q0001.title: Ohm's law: V = IR
q0001.short: "Ohm's law is V = IR: the voltage across a resistor is the current through it times its resistance, so I = V/R and R = V/I as well. 5 volts across 1 kΩ is 5 milliamps. It means current is proportional to voltage, a straight-line I–V curve. The caveat is that it only applies to ohmic, linear elements at a steady temperature. Diodes and LEDs aren't ohmic, and a bulb's resistance changes as it heats."

q0002.title: Ohm's law, conceptually
q0002.short: "Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is how much the material fights it. A voltage creates an electric field that pushes electrons, but they keep colliding with the atoms in the lattice, so they settle at an average drift speed proportional to the field. Double the voltage, double the drift speed, double the current. That's why V = IR is linear. The collisions are also where the I^2R heat comes f

q0003.title: Basic circuit analysis laws
q0003.short: "The core three are Ohm's law, KCL and KVL. KCL says currents into a node sum to zero, conservation of charge; KVL says voltages around a loop sum to zero, conservation of energy. From those you get series and parallel rules and the voltage and current dividers. For linear circuits you also have superposition and Thevenin/Norton equivalents, plus maximum power transfer. For anything bigger I'd use nodal analysis, whi

q0004.title: KCL and KVL explained
q0004.short: "KCL says the currents into any node sum to zero, so what flows in must flow out. That's conservation of charge. KVL says the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero, so the source voltage equals the sum of the drops. That's conservation of energy, because voltage is a potential. With Ohm's law, those two let you solve any circuit. They assume a lumped circuit; if a loop links a changing magnetic field, you get a

q0005.title: Solving KCL/KVL circuit problems
q0005.short: "I label nodes, pick a ground and assign current directions first. If the circuit reduces with series and parallel rules, I collapse it and use dividers. Otherwise I use nodal analysis: KCL at each unknown node with each current written as voltage difference over resistance, then solve the equations. Mesh analysis is the KVL alternative when there are many voltage sources. Finally I check that currents balance at eve

q0006.title: Power equations: P = VI
q0006.short: "Power is P = VI, voltage times current, which is energy per second. For a resistor you can substitute Ohm's law to get I^2R or V^2/R, whichever uses what you know. For AC, average power is V{rms}I{rms}\cos\varphi, so a pure capacitor or inductor averages zero. I use it all the time to check resistor wattage, regulator heat like (V{in} - V{out})\cdot I for an LDO, and battery life."

q0007.title: Why losses scale with current
q0007.short: "Losses in wires, traces and switches are I^2R, and the resistance is fixed by the conductor, so current is what you control. For a given power, P = VI, so raising voltage cuts current proportionally and cuts conduction loss with the square. That's why the grid uses high voltage and USB-PD goes to 20 volts. The V^2/R form doesn't contradict it, because that V is the drop across the wire. Switching and dielectric loss

q0008.title: Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation
q0008.short: "A voltage divider is two resistors in series across V{in}, with the output taken across the bottom one: V{out} = V{in}\,R2/(R1+R2). It comes straight from series current: I = V{in}/(R1+R2), and V{out} = IR2. The key caveat is that it assumes no load current. A load appears in parallel with R2 and pulls the output down, so dividers are for setting references and scaling signals, not for powering things."

q0009.title: RLC circuit analysis basics
q0009.short: "Treat R, L and C as impedances: R, j\omega L and 1/j\omega C. In series, the reactances cancel at \omega0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}, so impedance drops to R and current peaks. In the time domain you get a second-order equation, and the damping ratio \zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{C/L} decides the response: overdamped above 1, critically damped at 1, ringing below 1. Q = 1/(2\zeta) tells you how sharp the resonance is and how much it

q0010.title: LPF, HPF and BPF analysis basics
q0010.short: "I treat a filter as an impedance divider. An RC low-pass, R in series and C to ground, gives H = 1/(1 + j\omega RC): unity at DC, −3 dB and −45° at fc = 1/2\pi RC, then −20 dB per decade. Swap R and C for a high-pass with the same corner. For a bandpass, cascade a high-pass and a low-pass with enough impedance separation or a buffer, or use a series RLC with output across R, centred at 1/2\pi\sqrt{LC} with bandwidth

q0011.title: Passive components' parasitics
q0011.short: "Every real passive has the other two elements in it. A resistor has a little series inductance and a little shunt capacitance. A capacitor has ESR and ESL, so above its self-resonant frequency, around 20 MHz for a small 100 nF part, it acts like an inductor. An inductor has winding resistance and winding capacitance, so above its self-resonance it acts like a capacitor. They come from geometry: lead length, plate lo

q0012.title: Basic op-amp circuit analysis
q0012.short: "First check for negative feedback. If it's there, the op-amp holds both inputs at the same voltage and they draw no current, so I just do KCL at the inverting node. For an inverting amp the input current Vin over R1 flows through Rf, so gain is minus Rf over R1. For a non-inverting amp the feedback divider sets the inverting node equal to Vin, so gain is one plus Rf over R1. Same method for summing amps and integrat

q0013.title: Resistor symbol (US vs IEC)
q0013.short: "A resistor is a zigzag line in US-style schematics, or a plain rectangle in IEC drawings. It's a two-terminal part with no polarity. I label it with a reference designator like R1 and a value like 10 k. A potentiometer adds an arrow to the middle for the wiper, giving three terminals. A thermistor adds a diagonal line and a little t. I'd also mark junction dots so the connections are clear."

q0014.title: What resistance is
q0014.short: "Resistance is the opposition to current: R equals V over I, measured in ohms. Physically, electrons drift through a material and keep scattering off the lattice and impurities, which limits the current for a given voltage and turns energy into heat. For a uniform wire it's rho times length over area. V over I is a definition; Ohm's law says it's constant for ohmic materials like metals, but not for devices like diod

q0015.title: What resistance depends on
q0015.short: "Resistance depends on geometry and material, R equals rho L over A, so length, cross-section and resistivity. Resistivity changes with temperature: metals rise about 0.4 percent per kelvin, semiconductors fall. Then there's frequency through skin effect, voltage coefficient, mechanical strain, light, aging and humidity, and self-heating. In practice I pick the technology by which of those matters: thin-film for low

q0016.title: Realistic resistor model and parasitics
q0016.short: "A real resistor is the ideal R in series with a small inductance, from the leads and the current path, with a small capacitance across the whole thing from the terminations. High-value resistors go capacitive first: 10 k with 0.1 pF has a corner near 160 MHz. Low values go inductive. The best behaved is near the square root of L over C, roughly 80 ohms for a chip. Wirewound parts are the worst because they're coils.

q0017.title: Common resistor values (E-series)
q0017.short: "Resistor values come from the E-series: preferred numbers spaced logarithmically in each decade. E12 has 12 values and goes with 10 percent parts, E24 has 24 for 5 percent, and E96 has 96 for 1 percent. The spacing makes neighbors overlap within tolerance. The ones I use constantly are 10, 100, 1k, 4.7k, 10k, 100k, 1 meg, plus 22 or 33 ohms for series termination. For dividers I use E96 and then compute the real out

q0018.title: Common resistor packages and sizes
q0018.short: "SMD resistors are named in hundredths of an inch: 0402 is about 1 by 0.5 millimeters, 0603 is 1.6 by 0.8, 0805, 1206, and up to 2512 for around a watt. Power rating scales with size, roughly 1/16 to 1/10 watt for 0402 and 0603, 1/4 watt for 1206, 1 watt for 2512, and voltage rating scales too. Through-hole is mostly 1/4 watt axial, plus wirewound and chassis types for power. I'd pick by derated power, voltage, and h

q0019.title: Resistor failure modes
q0019.short: "The dominant failure for a resistor is open circuit from overheating or a pulse. Others are drift from heat, humidity or aging, mechanical cracking from board flex or thermal cycling, sulfur corrosion of silver terminations, and rarely a short from arcing or contamination. I prevent them by derating power to about half, checking voltage and pulse ratings, picking anti-surge or anti-sulfur parts when needed, and keep

q0020.title: Pull-up and pull-down resistors
q0020.short: "A pull-up or pull-down gives a node a known default level when nothing is driving it, so a CMOS input doesn't float and pick up noise, and so open-drain outputs can go high. I size it between two limits: small enough for rise time (RC) and to beat leakage, big enough that the current when pulled low is acceptable, V over R, and within the driver's sink rating. Typical values are 10 k for control lines, 4.7 k for I2C

q0021.title: Capacitor schematic symbols
q0021.short: "The capacitor symbol is two parallel plates with a gap, which is a picture of the real part: two conductors separated by a dielectric. You label it C1 with a value like 100 nF. For electrolytic or tantalum parts there's a polarized symbol: one plate is curved, or drawn as a box in IEC style, and there's a plus sign on the positive side. That matters because those parts are damaged if you reverse-bias them."

q0022.title: What capacitance is
q0022.short: "Capacitance is how much charge something stores per volt: C = Q/V, measured in farads. It's set by geometry and material, so for parallel plates it's \varepsilon A/d: bigger area, thinner gap or a higher-permittivity dielectric all increase it. The energy lives in the electric field, \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2. And because i = C\,dv/dt, you need current to change a capacitor's voltage, which is why capacitors hold rails stead

q0023.title: Dielectrics and permittivity
q0023.short: "A dielectric is an insulator that polarizes in an electric field: no free charges flow, but bound charges shift and molecular dipoles line up. In a capacitor that polarization partly cancels the field, so the plates hold more charge per volt. That's the relative permittivity \varepsilonr, multiplying capacitance in \varepsilon0\varepsilonr A/d. The dielectric also sets the voltage rating through its breakdown streng

q0024.title: Capacitor impedance equation
q0024.short: "A capacitor's impedance is 1/(j\omega C), or -j/(\omega C), with \omega = 2\pi f. It comes from i = C\,dv/dt: for a sinusoid, the derivative is multiplication by j\omega. The magnitude 1/(2\pi fC) drops with frequency, so it's open at DC and approaches a short at high frequency, and the phase is −90°, meaning current leads voltage. For example, 100 nF at 1 MHz is about 1.6 Ω."

q0025.title: Capacitor differential equation
q0025.short: "It's i = C\,dv/dt: current through a capacitor is proportional to the rate of change of its voltage. You get it by differentiating Q = CV. The integral form is v = v(0) + \frac1C\int i\,dt, so the capacitor integrates current and remembers its initial voltage. Consequences: constant voltage means zero current, so it's open at DC; constant current makes a linear ramp; and voltage can't jump instantly. With a resistor

q0026.title: Sign of capacitive reactance
q0026.short: "Negative. ZC = 1/(j\omega C) = -j/(\omega C), so the reactance is -1/(\omega C). That negative sign means current leads voltage by 90°, the opposite of an inductor's +j\omega L. Many books write XC as a positive magnitude and put the minus in Z = R - jXC, which is equivalent. The practical point is that inductive and capacitive reactances cancel in series, which is what resonance is."

q0027.title: Continuity condition and inductors
q0027.short: "The continuity condition says inductor current and capacitor voltage can't change instantaneously. Inductors resist changes in current: since v = L\,di/dt, an instant change in current would need infinite voltage, and the stored energy \tfrac12Li^2 can't change in zero time. That's why interrupting a coil's current produces a huge voltage spike, and why we put flyback diodes across relays and motors. Capacitors are

q0028.title: Capacitor initial vs DC steady state
q0028.short: "Initially, an uncharged capacitor acts like a short circuit, because its voltage can't change instantly: it's at 0 V but can take any current. At DC steady state it acts like an open circuit, because once the voltage stops changing, i = C\,dv/dt is zero. In between, it charges exponentially with \tau = RC. More generally, at the first instant it looks like a voltage source at whatever voltage it held before."

q0029.title: Inductor impedance at DC vs infinite frequency
q0029.short: "An ideal inductor's impedance is j omega L, so at DC it's zero, a short circuit, and as frequency goes to infinity it goes to infinity, an open circuit. On a log-log plot that's a straight line rising at 20 dB per decade. Time-domain, v equals L di/dt: it resists fast current changes. A real inductor has winding capacitance, so it peaks at its self-resonant frequency and then acts like a capacitor. The capacitor is

q0030.title: Realistic capacitor model and parasitics
q0030.short: "The realistic model is the ideal capacitance in series with ESR, the resistance of plates, terminals and dielectric loss, and ESL, the inductance of the current loop, with a large leakage resistance in parallel. Because of ESL, the part is only a capacitor below its self-resonant frequency, where impedance bottoms out at the ESR; above it, it's an inductor. A 100 nF ceramic with 1 nH is around 16 MHz. Real capacitor

q0031.title: Capacitor self-resonant frequency
q0031.short: "The self-resonant frequency is where the capacitor's capacitive reactance cancels its own ESL's inductive reactance: f equals one over two pi root of L times C. Below it the part is a capacitor, at it the impedance is just the ESR, above it the part is an inductor. A 100 nF ceramic with 1 nH is around 16 MHz. Bigger capacitance and more mounting inductance both lower the SRF, which is why we parallel several values

q0032.title: Bypass, decoupling and bulk capacitors
q0032.short: "A decoupling or bypass cap is a small ceramic, about 100 nF, right at the IC's supply pin. It supplies the fast current bursts the chip needs and shunts high-frequency noise to ground. A bulk capacitor is large, tens to hundreds of microfarads, near the power entry or load, holding the rail up through slower load steps while the regulator reacts. The difference is the frequency band: big caps have high ESL so they o

q0033.title: AC coupling capacitors
q0033.short: "An AC coupling capacitor in series blocks DC and passes AC, so two stages with different DC bias levels can connect. Together with the input resistance after it, it forms a high-pass filter with corner one over two pi R C, so I choose C so that corner is well below the lowest signal frequency. The cost is a startup settling time of a few R C, and I need a bias network after the cap to set the DC level."

q0034.title: Signals capacitors pass and block
q0034.short: "A capacitor blocks DC and low frequencies and passes high frequencies: impedance one over j omega C is infinite at DC and small at high frequency. In series with a resistor to ground it's a high-pass filter; across the signal to ground it's a low-pass. The corner is one over two pi R C, with a gentle 20 dB per decade roll-off. In the time domain it passes changes, edges and spikes, and blocks constant levels."

q0035.title: Build an LPF or HPF with one capacitor
q0035.short: "One resistor plus one capacitor does either. Low-pass: resistor in series, capacitor from the output to ground. High-pass: capacitor in series, resistor from the output to ground. The corner is one over two pi R C. I pick C from a standard value, compute R, keep R well above the source resistance and well below the load, and remember it's only 20 dB per decade. For a 1 kHz low-pass, 100 nF and 1.6 kΩ."

q0036.title: Capacitor failure modes
q0036.short: "Each type fails differently. Ceramics crack from board flex or thermal shock, usually becoming shorts. Aluminum electrolytics dry out: the capacitance falls and ESR rises, with life doubling for every 10 degrees cooler, and they can vent from overvoltage or reverse polarity. Tantalums fail short and can ignite after a surge, so derate 50 percent and limit inrush. Films self-heal and age gently. I derate voltage and

q0037.title: Capacitor voltage continuity condition
q0037.short: "The continuity condition says the voltage across a capacitor can't change instantly, so the voltage just after a switch equals the voltage just before. Capacitors resist changes in voltage. It follows from i equals C dv/dt: an instant jump needs infinite current, or infinite power for the stored energy. So an uncharged capacitor acts like a short at the first instant and an open circuit at DC steady state, and the c

q0038.title: Inductor schematic symbol
q0038.short: "An inductor is drawn as a coil: a lead, three or four humps, and another lead, labelled L1 with a value in henries, like 10 µH. Two parallel lines next to the coil mean it has a magnetic core, an arrow through it means it's adjustable, and two coils with dots are coupled windings or a transformer. A ferrite bead usually gets its own rectangle symbol because it acts more like a frequency-dependent resistor. For power

q0039.title: What is inductance?
q0039.short: "Inductance is the ratio of magnetic flux linkage to current, L = N\Phi/I, in henries. Its practical meaning is that it opposes changes in current: change the current and the changing flux induces a voltage that fights you, v = L\,di/dt. It stores energy in the magnetic field as \tfrac12 LI^2. It grows with turns squared, loop area and core permeability, and every current loop has some, which is why fast edges cause

q0040.title: Inductor impedance equation
q0040.short: "An ideal inductor's impedance is ZL = j\omega L = j2\pi fL. It comes from v = L\,di/dt: for a sinusoid, the derivative multiplies by j\omega. The magnitude \omega L rises linearly with frequency, so it's a short at DC and an open at very high frequency, and the j means voltage leads current by 90° with no power dissipated. For example, 10 µH at 1 MHz is about 63 Ω. In Laplace terms it's sL."

q0041.title: Inductor differential equation
q0041.short: "It's v = L\,di/dt: inductor voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of current, with current into the plus terminal. In integral form, i(t) = i(t0) + \frac1L\int v\,dt, so the current is the running integral of the voltage. A constant voltage gives a linear current ramp, constant current means zero voltage so it's a short at DC, and the current can't jump instantly without infinite voltage. That's the bas

q0042.title: Inductor reactance sign
q0042.short: "Positive. ZL = j\omega L, so the reactance is +\omega L, while a capacitor's is -1/(\omega C). Positive reactance means the voltage leads the current by 90°, the 'ELI' in 'ELI the ICE man', and the inductor absorbs reactive power. In a series LC you add the signed reactances, so the circuit looks capacitive below resonance and inductive above. A real inductor's reactance only stays positive up to its self-resonant f

q0043.title: Inductor current continuity condition
q0043.short: "The continuity condition says inductor current can't change instantaneously: iL(0^+) = iL(0^-). That comes from v = L\,di/dt: a jump in current would need infinite voltage, and it would change the stored energy \tfrac12 LI^2 in zero time. So inductors resist changes in current, while their voltage can jump. Practically, if you interrupt an inductor's current, its voltage spikes as high as needed to keep current flow

q0044.title: Inductor at t = 0⁺ and DC steady state
q0044.short: "When first excited from zero current, an inductor acts like an open circuit: its current can't jump, so it's still zero right after the step and the full voltage appears across it. At DC steady state it's a short, because constant current means L\,di/dt = 0; a real one shows just its DC resistance. In between, the current rises exponentially with \tau = L/R. If it was already carrying current, at the switch instant

q0045.title: Inductor impedance from DC to ∞
q0045.short: "At DC an ideal inductor's impedance j\omega L is zero, a short; as frequency goes to infinity it goes to infinity, an open. Plotted, Z is a straight line through the origin, or on log–log axes a line rising at 20 dB per decade with a constant +90° phase. A real inductor bottoms out at its DCR at low frequency, peaks at its self-resonant frequency because of winding capacitance, and turns capacitive above it."

q0046.title: Inductor saturation
q0046.short: "Saturation is when the core's flux density hits its material limit: the magnetic domains are all aligned, permeability collapses toward that of air, and inductance drops sharply. Since di/dt = V/L, the current then ramps much faster and spikes. That overstresses switches, trips current limits and adds heat, which in ferrite lowers the saturation current further. So you size an inductor's I{sat} above the worst-case

q0047.title: Realistic inductor model and parasitics
q0047.short: "The real inductor is the ideal L in series with winding resistance, DCR going up to ACR with frequency, with a parallel capacitance across the whole winding from turn-to-turn coupling, and a parallel resistor for core loss. That gives a self-resonant frequency one over two pi root L C. Below it, it's an inductor; at it, the impedance peaks; above it, it's a capacitor. A 10 microhenry coil with 5 picofarads resonates

q0048.title: What inductor cores do
q0048.short: "A core is magnetic material, ferrite or powdered iron, that concentrates the flux. Inductance goes as turns squared over reluctance, and a high-permeability core has far lower reluctance than air, so you get hundreds or thousands of times more inductance from the same turns, in less space. The costs are saturation, where inductance collapses at high current, and core loss. An air gap lowers the inductance but raises

q0049.title: Typical inductor core materials
q0049.short: "The main core materials are ferrite, powdered iron and its relatives like sendust and MPP, laminated silicon steel, and amorphous or nanocrystalline alloys. Ferrite is low loss for tens of kHz to a few MHz but saturates hard around 0.3 to 0.5 tesla. Powder cores have distributed gaps, so low permeability, around 1 tesla, and soft saturation, which suits DC-biased power inductors. Silicon steel is for line frequency.

q0050.title: Inductor loss mechanisms
q0050.short: "Two buckets: winding loss and core loss. Winding loss is I squared R, where the AC resistance is higher than DC because of skin and proximity effects. Core loss is hysteresis, proportional to the B-H loop area times frequency, plus eddy currents in the core, roughly f squared B squared, summarized by the Steinmetz equation k f to the alpha B to the beta. There's also fringing loss near a gap and capacitive loss at h

q0051.title: AC resistance (ACR) of inductors
q0051.short: "ACR is the effective series resistance of an inductor's winding at the operating frequency, and it's higher than DCR. Skin effect pushes current to the surface within a depth of delta, 66 micrometers in copper at 1 megahertz, so resistance rises as the square root of frequency for thick wire. Proximity effect from neighboring turns' fields adds more, especially with many layers. Litz wire, foil, fewer layers and int

q0052.title: Signals inductors pass and block
q0052.short: "An inductor's impedance j omega L is zero at DC and rises with frequency, so it passes DC and low frequencies and blocks high frequencies, the opposite of a capacitor. A series inductor into a load R is a low-pass filter with corner R over two pi L. Put the inductor to ground and it's a high-pass. With a capacitor you get a second-order LC low-pass at one over two pi root LC. In the time domain it resists fast curre

q0053.title: Build an LPF or HPF with one inductor
q0053.short: "Inductor in series with the load is a low-pass; resistor in series with the inductor to ground is a high-pass. The corner is R over two pi L. For a 15.9 kilohertz low-pass into 1 kilohm I need 10 millihenries. It's only practical at RF or on power lines, because at low frequency the inductors get huge. And real inductors have DCR, which limits the high-pass stopband, and an SRF above which they stop working."

q0054.title: Inductor failure modes
q0054.short: "The big one is saturation: above the saturation current the inductance collapses and the current ramps with only the resistance limiting it, which can destroy the switch in a converter, usually during start-up, load steps or shorts. Then thermal overstress from copper and core loss, which breaks down the insulation and causes shorted turns or an open winding. Mechanical failures such as cracked ferrite and broken te

q0055.title: Conductors, insulators, semiconductors
q0055.short: "It's about how many electrons are free to move, which band theory explains. A conductor like copper has no band gap, so there are about 10^{23} free electrons per cm³. An insulator like SiO₂ has a huge gap, around 9 eV, so essentially nothing gets free at room temperature. A semiconductor like silicon has a small gap, 1.1 eV, so a few carriers exist and, more importantly, doping, light or fields can change the condu

q0056.title: Skin effect
q0056.short: "Skin effect is AC current crowding toward a conductor's surface. The changing magnetic field inside the wire induces eddy currents that cancel current in the center and reinforce it at the edges. Current density falls off exponentially with skin depth \delta = \sqrt{\rho/(\pi f\mu)}: for copper about 65 µm at 1 MHz and 2 µm at 1 GHz. So effective area shrinks and resistance rises like \sqrt f. That's why inductors a

q0057.title: Photoelectric effect
q0057.short: "It's light knocking electrons out of a material. The key facts are that there's a threshold frequency, below which nothing happens however bright the light, and that the electrons' maximum energy depends on frequency, not intensity. Einstein explained it with photons: each photon has energy hf, gives it all to one electron, and KE{max} = hf - \phi, where \phi is the work function. In semiconductors the same idea, wi

q0058.title: Dielectric losses and their mechanisms
q0058.short: "Real dielectrics turn some AC field energy into heat. Mechanisms: leakage conduction, mainly at low frequency; polarization lag, where dipoles and ions can't reorient fast enough and lose energy to the lattice, peaking near the relaxation frequency; interfacial charge in composites; hysteresis in ferroelectric ceramics like X7R; and partial discharge at high voltage. We quantify it with the loss tangent: P = V^2\ome
terms: Class I vs Class II ceramic

q0059.title: How electricity works
q0059.short: "Electricity is charge moving and the energy it carries. A source like a battery creates a voltage, which is energy per unit charge. Connect a closed circuit and that voltage sets up a field in the wire, which pushes the free electrons that are already there, and that's current. Collisions with the metal's atoms are resistance, so V = IR, and energy gets delivered at P = VI. The electrons drift really slowly, fractio

q0060.title: How lightning works
q0060.short: "Lightning is a huge electrostatic discharge. In a thunderstorm, collisions between ice crystals and graupel separate charge: the cloud's middle ends up negative, and that induces positive charge on the ground. When the field gets high enough the air breaks down. A stepped leader of ionized air works its way down, an upward streamer meets it, and a return stroke of tens of kiloamps flows in microseconds, heating the

q0061.title: Energy bands where electrons move
q0061.short: "In a solid, atomic levels merge into bands. Current-carrying electrons move in the conduction band, the band above the band gap, where there are plenty of empty states to move into. In a semiconductor the valence band below the gap also carries current, via holes: missing electrons that act as positive carriers. A completely full band can't conduct and an empty one has no carriers, so you need electrons in the condu

q0062.title: P-type vs N-type semiconductors
q0062.short: "N-type and P-type are silicon doped on purpose so one carrier dominates. N-type uses a donor like phosphorus with five valence electrons, so the extra electron is free and electrons are the majority carrier. P-type uses an acceptor like boron with three valence electrons, which leaves a missing electron, a hole, that behaves like a mobile positive charge. Both are electrically neutral. The minority carrier is set by

q0063.title: Depletion region and how it forms
q0063.short: "The depletion region forms because electrons diffuse from the N side to the P side and holes go the other way. Each carrier that leaves exposes a fixed ionized dopant, positive donors on the N side and negative acceptors on the P side. That fixed space charge makes an electric field that pushes carriers back, and the field grows until drift balances diffusion. What's left is a carrier-free layer with a built-in pote

q0064.title: Common semiconductor materials
q0064.short: "Silicon is the workhorse because it's cheap, forms a great oxide, and has a good 1.12 eV gap. Germanium is the older, leakier, 0.66 eV material, now mostly used in SiGe. III-V compounds like GaAs, InP and GaN are used for RF and optoelectronics because they have high electron mobility and direct bandgaps that emit light. Silicon carbide and gallium nitride are wide-bandgap materials around 3.3 eV used for high-volta

q0065.title: What doping is and how it is done
q0065.short: "Doping is deliberately adding a tiny, controlled amount of impurity atoms to a semiconductor to set its carrier type and concentration. Pure silicon has only about 10^{10} carriers per cm³, so I add phosphorus or arsenic, which each donate an electron for N-type, or boron, which creates a hole for P-type. A few parts per million is enough to raise conductivity by orders of magnitude. It's done by ion implantation or

q0066.title: How doping improves performance
q0066.short: "Doping improves silicon in several ways. It raises the carrier density by many orders of magnitude, so resistivity drops from hundreds of kilohm-centimetres to well under an ohm-centimetre. It makes the carrier density set by design and stable over temperature instead of by thermal generation. It lets me choose N or P so I can build junctions and transistors, and it lets me tune threshold, breakdown, gain and contac

q0067.title: Which elements are used as dopants
q0067.short: "In silicon, donors are Group V atoms, with an extra valence electron: phosphorus, arsenic and antimony give N-type. Acceptors are Group III atoms with one fewer: boron mainly, and gallium, aluminium or indium in special cases, give P-type. Arsenic diffuses slowly so it's used for shallow source and drain; phosphorus diffuses faster and goes in wells; boron is the standard P-type dopant. In compound semiconductors th

q0068.title: Charge carrier mobility
q0068.short: "Mobility is how quickly carriers drift per unit of electric field: vd=\mu E, in cm²/V·s. It equals q\tau/m^, so it depends on how long a carrier travels between scattering events and how light it is. In silicon it's about 1350 for electrons and 480 for holes at room temperature, and it drops with higher temperature from lattice scattering and with higher doping from impurity scattering. Conductivity is q(n\mun+p\mup

q0069.title: Majority carriers in P-type vs N-type
q0069.short: "N-type has electrons as the majority carrier, P-type has holes. The majority density is about equal to the doping, say 10^{16} per cm³. The minority carrier is set by np=ni^2, so with ni=10^{10} it's only 10^{4} per cm³, twelve orders lower. Majority carriers carry the bulk current, but minority carriers matter at junctions: they set diode and BJT current and reverse leakage."

q0070.title: Electron vs hole mobility
q0070.short: "Electrons are more mobile: about 1350 versus 480 cm²/V·s in silicon, a ratio of roughly 2.8. Mobility is q\tau/m^. Electrons have a lighter conductivity effective mass and a simpler band to move in, while holes sit in the valence band with heavy and light hole bands and more scattering. That's why PMOS devices are drawn wider than NMOS, NPN transistors beat PNP, and N-type material has lower resistance at the same d

q0071.title: Why N-type has lower resistance
q0071.short: "Conductivity is q(n\mun+p\mup). At the same doping, N-type and P-type have the same majority density, but electron mobility (about 1350 cm²/V·s) is around 2.8 times the hole mobility (about 480). So N-type conducts about 2.8 times better. At 10^{16} per cm³ that's about 0.5 Ω·cm versus 1.5 Ω·cm. It narrows at heavy doping, and it only holds at equal doping."

q0072.title: How a diode works (PN junction)
q0072.short: "A diode is a PN junction. Where P and N meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving a depletion region of fixed ions and a built-in barrier of a bit under a volt. Forward bias lowers the barrier, and current grows exponentially, about ten times per 60 millivolts, so silicon looks 'on' around 0.6 to 0.7 volts. Reverse bias raises the barrier and only a tiny leakage current flows, until breakdown. That's the

q0073.title: Diode use cases
q0073.short: "I group diode uses by the property they exploit. One-way conduction gives rectifiers, reverse-polarity protection, OR-ing two supplies, and flyback diodes across inductive loads. Controlled breakdown gives Zener references and TVS surge clamps, plus the ESD diodes on every IC pin. And the junction itself makes LEDs, photodiodes, varactors and temperature sensors. The main cost is the forward drop, so in power paths

q0074.title: Draw the diode I–V curve
q0074.short: "Voltage on x, current on y. Forward bias: the current stays near zero and then rises exponentially, with a knee around 0.6 to 0.7 volts for silicon, roughly ten times more current per 60 millivolts. Reverse bias: a tiny flat leakage current, nanoamps. Then at the breakdown voltage it drops sharply downward. The axes aren't to scale, and for hand analysis I'd swap the curve for a model: ideal, constant 0.7 volt drop,

q0075.title: Diode operating regions
q0075.short: "Three regions, set by the voltage anode minus cathode. Forward bias: the barrier drops and current rises exponentially; past about 0.6 to 0.7 volts for silicon it's on, and I model it as a 0.7 volt drop. Reverse bias: the barrier rises, the depletion region widens, only nanoamps of leakage flow, so I treat it as open. Breakdown: at the breakdown voltage the reverse current shoots up while the voltage stays near V{BR

q0076.title: Find a diode's operating region
q0076.short: "I take VD as anode minus cathode. At or above the turn-on voltage, about 0.7 for silicon, it's forward conducting. Between minus the breakdown voltage and 0.7, it's off: reverse biased or only weakly forward. At or below minus V{BR}, it's in breakdown. In a circuit, the diode clamps its own voltage, so I remove it, find the open-circuit voltage across its terminals and compare that, or I assume a state, solve, and c

q0077.title: Kinds of diodes
q0077.short: "I group them by job. Conduction: standard rectifiers like the 1N4007 for high voltage but slow; small-signal 1N4148 for fast, low-current switching; ultrafast recovery for switching power; Schottkys for low forward drop and no reverse recovery but more leakage; and silicon carbide Schottkys for high-voltage power. Breakdown: Zeners for references and clamps, TVS diodes for surge and ESD. And optical or capacitive: L

q0078.title: Diode forward voltage: value and why
q0078.short: "About 0.6 to 0.7 volts for silicon at milliamp currents. It's not a hard threshold: the current is IS e^{V/VT}, and silicon's IS is around 10^{-14} amps because of its 1.1 eV bandgap, so you need about 11 decades times 60 millivolts, roughly 0.65 volts, to reach a milliamp. Lower-barrier devices drop less: Schottky 0.2 to 0.45, germanium 0.2 to 0.3. Wider-bandgap ones drop more: LEDs 2 to 3 volts, silicon carbide hi

q0079.title: Building an ideal diode
q0079.short: "For signals, an op-amp superdiode: the diode goes inside the op-amp's feedback loop, so its 0.6 volt drop is divided by the open-loop gain and the output follows the input for positive signals, at the cost of speed. For power, a MOSFET with a controller: the body diode points the right way, and the controller senses forward voltage and turns the gate on so the drop is just I R{DS(on)}, then turns it off fast if curr

q0080.title: Draw the NPN BJT symbol
q0080.short: "The BJT symbol is a base bar with the base lead on one side, and two angled lines on the other: collector at the top and emitter at the bottom. The emitter has an arrow. For an NPN the arrow points out, away from the base, because it's the base-emitter diode direction, P to N. For a PNP the arrow points in. Current goes into the collector and base and out of the emitter for an NPN, so IE=IC+IB."

q0081.title: BJT terminals: base, collector, emitter
q0081.short: "A BJT has a base, a collector and an emitter. The emitter injects carriers, the thin base controls the flow, and the collector collects the carriers. A small base current controls a large collector current. They aren't symmetric: the emitter is heavily doped, the base is thin and lighter, and the collector is lightly doped and large to handle voltage and heat. In an NPN, base and collector current go in and emitter

q0082.title: Use cases of a BJT
q0082.short: "BJTs are used as switches and amplifiers. As a switch, an NPN drives relays, LEDs and buzzers from a microcontroller pin, with a base resistor sized for saturation. As an amplifier, a common-emitter stage gives gain of about -gmRC with gm=IC/VT, and an emitter follower buffers a signal. Inside ICs they're used in differential pairs, current mirrors, bandgap references and temperature sensors because V{BE} is predict

q0083.title: BJT vs MOSFET comparison
q0083.short: "A BJT is current-controlled: base current into a forward-biased junction controls collector current, with a gain around 100. A MOSFET is voltage-controlled, with an insulated gate that draws essentially no DC current. The BJT has higher transconductance per milliamp, better matching and lower noise, so it suits precision analogue. The MOSFET has very low on-resistance, no base drive, positive temperature coefficient

q0084.title: BJT I-V characteristic curves
q0084.short: "The BJT output curve plots collector current against collector-emitter voltage for stepped base currents. Each curve rises steeply near the origin in saturation, then goes nearly flat in the forward-active region at IC\approx\beta IB with a slight Early-effect slope, and breaks down at high V{CE}. The input curve is a diode, with a knee near 0.65 V, and the transfer curve is exponential, a decade per 60 mV. A load l

q0085.title: How a BJT works
q0085.short: "In an NPN the forward-biased base-emitter junction injects electrons from the heavily doped emitter into the thin base. Most diffuse across before recombining, and the field of the reverse-biased base-collector junction sweeps them into the collector. That gives a collector current set by V{BE}, IC=ISe^{V{BE}/VT}, nearly independent of V{CE}. A small base current supplies the holes lost to recombination and back-inj

q0086.title: NPN vs PNP transistors
q0086.short: "NPN and PNP are doping mirror images. NPN is N-P-N with electrons as main carriers; PNP is P-N-P with holes. An NPN conducts when the base is 0.7 V above the emitter, current flows into the collector and out of the emitter, and it's the natural low-side switch. A PNP conducts when the base is 0.7 V below the emitter, with current into the emitter, and it's the natural high-side switch. Because holes are less mobile

q0087.title: BJT modes of operation
q0087.short: "A BJT's mode comes from the bias on its two junctions. Cutoff: both reverse, no current, open switch. Forward-active: base-emitter forward, base-collector reverse, V{BE}\approx0.7 V and IC=\beta IB, the amplifier mode. Saturation: both forward, V{CE}\approx0.2 V, current limited by the circuit, closed switch. Reverse-active: roles of emitter and collector swapped, with poor gain. I tell them apart by V{BE} and V{CE}

q0088.title: BJT current gain (beta)
q0088.short: "Beta is the ratio of collector current to base current in forward-active mode, typically 50 to 300 for small-signal transistors. It's linked to alpha, IC/IE (about 0.99), by \beta=\alpha/(1-\alpha). It comes from the fraction of injected carriers that reach the collector: a thin base and a heavily doped emitter give high beta. It's not a precise constant: it varies a lot between parts and with current and temperatur

q0089.title: Draw NMOS and PMOS symbols
q0089.short: "An NFET symbol is a gate plate separated from a broken channel line, drain on top, source on the bottom, and an arrow on the body pointing into the channel. The PFET is the same with the arrow pointing out, and I flip it so the source is on top at the supply. The arrow is the body-channel PN junction pointing from P to N, the broken line means enhancement-mode, normally off, and the gap shows the gate is insulated.

q0090.title: MOSFET terminals and their roles
q0090.short: "Four terminals: gate, drain, source and body. The gate is insulated by the oxide, draws no DC current, and its voltage relative to the source creates or removes the channel. The source supplies the carriers and is the reference for V{GS} and V{DS}. The drain collects them and usually connects to the load. The body is the silicon the channel lives in. Discrete parts tie it to the source internally, which is why they

q0091.title: Why source and body are tied
q0091.short: "Source and body. Discrete MOSFETs short them internally. It keeps the source-body PN junction from ever forward-biasing, and it removes the body effect: if the source sits above the body, the threshold voltage goes up, so with V{SB} = 0 the threshold stays put. The cost is the body diode from source to drain, so one FET only blocks one direction. In ICs, NMOS bodies usually share the grounded substrate, so you often

q0092.title: MOSFET use cases
q0092.short: "Three main areas. Switching: low-side NFETs driving motors, relays and LEDs from a GPIO, PFET high-side load switches, and the switches in buck converters, H-bridges and synchronous rectifiers. Digital: every CMOS gate and memory cell. Analog: in saturation it's a voltage-controlled current source for amplifiers, current mirrors and LDO pass elements, and in triode it's a voltage-controlled resistor for analog switc

q0093.title: Why MOSFETs are so widely used
q0093.short: "Four reasons. The gate is insulated, so it's voltage-driven and draws no current to stay on, which makes it trivial to drive from logic. When it's on it's just a small resistor, milliohms in modern parts, so conduction loss is low and paralleling works because R{DS(on)} rises with temperature. It's a majority-carrier device, so it switches fast without storage time. And for digital, CMOS pairs draw almost no static

q0094.title: BJT vs MOSFET (MOSFET perspective)
q0094.short: "A BJT is current-controlled through a forward-biased junction: it needs continuous base current, roughly IC/\beta, and when on it has a fixed-ish V{CE(sat)}. A MOSFET is voltage-controlled through an insulated gate: no DC gate current, and when on it's a resistor, R{DS(on)}. MOSFETs switch faster and parallel easily. BJTs have more transconductance per milliamp and lower noise, so they still win in some analog. And

q0095.title: MOSFET I-V curves
q0095.short: "I'd plot ID against V{DS} with a curve for each V{GS}. Below threshold there's no current. Above it, each curve rises roughly linearly from the origin, that's triode where the FET is a voltage-controlled resistor, then flattens into saturation where ID = \frac12 kn(V{GS}-Vt)^2. A dashed parabola V{DS} = V{GS} - Vt separates the regions. Curves get further apart for equal V{GS} steps because it's square-law, and they

q0096.title: How a MOSFET works
q0096.short: "Take an NMOS: a P-type body with N-type source and drain, and a gate on a thin oxide in between. With no gate voltage, it's two back-to-back diodes, so no current. A positive gate voltage first pushes holes away, then, past threshold, pulls enough electrons to the surface to form an N-type channel linking source and drain. V{DS} drives current through it, and more overdrive means more channel charge and lower resist

q0097.title: N-channel vs P-channel MOSFET
q0097.short: "The difference is the carrier in the channel. An N-channel FET has an electron channel in a p-type body, turns on with the gate above the source by more than Vt, and its source usually sits at ground. A P-channel FET is the mirror image: hole channel, gate must go below the source, source usually at the supply. Because holes are about 2 to 3 times less mobile than electrons, a PMOS needs to be 2 to 3 times wider to

q0098.title: Enhancement vs depletion mode MOSFET
q0098.short: "The mode tells you whether a channel exists at zero gate voltage. Enhancement mode has no channel at V{GS}=0, so it's normally off and you apply a gate voltage above Vt to create one. That's nearly every MOSFET. Depletion mode has a channel implanted at fabrication, so it conducts at zero gate voltage and you apply a gate voltage of the opposite polarity to cut it off. For an N-channel that means a negative threshol

q0099.title: MOSFET modes of operation
q0099.short: "There are three regions. In cutoff, V{GS} is below threshold, there's no channel, and the device is open. In triode, V{GS} is above threshold but V{DS} is less than the overdrive, so the channel spans the whole device and it behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor. In saturation, V{DS} is bigger than the overdrive, the channel pinches off at the drain, and the current flattens at about half k times overdrive squa

q0100.title: Find the MOSFET region and load line
q0100.short: "First compare V{GS} to Vt: below it, cutoff. Above it, assume saturation, compute ID=\tfrac12k(V{GS}-Vt)^2, get V{DS}=V{DD}-IDRD, and check that V{DS} is at least the overdrive. If it's not, the device is in triode and I re-solve with the triode equation. The load line is the straight line ID=(V{DD}-V{DS})/RD, and the operating point is where it crosses the transistor's curve for that V{GS}."

q0101.title: MOSFET body diode: origin and effects
q0101.short: "The body diode is the PN junction between the MOSFET's body and its drain, there because of how the transistor is built. With the body tied to the source, an NMOS has a diode with its anode at the source and cathode at the drain, so the FET can't block voltage in the reverse direction, and a PMOS is the opposite. It matters in half-bridges: during dead time inductor current flows through it at 0.7 to 1 V and it has

q0102.title: Why MOSFET gates fear overvoltage
q0102.short: "The gate is a capacitor with a very thin oxide, a few nanometers in logic and tens of nanometers in power FETs, so even a few volts makes a very high field. Silicon dioxide breaks down at about 10 MV/cm and the damage is permanent, which is why V{GS} maximums are only around ±8 to ±20 V. Plus the gate has no DC path and tiny capacitance, so a small ESD charge gives hundreds of volts, and gate-loop ringing or Miller

q0103.title: MOSFET W/L ratio and its effects
q0103.short: "W/L is channel width over channel length, and it sets the transistor's strength. In the model k=\mu C{ox}W/L, so drain current, transconductance and conductance all scale with W/L, and on-resistance scales with L/W. The cost is gate capacitance, which grows with W times L, so a stronger device loads its driver and uses more dynamic power. You use wider devices for speed and drive, longer L for output resistance and

q0104.title: Identify an unnamed analog circuit
q0104.short: "I find the ports and look for the telltale features: feedback to an amplifier input means regulation, like an LDO with V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2); a clock with flying capacitors and diodes is a charge pump giving about 2V{in} minus drops; two matched FETs with a diode-connected reference is a current mirror copying current by the W/L ratio; a single NMOS with pull-ups either side is a level shifter; and series R, L with

q0105.title: CMOS and the CMOS buffer
q0105.short: "CMOS means complementary MOS: every gate has a PMOS pull-up network to V{DD} and an NMOS pull-down network to ground, driven by the same inputs, so exactly one side is on at a time and there's no static current. The basic cell is the inverter: PMOS on top, NMOS on the bottom, gates tied as input, drains tied as output. A single stage always inverts, so a buffer is two inverters in series, usually with the second one

q0106.title: Why CMOS is used everywhere
q0106.short: "Mainly power. In CMOS the PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down are complementary, so one is always off and there's no static current, only leakage. You pay energy only when a node switches, about CV^2 per cycle. On top of that, outputs swing rail to rail for big noise margins, inputs are gates that draw no DC current so fan-out is huge, and MOSFETs scale and integrate densely. The costs are dynamic power at high frequenc

q0107.title: PMOS high side, NMOS low side
q0107.short: "PMOS on the high side, NMOS on the low side, because a MOSFET is controlled by V{GS} and you want each source tied to a fixed rail. The NMOS source sits at ground, so a gate at V{DD} turns it fully on; the PMOS source sits at V{DD}, so a gate at 0 V turns it fully on. Swap them and each becomes a source follower that loses a threshold voltage. In power stages, though, the high side is often an NMOS anyway for its lo

q0108.title: TTL vs CMOS logic families
q0108.short: "TTL is bipolar logic: multi-emitter BJT inputs and a totem-pole NPN output, 5 V only. CMOS uses complementary MOSFETs. TTL draws static current, a few mW per gate, and its inputs source current; CMOS draws almost nothing static and its inputs are high impedance but must not float. TTL thresholds are fixed at 0.8 and 2.0 V with outputs guaranteed only to 2.4 V, while CMOS swings rail to rail with thresholds that scal

q0109.title: Shoot-through in CMOS gates
q0109.short: "Shoot-through is when the PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage are on at the same time, so current goes straight from V{DD} to ground. It happens during every input transition, between V{tn} and V{DD} - V{tp}, peaking near mid-rail. It's worst with slow edges or floating inputs. Prevent it with fast edges, Schmitt-trigger inputs, tied-off unused pins, and in drivers or power stages by giving each FET its own gate signal wi

q0110.title: CMOS power and efficiency analysis
q0110.short: "CMOS has no DC path in steady state, so power is mostly dynamic: every low-to-high transition draws CV{DD}^2 from the supply, half stored on the load and half burned in the PMOS, and the discharge burns the stored half in the NMOS. Average power is \alpha CV{DD}^2f: linear in frequency, quadratic in supply and swing, independent of transistor resistance. Rise and fall time only matter through short-circuit current,

q0111.title: Achieving faster slew rates in CMOS
q0111.short: "Slew rate is I/C, so to go faster I increase drive current, reduce capacitance, or reduce swing. In CMOS that means wider output transistors for lower on-resistance, more gate overdrive or a higher supply, and a tapered chain of inverters, each about 3 to 4 times larger than the last, to drive big output devices. I'd also cut the load capacitance by shortening traces and reducing fan-out. The trade-off is peak curre

q0112.title: CMOS input ESD and overvoltage protection
q0112.short: "I'd use layers. At the pad, two big diodes steer ESD current to V{DD} or ground, with a rail clamp between the rails to sink it. Then a series resistor of a few hundred ohms and a small secondary clamp at the gate, which see only what leaks through. On the board, a TVS at the connector for IEC-level events, and a series resistor sized so that a DC overvoltage only pushes a milliamp or two through the clamp diode. Th

q0113.title: CMOS buffer driving a series RC load
q0113.short: "Treat the buffer as a switch to V{DD} or ground. On the positive step the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off: current V{DD}/R flows from the supply into the capacitor and decays with \tau=RC while the capacitor voltage rises exponentially. On the negative step the NMOS is on and the PMOS is off: the capacitor discharges through the resistor into the NMOS, so the current reverses and again decays. The output is a square

q0114.title: Swapped PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage
q0114.short: "Swapping them puts the NMOS on top and the PMOS on the bottom, so each source is the output node. The NMOS then can only pull the output up to V{DD}-V{tn}, since it turns off once its V{GS} falls to Vt, and the PMOS can only pull it down to V{tp}. So the output no longer reaches the rails, the body effect makes it worse, the edges get slower near the limits, and the stage becomes non-inverting. That's why CMOS has t

q0115.title: Common-mode vs differential gain, CMRR
q0115.short: "Split two inputs into a difference and an average. Differential gain is the gain on the difference and common-mode gain is the gain on the average, so the output is AdVd+A{cm}V{cm}. Ideally Ad is large (or the designed gain) and A{cm} is zero, so the common-mode rejection ratio Ad/A{cm} is infinite. In practice mismatch leaves a small A{cm}: a four-resistor difference amp with 1% resistors and a gain of 10 has a wor

q0116.title: Gain-bandwidth product
q0116.short: "The gain-bandwidth product is the constant you get by multiplying gain by frequency along the amplifier's roll-off. A voltage-feedback op-amp has a huge DC gain with a dominant pole at a low frequency, then falls 20 dB per decade, so gain times frequency is constant and equals the unity-gain frequency. With feedback, closed-loop bandwidth is the GBW divided by the closed-loop noise gain, so a 1 MHz op-amp running at

q0117.title: What sets slew rate and rise time
q0117.short: "Slew rate is the largest-signal limit: the maximum dV/dt, set by the current available to charge a capacitor. In an op-amp it's the input stage tail current divided by the compensation capacitor, I/Cc, like 10 µA over 20 pF gives 0.5 V/µs. Rise time is the small-signal limit from bandwidth, about 0.35 over the -3 dB bandwidth, or 2.2 RC. Small steps are bandwidth-limited exponentials; big steps ramp linearly at the

q0118.title: Pros and cons of fast vs slow slew rates
q0118.short: "Fast slew rates give better timing margin, less jitter, lower switching loss in power stages and less distortion in amplifiers. The cost is more high-frequency content, so more EMI, ground bounce, crosstalk, ringing and overshoot, and you start to need termination. Slow slew rates are quiet and easy on EMC but eat timing margin and raise switching loss. So I choose the slowest edge that meets timing and tune with dr

q0119.title: Biasing an amplifier
q0119.short: "Biasing sets the DC operating point so the transistor stays active and the signal can swing symmetrically. For a BJT I use voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor: the divider sets the base voltage, IE=(VB-V{BE})/RE, so the current depends on resistors, not on \beta, and the emitter resistor gives negative DC feedback. The divider current is about ten times the base current, and the collector sits near mid-sup

q0120.title: Why BJTs are often used for amplifiers
q0120.short: "Mostly because of transconductance. A BJT's gm is IC/VT, about 39 mS per milliamp, whereas a MOSFET's is 2ID/V{ov}, around 4 to 10 mS. So a BJT gives more gain per stage, more bandwidth per mA, lower input-referred voltage noise, a higher intrinsic gain (VA/VT in the thousands) and better offset matching. The costs are base current, a more nonlinear exponential law and temperature drift. MOSFETs win on input resista

q0121.title: What an op-amp is and how it works
q0121.short: "An op-amp is a high-gain differential amplifier: the output is a huge gain, around 10^5 or more, times the difference between its two inputs. Open-loop it just saturates, so you wrap negative feedback around it. Then it forces the two inputs to nearly the same voltage, and the closed-loop gain is set by external resistors, roughly 1/\beta, instead of by the op-amp's own loose gain. Inside it's an input differential

q0122.title: Op-amp symbol and its two inputs
q0122.short: "An op-amp is a triangle pointing in the direction of signal flow. Two inputs on the flat side: the minus input is inverting, the plus input is non-inverting. One output at the tip. The output is the gain times plus minus minus. So a signal into plus comes out in phase and a signal into minus comes out inverted, which is why negative feedback is wired back to the minus input. I'd also add the two supply pins, positiv

q0123.title: Connections needed to wire an op-amp
q0123.short: "Beyond the two inputs and the output, an op-amp needs a positive and negative supply, so power pins, with a 100 nF decoupling capacitor close to them. For a linear amplifier it also needs a feedback path from the output to the inverting input. Both inputs need a DC path to a defined voltage, because bias current flows into them and a floating input drifts to a rail. Then I check the common-mode range and output swin

q0124.title: The three ideal op-amp rules
q0124.short: "The ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance, so no current flows into the inputs; zero output impedance, so the output is an ideal voltage source; and infinite gain. With negative feedback, infinite gain forces the difference between the inputs to zero, the virtual short, so V+ = V-. With these I can solve a circuit with just KCL. For an inverting amp the minus node is a virtual ground, the input current all flows

q0125.title: Inverting and non-inverting op-amp circuits
q0125.short: "Inverting: plus input to ground, signal through R{in} into the minus node, Rf from the output back to that node. The minus node is a virtual ground, so gain is -Rf/R{in}. Non-inverting: signal on the plus input, and Rf and Rg form a divider from output to ground feeding the minus input. The virtual short makes V{out}(Rg/(Rg+Rf)) = V{in}, so gain is 1 + Rf/Rg. Inverting has input impedance R{in} and can attenuate; no

q0126.title: DC gain of an op-amp
q0126.short: "Open loop, an op-amp's DC gain is very large, typically 10^5 to 10^6, or 100 to 120 dB, though it's loosely specified. In a circuit what matters is the closed-loop gain, set by the feedback resistors: 1/\beta, such as 1 + Rf/Rg. The finite open-loop gain only adds a small error of about G/A0, so a gain of 10 on a 10^5 part is off by 0.01%. And that high gain only holds at low frequency: a dominant pole rolls it off

q0127.title: Open-loop op-amp: the comparator
q0127.short: "Open loop, the op-amp's gain of 10^5 or more acts on the tiny difference between its inputs, so the output slams to a rail depending on which input is higher. That makes it a comparator, a one-bit ADC. The linear region is only ~100 µV wide. Noise near the threshold causes chatter, so you add positive feedback for hysteresis, a Schmitt trigger. In practice, dedicated comparators are better than op-amps for this beca

q0128.title: Why prefer non-inverting op-amp stages
q0128.short: "Non-inverting stages are often preferred because the input goes straight into the op-amp's high-impedance plus terminal, so they don't load the source or turn its resistance into a gain error. They also don't invert, can be built as a unity-gain buffer, and for the same signal gain have slightly better bandwidth. The downsides: the gain is at least one, and both inputs swing with the signal, so common-mode range and

q0129.title: Bode magnitude and phase of a first-order filter
q0129.short: "For a first-order low-pass I'd draw magnitude in dB and phase versus log frequency. Magnitude is flat at 0 dB, is 3 dB down at the corner fc = 1/(2\pi RC), and then falls at −20 dB per decade. Phase goes from 0 to −90 degrees, with exactly −45 at the corner. A high-pass is the mirror image: rising 20 dB per decade up to the corner then flat, phase from +90 to 0, +45 at the corner."

q0130.title: First-order LPF and HPF circuits
q0130.short: "The RC low-pass is a series resistor with a capacitor to ground, output across the capacitor. The capacitor shorts out high frequencies. The high-pass swaps them: series capacitor, resistor to ground, output across the resistor, so the capacitor blocks DC. Both have a corner at 1/(2\pi RC). You can build the same filters with an inductor, series L plus a resistor to ground for a low-pass, but RC is usually preferred

q0131.title: Roll-off rate of a first-order low-pass
q0131.short: "A first-order low-pass rolls off at 20 dB per decade, about 6 dB per octave, above its corner. The reason is that for f \gg fc the magnitude is just fc/f: ten times the frequency gives one tenth of the amplitude, which is minus 20 dB. It's the capacitor behaving like a short, so the filter acts as an integrator. The slope is asymptotic: minus 3 dB at the corner and minus 20 dB at ten times the corner. Each extra pol

q0132.title: What bandwidth characterizes
q0132.short: "Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a system passes within 3 dB of its passband gain: DC to the corner for a low-pass, upper minus lower edge for a band-pass. It characterizes speed: rise time is about 0.35 over the bandwidth. It also sets how much noise gets in and, through Shannon, how much information you can send. For an op-amp, closed-loop bandwidth is about GBW over gain."

q0133.title: The −3 dB point and how much passes
q0133.short: "The 3 dB point is where the gain has dropped to 0.707 of the passband, which is half the power. For an RC filter it's 1/(2\pi RC) with 45 degrees of phase shift. After that the response keeps falling at 20 dB per decade for a first-order filter: it's not a cliff. At the corner 70.7 percent of the voltage and 50 percent of the power get through; at twice the corner about 45 percent; at ten times about 10 percent, whi

q0134.title: Ways to raise a clock frequency (PLL)
q0134.short: "A PLL, used as a frequency multiplier. A stable low-frequency reference like a crystal feeds a loop containing a VCO and a divide-by-N in the feedback path. The loop locks the divided VCO to the reference, so the output is N times the reference: 25 MHz times 40 gives 1 GHz. It's preferred over a very high-frequency crystal because it's flexible and the reference is clean and cheap. Simpler options exist, like an XOR

q0135.title: How a PLL works
q0135.short: "A PLL is a feedback loop that locks an oscillator's phase to a reference. A phase-frequency detector compares the reference to the VCO output divided by N and generates pulses proportional to the phase error. A charge pump and loop filter turn that into a control voltage, which steers the VCO. When the divided clock has the same frequency as the reference and a constant phase offset, the control voltage stops changi

q0136.title: PLL building blocks and their roles
q0136.short: "A charge-pump PLL has a reference oscillator, a phase-frequency detector, a charge pump, a loop filter, a VCO, and a divide-by-N feedback divider. The PFD turns the timing error between reference and divided VCO into UP/DOWN pulses, the charge pump turns those into current, the loop filter integrates it into a control voltage, the VCO converts that to frequency, and the divider feeds it back. Fractional-N adds a sig

q0137.title: Draw a PLL block diagram
q0137.short: "Left to right: reference clock into a phase-frequency detector; its UP and DOWN outputs drive a charge pump; that feeds a loop filter, an R–C network; the filter's control voltage drives the VCO, whose output is f out. A divide-by-N block takes f out and feeds it back to the second input of the PFD, closing the loop. I'd label f ref, UP/DOWN, the pump current, V control, f out and f out over N, and write f out equal

q0138.title: PLL locking too fast or too slow
q0138.short: "It's the loop bandwidth trade-off. Too fast, meaning wide bandwidth, and the output inherits reference and charge-pump noise multiplied by N, reference spurs, and may overshoot or even go unstable as the bandwidth nears the reference frequency. Too slow and the lock time gets long, so startup and frequency changes lag, and the loop can't suppress the VCO's own noise and drift, so jitter rises, and it can't track inp

q0139.title: Why a crushed clock window hurts
q0139.short: "I take the clock window as the time you have each cycle for launch, logic, setup, skew and jitter. If you crush it, with a faster clock, jitter, duty-cycle error or PLL overshoot, you get setup and hold violations and metastability in synchronous logic, minimum-pulse-width failures in flops and memories, SNR loss in ADCs through aperture jitter, and eye closure and bit errors in serial links and DDR. Circuits see th

q0140.title: What kind of load is a SoC/CPU?
q0140.short: "A SoC is best described as a capacitive, time-varying current sink. It's CMOS, so power goes into charging and discharging capacitance every cycle: \alpha C V^2 f. On average it looks resistive, like 17 milliohms for a 54 amp core, but that's just V over I, and it changes with the workload. It isn't really inductive. The inductance is in the package and board, and with fast current steps it causes droop, which is wh

q0141.title: Maximum power transfer condition
q0141.short: "Maximum power goes to the load when the load resistance equals the source resistance, or for AC when ZL = Zs^. The load power is Vs^2RL/(Rs+RL)^2, and setting the derivative to zero gives RL = Rs, with P{max} = Vs^2/(4Rs). The catch is that efficiency is only 50% at that point, so it's used in RF and signal chains, not in power supplies, where you want low source impedance instead."

q0142.title: Why many capacitors on a power rail
q0142.short: "They're decoupling capacitors, acting as local charge reservoirs so fast current bursts don't pull the rail down. There are many because a real capacitor has ESR and inductance, so each one is only a low impedance over a limited band, above its self-resonant frequency it looks like an inductor. Paralleling several small parts divides the inductance and gives low impedance out to hundreds of megahertz. One massive ca

q0143.title: What is bulk capacitance?
q0143.short: "Bulk capacitance is the large capacitance, tens to thousands of microfarads, at a board's power entry or a regulator's input or output. It's the local energy tank: it supplies load steps while the regulator catches up, smooths converter input ripple, and provides hold-up. You size it from C = I\Delta t/\Delta V or from energy. It's slow, though. Big capacitors are inductive above a few hundred kilohertz, so small ce

q0144.title: Inductive flyback and protection
q0144.short: "Inductive flyback is the voltage spike when you suddenly interrupt current through an inductor. Since v=L\,di/dt, the inductor forces the current to continue by driving its voltage as high as needed, up to kilovolts if there's no path. It's unwanted with relays, motors and solenoids, where it can kill the driver, so you add a freewheel diode, or a diode with a Zener or a TVS, or a snubber. It's wanted in boost and f

q0145.title: PWM and its characteristics
q0145.short: "PWM is switching a signal fully on and off at a fixed frequency and varying the on-time fraction, the duty cycle D. The average is D\cdot V, for example 1.5 V from a 5 V signal at 30%, but the RMS is V\sqrt D, which sets heating. A filter or a slow load averages it. The main benefit is efficiency, since the switch is either on or off. Frequency is the trade-off: higher means smaller filters but more switching loss a

q0146.title: Wide-bandgap semiconductors: SiC, GaN
q0146.short: "The main ones are silicon carbide and gallium nitride, with gallium oxide and diamond in research. Their wide bandgap gives a critical field about ten times silicon's, so the drift region can be much thinner. That gives much lower on-resistance for a given voltage, smaller capacitances and faster switching, so higher efficiency and frequency with smaller magnetics. SiC fits high voltage, GaN fits up to roughly 650 v

q0147.title: Ways to step voltage up or down
q0147.short: "To step down you can use a divider, a Zener, a linear regulator or LDO, or a buck converter. To step up, a boost converter, a charge pump, or a transformer-based converter; buck-boost and SEPIC when the input crosses the output. For a power rail you don't use a divider or Zener since the output moves with load and wastes power. You use an LDO when the drop and current are small and you want low noise, because effici

q0148.title: Why not a divider for a power rail
q0148.short: "A divider's output is a Thevenin source with output resistance R1\parallel R2, so the voltage drops with load current, and a rail's load changes all the time. To make it stiff you'd need tiny resistors that waste far more power than the load uses, and it still isn't regulated against input changes. For 5 V to 3.3 V at 20 mA it would burn watts for 66 milliwatts. Use an LDO or buck, which use feedback to hold the out

q0149.title: When a voltage divider is applicable
q0149.short: "A divider works when the load draws negligible current compared with the divider's own current, so the output is just the resistor ratio. Typical uses are regulator feedback networks, scaling a voltage into an ADC or comparator (ideally through a buffer), enable-pin under-voltage thresholds, and bias networks. Rule of thumb: the load should be about 100 times the Thevenin resistance for 1% error. Then pick the resis

q0150.title: Design a power supply
q0150.short: "I'd start with requirements: input range, outputs, currents, ripple, efficiency, environment. For 12 V to 3.3 V at 2 A I'd use a synchronous buck rather than an LDO, which would waste 17 W. At 500 kHz that gives about D = 0.275, an 8.2 µH inductor, about 40 µF of ceramic output capacitance, and a feedback divider for the 0.6 V reference. Then I'd add soft start, current limit, UVLO, thermal protection and input prot

q0151.title: Supply overshoot and undershoot
q0151.short: "Undershoot makes logic slower, because gate delay rises as the supply drops, so you get timing failures, brown-outs, bad memory writes and analogue errors. Overshoot stresses devices, since it can exceed absolute-maximum ratings, and it increases power as V^2. It's tolerable for loads with wide input range or their own regulation, like motors, heaters or LEDs, and for brief events within spec. Low-voltage digital co

q0152.title: Parameters to track in a supply
q0152.short: "I'd track output voltage and its regulation against load and line, ripple and noise, transient response and loop stability, then input and output voltage and current to get efficiency and loss, plus quiescent current and temperature. Beyond that, start-up behaviour like soft-start and inrush, and protection thresholds: current limit, under-voltage lockout, thermal shutdown and power-good. At runtime I'd monitor volt

q0153.title: Specs for buying or designing a supply
q0153.short: "I'd start from the load and spec the output voltage and tolerance, continuous and peak current, ripple and noise, regulation and transient response. Then efficiency including no-load power, the input range and surge/inrush behaviour, protections like over-current and over-temperature, thermal derating, and certifications and cost. I'd size continuous current at about 70-80% of the rating, cover the peak, and verify

q0154.title: Energy conservation in power design
q0154.short: "Energy conservation says input power equals output power plus losses, almost always heat: P{in}=P{out}+P{loss}. It's a tool and a goal. As a tool, it gives me unknown currents: a 90% efficient converter making 6.6 W from 12 V draws 0.61 A. As a goal, wasted energy is heat and battery life: an LDO from 12 to 3.3 V at 2 A wastes 17 W while a buck wastes under 1 W."

q0155.title: Solve for the missing V or I
q0155.short: "Output power equals efficiency times input power: V{out}I{out}=\eta V{in}I{in}. Solve for the missing one. With 12 V in at 0.5 A and 3.3 V out, the ideal output current is 12\times0.5/3.3=1.82 A, or 1.64 A at 90% efficiency. I'd state the efficiency assumption, check direction (buck raises current, boost lowers it, LDO keeps it the same) and flag any result that implies more than 100% efficiency."

q0156.title: Name some voltage regulators
q0156.short: "I'd group them by how they work. Linear regulators, like a 7805, LM317 or an LDO, burn the excess voltage as heat, so they're simple and quiet but only step down. Switching regulators use an inductor and a switch, buck to step down, boost to step up, buck-boost for both, flyback for isolation, and they hit roughly 90 percent efficiency. Charge pumps use capacitors to double or invert a voltage at low current. And sh

q0157.title: Buck converter vs LDO trade-offs
q0157.short: "An LDO burns the extra voltage as heat in a series pass element, so its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, and it only steps down. A buck switches and uses an inductor to transfer energy, so it's around 90 percent efficient regardless of the voltage drop. The trade is that the LDO is tiny, quiet and fast, while the buck needs an inductor, has ripple and EMI, and needs careful layout. Big drop or high current, buck;

q0158.title: When an LDO beats a buck
q0158.short: "An LDO is more efficient when the voltage drop is small or the load is tiny. Its efficiency is about Vout over Vin, so it beats a buck whenever that ratio is higher than the buck's efficiency, like 3.6 volts down to 3.3 at 92 percent. At very light loads, a buck's own quiescent current and switching overhead can exceed the load, so a nano-amp-class LDO can win. At a big drop and real current, the buck always wins."

q0159.title: AC-AC, AC-DC, DC-DC, DC-AC converters
q0159.short: "It's a grid by input and output. AC to AC is a transformer, variac, or TRIAC phase control. AC to DC is a rectifier, usually a diode bridge plus a filter capacitor, often with a PFC stage. DC to DC is linear regulators, charge pumps and switching converters like buck, boost and flyback. DC to AC is an inverter: an H-bridge or three-phase bridge with PWM. They chain: a wall adapter is AC-DC then DC-DC, and a motor dr

q0160.title: Bridge rectifier operation
q0160.short: "A bridge rectifier is four diodes in a diamond: AC across one diagonal, load across the other. On one half-cycle two diodes conduct and on the other half-cycle the other two do, but current always goes through the load in the same direction, so you get the absolute value of the input, pulsating DC at twice the line frequency. Two diodes are in the path, so you lose about 1.4 volts, and you add a capacitor to smooth

q0161.title: Why step-down regulators dominate
q0161.short: "Because supplies are usually higher than what the chips need, and chips keep going lower in voltage to save CV-squared-f power. Distributing at a higher voltage also means less current and less I-squared-R loss, so you convert down at the point of load. Step-down converters are also simpler: a buck has continuous output current and no right-half-plane zero, while a boost has higher input current, a pulsed output and

q0162.title: Power supply efficiency: definition, measurement
q0162.short: "Efficiency is output power over input power, so it's the fraction of source energy that reaches the load; the rest is loss and becomes heat. I measure Vin, Iin, Vout and Iout together, with Kelvin sensing at the converter pins, an electronic load, and a warmed-up unit, and I sweep load and input voltage because efficiency is a curve. It matters for heat, battery life, size and cost, reliability, and regulations."

q0163.title: Pin, Pout, efficiency: find the third
q0163.short: "Efficiency is output power over input power. Given two, rearrange: eta is Pout over Pin; Pout is Pin times eta; Pin is Pout divided by eta. For example, 5 watts out at 90 percent needs 5.56 watts in, losing 0.56. Input must always be larger than output, and for cascaded stages you multiply the efficiencies."

q0164.title: Where lost power goes and why it hurts
q0164.short: "Lost power becomes heat. The energy not delivered to the load is dissipated in FET and inductor resistance, switching transitions, magnetic cores and the controller's bias. That raises junction temperature by loss times thermal resistance, which risks thermal shutdown and shortens component life, shifts parameters like on-resistance, wastes battery energy, and forces larger heatsinks and more cost. So I compute the

q0165.title: Quiescent current of a regulator
q0165.short: "Quiescent current is what a regulator draws from its input just to operate, with no load: the bias for the reference, error amp, feedback divider and control. For an LDO it's the ground-pin current. It matters because it never goes away: in a battery device that sleeps at microamps, it can dominate standby current and light-load efficiency. For example, 50 microamps on a coin cell kills standby life, so for always-o

q0166.title: Design a power architecture from a spec
q0166.short: "I'd clarify input range, accuracy, noise, sequencing and thermal limits first, then build a power budget. For a 12 volt input with 5, 3.3, 1.8 and 1 volt rails plus a clean analog 1.8, it's about 27 watts out. I'd use a buck on each rail, fed directly from the input, around 90 percent efficient overall, with a low-noise LDO from 3.3 volts for the analog rail. Then I'd check input current at minimum voltage, sizing,

q0167.title: Multiple output voltages from one supply
q0167.short: "Per-rail switching regulators are the default: bucks for rails below the input, boost or buck-boost for ones above, and an inverting converter or charge pump for negative rails. LDOs suit small, clean rails, but their input current equals output current, so cascading them doesn't cut total loss. For compact designs I'd use a PMIC, multi-output buck or SIMO converter, and for isolated or mains-fed rails a multi-windi

q0168.title: Same voltage, different noise rails
q0168.short: "I'd keep the noisy and quiet loads from sharing a path. The digital 3.3 V comes from a buck, and the analog 3.3 V comes from a low-noise LDO fed from a slightly higher rail, with an LC or ferrite filter if the LDO's PSRR at the switching frequency isn't enough. I'd compute the required attenuation from the ripple and the noise budget, damp any LC filter, and manage the switcher with frequency choice, sync or spread

q0169.title: Large dropout but clean, efficient rail
