q0169.short: "A buck takes the big drop efficiently, down to just above the target, and then a low-noise LDO takes the last few hundred millivolts and cleans the rail. For 12 to 3.3 volts at an amp, the buck goes to about 3.6 volts and the LDO drops 0.3 volts, so it only dissipates 0.3 watts and the chain is around 84 percent efficient. I choose the headroom as the smallest value that still gives enough PSRR at the switching freq

q0170.title: Intermediate bus converter and when needed
q0170.short: "An intermediate bus converter is the first stage of a two-stage architecture: it steps a high input like 48 volts down to an intermediate bus like 12, often isolated and fixed-ratio, and point-of-load buck converters near each chip then make the final rails. It's needed because distributing at high voltage cuts I-squared-R loss, and because a single stage from 48 volts to 1 volt needs a duty cycle near 2 percent, wh

q0171.title: Power sequencing: why, order, timing
q0171.short: "Power sequencing is controlling the order and timing of supply rails turning on and off. It's needed because multi-rail chips can be damaged or left in undefined states if, say, the I/O is powered while the core isn't, since ESD diodes back-power the core or latch-up occurs. The order comes from the datasheets: sequence sections and absolute max ratings like I/O not exceeding core by 0.3 volts. The timing is usually

q0172.title: Implementing power sequencing
q0172.short: "The simplest is to chain regulators: the power-good pin of one, pulled up through a resistor, drives the enable of the next, so each rail starts only when the previous is valid. For extra delay I add an RC on the enable, with t=RC\ln[V{cc}/(V{cc}-V{th})], though tolerance is loose. For more control I use a voltage supervisor, or a sequencer IC or PMIC, or an MCU or CPLD reading PGs. Tracking pins and load switches h

q0173.title: What is a buck converter
q0173.short: "A buck converter is an efficient switching regulator that steps a voltage down. A transistor chops the input on and off at a fixed frequency, and an inductor and capacitor average it, so the output is the input times the duty cycle. A feedback loop adjusts the duty cycle to hold the output constant. It's efficient because the switch is either fully on or fully off, so almost no power is lost, unlike a linear regulat

q0174.title: How a buck converter works
q0174.short: "A buck has two states. When the high-side switch is on, the inductor sees V{in}-V{out} and its current ramps up while feeding the load. When the switch turns off, the inductor current keeps flowing through the diode or low-side FET, the inductor sees -V{out}, and the current ramps down. The output capacitor smooths the ripple. In steady state the up and down ramps balance, so V{out}=D\,V{in}. A feedback loop adjusts

q0175.title: Draw a buck converter circuit
q0175.short: "I'd draw the input source with a capacitor across it, then a high-side NFET from the input rail to a switch node. From the switch node, a diode down to ground with the cathode at the node, and an inductor going right to the output. At the output, a capacitor to ground in parallel with the load. A feedback divider goes back to the controller, which drives the FET gate with PWM. For a synchronous buck I replace the di

q0176.title: Buck converter applications
q0176.short: "Bucks are everywhere you need an efficient step-down: point-of-load rails like 12 V or 5 V down to 3.3 V, 1.8 V or 1 V for processors, FPGAs and memory; battery-powered devices where efficiency sets runtime; automotive and industrial buses stepped down to logic rails; and CPU core rails, which are multiphase bucks. The same stage regulates current for LED drivers and chargers. I'd use an LDO instead for tiny dropout

q0177.title: SIMO buck converter
q0177.short: "SIMO means single-inductor multiple-output: one input, one shared inductor, several regulated rails. The inductor is time-multiplexed: it's charged from the input and then dumped into one output at a time, usually in discontinuous mode so each slot starts at zero current. The win is area and cost, because one inductor replaces several. The costs are cross-regulation between outputs, high peak inductor currents, a sh

q0178.title: What sets a buck's output voltage
q0178.short: "In the power stage, the duty cycle and input set the output: V{out}=D\,V{in} in continuous conduction, because the inductor can't sustain a DC voltage, so the average switch-node voltage must equal V{out}. In a real regulator the feedback loop picks D: a divider scales V{out} to a reference, and the loop adjusts D until they match, so V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2). The formula changes with losses and in discontinuous mode.

q0179.title: What is duty cycle
q0179.short: "Duty cycle is the fraction of each switching period that the switch is on: D=t{on}/T, between 0 and 100 percent. It's independent of frequency: at 500 kHz, 27.5 percent is a 550 ns on-time. In a buck the switch node is a pulse train whose average is D\,V{in}, so duty cycle sets the output voltage, and the feedback loop adjusts it to regulate."

q0180.title: How to calculate duty cycle
q0180.short: "Ideally, duty cycle is V{out}/V{in}, so 12 V to 3.3 V is 27.5 percent. In a real converter I add the drops: for a synchronous buck D=\frac{V{out}+I(R{ls}+R{DCR})}{V{in}-I(R{hs}-R{ls})}, which at 2 A is about 28 percent, and with a Schottky diode closer to 30.7 percent. I can also read it from the scope as on-time over period, or get it from I{in}/I{out}. All of that assumes continuous conduction."

q0181.title: Buck at 100% and 0% duty
q0181.short: "At 100 percent duty the high-side is always on, there's no switching or ripple, and V{out} is the input minus the drops across the switch and inductor, so the converter is in dropout and not regulating. At 0 percent the high-side is always off, the inductor current ramps down at V{out}/L, and the output decays; in a forced-PWM synchronous buck the current even reverses and feeds energy back to the input. In real par

q0182.title: Duty cycle from a Vout/Vin ratio
q0182.short: "For a buck in continuous conduction, duty cycle equals the ratio: D=V{out}/V{in}, from volt-second balance. A ratio of 0.275 is 27.5 percent, which at 500 kHz is a 550 ns on-time. I'd check that against the minimum on-time. It's a bit higher with real drops, and in discontinuous mode at light load the ratio alone isn't enough: D=M\sqrt{K/(1-M)} with K=2L/(RT)."

q0183.title: Vout from duty cycle and Vin
q0183.short: "Yes, in continuous conduction: V{out}=D\,V{in}, so 27.5 percent of 12 V is 3.3 V. Real drops pull it down a bit. In discontinuous mode at light load the output is higher for the same duty cycle, so I'd need the load, inductance and frequency too. And in a closed-loop regulator, D isn't an independent input; the feedback loop sets it to hold V{out}."

q0184.title: DC load-line and its tradeoffs
q0184.short: "A DC load line, or droop, is a deliberate drop in output voltage with load current: V{out}=V{ref}-R{LL}I{out}, made by sensing current and subtracting it from the setpoint. It lets the output use the whole tolerance window during a load step instead of half, so you need less output capacitance and see less overshoot, and the load runs at lower voltage and power when busy. The costs are worse DC accuracy, a lower vol

q0185.title: Draw all the buck waveforms
q0185.short: "Switch node is a 12 V pulse that sits at about minus a diode drop when off, averaging 3.3 V. Inductor voltage is that minus V{out}: plus 8.7 V then minus 3.3 V. Integrate it and the inductor current is a triangle about 1 A peak to peak around 2 A. The capacitor current is that triangle with the load average removed, so its integral is a small parabolic ripple of ten-ish millivolts. Input current is the inductor curr

q0186.title: Purpose of output inductor and capacitor
q0186.short: "The inductor stores energy and releases it, so the chopped 12 V pulse becomes a smooth current without burning power; it's the lossless alternative to a series resistor. The capacitor absorbs the inductor's current ripple and holds the output voltage steady, and it supplies load steps until the inductor catches up. Together they're a second-order low-pass with a corner well below the switching frequency, here 16 kHz

q0187.title: Inductor and capacitor current directions
q0187.short: "The inductor current flows from the switch node toward the output in both states; it ramps up when the high-side FET is on and the current comes from the input, and it ramps down during the off state, with the current coming up through the diode or low-side FET from ground. The capacitor current is iL minus the load current, so it's positive, charging, when the inductor current is above the average and negative, dis

q0188.title: Why inductor current is a linear ramp
q0188.short: "It follows from v = L\,di/dt. In the on state the inductor sees roughly V{in}-V{out}, constant, so the current rises linearly with slope (V{in}-V{out})/L. In the off state it sees -V{out}, constant, so it falls linearly at V{out}/L. The slope depends only on those voltages and L, not on the load; the load just sets the average of the triangle. It's only approximately linear, assuming small ripple and negligible resi

q0189.title: Is the output capacitor voltage a linear ramp
q0189.short: "A constant capacitor current gives a linear ramp, but in a buck the capacitor current is a triangle, the inductor current minus the load. The integral of a triangle is a parabola, so the capacitor voltage is made of parabolic arcs, with its extremes where the capacitor current crosses zero. It only looks like a linear ramp when ESR dominates, because the ESR drop follows the current. Ripple is about \Delta I/(8fC),

q0190.title: When the output capacitor charges and discharges
q0190.short: "The capacitor charges when the inductor current is above the load current and discharges when it's below, because the capacitor current is just inductor current minus load current. In steady state that's the top half and bottom half of the inductor triangle, not the on and off states: the capacitor starts charging halfway up the on ramp and stops halfway down the off ramp, and charging lasts exactly half a period. I

q0191.title: Inductor voltage polarity in a buck
q0191.short: "With the current flowing from the switch node to the output, the voltage across the inductor is positive on the switch-node end during the on state, plus 8.7 V in my example, and the current ramps up as it stores energy. In the off state the high-side FET opens, the inductor keeps its current, so its polarity reverses: the switch-node end goes negative relative to the output, minus 3.3 V, and the current ramps down

q0192.title: When the inductor sinks and supplies current
q0192.short: "The inductor current always flows toward the output, so I think in power terms. During the on state the input is connected, the inductor has 8.7 V across it and rising current, so it absorbs energy, it's sinking power from the input. During the off state the input is disconnected and the inductor's voltage reverses, so it delivers its stored energy to the output, supplying the load. In steady state those energies ma

q0193.title: Why a buck needs an input capacitor
q0193.short: "The buck draws pulsed current from the input, only while the high-side FET is on, with a small average and tall pulses. A real source and its wiring have inductance and can't supply those fast pulses, so the input capacitor sits at the FET as a local reservoir, supplying the pulses and getting recharged smoothly. Without it the input would droop and ring, the switch node could overshoot beyond the FET rating, EMI wo

q0194.title: Voltage and current ripple from circuit analysis
q0194.short: "Ripple is the peak-to-peak switching-frequency variation of the inductor current and the output voltage. The inductor current ramps by V\cdot t/L each state, so \Delta I=V{out}(1-D)/(Lf), about 1 A in my example. The capacitor sees that as a triangle with zero average, so the capacitive voltage ripple is \Delta I/(8fC), about 11.6 mV, plus \Delta I\cdot ESR. Bigger L, higher f, bigger C and lower ESR all reduce it,

q0195.title: What sets the inductor current slope
q0195.short: "The slope is the voltage across the inductor divided by L. In the on state that's (V{in}-V{out})/L, rising 1.85 A/µs in my 12 V to 3.3 V, 4.7 µH example, and in the off state it's -V{out}/L, falling 0.7 A/µs. The load current doesn't change the slope, only the offset; the duty cycle only decides how long you stay on each one. In real parts, resistive drops, diode drop, tolerance and saturation modify it slightly."

q0196.title: What sets output capacitor voltage slope
q0196.short: "The slope is iC/C. In a buck the capacitor current is the inductor current minus the load current, a triangle of plus and minus half the ripple current, so the voltage slope swings between about minus and plus 23 mV/µs in my example (0.51 A over 22 µF) and is zero at the ripple extremes. So the ripple current and C set it. In a load step it is \Delta I/C, and at start-up the soft-start ramp times C sets the inrush."

q0197.title: Why the buck needs a diode
q0197.short: "The diode is the freewheeling path. When the high-side FET opens, the inductor current can't stop, so the inductor forces the switch node negative until something conducts. The diode does that at about minus 0.4 V and lets the current ramp down through the load. Without it the node would fly down until the FET avalanches or the controller's switch pin breaks: in my example the inductor holds about 15 µJ at turn-off,

q0198.title: Buck with an ideal diode
q0198.short: "An ideal diode removes the forward-drop loss: for 12 V to 3.3 V at 2 A with a 0.5 V Schottky that's 0.73 W of 6.6 W, so efficiency goes from about 90% toward 100%, and the gain is bigger at lower output voltages. It also makes the off-state switch node exactly 0 V, the duty cycle exactly V{out}/V{in}, and removes reverse-recovery spikes. What it doesn't change is that it can't conduct backwards, so you still get DCM

q0199.title: Switch node voltage in the off state
q0199.short: "Just below ground: the inductor current keeps flowing, so the switch node is pulled down until the freewheel path conducts. With a Schottky that's about minus 0.4 V; with a synchronous low-side FET it's minus I\,R{ds(on)}, tens of millivolts, with brief dips to about minus 0.7 V in dead time on the body diode. The one exception is DCM: after the inductor current hits zero the node floats and rings around V{out}."

q0200.title: Source of inductor current in the off state
q0200.short: "By KCL at the switch node, with the high-side FET open the inductor current has to come through the diode, or the low-side FET, from ground. So it circulates: ground, diode, switch node, inductor, load, back to ground; the input isn't in the loop. The energy comes from the inductor's magnetic field, built up during the on time, about 9.6 µJ per cycle in my example. The capacitor only fills in the gap when the induct

q0201.title: Buck power bridge type and why
q0201.short: "Most buck converters use a half bridge of two NFETs with synchronous rectification: a high-side NFET to V{in} and a low-side NFET to ground, driven complementary with dead time. The low-side FET replaces the diode because I\cdot R{DS(on)} is far below a diode's fixed 0.3 to 0.7 V drop, which matters most at low output voltage and high current. NFETs on both sides because electrons are more mobile than holes, so an N

q0202.title: Freewheel diode: why and what if removed
q0202.short: "The diode is the freewheel path. When the high-side switch opens, the inductor current can't jump, so the switch node swings negative until the diode turns on at about minus 0.4 V and carries the current while it decays. Remove it and the inductor generates whatever voltage it needs, L\,di/dt, so SW slams negative at around 10 V per nanosecond until some FET or pin avalanches. That dumps the inductor's stored energy

q0203.title: Synchronous rectification pros and cons
q0203.short: "Synchronous rectification replaces the freewheel diode with a low-side MOSFET driven complementary to the high side. It wins on efficiency: loss is I^2R{DS(on)} instead of Vf\cdot I, so at 3.3 V out and 2 A you cut roughly 650 mW to about 30 mW. The costs are a second gate driver, dead time to avoid shoot-through with body-diode loss during it, gate-drive power at all loads, and negative inductor current at light lo

q0204.title: High-side NFET vs PFET trade-offs
q0204.short: "An NFET is the better switch and a PFET is the easier one to drive. NFETs have two to three times lower R{DS(on)} per area because electrons are more mobile than holes, so less gate charge and capacitance and lower cost, but a high-side NFET needs its gate above V{in}, so a bootstrap or charge pump, and it can't reach 100% duty without refresh. A high-side PFET just pulls its gate down relative to V{in} and supports

q0205.title: Symmetrical power bridge pros and cons
q0205.short: "I'd take symmetrical to mean two identical FETs in the half bridge. Pros: one part number, identical drive and timing, and bidirectional capability, so it's good near 50% duty and for inverters or bidirectional converters. Con: in a buck the high side conducts D and hard-switches while the low side conducts 1-D with near-zero-voltage switching, so equal sizing wastes silicon at small duty. For fixed area the optimal

q0206.title: Design a high-side NFET drive
q0206.short: "The high-side NFET's source is the switch node, so its gate has to go to V{in} plus about 5 V. I'd use a bootstrap: a gate driver whose supply pin is a capacitor from BST to SW, charged through a Schottky from a 5 V rail while the low side is on. Size it as C\ge Qg/\Delta V, for example 12 nC over 0.3 V is 40 nF, then use 100 nF. Considerations: refresh limits max duty, pre-biased start-up, SW undershoot and dv/dt i

q0207.title: Shoot-through and dead time
q0207.short: "If both are on, V{in} is shorted to ground through two small R{DS(on)}s. Real current is tens to hundreds of amps for nanoseconds, limited by saturation and the input cap, but it wastes energy every cycle, heats the FETs, droops V{in} and can destroy them. Avoid it with dead time, ideally adaptive, or non-overlapping gate logic. Also guard against dv/dt-induced turn-on through the Miller capacitance with a low-imped

q0208.title: Body diode in the off state, SW waveform
q0208.short: "In the off state the inductor current keeps flowing through the low side. During the dead time both FETs are off, so it flows through the low-side body diode and SW sits about one diode drop, 0.7 to 1 V, below ground. Then the low-side channel turns on and SW comes up to about minus I\,R{DS(on)}, tens of millivolts. Before the high side turns on there's another dead-time shelf. When the high side turns on the diode

q0209.title: Design considerations from body diode behavior
q0209.short: "The body diode conducts in dead time at about 0.7 to 1 V and then must be forced off by the high-side turn-on. So I'd budget its conduction loss V{SD}Itdf and its recovery loss Q{rr}V{in}f, set dead time as short as is safe, probably adaptive, check the negative SW voltage against the controller's rating, watch the recovery spike and ringing for EMI and overshoot, check the diode's current and thermal rating, and ch

q0210.title: Reducing body diode effects
q0210.short: "Attack each mechanism. Shorten the dead time with adaptive control so the diode conducts as little as possible, which cuts both conduction and stored charge. Add a Schottky in parallel, but only co-packaged or monolithic, since nanohenries of loop inductance stop it taking the current. Choose a FET with low Q{rr} and soft recovery. Slow the high-side turn-on or add a snubber and tighten the layout to tame the recove

q0211.title: Why buck beats LDO efficiency
q0211.short: "An LDO is a series resistor: all the output current passes through it and it burns (V{in}-V{out})\times I{out}, so efficiency is about V{out}/V{in}, 27% for 12 V to 3.3 V. A buck uses switches that are either fully on or fully off, so they dissipate almost nothing, plus an inductor and capacitor that store and return energy instead of dissipating it. Power is conserved, so the input current drops to D\cdot I{out}. R

q0212.title: Sizing L and C for ripple spec
q0212.short: "Size the inductor from the ripple current: L=\dfrac{V{out}(1-D)}{f\,\Delta I} with \Delta I about 30% of full load. Then the output capacitor from \Delta V\approx\dfrac{\Delta I}{8fC}+\Delta I\cdot ESR, so C\ge\dfrac{\Delta I}{8f(\Delta V-\Delta I\cdot ESR)}. For 12 V to 3.3 V, 3 A, 600 kHz, 20 mV: 4.7 µH and about 10 µF effective, so 22 µF nominal after ceramic derating. Then check the inductor's saturation current

q0213.title: Component-by-component loss and ripple
q0213.short: "I'd go part by part. The high-side FET has conduction loss D\,I^2R and the largest switching loss; the low-side FET has the largest conduction loss plus dead-time and recovery loss; the driver adds QgVf and quiescent current; the inductor loses in DCR and core and sets the ripple current; the output capacitor barely affects efficiency but sets the voltage ripple through C and ESR; the input capacitor carries pulsed

q0214.title: Ways to increase buck efficiency
q0214.short: "First I'd find the dominant loss. At heavy load it's conduction, so lower-R{DS(on)} FETs (low side first), a lower-DCR inductor and, at high current, multiphase. For switching loss, lower the frequency with a bigger inductor, pick low-Qg/low-Q{rr} FETs, tune dead time adaptively and trade edge speed against EMI. At light load use PFM or diode emulation and low quiescent current. And if possible lower V{in}, since sw

q0215.title: Ways to decrease buck ripple
q0215.short: "Output ripple is \Delta IL/(8fC)+\Delta IL\cdot ESR with \Delta IL=V{out}(1-D)/(Lf), so increase L, C or f, or reduce ESR. Frequency is the strongest lever: the capacitive ripple goes as 1/f^2. Beyond that, interleave multiple phases to cancel ripple current and raise its frequency, add a second-stage LC or ferrite-bead filter, or a post-LDO. High-frequency spikes need layout and local small capacitors, not more bul

q0216.title: Switching frequency vs efficiency and ripple
q0216.short: "Higher switching frequency lowers ripple and shrinks L and C: inductor ripple current goes as 1/f and the capacitor ripple as 1/f^2. But overlap, C{oss}, gate-drive, dead-time and recovery losses all scale with f, so efficiency drops. With a fixed inductor, efficiency peaks at a moderate frequency (about 300 kHz in my example) because lower ripple current also cuts RMS and core loss. With the inductor scaled to hold

q0217.title: Biggest efficiency loss sources in a buck
q0217.short: "At nominal load: the low-side FET (conducts 1-D of the cycle, so the biggest I^2R), then the high-side FET (conduction plus all the hard switching loss), then the inductor (DCR plus core). Capacitors and feedback are negligible. In a 12 V to 3.3 V, 2 A example, about 180, 140 and 120 mW of 457 mW. The ranking shifts: at light load fixed losses (gate drive, recovery, quiescent) dominate; at high V{in} or high frequen

q0218.title: Why reduce output ripple
q0218.short: "Ripple uses up the load's supply tolerance and couples into sensitive circuits: ADC noise, VCO and PLL spurs, audio and sensor error, through finite PSRR that gets worse at high frequency. It also means higher peak and RMS current, more inductor core loss, capacitor heating and conducted EMI. For example, 10 mV of ripple on a VCO with 5 MHz/V pushing gives about a -26 dBc spur before filtering. But reducing it costs

q0219.title: When ripple matters less
q0219.short: "Ripple matters less when the load tolerates it or doesn't see it: a digital rail with plus or minus 10% tolerance, a load behind an LDO or filter with good rejection at f{sw}, or loads that average it, such as heaters, motor windings, and LEDs driven at average current. Then I'd raise the ripple ratio, using a smaller inductor and capacitor for lower cost and faster transients, while still checking peak current, EMI

q0220.title: Switching frequency upper and lower limits
q0220.short: "Upper limit: switching loss scales with frequency, the pulse can't be shorter than the minimum on-time (f{max}=D/t{on,min}, 2 MHz for 12 V to 1.2 V with 50 ns), plus core loss, EMI and edge times. Lower limit: L and C scale as 1/f, so 1 A and 10 mV at 20 kHz needs 120 µH and 625 µF, the loop crossover must stay below f{sw}/10, and below 20 kHz it's audible. At 1 THz the period is 1 ps, shorter than any FET edge; at

q0221.title: How switching frequency affects performance
q0221.short: "Higher switching frequency means less ripple and smaller inductors and capacitors, and it lets the loop be faster. The cost is that every per-cycle loss, like gate charge, switch-node capacitance and transition overlap, scales linearly with frequency, so efficiency and heat get worse. It also pushes against the minimum on-time limit for big step-downs and moves your EMI harmonics around. So you pick a frequency that

q0222.title: Dropout, Vin, Vout, Iout effects on a regulator
q0222.short: "Dropout is the minimum headroom between input and output an LDO needs to regulate, about load current times pass-device resistance. For an LDO, efficiency is V{out}/V{in} and PSRR collapses near dropout. A buck has the equivalent as a maximum duty cycle limit, where it needs about V{out} plus I\cdot(R{on}+DCR). In a buck, more V{in} means more ripple and more switching loss; more V{out} helps efficiency; and output

q0223.title: Output voltage sensing and feedback network
q0223.short: "The output voltage is sensed with a resistor divider into the feedback pin. The error amp compares that pin to an internal reference, usually around 0.6 to 1 V, and the loop adjusts the duty cycle until they match, so V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2). The divider is needed because the reference is lower than the output and because it lets you program the rail with two resistors. There's usually a feed-forward cap across the t

q0224.title: Feedback divider resistance too high or too low
q0224.short: "Too high, and the feedback pin's bias current flows through the top resistor and shifts the output, leakage and noise pickup get worse, and the resistance plus pin capacitance makes a pole that can eat phase margin. Too low, and the divider itself draws current all the time, which hurts efficiency at light load and battery life. So you pick something in the tens to hundreds of kΩ, within the datasheet's recommendati

q0225.title: Ways to sense output current
q0225.short: "The simplest is a series sense resistor with a current-sense amplifier: accurate, but it costs I^2R loss. To avoid the loss, converters sense the inductor's DCR with an RC network (time constant L/DCR) or the MOSFET's R{DS(on)} while it's on, or use a SenseFET mirror, but those drift with temperature. For isolation or high current you use a Hall sensor or a current transformer."

q0226.title: Where to sense buck output current
q0226.short: "For control and fast protection I sense the inductor or switch current, before the output capacitor, because that's the real state of the power stage and it isn't filtered yet. For accurate load current or telemetry I sense after the capacitor in series with the load, where it's smooth DC and the common-mode is just V{out}. Sensing right after the inductor still shows the ripple. And the input side is for input curr

q0227.title: Signals used in the buck control loop
q0227.short: "The key one is V{out} through the feedback divider into the error amplifier, which sets the duty cycle. In current-mode control the inductor current is the inner loop and also gives cycle-by-cycle limiting. V{in} is used for feed-forward in voltage mode and for UVLO. Switch-node or low-side current detects zero crossing for light-load modes, and temperature, bias voltage and a power-good window on V{out} cover prote

q0228.title: Buck operating modes (CCM, DCM, PFM)
q0228.short: "There are two axes. Inductor current: continuous (CCM), where it never hits zero; discontinuous (DCM), where it returns to zero and rests; and forced CCM, where a synchronous low side lets it go negative. Modulation: PWM, fixed frequency with varying duty, and PFM or burst mode, fixed-size pulses at a rate set by the load. Real converters switch between them automatically: CCM-PWM at heavy load, DCM in the middle, P

q0229.title: DCM vs CCM in a buck converter
q0229.short: "In CCM the inductor current never reaches zero; in DCM it falls to zero and rests for part of the cycle, so there are three switching states instead of two. The boundary is at I{out}=\Delta IL/2. In CCM the output is D\,V{in} regardless of load; in DCM the gain depends on the load, so the duty cycle must shrink as the load drops. DCM also has higher peak current, ringing at the idle interval, and a more first-order

q0230.title: Improving buck efficiency at light load
q0230.short: "At light load the losses that don't scale with load, gate drive, switch-node capacitance and quiescent current, dominate the efficiency number. So you cut them: use PFM or burst mode so pulses and switching losses scale with load, diode emulation so you don't circulate reverse current, a low-quiescent-current controller and a high-value feedback divider, and in multiphase designs shed phases. At microamp loads an ul

q0231.title: Explain PFM operation in a buck
q0231.short: "PFM is a light-load mode where the converter fires fixed-size pulses only when the output droops below a threshold. Each pulse ramps the inductor to a fixed peak, then it discharges to zero into the output, and the converter sleeps until the output sags again. Pulse rate is proportional to load, so switching losses scale down with the load and efficiency stays high. The trade-offs are more, lower-frequency ripple an

q0232.title: PFM versus PWM in buck converters
q0232.short: "PWM keeps the frequency fixed and varies the pulse width; PFM keeps the pulse size fixed and varies how often it fires. PWM gives a clean fixed-frequency spectrum, low ripple and fast response, but poor light-load efficiency because it switches constantly. PFM scales switching losses with load so it's efficient at light load, but has larger low-frequency ripple, smeared EMI and a slower response to load steps. ICs c

q0233.title: Output ripple in PFM versus PWM
q0233.short: "PWM ripple is small and at the switching frequency: in CCM about \Delta IL/(8Cf) plus ESR, and it shrinks further in DCM as the pulses get shorter. PFM ripple comes from a fixed-size charge packet each pulse, about Q/C, which doesn't shrink with load; it just occurs less often. So at light load PFM ripple is roughly ten times PWM's, similar to full-load PWM in amplitude, but at a low and variable frequency that can

q0234.title: Inductor current in PFM mode
q0234.short: "In PFM the inductor current is a train of triangular pulses with zero current in between. Each pulse ramps up at (V{in}-V{out})/L to a fixed peak, ramps back down at V{out}/L to zero, where the low side shuts off. Then the inductor sits idle while the capacitor feeds the load. The pulse shape doesn't change with load, only how often they occur. Peak current is much higher than the average, and near half the peak the

q0235.title: Inductor and capacitor cycle in PFM
q0235.short: "Asleep, the capacitor feeds the load and the output droops. When it hits the threshold, the high-side FET turns on, the inductor current ramps up and stores energy; once it exceeds the load current the capacitor charges. Then the low side takes over, the inductor releases its energy into the output as the current ramps down, and the capacitor keeps charging until the inductor current drops below the load. At zero cu

q0236.title: What a multiphase buck is
q0236.short: "A multiphase buck is N buck power stages that share one output capacitor and one load but switch at evenly staggered times, 360 over N degrees apart. Each phase carries about one N-th of the current. The inductor currents add at the output and their ripples partly cancel, so the capacitor sees much less ripple, at N times the switching frequency. That lets you deliver high current, respond quickly to load steps and

q0237.title: Multiphase vs single-phase trade-offs
q0237.short: "Multiphase gives you more current, lower and higher-frequency output ripple, a faster transient response because the effective inductance is L over N, and heat spread over several stages. The costs are more parts and area, a more complex controller with current balancing, fixed losses that multiply with the phase count, and a harder layout. At the same total silicon the conduction loss doesn't change, so I'd pick mu

q0238.title: How multiphase bucks work and their challenges
q0238.short: "A multiphase buck has one voltage loop that sets total current and a PWM generator that gives each phase a staggered pulse. The main challenge is current sharing: the phases are connected through milliohms, so a 0.1 percent duty error at 12 V can push about 3 amps into one phase. So the controller senses each phase current, usually through the inductor DCR, and trims duty to balance. Other challenges are small sense

q0239.title: When to use a multiphase buck
q0239.short: "I'd use a multiphase buck when one stage can't meet the current, transient or thermal requirements: high current, typically tens of amps or more, at low voltage like a processor core; tough load steps where I need a small effective inductance; and limits on heat or component height. I'd choose the number of phases from the largest of current over derated per-phase rating, slew needed over slew per phase, and thermal

q0240.title: How multiphase increases output current
q0240.short: "The phase inductor currents all feed the same output node, so by KCL they add: four phases at 15 A each deliver 60 A. Each stage only needs FETs, an inductor and a package rated for its own share, so the single-stage limits go away. In practice the total is N times the derated phase limit divided by one plus the sharing error, and I'd check inductor peak current against saturation and think about what happens if one

q0241.title: Multiphase impact on efficiency
q0241.short: "Multiphase efficiency depends on the loss. Conduction loss is I^2R: with the same per-phase parts it falls as 1 over N, but for the same total silicon it is unchanged. Switching loss in total is about the same. Gate drive, driver quiescent and core loss grow with the number of phases, so at light load a multiphase buck is less efficient unless it sheds phases. So it's better at high load and needs phase shedding to

q0242.title: Multiphase and heat density
q0242.short: "Heat density is watts per area, and it is what limits a part. A single-phase 60 amp converter puts all its loss, around 5 watts at 1 volt, into one pair of FETs and one inductor. With four phases, each stage dissipates about a quarter of that, so temperature rise, which is power times thermal resistance, drops several-fold per package, and the heat is spread over more board. It's not exactly one over N because neigh

q0243.title: Multiphase and transient response
q0243.short: "A multiphase buck responds faster for two reasons. When the load steps, all phases ramp together, so the effective inductance is L over N and the total current slews N times faster, so the capacitor has to cover a much shorter gap. And the effective sampling frequency is N times f sw, so the control loop can have a higher bandwidth. For a 12 V to 1 V rail with a 30 amp step, four phases cut the ideal droop by about

q0244.title: What stability means in a buck
q0244.short: "Stability means disturbances like load steps and noise die out instead of growing. In the small-signal model, that means all closed-loop poles are in the left half-plane. In practice I check the loop gain on a Bode plot: at the crossover frequency where gain is 0 dB, the phase margin should be about 45 to 60 degrees, and the gain margin 6 to 10 dB or more. The buck is tricky because its LC output filter adds up to 1

q0245.title: Stable, marginal and unstable bucks
q0245.short: "Stable: a load step gives a dip and a damped recovery, and the ringing is at about the crossover frequency. Marginally stable: zero phase margin, poles on the imaginary axis, so a constant-amplitude oscillation. Unstable: poles in the right half-plane, so the oscillation grows until the duty cycle clamps or the current limit trips, which stresses the parts. Low phase margin also amplifies noise near crossover, so no

q0246.title: The output LC filter as a system
q0246.short: "It's a second-order, linear low-pass filter: an inductor and capacitor give two poles at the resonant frequency 1 over 2 pi root LC. It's underdamped, with a quality factor set by the load, the ESR and the inductor DCR, so the Bode plot has a resonant peak, then falls at minus 40 dB per decade with 180 degrees of phase lag. Light loads have higher Q. The ESR adds a zero that gives back phase. That resonant double po

q0247.title: How L and C values affect stability
q0247.short: "L and C set the LC resonance, f0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}), and its Q. In voltage mode the compensator zeros are placed around that resonance, so bigger L or C moves it below the zeros and costs phase margin, while smaller values move it toward crossover and can push the peak through 0 dB. The capacitor ESR makes a zero that adds phase lead, so swapping electrolytics for ceramics often breaks stability. Also tolerance and c

q0248.title: What happens in a load transient
q0248.short: "When the load steps up, the inductor current can't jump, since it only ramps at V in minus V out over L, so the output capacitor supplies the extra current. You see an immediate ESR step, then the capacitor droops at delta I over C. The loop senses the droop, raises the duty cycle, and the inductor ramps up until its current matches the new load, at which point the droop bottoms out. The inductor then overshoots sli

q0249.title: Characterizing transient response
q0249.short: "I characterize it in the time domain with a load step of defined size and slew rate: peak undershoot and overshoot, recovery time to a stated band like plus or minus one percent, and ringing, which gives the damping. In the frequency domain I measure the loop gain by injection to get crossover and phase and gain margin, and I look at closed-loop output impedance against the target impedance, delta V allowed over del

q0250.title: Feedforward capacitor in a buck
q0250.short: "A feedforward capacitor goes across the upper feedback resistor. At DC it does nothing, but at higher frequency it bypasses R1, giving a zero at 1 over 2 pi R1 Cff and a pole at 1 over 2 pi R1-parallel-R2 times Cff. Between them it adds phase lead, up to about 38 degrees for a 3.3 V output from 0.8 V reference, which improves phase margin and speeds up transient response. I'd use it with ceramic-only outputs that ha

q0251.title: Buck control topologies compared
q0251.short: "I group buck control by when the controller decides to switch. Voltage mode compares an error amplifier output to a fixed ramp: simple and quiet, but a second-order plant needs type III compensation. Current mode adds an inner inductor-current loop, which makes the plant first-order, rejects line changes and gives cycle-by-cycle current limit, but needs slope compensation and is noise-sensitive. Ripple-based schemes

q0252.title: Voltage mode vs current mode control
q0252.short: "Voltage mode has one loop: the error amplifier output is compared to a fixed ramp to set duty, and the plant is the full second-order LC, so it needs type III compensation. Current mode adds an inner loop on the inductor current: the outer loop sets a current command and the switch turns off when the inductor current reaches it. The inductor then looks like a current source, so the plant is first-order, compensation

q0253.title: Subharmonic oscillation explained
q0253.short: "Subharmonic oscillation is a cycle-by-cycle instability in fixed-frequency peak current-mode control. If the inductor current starts a cycle slightly high, it hits the peak threshold sooner, the on-time is shorter, the off-time is longer, and the current falls more, so the next cycle's error has the opposite sign and is multiplied by m2 over m1, which is D over one minus D. Below 50 percent duty that shrinks, above

q0254.title: Peak current mode below and above 50% duty
q0254.short: "In peak current mode a disturbance, like noise tripping the comparator early or a load step, shows up as a current error that flips sign each cycle and is multiplied by D over one minus D. Below 50 percent that's less than one, so the error dies out and noise only adds a bit of jitter. Above 50 percent it's greater than one, so the error grows every cycle, giving alternating long and short pulses at half the switchi

q0255.title: Slope compensation and when it's needed
q0255.short: "Slope compensation is an artificial ramp added to the sensed inductor current in fixed-frequency peak current-mode control. Without it, an error in the inductor current is multiplied by D over one minus D every cycle, so above 50 percent duty it grows into subharmonic oscillation. With a ramp of slope m a the multiplier becomes minus m2 minus m a over m1 plus m a, so a ramp of at least half the inductor's down-slope

q0256.title: Buck IC: integrated vs external parts
q0256.short: "The control brain is inside the IC: reference, error amp, oscillator, PWM comparator, protection, soft start and gate drivers. For small and medium currents the two power FETs are inside too. What stays external is energy storage and anything that needs tolerance: the inductor, input and output capacitors, the bootstrap cap, and the feedback divider on adjustable parts. Compensation is internal on easy-to-use parts

q0257.title: How to select a buck converter IC
q0257.short: "I start with requirements: input range including transients, output voltage and current, ripple, efficiency, size, quiescent current. Then I filter by input voltage with margin, current rating and current limit, and check the duty cycle against the IC's minimum on-time at my chosen frequency. I estimate losses and junction temperature, then look at control mode, light-load behaviour, protections, package and cost. I

q0258.title: Spec the buck inductor and capacitors
q0258.short: "I size the inductor at maximum input for a 20 to 40% ripple current, L = V{OUT}(1-D)/(f{SW}\Delta I), and make sure its saturation current clears the IC's current limit. The output cap has to satisfy ripple and the load transient, using effective capacitance after DC-bias derating, and fit the loop's allowed range. The input cap is sized for RMS current, I{OUT}\sqrt{D(1-D)}, and voltage ripple, with ceramics at the

q0259.title: Inductor saturation current and DCR vs ACR
q0259.short: "Saturation current matters because when the core saturates the inductance collapses, the current slope V/L shoots up, and you overshoot the IC's current limit, stress the FETs and can ratchet in a short. So I pick I{sat} above the IC's maximum current limit, derated for temperature, not just load plus half ripple. DCR is the copper resistance that sets full-load conduction loss. ACR is the effective resistance at th

q0260.title: What sets minimum and maximum L and C
q0260.short: "Minimum L is set by ripple, peak current against the current limit, staying in CCM at light load, and slope compensation on peak-current-mode parts. Maximum L is set by transient slew, since current can only change at V/L, by the LC corner limiting loop bandwidth, and by saturation and DCR in a real part. Minimum C comes from ripple, load-step droop and the compensation's required range. Maximum C comes from soft-st

q0261.title: How output L and C affect stability
q0261.short: "The output LC is a second-order plant with a double pole at 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) and up to 180° of phase lag, so it eats phase margin. Bigger L or C moves the pole down and forces a lower crossover or different compensation. ESR adds a zero at 1/(2\pi\,ESR\,C) that gives phase lead, but ceramics have almost none. Light load raises the Q of the peak, so it's the worst case. Current-mode control removes the second pole,

q0262.title: Sensing buck output voltage and current
q0262.short: "Output voltage is sensed with a resistor divider into the feedback pin, which the error amp compares with an internal reference: V{OUT} = V{REF}(1+R1/R2). Current is sensed in one of four ways: a series sense resistor, the voltage across the FET's R{DS(on)}, an RC across the inductor that reproduces IL\cdot DCR, or a sense-FET that mirrors the switch current. They trade accuracy against loss, temperature drift and n

q0263.title: Design a buck converter
q0263.short: "I'd start with requirements: input range, output voltage and current, ripple, transient and efficiency. For 12 V to 3.3 V at 3 A I'd choose a synchronous current-mode buck around 500 kHz, with 6.8 µH for about 30% ripple and saturation above the IC's current limit, five 22 µF ceramics for output, ceramics plus a damping bulk cap at the input, and a divider with a 0.8 V reference. Then estimate loss, junction tempera

q0264.title: Simple circuit to switch and regulate a buck
q0264.short: "I divide the output to a feedback voltage and use an error amplifier against a reference to make a control voltage. A comparator compares that voltage to a sawtooth ramp, so duty is control voltage over ramp amplitude, and drives the switch through a gate driver. If the output rises, the error amp lowers the control voltage and the duty cycle falls. The even simpler option is a comparator with hysteresis that turns

q0265.title: Buck failure modes, detection and prevention
q0265.short: "By block: in the switches, shoot-through and switch-node overshoot, prevented with dead time and a tight hot loop; in the inductor, saturation, prevented by choosing I{sat} above the current limit; on shorts, current runaway handled by current limit with foldback and hiccup; on the input, hot-plug ringing to twice V{IN} and brown-outs, handled by damping, TVS and UVLO; on the output, overshoot and overvoltage handle

q0266.title: Debug a buck that isn't regulating
q0266.short: "I'd power it from a current-limited supply after checking for shorts, then work down the chain: V{IN} at the pins, EN and UVLO, internal rails, then the switch node to see whether it's switching. If it isn't, it's enable, UVLO or a fault latch. If it is, I check the FB pin against the reference: that tells me whether the divider is wrong or the converter is limited by current limit, saturation or the load. Noisy swi

q0267.title: Validating and characterizing a buck converter
q0267.short: "I'd test static, dynamic, protection, stress and corners. Static: accuracy, line and load regulation, efficiency and ripple across load and input voltage. Dynamic: load and line steps, and loop gain with an injection resistor and network analyzer to get crossover and phase margin at light and heavy load. Then start-up, soft-start and pre-bias, protections like current limit, short circuit, UVLO and thermal, stress o
terms: Loop gain ($T$), phase margin (PM), gain margin (GM)

q0268.title: How a buck converter ages
q0268.short: "The weak link is the electrolytic capacitor: electrolyte evaporates, so ESR rises and capacitance falls, and life halves for every 10 °C of heating. That raises ripple and droop and shifts the loop. Ceramics lose a few percent capacitance per decade of time and can crack. Inductors age through insulation and core heating; silicon and solder suffer thermal-cycling fatigue that raises thermal resistance and R{DS(on)}.

q0269.title: Buck performance over PVT
q0269.short: "Process is part-to-part spread: reference, oscillator, current limit, FET resistance, and L and C tolerance. Voltage is input range, output and load: at high input, duty is smallest, ripple and switching loss are highest and on-time is shortest. Temperature raises DCR and R{DS(on)} so efficiency falls when hot, ferrite saturates earlier, ceramic capacitance and electrolytic ESR shift. I'd find the worst corner for e

q0270.title: What a boost converter is
q0270.short: "A boost converter is a switching regulator whose output is higher than its input, built from an inductor, a switch, a diode and a capacitor. With the switch on, the inductor charges from the input. When it opens, the inductor current has to keep flowing, so the inductor voltage flips and adds on top of V{in}, pushing current through the diode into the output. Volt-second balance gives V{out} = V{in}/(1-D). Energy is

q0271.title: Boost converter operation cycle
q0271.short: "With the switch on, the inductor sits across V{in}, current ramps up at V{in}/L, the diode blocks, and the output capacitor feeds the load. When the switch turns off, the inductor current has to continue, so the switch node rises, the diode conducts, and the inductor delivers current into the output, now ramping down because the voltage across it is V{in}-V{out}. In steady state the up and down ramps match, giving V

q0272.title: Drawing a boost converter circuit
q0272.short: "Input on the left, inductor in series, then a switch node. From the switch node a MOSFET goes to ground, and a diode goes to the output with its anode on the switch node. The output has a capacitor to ground and the load. So it's source, inductor, diode, output, with the switch pulling the middle node to ground. I'd mark the switch node, the inductor current, the diode direction and ground, and mention the feedback

q0273.title: Boost converter applications
q0273.short: "Anywhere the source is below the rail you need. Single Li-ion cell to 5 V for power banks and speakers, two AAs to 3.3 V for microcontrollers, a battery to a high-voltage LED string, display and flash bias supplies. At higher power, a boost is the standard PFC front end, taking rectified mains to about 400 V, and solar MPPT stages use one too. The catch is that input current is I{out}/(1-D), so you have to design fo

q0274.title: Why boosts are less efficient than bucks
q0274.short: "Two things: current and the diode. In a boost the inductor and switch carry I{out}/(1-D), more than the load current, and conduction loss goes with current squared, so DCR and R{DS(on)} losses are bigger. In a non-synchronous boost the diode also carries the full load current at VF, which is about 8% of a 5 V, 1 A output. Add pulsed output current, higher switch-node voltage and duty-cycle limits. With synchronous r

q0275.title: Roles of boost diode, inductor, capacitor
q0275.short: "The inductor is the energy store: it charges while the switch is on and then forces its current into the output when the switch opens, which is what lifts the voltage. The diode is the one-way valve: it carries the inductor current to the output in the off-time and blocks in the on-time so the output capacitor isn't shorted to ground. The capacitor holds the output steady: it supplies the load during the on-time and

q0276.title: Boost inductor flyback voltage
q0276.short: "When the boost switch opens, the inductor current has to continue, so its voltage reverses and the switch node rises until the diode conducts. That clamps the node at V{out}+VF, so the flyback energy goes into the output instead of a spike. That is both how the boost steps up and what sets the switch voltage stress. If the current has no path, say an open diode or open load with no OVP, the voltage runs up as I\sqrt

q0277.title: LDO meaning and dropout advantage
q0277.short: "LDO means low-dropout regulator, a linear regulator that can keep regulating with only a small difference between input and output. Dropout is the minimum V{in}-V{out} it needs, like 200 mV at 500 mA for a MOSFET pass device, roughly load current times R{DS(on)}. Low dropout is useful because you can run from a battery close to the output voltage until it's nearly empty, and because efficiency is about V{out}/V{in},

q0278.title: How an LDO works
q0278.short: "It's a pass transistor in series with the load plus a feedback loop. A divider scales the output down to a feedback voltage, an error amplifier compares it with a reference and drives the pass transistor's gate. If the output sags, the amp turns the transistor on harder; if it rises, it backs off. In steady state the feedback equals the reference, so V{out}=V{ref}(1+R1/R2). The transistor is a variable resistor that

q0279.title: LDO as a variable series resistor
q0279.short: "A variable series resistor. The pass transistor drops V{in}-V{out} at the load current, so it looks like R=(V{in}-V{out})/I{out}, and the feedback loop keeps adjusting that value to hold the output constant. So the loss is I^2R=(V{in}-V{out})I{out} and the efficiency is V{out}/V{in}. In dropout it bottoms out at R{DS(on)}. At AC, the loop makes the output impedance look inductive over its bandwidth."

q0280.title: LDO trade-offs vs step-down regulators
q0280.short: "LDOs are simple, quiet and small, with fast transient response and no EMI, but their efficiency is V{out}/V{in} and the lost power is heat, so they only work at small headroom or low current. Buck converters are efficient at large step-downs and high currents but need an inductor, make switching noise and EMI, and cost more area. So: small headroom or sensitive analog, LDO; big headroom or high current, buck; and if

q0281.title: External parts an LDO needs
q0281.short: "An input capacitor close to the IN pin, an output capacitor close to the OUT pin with the value and ESR the datasheet requires because it's part of the loop, and for adjustable parts two feedback resistors. Optionally an enable connection, a pull-up on power-good, a noise-reduction or soft-start capacitor, a feed-forward cap, reverse-current protection, and copper for heat. I'd check ceramics for DC-bias derating."

q0282.title: Where LDO power loss goes
q0282.short: "It becomes heat in the pass transistor: (V{in}-V{out})\times I{out} plus V{in}IQ. 5 V to 3.3 V at 500 mA is 0.85 W. That heat flows through the package and PCB, raising the junction by P\times\theta{JA}, 51 °C at 60 °C/W. If it passes the limit, thermal shutdown kicks in. I reduce it by lowering headroom (pre-regulate with a buck, or drop some voltage in a series resistor), improving copper and airflow, or switching

q0283.title: LDO efficiency vs current and dropout
q0283.short: "Efficiency is V{out}I{out}/[V{in}(I{out}+IQ)], essentially V{out}/V{in} when the load is much bigger than IQ, so it's flat versus load current. Output current matters at light load, where IQ dominates, and at heavy load through dropout: V{DO}=I\,R{DS(on)} raises the minimum input, and at that minimum the best efficiency is V{out}/(V{out}+V{DO}). E.g. 3.3 V with 200 mV dropout gives 94%, but headroom of 1.7 V gives o

q0284.title: How a charge pump works
q0284.short: "A charge pump uses switches and capacitors, no inductor. In phase one a flying capacitor is charged to V{in}. In phase two it's re-wired in series with the input and dumps its charge into the output capacitor, so the output is about 2V{in}. Input current is roughly twice the output current, and the output droops with load like 2V{in}-I{out}R{out}, where R{out} depends on 1/(fC) and the switch resistance."

q0285.title: How a charge pump raises voltage
q0285.short: "It's series stacking. Charge a capacitor to V{in}, then in the next phase put its bottom plate on V{in}, so its top plate is at 2V{in}, and connect that to the output. Energy is conserved because the input supplies charge twice per cycle but the output only gets it once: input current is twice output current. More stages stack more clock swings, about (N+1)V{in}, at the price of more droop and diode drops."

q0286.title: Drawing a charge pump circuit
q0286.short: "Voltage doubler: flying capacitor in the middle. S1 connects its top plate to V{in} and S2 its bottom plate to ground in phase one, charging it to V{in}. In phase two S3 connects the bottom plate to V{in} and S4 connects the top plate to the output, so the output is 2V{in}. Output capacitor and load to ground. Non-overlapping clocks. The passive version uses two diodes and a clock-driven capacitor."

q0287.title: What charge pumps are used for
q0287.short: "Anywhere I need a voltage outside the supply at low current without an inductor: negative rails from a positive supply, RS-232 levels, white-LED backlight and flash drivers with 1x/1.5x/2x modes, gate drive above the rail, and on-chip high voltage for flash programming. They're small and quiet but limited to a few hundred milliamps with efficiency capped by the ratio. For amps or flexible ratios I'd use an inductive

q0288.title: Charge pump efficiency analysis
q0288.short: "Input current is n times output current, so ideal efficiency is V{out}/(nV{in}). Under load V{out}=nV{in}-I{out}R{out}, so conduction efficiency is 1-I{out}R{out}/(nV{in}), with R{out} from 1/(fC) and the switch resistance. Add gate-drive and quiescent overhead. A regulated pump wastes the excess ratio, so efficiency is V{reg}/(nV{in}), which is why parts hop between 1x, 1.5x, 2x."

q0289.title: Specifying charge pump capacitors
q0289.short: "Flying cap from the slow-switching resistance 1/(fC): pick it so that's no more than the switch-limited resistance, about 1 µF at 500 kHz. Output cap from ripple I/(2fC) plus ESR. Then spec effective capacitance after DC-bias derating, voltage rating 1.5x or more, low ESR, and RMS current: 2I{out} in the flying cap. Place close to the pins."

q0290.title: Battery chemistries and how to choose
q0290.short: "Primary, single-use: alkaline, zinc-carbon, lithium coin cells like a CR2032, lithium thionyl chloride. Rechargeable: lead-acid, NiCd, NiMH, and the lithium family: Li-ion, LiPo, LiFePO4. To choose I start from requirements: total energy in Wh, peak current, size and weight, temperature range, recharge or not, shelf life, cost and safety. Microamp sensor for ten years is a coin cell, a remote is alkaline, a phone or

q0291.title: How to characterize a battery
q0291.short: "I'd measure it like a device under test. Capacity: charge with CC/CV, rest, then constant-current discharge to cutoff and integrate current. Open-circuit voltage versus state of charge, with rests, for the fuel gauge. Internal resistance from a current pulse: the instant voltage step over the current. Then repeat across C-rates and temperatures, and measure self-discharge over weeks and capacity and resistance fade

q0292.title: Desirable battery characteristics
q0292.short: "Desirable: high energy density, so it's small and light for the runtime; low internal resistance, so it can deliver high current without sagging or heating; a flat, stable voltage; long cycle life and low self-discharge; wide temperature range; fast charging; safe under abuse; and low cost with the right form factor. They trade off: more energy usually means less power, life or safety, so which ones matter depends o

q0293.title: Battery specs to check when buying
q0293.short: "I'd start from my power budget to get required watt-hours with margin and the peak current. Then check the datasheet: nominal, full and cutoff voltage against my regulator; capacity and the rate and temperature it was measured at; continuous and pulse current; internal resistance; cycle life definition; self-discharge; temperature range; charge limits. Then practicals: dimensions with swelling margin, built-in prote

q0294.title: Measuring battery voltage and current
q0294.short: "Voltage goes in parallel, current in series. On the bench: a DMM across the terminals for voltage, and for current either break the circuit with the DMM in current mode, minding its burden voltage, or use a shunt and measure the voltage across it. In a product: a resistor divider into the ADC for voltage, since 4.2 V exceeds a 3.3 V ADC, and a milliohm shunt with a differential amplifier for current. Use Kelvin sens

q0295.title: What to monitor for battery safety
q0295.short: "Voltage, current and temperature, continuously, per cell. Overvoltage around 4.2 volts a cell and undervoltage around 3 volts. Overcurrent with a fast short-circuit trip. Temperature with an NTC: no charging when it's near freezing, and cut off when it's hot. On top of that, cell imbalance, resistance growth and swelling. If a limit is hit, open a MOSFET or contactor and stop the charger, and have a fuse as the back

q0296.title: Charging and discharging a battery safely
q0296.short: "Use a charger IC and CC/CV: check temperature (about 0 to 45 °C) and voltage first, pre-charge gently at around 0.1C if the cell is deeply discharged, then charge at constant current, like 0.5C, until 4.2 V with about 1% accuracy, then hold 4.2 V while current tapers, terminate at about C/10, and have a safety timer. For discharge, stay within rated current and cut off at about 3 V. Put protection (OV, UV, OC, short

q0297.title: Li-ion chemistry in consumer electronics
q0297.short: "Lithium-ion, packaged as lithium polymer pouch cells in phones and wearables, and as cylindrical cells like the 18650 in laptops and tools. The reasons: much higher energy density, two to three times NiMH and many times lead-acid; a 3.7 V cell so one cell can run the electronics; low self-discharge; no memory effect; good power and cycle life. The cost is a charger, protection circuit and safety care."

q0298.title: What LiPo stands for
q0298.short: "LiPo is lithium polymer, also lithium-ion polymer. It isn't a new chemistry: it's a lithium-ion cell where the electrolyte is held in a polymer gel instead of being a free liquid, which lets the cell be built as a flexible aluminum-laminate pouch instead of a rigid can. That gives thin, custom shapes. Voltage, 3.7 nominal and 4.2 full, and safety concerns are the same as lithium-ion, and the 'polymer' in consumer ce

q0299.title: LiPo trade-offs versus other batteries
q0299.short: "LiPo wins on form factor, weight and energy density, with low internal resistance for high current: it can be thin and any shape. The trade-offs: it's mechanically fragile with no hard can, it swells with age or abuse, it needs a protection circuit and careful charging like any lithium cell, cost per kWh is often higher than cylindrical cells, and cycle life and safety are worse than LiFePO4. Versus primary lithium

q0300.title: Other lithium chemistries and their trade-offs
q0300.short: "Lithium-ion is a family named by the cathode. LCO gives the most energy in a small cell but is the least stable, used in phones. NMC is the balanced workhorse for tools, e-bikes and EVs. NCA is higher energy still. LMO is cheap and high current but short-lived. LiFePO4 is 3.2 V, very safe and thousands of cycles, but lower energy and a flat curve. LTO is about 2.4 V, low energy, but charges extremely fast and lasts

q0301.title: LiPo aging and end of life
q0301.short: "No. LiPos wear out from both cycling and calendar time, losing capacity and gaining internal resistance. End of life is usually 80 percent capacity, a few hundred to a thousand cycles for LCO/NMC. Causes: the SEI layer growing on the anode, lithium plating from cold or fast charging, cathode degradation at high voltage, and electrolyte decomposition producing gas, which makes pouch cells swell. Heat, high state of c

q0302.title: LiPo cell materials
q0302.short: "Cathode: a lithium metal oxide like LCO or NMC with carbon and binder on aluminum foil. Anode: graphite on copper foil. A porous polyethylene or polypropylene separator in between, all soaked in lithium salt, usually LiPF6, in organic carbonate solvents, gelled in a polymer for LiPo. It's sealed in an aluminum-and-plastic laminate pouch with Al and Ni tabs, plus a small protection board. Aluminum goes on the cathode

q0303.title: Battery internal resistance
q0303.short: "Internal resistance is the series resistance inside the cell, so the terminal voltage is the open-circuit voltage minus I times R. It causes voltage sag, I-squared-R heating, and limits peak current and power. It isn't constant: it rises a lot in the cold, because ion transport and reaction kinetics slow down, it grows with aging as the SEI thickens, it rises at low state of charge, and it depends on frequency: a 1

q0304.title: Battery management system features
q0304.short: "A BMS is the electronics that keeps a pack safe, healthy and informative. It measures cell voltages, pack current and temperature; protects against overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent, short circuit and over-temperature by opening MOSFETs or contactors, with the fast ones in hardware; estimates state of charge and health; balances series cells, usually passively with bleed resistors; controls charging limits; and

q0305.title: LiPo cell voltage range and why
q0305.short: "A LiPo cell is 3.7 volts nominal, 4.2 volts fully charged, and about 3.0 volts empty. The cell voltage is the cathode potential minus the anode potential, so it tracks how much lithium is in each electrode. Above 4.2 you oxidize the electrolyte and plate lithium, and if you over-discharge well below about 2.5 volts you start dissolving the copper current collector. So the usable window is 3.0 to 4.2, storage is arou

q0306.title: Temperature effects on LiPo performance
q0306.short: "Cold makes a LiPo's internal resistance shoot up, roughly 2.5 times at 0 degrees C and 6 times at minus 20, so you get more voltage sag, an earlier cutoff and less usable capacity, which mostly recovers when it warms up. Charging in the cold is worse because lithium plates as metal instead of intercalating, which is permanent damage, so chargers block charging below about 0 degrees. Heat improves performance but spe

q0307.title: What to monitor in a LiPo circuit
q0307.short: "Three things: per-cell voltage, current in both directions, and temperature. Voltage keeps each cell in its roughly 3.0 to 4.2 V window, current from a shunt gives overcurrent protection and lets me coulomb-count, and an NTC on the cell enforces the charge and discharge temperature windows. From those I derive state of charge, state of health and cycle count. Each one has a threshold tied to an action, such as openi

q0308.title: Determining state of charge and why it's hard
q0308.short: "SoC can't be measured directly, only estimated. Voltage lookup uses the open-circuit voltage curve, but that curve is flat, about 6 mV per percent, and it sags by I R under load. Coulomb counting integrates current and works under load, but sensor offset accumulates, 10 mA on a 2 amp-hour cell is about 12 percent per day, and it needs a starting point and the correct capacity. So gauges fuse them with a Kalman filte

q0309.title: Why SoC accuracy matters
q0309.short: "SoC accuracy decides when you stop charging and discharging, so errors push cells out of the safe window or force you to carry reserve. A plus-minus 5 percent error costs about 10 percent of the battery you paid for, and on a 75 kilowatt-hour EV, 5 percent is about 3.75 kWh or more than 20 kilometres. It also drives runtime prediction and user trust. The level of accuracy you need depends on the application, since b

q0310.title: When SoC accuracy matters most
q0310.short: "Accuracy matters in proportion to the consequence of being wrong. It matters most in drones, medical devices, EVs and grid storage, where an error means a crash, a patient at risk, or real money in unused battery. It matters less in cheap or replaceable products like toys or remotes, where a voltage cutoff protects the cell. Technically, it also depends on load and where you are on the curve: voltage is fine near em

q0311.title: How battery capacity is measured
q0311.short: "You fully charge the cell, let it rest, then discharge it at a constant current to the cutoff voltage and integrate current over time: capacity in amp-hours is the sum of current times time step. It's done with a battery cycler or electronic load, ideally in a temperature chamber. Capacity depends on conditions, so you state them: the rated value is usually at about C over 5 and room temperature. Higher current or c

q0312.title: Determining LiPo state of health
q0312.short: "I'd check three things. Capacity: charge fully, discharge slowly to cutoff, and compare to rated; state of health is the ratio, and about 80 percent is a typical end-of-life line. Internal resistance: apply a current pulse and take the voltage drop over the current, or use a 1 kHz meter; it rises with age and limits power. Then self-discharge, cell-to-cell mismatch and physical signs like swelling. In a product, a f

q0313.title: Why charging and monitoring ICs matter
q0313.short: "Lithium cells need tight, closed-loop control, and ICs give that safely. A charger IC runs the whole profile: precharge, constant current, constant voltage at 4.2 V within about one percent, termination, plus NTC temperature checks and a safety timer. A protection IC with back-to-back FETs cuts off overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent and short circuits in microseconds to milliseconds without firmware. A fuel gaug

q0314.title: Cell balancing: why, when, what if missing
q0314.short: "Balancing keeps every cell in a series pack at the same state of charge. Series cells carry the same current but differ in capacity, self-discharge and resistance, so they drift apart. Then the first cell to hit 4.2 volts ends the charge and the first to hit cutoff ends the discharge, so capacity is limited by the weakest cell, and a strong cell can be overcharged while the pack total looks fine. Passive balancing b

q0315.title: What a LiPo C rating means
q0315.short: "The C rating is the maximum current as a multiple of the battery's capacity. 1C is the current that would empty it in an hour, so a 2200 milliamp-hour 30C pack can deliver 30 times 2.2, or 66 amps, and runs flat in two minutes. It's really a limit set by internal resistance and heat: at 66 amps the cell sags and dissipates tens of watts. Ratings usually come as continuous and burst, they aren't standardized, so I si

q0316.title: LiPo discharge and charge curves
q0316.short: "Discharge: a full cell is 4.2 V, drops by I times R when loaded, then follows a long plateau around 3.6 to 3.8 V, with a knee near 3.4 and a cliff at the 3.0 V cutoff. More current or cold slides it down and ends it sooner. Charge is constant current until the cell hits 4.2 V, with the voltage rising, then constant voltage at 4.2 V while the current decays exponentially, terminating at about C over 20. In a model, 1

q0317.title: When LiPos charge fastest
q0317.short: "They charge fastest during the constant-current phase, from low state of charge to about 80 or 85 percent, where the charger delivers its full current and the cell accepts it. After the voltage hits 4.2 volts the charger holds it and the current decays, so the last 15 percent is slow: in my model it's 26 minutes at 1C after 51 minutes for the first 85 percent. Warm, mid-SoC cells with low resistance are fastest; col

q0318.title: Safe LiPo charging rate limits
q0318.short: "For a standard LiPo the safe charge rate is about 0.5C to 1C, so 1 to 2 amps for a 2 amp-hour cell. Some cells are rated for 2C or more, but the datasheet is the limit. The constraints are lithium plating, which gets worse at low temperature and high state of charge, and I squared R heating. Faster has diminishing returns, since 2C only saves about 30 percent of total time versus 1C, so I charge at 1C or below withi

q0319.title: What happens when a LiPo is overcharged
q0319.short: "Overcharging is pushing a cell above 4.2 volts or past what the anode can hold. A little over mostly shortens life. Further over, the electrolyte oxidizes and makes gas so the pouch swells, and extra lithium plates as metal on the anode, which can grow dendrites. The energy has nowhere to go but heat, which speeds up the reactions, and eventually the separator melts, the cell shorts and thermal runaway starts. It's

q0320.title: How to charge a LiPo: steps and precautions
q0320.short: "First inspect the pack and don't charge anything swollen or damaged. Set the right chemistry, cell count and a current of 0.5 to 1C, connect the balance lead for series packs, and check the temperature is between about 0 and 45 degrees. A deeply discharged cell gets a gentle precharge. Then constant current until 4.2 volts per cell, constant voltage with the current tapering to about C over 10 to C over 20, then ter

q0321.title: Constant-current and constant-voltage charge phases
q0321.short: "Constant current first: the charger regulates the current, say 1C, and the cell voltage climbs because terminal voltage equals open-circuit voltage plus I times R, until it reaches 4.2 volts. Then constant voltage: it holds 4.2 volts and the current decays exponentially as the open-circuit voltage approaches 4.2, with a time constant of about R Q over the OCV slope. It ends when the current drops to about C over 20

q0322.title: What to monitor while charging a LiPo
q0322.short: "Per-cell voltage, current, temperature and time. Each cell must stay at or below 4.2 volts and I watch the spread in a series pack. Current should hold at the set value in CC, then taper in CV until about C over 20 to C over 10, where I terminate. Temperature from an NTC, within about 0 to 45 degrees and without a fast rise. And a safety timer as a backstop. A healthy charge is flat current, voltage pinned at 4.2, c

q0323.title: Design a LiPo charge/discharge circuit
q0323.short: "I'd gather requirements, then use a charger IC with power path from USB, a battery with a protection IC and dual MOSFETs, and a buck-boost or LDO to the load, plus an NTC and optionally a fuel gauge. For a 2 amp-hour cell on USB, charge at 500 milliamps; a resistor programs it, and a linear charger dissipates about 0.65 watts. Because the cell swings 3.0 to 4.2 volts, a 3.3 volt rail wants a buck-boost; an LDO works

q0324.title: LiPo storage charge
q0324.short: "Storage charge is the level you leave a LiPo at when it's not in use, about 3.8 volts per cell, roughly 50 percent. Full charge accelerates calendar aging and gas, especially when warm, and leaves more stored energy if something fails. Empty is worse in a different way: self-discharge and parasitic drain can pull the cell below about 2.5 to 3 volts into over-discharge, which damages the anode and, deep enough, disso

q0325.title: Why charging and monitoring ICs matter
q0325.short: "A lithium cell has a very tight safe window: about 4.2 V per cell within a percent or so, limited current, and a temperature range for charging. A charger IC enforces that automatically with CC/CV control, precharge for deep-discharged cells, termination, a safety timer and NTC temperature checks. A monitor or BMS IC adds over-voltage, under-voltage, over-current and short-circuit cutoff and reports state of charge.

q0326.title: Balance charging and when it is needed
q0326.short: "Balance charging makes every cell in a series pack finish at the same voltage, not just the pack total. Series cells get the same current but differ in capacity and starting charge, so one hits 4.2 V first. The charger uses a tap on each cell to see that, then bleeds the full cell through a resistor, or moves charge to weaker cells, while the rest catch up. You need it for any pack of two or more series cells, espec

q0327.title: Dangers of lithium batteries and prevention
q0327.short: "The main danger is thermal runaway. Lithium cells have a flammable electrolyte and a lot of stored energy, and abuse like overcharge, overdischarge, shorting, puncture or heat makes them self-heat until they vent and burn, sometimes with toxic gas. You prevent it in layers: cell-level separator and vent, a protection IC with voltage, current and temperature cutoffs plus a fuse, a proper CC/CV charger with a temperat

q0328.title: Handling and disposing of LiPos
q0328.short: "LiPos are soft pouch cells holding a lot of energy and a flammable electrolyte, so puncture, crush, heat or shorted terminals can start an internal short and thermal runaway, even hours later. So I store them insulated, at a partial charge, cool, in a fire-safe bag, charge them only with the right charger and never unattended, and retire swollen ones. At end of life they go to battery recycling, with the terminals t

q0329.title: Why puncturing a LiPo is dangerous
q0329.short: "A LiPo is a thin stack of electrodes separated by a micron-scale separator in a soft foil pouch. A puncture bridges the electrodes, creating an internal short: the cell's energy dumps through a tiny spot, heating it fast, melting the separator and starting thermal runaway. Air and moisture entering make it worse. No protection circuit or fuse can help because the short is inside the cell, and damage can be delayed,

q0330.title: LiPo overcharge and overdischarge damage
q0330.short: "Overcharging above about 4.2 volts pulls too much lithium out of the cathode, plates lithium on the anode and oxidizes the electrolyte, so you get gas, swelling, heat and potentially thermal runaway. Overdischarging below about 3 volts breaks down the anode's protective layer and can dissolve the copper collector, which then forms dendrites on recharge and risks an internal short. So overcharge is the immediate haza

q0331.title: Short-circuiting a LiPo
q0331.short: "A LiPo has milliohm-level internal resistance, so a short is limited almost only by that: one 4.2 V cell at 50 milliohms gives about 84 amps, and a 4S hobby pack with 20 milliohms gives around 840. That puts hundreds of watts to kilowatts of I^2R into the cell and wiring, heating it by many degrees per second toward venting and thermal runaway. So you need layered protection: a properly rated fuse, a fast short-circ

q0332.title: Why heat is a big concern for LiPos
q0332.short: "Heat is a concern for three reasons. Current through the cell's internal resistance makes I squared R heat inside a small sealed package. Higher temperature speeds up the side reactions that age the cell, roughly doubling degradation per 10 degrees as a rule of thumb. And above about 80 to 130 degrees the cell's decomposition reactions are exothermic, so heat makes more heat and you get thermal runaway. So we limit

q0333.title: What motors and solenoids are, and uses
q0333.short: "A motor converts electrical energy into rotation and a solenoid converts it into a short linear push or pull, both using a coil that creates a magnetic field. A solenoid is a coil with a movable plunger and a spring, good for locks, valves and relays. A motor has coils on a rotor in a magnetic field, so current produces torque, used for fans, pumps, wheels and drones. Electrically both are inductive loads, a resista

q0334.title: How motors and solenoids work
q0334.short: "Both use the fact that current makes a magnetic field and a field pushes on current. A solenoid is a coil with an iron plunger that the field pulls in to close the air gap, with a spring to return it; force grows with turns times current and gets much stronger as the gap shrinks. A brushed motor has a rotor coil in a magnet's field, so F equals BIL on each side gives torque proportional to current, and the commutato

q0335.title: Why coils are used in motors and solenoids
q0335.short: "A coil multiplies the magnetic effect of the current: each turn carries the same current and their fields add in the same direction inside the coil, so field and force scale with ampere-turns NI, and iron inside makes it far stronger.
