The same configuration is an inductor with L proportional to N squared, so these loads store energy and resist current changes. For fixed copper and ampere-turns, more turns means less

q0336.title: When a motor or solenoid draws most current
q0336.short: "A motor draws the most current when it's stalled or just starting, because there's no back-EMF to oppose the supply: I equals V minus Ke omega over R, so at zero speed it's V over R, say 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm, versus half an amp at free-running speed. Inductance only delays it by a few milliseconds. The same goes for a jammed or heavily loaded motor. A DC solenoid draws its maximum, V over R, at steady stat

q0337.title: When a motor or solenoid draws least current
q0337.short: "For a motor, the steady-state minimum is at no load and top speed: the back-EMF almost equals the supply, so the current is just what's needed to overcome friction, about half an amp versus 12 amps at stall in my example. The absolute minimum is the instant of turn-on, when the inductor makes the current start at zero. If the shaft is driven faster than no-load speed, the current goes negative: regeneration. For a s

q0338.title: Steady state at minimum and maximum current
q0338.short: "At steady state the inductor drops nothing, so the winding is its resistance plus back-EMF. At maximum current the motor is stalled: no back-EMF, I equals V over R, maximum torque, and all the input power V squared over R, 144 watts in my 12 V, 1 ohm example, becomes winding heat, so it burns out in seconds. At minimum current it's free-running: back-EMF nearly equals the supply, current is just friction, about half

q0339.title: Motors and solenoids as electrical loads
q0339.short: "Motors and solenoids are inductive loads: a coil resistance in series with an inductance, plus for a motor a back-EMF that depends on speed. The inductance means the current can't change instantly, so it ramps with L over R and, when you switch off, the stored energy causes a voltage spike across the switch, so you need a flyback diode or snubber. In AC the current lags the voltage, giving a power factor below one.

q0340.title: Flyback voltage
q0340.short: "Flyback voltage is the spike you get when you interrupt current in an inductive load. Since v equals L di dt, when the switch opens the coil forces its current to keep flowing and generates whatever reverse voltage it takes, limited only by parasitic capacitance or breakdown, so it can destroy the switch. The fix is a flyback diode across the coil to give the current a path, clamping the switch to the supply plus 0.

q0341.title: What back EMF is
q0341.short: "Back-EMF is the voltage a spinning motor generates: a coil moving in a magnetic field induces a voltage proportional to speed, e equals Ke omega, and by Lenz's law it opposes the supply. So the current is V minus back-EMF over R: huge at stall, small at speed, and voltage essentially sets speed while current sets torque. It also gives free speed information for sensorless control and is what makes regenerative braki

q0342.title: 12 V across a 1 ohm coil: 12 A?
q0342.short: "Not instantly, and for a motor usually not at all. Twelve amps is V over R, the limit. The coil is an inductor, so the current rises as 12 times one minus e to the minus t over tau, with tau equal to L over R. A DC solenoid reaches 12 amps in steady state after about five time constants, and that's 144 watts, so it will burn out. A motor draws 12 amps only at stall: spinning, back-EMF cuts it to maybe half an amp. I

q0343.title: What inrush current is
q0343.short: "Inrush current is the surge a load draws when first switched on, above its steady running current. For a motor it's because at standstill there's no back-EMF, so only the winding resistance limits the current, roughly V over R, 12 amps for a 12 volt, 1 ohm motor versus maybe 5 amps running; it lasts until the rotor speeds up. AC solenoids also have it, while the plunger is open. It sags supplies and trips protection

q0344.title: Every case where motors and solenoids peak
q0344.short: "A motor's current is V minus Ke omega over R, so it peaks when speed is low relative to the supply: startup, stall, jams and heavy load, V over R, so 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm. The biggest normal case is reversing the supply while spinning, plugging, where back-EMF adds to the supply, so about 2V over R, 23.5 amps. Shoot-through in a bridge is bigger still. A DC solenoid peaks at V over R in steady state, or hi

q0345.title: Inductor continuity vs motor inrush
q0345.short: "Inductors don't limit how large the current gets, only how fast it changes: v = L\,di/dt. So the current starts at zero and ramps at V/L. A motor winding has tiny L, so that's thousands of amps per second. At standstill there's no back-EMF, so the final current is just V/R, many times the running current. It rises with a time constant L/R of about a millisecond, far faster than the rotor can speed up and build back-

q0346.title: Motor vs generator
q0346.short: "A motor and a generator are the same machine with the energy flowing in opposite directions. A motor converts electrical power to mechanical: current in the field makes torque. A generator converts mechanical to electrical: moving conductors in a field make a voltage. Inside every running motor there's also a back-EMF Ke\omega. If you drive the shaft faster than V/Ke, that back-EMF exceeds the supply, the current re

q0347.title: Motor vs solenoid
q0347.short: "Both are coils that turn current into mechanical force and both are inductive loads that need flyback protection. A motor makes continuous rotation with torque proportional to current and a back-EMF that limits its current as it speeds up. A solenoid pulls an iron plunger in over a short linear stroke: force goes roughly as current squared and rises sharply as the gap closes. Motors for continuous motion, solenoids

q0348.title: Parts of a brushed motor, rotating vs static
q0348.short: "A brushed DC motor has a stator that doesn't move: the housing, the permanent magnets or field windings, the end caps, the brush holders and the brushes. The rotor, or armature, spins: the shaft, laminated iron core, copper windings and the commutator. Bearings let the shaft turn. The brushes stay still and press on the rotating commutator to feed current into the windings and reverse it each half turn, so torque st

q0349.title: Types of motors and their uses
q0349.short: "Brushed DC: simple, cheap, voltage sets speed, good for toys, pumps and automotive actuators. Brushless DC: electronic commutation, efficient and long-lived, used in drones, fans, drives and EVs. Steppers move in discrete steps with holding torque, so they're used for open-loop positioning such as 3D printers. AC induction motors run off mains and are rugged, used in appliances and industry. Servos are any motor plu

q0350.title: What are linear motors?
q0350.short: "A linear motor is a rotary motor unrolled flat: a magnet track and a coil carrier, the forcer, that moves along it. Force is proportional to current, F = KfI, and the moving coil generates a back-EMF Kev, same as a rotary motor. The big win is direct drive: no lead screw, belt or gearbox, so no backlash and very high speed and precision. The downsides are cost, heat, limited force without gearing, strong magnet attr

q0351.title: Phone vibration motors (ERM and LRA)
q0351.short: "Two kinds. ERMs are tiny brushed DC motors with an off-centre weight; the force is m e\omega^2, so strength and frequency rise together with voltage, and they're a bit slow to spin up. LRAs are voice-coil actuators: a mass on a spring driven by an AC signal at its resonance, around 150 to 250 hertz. They respond in milliseconds, so they give crisp, programmable haptics, and amplitude is independent of frequency. Mos

q0352.title: Motor torque-speed, current and voltage curves
q0352.short: "With V = IR + Ke\omega and T = KtI, torque falls linearly with speed from stall torque KtV/R at zero rpm to zero at the no-load speed V/Ke. Current is proportional to torque, so it's highest at stall and lowest at no-load. Back-EMF rises with speed, so the remaining voltage across the winding, IR, shrinks. Peak power is at half stall torque and half no-load speed, but efficiency peaks at low torque near no-load spee

q0353.title: Torque is current, speed is voltage
q0353.short: "Torque goes with current and speed goes with voltage. The Lorentz force on the winding gives T = KtI, so more current means more torque; that's why stall, the highest torque, is also the highest current, V/R. Spinning generates a back-EMF Ke\omega that opposes the supply, so \omega \approx (V - IR)/Ke: speed tracks voltage, minus a load-dependent drop. Kt and Ke are the same number in SI units, by energy conservatio

q0354.title: How to spec a brushed motor
q0354.short: "I work from the load backwards. Get the output torque and speed, continuous and peak, plus duty cycle, supply voltage, size and life. Pick a gear ratio that sets motor torque as load torque over N\eta and motor speed as N times load speed. Then check the motor: continuous torque under its rated continuous value, peak under stall, and enough voltage for back-EMF plus IR with margin. Current is torque over Kt, which s

q0355.title: Motor noise and how to reduce it
q0355.short: "Motor noise has electrical and acoustic parts. Electrically, brush commutation interrupts inductive coil current, so L\,di/dt spikes and arcs produce broadband noise that couples onto the leads and the supply, along with PWM edges and start-up current steps. I'd suppress at the source with a 100 nF ceramic across the terminals plus small capacitors to the case, add ferrite beads to make an LC filter, then use decoup

q0356.title: What is arcing?
q0356.short: "Arcing is a discharge through ionised gas between two conductors, hot plasma that conducts at a low voltage once it's lit. It starts either from breakdown of a gap by high voltage, or, the common case, when you interrupt current in an inductor: v = L\,di/dt drives the opening gap's voltage up until air breaks down, and DC has no zero crossing to put it out. It erodes contacts and brushes, makes EMI, and can start fi

q0357.title: What are brushes?
q0357.short: "Brushes are the stationary conductive contacts, usually carbon, spring-pressed against the commutator on the rotor. They feed current from the motor terminals into the spinning windings, and together with the commutator's segments they reverse the current in each coil at the right angle, so the torque stays in one direction. The trade-off is that they wear, drop about a volt, create friction and spark slightly, whic

q0358.title: What brushes are made of
q0358.short: "Most brushes are carbon-graphite. Graphite is conductive and a natural solid lubricant, so it slides with low friction and leaves a stable film on the copper commutator, and the slightly resistive carbon helps commutation. Variants: electrographite for better performance, metal-graphite with copper or silver for lower drop and higher current in low-voltage motors, and precious-metal fingers in tiny motors. It's a tr

q0359.title: Concerns about brushes
q0359.short: "The concerns are wear and finite life, electrical drop and loss, arcing noise, and speed and current limits. Brushes wear and make dust, typically thousands of hours. They drop about a volt each, which matters at low voltage. Commutation of an inductive coil causes sparks and EMI. Too much current density overheats them, and at high speed they bounce. Humidity, altitude and contamination change their behaviour and s

q0360.title: Why brushes wear out
q0360.short: "Brushes wear from three things at once. Mechanical: friction against the moving commutator removes material in proportion to spring force times sliding distance. Electrical: commutation sparks erode the contact, and current heats the contact spots. Chemical and environmental: graphite needs a film and humidity to lubricate, so dry air, altitude, oil or silicone make it wear fast. A rough or out-of-round commutator m

q0361.title: Replace the brushes or the motor?
q0361.short: "It depends on serviceability, condition and cost. If the motor has accessible brush holders and a standard kit, and the commutator is round with a good film, the bearings and windings are fine, then replacing the worn brushes restores it cheaply. If the commutator is grooved, burnt or below minimum size, or windings or bearings are failing, or the motor is a sealed consumable, replace the motor. Compare repair cost

q0362.title: How brushes stay in contact
q0362.short: "Springs push the brushes onto the commutator. Each brush slides in a holder box, and a spring behind it, a coil spring, a constant-force strip spring, or a torsion arm, keeps a set pressure, around 1.5 to 2.5 psi for carbon, as the brush wears down. A flexible copper pigtail carries the current so the spring doesn't. In small motors the brush is itself a springy metal finger. Too little force means bounce and sparki

q0363.title: How BLDC motors work
q0363.short: "A BLDC motor has permanent magnets on the rotor and three coils on the stator, so there's no brush or commutator. An electronic inverter energises two of the three phases at a time to create a stator field, and steps to the next pair every 60 electrical degrees so the rotor keeps chasing the field. It knows the rotor position from Hall sensors or from back-EMF. So it's really a three-phase synchronous motor, but bec

q0364.title: Controlling BLDC motors
q0364.short: "I think in three layers. Commutation chooses the active phases from rotor position, using Hall sensors, back-EMF zero-crossings or an encoder. Modulation uses PWM on a three-phase bridge to set the voltage. On top are a current loop and a speed loop. The simple version is six-step with Hall sensors, which is cheap but has torque ripple; the high-performance version is field-oriented control, which regulates the d an

q0365.title: BLDC from a microcontroller
q0365.short: "I can't drive a BLDC from GPIO. I need a three-phase bridge of six N-MOSFETs, a gate driver to level-shift and supply gate current, and an MCU with complementary PWM and dead-time to command it. Feedback comes from Hall sensors or back-EMF, a shunt plus amplifier for current, and a divider for bus voltage. I'd add a hardware overcurrent trip into the timer's break input, a bulk DC-link capacitor, and local supplies.

q0366.title: Brushless vs brushed advantages
q0366.short: "Brushed motors commutate mechanically; brushless motors commutate electronically, and nearly every advantage follows from that. No brushes means no wear, so longer life, no arcing, so less EMI and no sparks, and no brush friction or voltage drop, so higher efficiency. The winding sits on the stator against the housing, so it cools better and handles more continuous power, and top speed isn't limited by the commutato

q0367.title: Motor poles and performance
q0367.short: "Poles are the permanent-magnet poles on the rotor; p pole pairs means p electrical cycles per revolution, so fe = p\cdot\text{rpm}/60. More poles gives more torque at lower speed for the same size, thinner back-iron, finer Hall resolution and, with the right slot count, less cogging. The cost is a higher electrical frequency for the same rpm, which raises iron and switching losses and demands a faster controller. Fe

q0368.title: Specifying a BLDC motor
q0368.short: "I work backwards from the load: continuous and peak torque, speed, duty and supply voltage. Power is T\omega. I choose Kt so that the current at continuous torque is within the continuous rating and the back-EMF plus IR at top speed is under about 85% of the supply. Then I check heating, I^2R times thermal resistance, and peak torque against the current limit. Finally I check sensors, pole count and frequency, size,

q0369.title: What is an ESC
q0369.short: "An ESC is the electronics that sits between a battery and a motor and converts a throttle command into power for the motor. For a brushless motor it's a three-phase inverter, six MOSFETs plus a microcontroller, that senses rotor position, usually from back-EMF, commutates the phases in sequence and PWMs them to set speed. It also adds protection like current limiting and undervoltage cutoff, often a 5 V BEC, and tel

q0370.title: Why brushless motors need ESCs
q0370.short: "Because a brushless motor has no commutator. In a brushed motor the brushes switch the coil current automatically as the rotor turns. With permanent magnets on the rotor and fixed coils, something electronic has to do that switching, and that's the ESC. Plain DC just creates a fixed field, so the rotor locks to it and draws huge current. The ESC reads rotor position, steps the phase currents, sets speed with PWM, li

q0371.title: ESC vs single-phase motor driver
q0371.short: "A single-phase driver is an H-bridge: it gives a brushed motor a direction and a PWM duty, and the commutator does the smart part mechanically. An ESC drives three phases with six switches and must do the commutation itself, so it needs rotor position from Hall sensors or back-EMF, and firmware for startup and sequencing. ESCs also add a throttle protocol, braking and regeneration, current and thermal protection, a

q0372.title: ESC components and subsystems
q0372.short: "An ESC has four groups of parts. The power path: input connector, DC-link capacitors and a three-phase bridge of six MOSFETs. The control path: a microcontroller running commutation, with a gate driver, bootstrap and dead-time between it and the FETs. The sensing: back-EMF dividers into comparators or ADC, a shunt for current, and voltage and temperature sensors. And the support: a BEC and logic regulators, throttle

q0373.title: Interfacing with ESCs
q0373.short: "The ESC takes battery power, a signal-plus-ground from the controller, and optionally returns telemetry; three wires go to the motor. The command is either an analog RC pulse of 1 to 2 ms, Oneshot or Multishot for faster updates, or digital DShot, which sends a 16-bit packet with 11-bit throttle and a CRC at 150 to 1200 kbit/s. Bigger systems use UART or CAN. The controller is usually a flight controller or MCU with

q0374.title: Design an ESC
q0374.short: "I'd clarify the spec first: say 4S, 30 A continuous, 60 A burst, DShot input, 5 V BEC. Architecture: sensorless six-step on a small MCU, three half-bridges of 40 V low-R{ds(on)} MOSFETs, a three-phase gate driver with bootstrap and dead-time, back-EMF dividers, a low-side shunt and a buck BEC. Sizing: about 7 W total loss at 30 A, bus capacitors for 15 A ripple, 1 µF bootstrap. Then firmware for startup and protecti

q0375.title: Specifying an ESC
q0375.short: "I start from the battery and motor. Voltage: the ESC must be rated for the pack's maximum, 16.8 V for 4S, with margin. Current: take the motor's measured full-throttle current on the real prop, and choose an ESC with continuous rating 25 to 50% above it, checking burst duration. Then compatibility: protocol like DShot, firmware that supports the motor's electrical rpm, BEC if needed, protections, telemetry. Finally

q0376.title: What is a stepper motor
q0376.short: "A stepper is a brushless motor that moves in fixed angular steps, one per pulse to the driver, so you can position it by counting pulses, usually open loop. The common hybrid type has two phases and 50 rotor teeth, giving 1.8 degrees per step, 200 per revolution. It has high holding torque at standstill, but torque falls with speed and it can lose steps if overloaded. Windings are bipolar or unipolar."

q0377.title: How a stepper motor works
q0377.short: "A stepper moves by walking a magnetic field in small jumps. Energise a coil and the rotor, a magnet or toothed iron, aligns with it; switch to the next coil and the equilibrium moves one step, so the rotor follows. In a 2-phase, 50-tooth motor, four steps make one electrical cycle, 7.2 degrees, each step 1.8. Driving the phases as sine and cosine gives microsteps. It runs open loop by counting pulses, and the driver

q0378.title: Stepper motor applications
q0378.short: "Steppers are used where I want accurate positioning at low to moderate speed without feedback: 3D printers and CNC axes, printers and scanners, camera focus mechanisms, syringe pumps, valves and dampers, telescope mounts and gauge needles. They fit because position equals step count, they hold torque at standstill, they give high low-speed torque without a gearbox, and they're cheap with simple drivers. They're a po

q0379.title: Stepper advantages over other motors
q0379.short: "A stepper's big advantages are open-loop positioning without an encoder or tuning, full holding torque at standstill, high torque at low speed so it can drive loads directly, no brushes, and low cost with a simple step/dir interface; error also doesn't accumulate. The downsides are torque falling with speed, low efficiency and heat because it always draws full current, resonance, and silent missed steps. So steppers

q0380.title: Stepper from a microcontroller
q0380.short: "I use a step/direction driver such as an A4988, DRV8825 or TMC2209: it contains the dual H-bridge, current chopper and microstep sequencer. The microcontroller sends STEP pulses, a DIR level, an enable and microstep-select lines. I add a separate motor supply well above the rated voltage, say 24 V, with a bulk capacitor at the driver, a common ground, and a current limit set via VREF. In firmware I generate steps wi

q0381.title: Specifying a stepper motor
q0381.short: "I work backwards from the load: compute the torque including friction, gravity and acceleration, for example T=FL/(2\pi\eta) for a lead screw, and the step rate needed for the speed. Then I pick a motor whose pull-out torque at that speed and my supply voltage is at least 1.5 to 2× the requirement, not just a big holding torque. I check inertia ratio, winding inductance versus speed, rated current and heating at hol

q0382.title: How steppers hold position
q0382.short: "A stepper holds position by magnetic alignment. With the right coils energised with steady current, the rotor sits in a stable equilibrium, and any displacement creates a restoring torque like a spring, roughly Th\sin(Nr\Delta\theta), so no feedback is needed. Holding torque is the peak of that restoring torque; beyond it the rotor slips by whole electrical cycles. The cost is continuous current and heat; reducing t

q0383.title: What is a servo motor?
q0383.short: "A servo motor is a motor with a position sensor and a controller built around it, so it goes to a commanded angle and holds it. The controller compares the command with the sensor reading and drives the motor to shrink the error. Hobby servos use a small DC motor, gearbox and potentiometer, commanded by a 1 to 2 ms pulse every 20 ms. Industrial ones use brushless motors with encoders. The feedback is what makes it a

q0384.title: How a servo works inside
q0384.short: "The servo measures the width of a 1 to 2 ms pulse that arrives every 20 ms and treats it as a target angle. A potentiometer on the output shaft reports the actual angle. The control chip subtracts them to get an error and drives an H-bridge so the motor turns toward the target, roughly proportional to the error, stopping inside a small deadband. A gearbox trades motor speed for torque. Push on the shaft and the erro

q0385.title: Servo motor applications
q0385.short: "Servos go wherever something has to be at a position or follow a trajectory and hold it against load: RC steering and control surfaces, robot arm joints, camera pan-tilts and gimbals, CNC and 3D printer axes, pick-and-place machines, throttle and valve actuators. I'd use a servo when I need angle or trajectory with disturbance rejection. A plain motor is for constant speed and a solenoid for on-off strokes. Sizing s

q0386.title: Servo advantages over other motors
q0386.short: "A servo's advantage is feedback: it knows where it is, so it's accurate under any load, holds position by pushing back and reports when it fails to arrive. Its torque stays flat out to rated speed with brief higher peaks, whereas a stepper's torque falls with speed. It's efficient because current follows load, while a stepper burns full current at rest. Disadvantages are cost, complexity and tuning, so I'd pick a st

q0387.title: Controlling a servo from an MCU
q0387.short: "I generate a 50 Hz pulse with the MCU's hardware timer, 1 to 2 ms wide, e.g. 1 MHz tick, period 20,000, compare 1000 to 2000. The servo gets its own 5 to 6 V supply sized for stall current, with a bulk capacitor near it, because the MCU can't supply those spikes. Grounds are common, and I put a few hundred ohms in series with the signal. For a DIY servo from a DC motor I'd add an H-bridge, encoder and a PID loop."

q0388.title: How to spec a servo motor
q0388.short: "I'd work from the load: compute the motion profile, then peak torque as inertia times acceleration plus friction and gravity, and RMS torque for thermal duty. Pick a gear ratio, remembering reflected inertia drops as N squared. Check the motor's torque-speed curve covers the peak and the RMS is below continuous with margin. Then supply voltage and current, feedback resolution, size and environment. For a hobby servo

q0389.title: Why servos are so precise
q0389.short: "A servo is precise because it measures the shaft position and keeps correcting the error, so precision comes from the sensor and loop, not the motor. A high-resolution encoder, say 17 bits is about 0.003 degrees, gearing that makes output steps finer, high loop gain for stiffness and an integral term that drives steady-state error to zero. Resolution isn't accuracy though: backlash, flex, friction and sensor error s

q0390.title: Motor and solenoid failure modes
q0390.short: "Main failure modes are thermal, electrical and mechanical. Stall or overload makes current V over R, and the winding overheats in seconds, so use current limiting, thermal protection and stall detection. Switching off the coil produces an inductive spike that kills drivers, so use a flyback diode or snubber. Brushes, bearings and plungers wear or stick, and solenoids burn out if held on beyond their duty cycle, so p

q0391.title: Dangers of motors and solenoids
q0391.short: "Dangers are to people, equipment and the system. People: pinching and entanglement, a 20 kg·cm servo gives about 100 N at 2 cm; unexpected restart after a reset; burns from stalled motors; shock from mains or high-voltage supplies; fire from battery shorts. Equipment: inductive spikes that kill drivers, regeneration that raises the supply, stall overheating. Mitigation: low voltage, guards, torque and current limits

q0392.title: What to measure on a motor or solenoid
q0392.short: "I'd measure by purpose. Protection: current, winding temperature and supply voltage. Control: speed and position from an encoder or back-EMF, and torque, which comes from current since torque is about Kt times current. Health: input power, efficiency, vibration, and trends like winding resistance, which also gives temperature. For solenoids I'd add the current waveform and stroke time to know whether the plunger act

q0393.title: Monitoring a motor with sensors
q0393.short: "One chain per quantity. Current: low-value shunt, current-sense amplifier and ADC, with a comparator for fast trips, or a Hall sensor if I need isolation. Temperature: NTC thermistor on the housing through a divider, RTD or thermocouple for accuracy or range, IR if contactless. Speed and position: encoder or Hall sensors into a timer. Bus voltage: divider to ADC. Vibration: accelerometer. I'd synchronise sampling to

q0394.title: Acting on motor monitoring data
q0394.short: "I'd match the response to severity. Shorts trip a hardware comparator immediately. Overcurrent gets cycle-by-cycle limiting. Slow overload and heat use an I squared t or thermal model to derate smoothly, then shut down with hysteresis. Stall, meaning high current and no motion for a set time, stops the drive, retries a few times and latches. I'd also compensate for supply droop, limit decel to avoid regeneration, ru

q0395.title: Measuring motor or solenoid current
q0395.short: "Most commonly a milliohm-scale shunt resistor plus a current-sense amplifier into the ADC: 20 A through 2 mΩ is 40 mV, gain 75 gives 3 V. Low-side is simple but only sees on-time current; high-side or in-line sees more but needs a high-common-mode amplifier. Hall sensors give isolation, MOSFET RDS(on) sensing saves a part but drifts with temperature. Because PWM chops the current I sample mid on-time or filter, and

q0396.title: Detecting motor or solenoid temperature
q0396.short: "The common options are an NTC thermistor in a divider, cheap and sensitive, an RTD like Pt100 for accuracy, a thermocouple for high temperatures, or an IC sensor for board temperature. For protection a thermal fuse or bimetal switch needs no electronics. And since copper resistance rises about 0.4 percent per kelvin, I can infer average winding temperature from its resistance. I'd embed the sensor in the winding if

q0397.title: Which motor temperatures matter
q0397.short: "Several temperatures matter. The winding, average and hot spot, limits insulation life, so I embed a thermistor or use resistance. The stator and housing lag but are easy to measure. For permanent-magnet motors the rotor magnets matter: NdFeB loses about 0.1 percent flux per kelvin and can demagnetise, but you can't sense it directly, so I estimate it. Bearings have a grease limit, brushes wear, and the MOSFET junct

q0398.title: Contactless temperature of moving motors
q0398.short: "Infrared: a thermopile sensor or IR thermometer reads the surface from a distance, and a thermal camera gives an image. The catch is emissivity: black or painted surfaces are around 0.95 but shiny metal might be 0.1, so a bare shaft at 100 °C can read about 36 °C. Fix with matte tape or paint. Without optics, I can infer temperature from winding resistance or back-EMF constant, use a thermal model, or use telemetry

q0399.title: How motors degrade with age
q0399.short: "Motors drift as they age. Bearings wear and grease degrades, so friction and no-load current rise, with more noise and heat. Brushes shorten and the commutator grooves, increasing contact resistance and sparking. Insulation ages and can short turns; magnets can lose strength, lowering the torque constant so you need more current per newton-metre. Efficiency falls, a 73 percent motor might drop to 61. Reliability fol

q0400.title: Stresses on a motor over its life
q0400.short: "Four groups. Thermal: steady heat ages insulation and cycling fatigues joints. Electrical: inrush is V over R, so a 12 V, 1.2 ohm motor sees 10 A at start, 25 times the heating of a 2 A run; plugging can double stall current; plus inductive spikes and PWM edges stressing insulation and bearings. Mechanical: start-stop shocks, side loads, vibration, overspeed. Environmental: moisture, dust, chemicals. I'd soft-start,

q0401.title: Thin coil wire versus high current
q0401.short: "The premise is off: many turns of thin wire gives higher resistance and lower current, and force depends on ampere-turns, so you pick turns to match your supply. 4500 turns of 0.12 mm wire draws about 45 mA at 12 V. Large currents occur only at start, stall or overload; a running motor's back-EMF limits current, and solenoids are rated by duty cycle. Coils don't always burn out; they fail when heat outruns cooling,

q0402.title: Why measure motor/solenoid speed and position
q0402.short: "Voltage only sets what a motor tries to do. Load, supply and temperature change what it actually does, so for speed control, positioning, BLDC commutation, stall and jam detection and diagnostics you need to measure speed or position and close the loop. For a solenoid the equivalent is knowing the plunger arrived, how hard it hit, and whether it jammed, so you can drop to a hold current, soften the landing and flag

q0403.title: Measuring motor RPM
q0403.short: "I'd get a pulse train from an encoder, a Hall sensor on a magnet, or an optical interrupter, and convert with rpm equals 60 times frequency divided by pulses per rev. At high speed I count pulses in a fixed window; at low speed I time the period between pulses with a hardware timer. No sensor? Back-EMF is proportional to speed, so I can measure terminal voltage during a PWM off-time. For lab checks I'd use an optica

q0404.title: Determining motor position
q0404.short: "I'd pick between absolute and incremental. Absolute options are a potentiometer, a magnetic angle sensor (12 bits or more, contactless) or an absolute encoder. Incremental means an optical quadrature encoder, which needs homing at power-up. Brushless motors have Hall sensors good for commutation (about 60 electrical degrees). Steppers count steps if they don't slip. The gear ratio multiplies output resolution but ad

q0405.title: Rotary encoder and speed measurement
q0405.short: "A rotary encoder converts shaft rotation into electrical pulses. An incremental quadrature encoder gives two square waves, A and B, 90 degrees apart, so the phase order gives direction and counting every edge gives four times the line count, plus an index pulse once per rev. For speed I count edges over a fixed window, rpm equals 60 times counts over CPR times window, or time between edges at low speed. Absolute enc

q0406.title: Measuring solenoid speed
q0406.short: "I'd time the plunger between two known points: optical or Hall gates a set distance apart, velocity equals distance over time, with a hardware timer. Or I differentiate a position sensor like a linear Hall or LVDT, with filtering. Without a sensor, the coil gives velocity through the motional back-EMF, i\,dL/dx\,v, which makes a dip in the current during the stroke. Lab check with a high-speed camera or laser."

q0407.title: Measuring solenoid position
q0407.short: "For just home or extended, a limit switch, reed or Hall switch. For continuous position: a linear Hall sensor with a magnet on the plunger (nonlinear, so linearise), an LVDT (precise, contactless, needs excitation), a linear pot, or an optical strip. Sensorless: inductance depends on air gap, so a small test pulse measures L and hence position, best near the closed end. I'd pick on resolution, linearity, temperature

q0408.title: BEMF speed sensing for motors and solenoids
q0408.short: "Back-EMF is proportional to speed, E equals Ke omega. The terminal voltage is IR plus L di/dt plus E, so I measure it when the current is zero: switch the drive off during the PWM off-time, wait for the freewheel current to decay, and sample the terminal through a divider into an ADC. Speed is that voltage over Ke. Otherwise subtract the I times R drop during on-time. It fails at low speed and drifts with temperatur

q0409.title: How to drive an inductive load
q0409.short: "I'd use a logic-level N-MOSFET as a low-side switch with the load between the supply and the drain, a gate resistor and pull-down, and a flyback diode across the load so the inductor current has a path when the FET turns off. Size the FET for voltage margin and stall or inrush current, then use PWM for speed or hold current. For two directions or protection and diagnostics, step up to an H-bridge or a driver IC."

q0410.title: Adding motor braking to a drive
q0410.short: "A single low-side switch can only coast. To brake I give the motor's back-EMF a short-circuit path: in a half-bridge, turn on the low-side FET; in an H-bridge, turn on both low sides. The motor then acts as a generator into its own resistance and stops in a time constant of tens of milliseconds instead of seconds. I'd check the brake current, E over R, against FET and winding ratings, limit it with PWM if needed, an

q0411.title: Driving a motor in both directions
q0411.short: "An H-bridge: four switches around the motor. Turning on the top-left and bottom-right sends current one way; top-right and bottom-left the other way. PWM one switch for speed. Never turn on both switches of one leg, so I add dead time or use a driver IC with shoot-through protection. Body diodes carry freewheel current, both low sides give braking, all off is coast. The MCU drives it with PWM plus a direction pin or

q0412.title: Kinds of motor braking
q0412.short: "Five kinds: coast, which is just letting friction work; dynamic braking, shorting the terminals or adding a resistor so the motor dissipates its energy as a generator; plugging, reversing the voltage for the fastest stop at high current; regenerative braking, returning energy to the supply with a bridge; and mechanical brakes for holding torque and fail-safe. Electrical braking loses torque as speed drops, so combin

q0413.title: Protection for inductive load drives
q0413.short: "Layers. For the kick, a flyback diode, or a diode plus Zener or TVS for faster release. For the gate, a series resistor, pull-down and maybe a gate Zener. For over-current, a sense resistor with current limit, plus a fuse; motors stall at V over R. Thermal shutdown. On the supply side, reverse-polarity protection, a TVS for surges and bulk capacitance for regeneration. In bridges, dead time. Plus a capacitor across

q0414.title: Drive switch trade-offs: EMR, SSR, MOSFET, BJT, IGBT
q0414.short: "Relay: contacts, zero on-state loss, isolation, AC or DC, but slow, wears, can't PWM, and DC inductive arcs hurt. SSR: isolated, silent, but about a volt drop (triac types) and AC-only unless MOSFET-based. MOSFET: voltage-driven, milliohm resistance, fast, the default for low-voltage PWM. BJT: cheap, current-driven, 0.2 to 0.7 V drop. IGBT: high voltage and current with constant drop, slower. 12 V motor: MOSFET. Mai

q0415.title: Faster solenoid drive: velocity and cycle rate
q0415.short: "Cycle time is pull-in plus release plus return. For pull-in I over-excite: a high voltage for the first few milliseconds, then PWM down to a hold current, since force goes as current squared and a closed plunger needs much less. For release I replace the plain flyback diode with a Zener or TVS so the coil sees a high reverse voltage and the current collapses fast. Add soft landing to stop bounce, and mechanical twea

q0416.title: Specifying a motor/solenoid driver IC
q0416.short: "I'd start from the motor's supply range including transients, stall and running current. Then check the IC's operating voltage with headroom, continuous current thermally using hot R{DS(on)} and R{\theta JA}, peak or limit above inrush, then features: interface and logic level, PWM frequency, current regulation, decay modes, protections (OCP, OTP, UVLO, shoot-through, fault pin), sleep current, package and cost. Fin

q0417.title: Specifying discrete transistors for a drive
q0417.short: "Voltage: at least twice the supply plus clamp, e.g. 40 V on a 12 V rail. Current: size from stall or the current limit, but the real limit is heat, so use hot R{DS(on)} at my actual gate voltage, which means logic-level for 3.3 or 5 V drive, and compute I^2R plus switching and gate loss against thermal resistance. Then gate charge and the Q{gd}/Q{gs} ratio for drive and Miller immunity, SOA or avalanche if unclamped

q0418.title: What limits switching frequency
q0418.short: "Mainly loss and timing. Switching loss, half V I times rise-plus-fall time times f, plus gate-drive, C{oss} and diode recovery losses, all scale with frequency and add to conduction loss until the thermal limit. Then dead time, minimum on-time and blanking eat a bigger share of a shorter period, gate drivers can only supply so much current, and the timer resolution caps the frequency. EMI rises too. The lower bound

q0419.title: Increasing the switching frequency
q0419.short: "I'd cut each limiter: shorten the switching edges with a stronger gate driver, lower Rg and low-Q{gd} FETs, tighten the layout to keep ringing down, use synchronous rectification to kill diode recovery, and go to GaN or SiC if I need MHz. Reduce dead time and blanking, give the timer resolution, and manage EMI and heat. For a motor, I might not raise the device frequency at all: a unipolar bridge or interleaving dou

q0420.title: Draw an H-bridge circuit
q0420.short: "An H-bridge is two half-bridges: each leg has a high-side and a low-side switch, and the motor sits between the two middle nodes. Turn on top-left plus bottom-right and current flows one way; top-right plus bottom-left reverses it; both low sides shorts the motor for braking; all off lets it coast. With MOSFETs I draw NFETs low and PFETs, or bootstrapped NFETs, high, include the body diodes for the inductive freewhe

q0421.title: Draw a half-bridge circuit
q0421.short: "A half-bridge is two switches in series from the supply to ground, with the output at the middle node. High side on gives the supply, low side on gives ground, both off lets an inductive load clamp through a body diode. I'd use two NFETs with body diodes, a bootstrapped gate driver for the high side, and dead time so the two never overlap. The average output is duty cycle times supply, and with an LC filter it becom

q0422.title: How a half/H-bridge works
q0422.short: "A half-bridge connects the output to the supply or to ground, and PWM duty sets the average output. The inductive motor current can't stop when the top switch opens, so it freewheels through the bottom FET or its body diode. An H-bridge is two half-bridges with the motor in between: one leg high and the other low gives one direction, the opposite gives reverse, and PWM on one leg, or on both in anti-phase, sets spee

q0423.title: H-bridge vs half-bridge trade-offs
q0423.short: "A half-bridge is one leg of two FETs; it drives a load between its output and a fixed rail, so the load sees zero to the supply and a motor only turns one way. An H-bridge is two legs with the load floating between them, which gives plus or minus the full supply, so reverse, brake and regeneration, but it needs twice the FETs and drivers, and has twice the conduction loss. Use a half-bridge for fans, solenoids and b

q0424.title: Braking a motor with half/H-bridges
q0424.short: "I'd brake with a half-bridge by turning on the low-side FET, which ties both motor terminals to ground, so the back-EMF drives current through the winding and the motor slows. An H-bridge can do that with both low sides, or can plug by applying reverse voltage, which makes current (V+E)/R, about twice as much, and stops several times faster. The stress is peak current, winding heating, a torque jolt on the gears and

q0425.title: Asymmetrical half-bridge vs symmetrical H-bridge
q0425.short: "An asymmetrical half-bridge is one where the two FETs differ or where the load only sees one polarity, so I'd use it for unidirectional loads and buck converters at lopsided duty cycles; resizing the FETs to match the duty cycle cuts conduction loss, 20% at D = 0.1. I need a symmetrical H-bridge when the load must see both polarities or zero DC average: reversing motors, voice coils, class-D speakers and transformer

q0426.title: High-side NFET advantages and challenges
q0426.short: "An NFET is the better switch because electrons are two to three times more mobile than holes, so for the same die it has lower on-resistance and gate charge, and it's cheaper with more choices. The challenge on the high side is that its source is the switch node, so the gate has to be a few volts above the supply, which needs a floating gate supply: a bootstrap capacitor or charge pump. That limits duty cycle and co

q0427.title: Drive circuit for a high-side NFET
q0427.short: "A high-side NFET needs its gate about 10 V above its source, and the source is the switch node, so I need a gate supply that floats with it. I'd use a half-bridge driver with a bootstrap: a fast diode from the 10 V supply to a capacitor that sits between the boot pin and the switch node. It charges when the low side is on and lifts the gate drive when the high side turns on. Size it as gate charge over allowed droop

q0428.title: PFET and NFET on together: shoot-through
q0428.short: "Turning on the PFET and NFET in the same leg shorts the supply to ground through two on-resistances, so you get big current spikes, heat, rail droop and often a dead FET. It happens with overlapping gate edges, tied gates, mismatched turn-off and turn-on delays, or Miller-coupled dv/dt. I prevent it with separate gate drives and dead time, a driver with built-in shoot-through protection, faster turn-off than turn-on

q0429.title: Drive an inductive load from a GPIO
q0429.short: "I'd use a low-side logic-level N-channel MOSFET: load from the supply to the drain, source to ground, GPIO to the gate. A flyback diode across the load takes the inductive kick, a 100 k pull-down on the gate keeps it off when the MCU is in reset, a 100 to 220 Ω series gate resistor limits GPIO current and ringing, and a bulk capacitor supports the supply. If the load is on a different or noisy supply, add isolation

q0430.title: Why a gate pulldown resistor
q0430.short: "A MOSFET gate is a capacitor with a huge DC resistance, so if the driving pin is in reset, booting or set as an input, the gate floats and drifts with leakage and noise, and can drift above threshold. Then the FET half-turns on and either fires the load at power-up or sits in its linear region burning power. A 10 to 100 kΩ pulldown from gate to source gives the gate a defined path to ground so it defaults off, and c

q0431.title: Gate series resistor and parasitic oscillation
q0431.short: "The gate is a capacitor, and the wire and package feeding it add nanohenries of inductance, so a fast driver edge makes a series LC that rings at tens of megahertz and overshoots the gate; with enough gain and feedback through the Miller capacitance it can even oscillate. A series gate resistor damps the loop, requiring R\ge2\sqrt{L/C}, caps the GPIO's peak current, and slows the edge to cut dv/dt and EMI, at the co

q0432.title: Why isolation matters, and its trade-offs
q0432.short: "Isolation matters for safety (keeping hazardous voltage away from people and logic), for protection (a shorted FET can't put the motor rail on the MCU pin), and for noise, because switching current on a shared ground shifts the MCU's reference by volts. It also gives floating references for high-side drives and sensors. The trade-offs are cost, area, an isolated power supply, delay and limited bandwidth, optocoupler

q0433.title: Which kinds of isolation to use
q0433.short: "It depends on what crosses the barrier and how strong it needs to be. For logic and PWM I'd use a digital isolator, or an optocoupler if it's slow. For a high-voltage bridge, an isolated gate driver with an isolated supply. For motor current sensing, an isolated amplifier or delta-sigma modulator. For buses like CAN or RS-485, an isolated transceiver, and for power, an isolated DC-DC. The grade is set by the standar

q0434.title: Opto-isolation and its trade-offs
q0434.short: "An optocoupler is an LED and a photodetector, usually a phototransistor, in one package with an insulating gap, so only light crosses and the two sides are galvanically isolated. The key spec is CTR, output current over LED current, which varies with temperature and drops with age. Trade-offs: slow with distorted pulse widths, milliamps of input current, limited common-mode immunity, and aging, in return for low cos

q0435.title: Design an opto-isolated gate drive
q0435.short: "I'd bias the LED at about 10 mA from the GPIO: (3.3 − 1.2)/10 mA is 210 Ω, so 200 Ω, active-high so reset means off. On the output side I'd run the phototransistor from an isolated 12 V as an emitter follower into a pulldown, which is non-inverting, defaults off and goes to about 11 V at end-of-life CTR, then buffer it with an NPN/PNP pair into a 10 Ω gate resistor with a gate-source pulldown, because a plain pull-u

q0436.title: What is galvanic isolation?
q0436.short: "Galvanic isolation means two circuits have no direct conductive path, so no DC current, yet they still exchange signal or power through light, a magnetic field or an electric field across a capacitor. It lets the two sides sit at completely different voltages, breaks ground loops and contains faults. But the barrier has a little capacitance, so fast common-mode transients still cross, it has a finite voltage rating,

q0437.title: High-side PFET challenges at high supply voltage
q0437.short: "A PFET high-side switch needs its gate pulled below the supply, so with a 48 V motor and a 3.3 V MCU the logic can't drive it directly: VGS would be minus 45 V, always on and beyond the gate rating. You need a level shifter, a small NFET rated for the full supply, a Zener clamp so the gate-source never exceeds about 12 V, and resistors that make turn-on and turn-off slow and lossy. Add the PFET's higher on-resistanc

q0438.title: Design a high-side PFET drive
q0438.short: "PFET source on the bus, drain to the load. A small 100 V NFET level shifter, driven from the GPIO through a series resistor with a pulldown, pulls the PFET gate down through a 10 k resistor. A 10 k pull-up from gate to source holds the PFET off, and a 12 V Zener from gate to source clamps VGS so it can't exceed the rating at any supply voltage. That gives about −12 V of VGS when on and 0 when off, with 3.6 mA standi

q0439.title: Ways to measure current
q0439.short: "You convert current to a voltage. The common ways are a series sense resistor with an amplifier, which is cheap, accurate and DC-capable but dissipates power; using an existing resistance like a MOSFET's Rds(on) or inductor DCR, which is free but inaccurate; and magnetic sensing, Hall sensors or current transformers, which give isolation and low loss but cost more and drift. For a low-voltage board I'd default to a

q0440.title: Why measure current
q0440.short: "Four reasons. Protection, because current is what overheats and destroys hardware, so you need a fast overcurrent trip. Control, because converters use inductor current for current-mode control and motors produce torque proportional to current. Monitoring, because integrating current gives battery state of charge and multiplying by voltage gives power. And diagnostics, like detecting a stalled motor or missing load.

q0441.title: Magnetic current sensing pros and cons
q0441.short: "Magnetic sensing measures the field around the conductor instead of a voltage drop. Hall sensors detect the field directly and work at DC and AC. Current transformers and Rogowski coils use Faraday induction, so they only see AC. The big advantages are isolation, almost no insertion loss and high current range. The downsides are cost, size, offset and temperature drift, sensitivity to stray fields, and poor accuracy

q0442.title: Current sensing tradeoffs compared
q0442.short: "A shunt plus current-sense amp is the accurate, cheap, DC-capable default, but it dissipates I-squared-R and has no isolation. Rds(on) or inductor DCR sensing is lossless and free but only 10 to 20 percent accurate, so it's for protection. Hall and CT sensors give isolation, no loss and high current range, but cost more, drift, and are poor at low current, and CTs are AC only. I'd choose by current level, isolation

q0443.title: How a sense resistor works
q0443.short: "A sense resistor is a small precise resistor in series with the load. All the load current flows through it, so the voltage across it is I \times R. I measure that millivolt-level drop with a current sense amplifier and an ADC and divide by the resistance to get current. It's small to limit loss, a few milliohms, and I connect the sense lines directly to its pads, Kelvin style, so only the resistor is in the measure

q0444.title: Sense resistor pros and cons
q0444.short: "Sense resistors are cheap, small, linear and accurate, they work from DC to high frequency, and they handle overloads. The downsides are that they dissipate I^2R and drop voltage so they don't scale to very high current, their tiny signal means amplifier offset limits low-current accuracy, resistance drifts with temperature, parasitic inductance corrupts fast edges, and there's no isolation. They also need Kelvin ro

q0445.title: Specifying a sense resistor
q0445.short: "I find the allowed window for the resistance. The upper limit is set by voltage drop and power at maximum current, R \le \min(V{drop}/I{max}, P/I{max}^2). The lower limit is set by the smallest current I need to measure: the signal must beat amplifier offset, so R \ge V{os}/(\varepsilon I{min}). Then I pick a low-TCR, low-ESL part rated at least twice the dissipation. Too big wastes power and drops voltage; too smal

q0446.title: Sense resistor from ADC range
q0446.short: "I take the ADC full-scale voltage, divide by the maximum current with about 10 percent headroom, and that gives the largest resistor: Rs = V{FS}/(1.1 I{max}). Then I check power I^2R, voltage drop, and resolution per LSB. If the result is silly, like 27 ohms at 100 milliamps, I use a small shunt and an amplifier instead. For bidirectional current I use half the range, since zero sits at mid-scale."

q0447.title: High-side vs low-side current sensing
q0447.short: "Low-side puts the shunt between load and ground: simple, cheap, near-zero common-mode, but it lifts the load's ground by IRs and can't see a short-to-ground fault. High-side puts it between supply and load: load stays grounded and short-to-ground is detected, but the amplifier must handle bus-level common-mode voltage and have good CMRR. I use high-side when the load must be grounded or for protection, and low-side

q0448.title: Sensing current with MOSFET Vds
q0448.short: "A fully-on MOSFET is a small resistor, so I = V{DS}/R{DS(on)}. You measure drain-source voltage with a comparator or amplifier and get current with no added loss, part or board space, which is why it's used for overcurrent protection. The cons are accuracy: R{DS(on)} rises 50 percent or more when hot and varies part to part, it only works while the FET is fully on and after the switching edge settles, and the signal

q0449.title: What a current sense amplifier is
q0449.short: "A current sense amplifier takes the small voltage across a shunt, rejects the large common-mode bus voltage it sits on, multiplies the difference by a precise fixed gain like 20 or 50, and outputs a ground-referenced voltage for an ADC or comparator, often with a reference pin for bidirectional current. Inside it's a difference amplifier with trimmed matched resistors, so V{out} = G\,I\,R{sense} + V{ref}. Key specs

q0450.title: When you need a CSA
q0450.short: "You need a CSA when you can't feed the shunt voltage straight into the ADC: the signal is millivolts and the ADC step is about a millivolt, so resolution is poor; the shunt sits on a high-side bus voltage the ADC can't tolerate; or the current is bidirectional and needs a level shift. A gain of 50 turns 50 millivolts into volts and also rejects common-mode noise. I don't need one if the ADC has a small differential

q0451.title: CSA versus a regular op-amp
q0451.short: "A CSA is a difference amplifier in an IC, but built for shunt sensing: its gain-setting resistors are on-die and trimmed so CMRR is 100 to 120 dB, where discrete 0.1 percent resistors give only about 80 dB; its inputs can sit above its own supply so it works on a high-side bus; and its offset is microvolts rather than millivolts. A plain op-amp is more flexible and fine when the bus is within the supply and accuracy

q0452.title: How to spec a CSA
q0452.short: "I'd work from system requirements to parameters. Topology fixes the common-mode range I need. The shunt and ADC range set the gain, limited by output swing and rounded to what's available. Offset divided by the shunt gives my minimum current, so I check it against my lowest current, and CMRR against the bus voltage. Then bandwidth at that gain against my PWM or protection time, output swing and REF, supply and prote

q0453.title: Choosing CSA gain from ranges
q0453.short: "Maximum gain is the largest usable output voltage divided by the shunt voltage at full current: G{max}=V{out,max}/(I{max}Rs). Usable means within both the ADC range and the CSA's output swing, with some headroom. I round down to a standard gain such as 20, 50, 100 or 200, and check amps per LSB. Example: 5 A on 10 mΩ gives 50 mV, so with a 3.2 V swing G max is 64 and I'd choose 50, giving 2.5 V. For bidirectional cu

q0454.title: Why protect against over/undervoltage and overcurrent
q0454.short: "Every component has limits, and real systems leave the nominal range: shorts, hot-plug spikes, wrong adapters, sagging batteries. Overcurrent is a heating problem since power goes as I squared R. Overvoltage causes breakdown of oxides and capacitors. Undervoltage makes logic misbehave and FETs run half on. So I layer protection: a fuse or eFuse and TVS at the input, current limit and thermal shutdown in the regulato

q0455.title: Design an over/undervoltage and overcurrent detector
q0455.short: "I'd use a window comparator: a resistor ladder from the rail with two taps, each going to a comparator against a 1.24 V reference, one for overvoltage and one for undervoltage, with a little hysteresis so it doesn't chatter. The trip is the reference times the total divider over the lower part. For current I'd put a milliohm shunt in the rail, amplify it with a current-sense amp, and compare to the same reference. T

q0456.title: What to do when a fault is detected
q0456.short: "It depends on how bad the fault is. The gentlest is to just flag it so firmware can react. Then limiting, like current limit or foldback. Then shutdown, either latched or with auto-retry or hiccup so a persistent short sees only a few percent duty. For overvoltage I can clamp with a TVS or crowbar a rail and blow a fuse, or disconnect the load. I match the response speed to the hazard, and in an embedded system I us

q0457.title: Protecting a power supply from overcurrent and overvoltage
q0457.short: "For overcurrent, a cycle-by-cycle peak limit stops the inductor from saturating, plus a valley limit or frequency foldback because in a hard short the inductor only has a diode drop to ramp down and current can ratchet up. Then hiccup and thermal shutdown. For overvoltage, the controller's OVP on the feedback turns off the high side, but since a shorted FET or an open feedback resistor defeats that, I'd add an indep

q0458.title: Over/undervoltage on an embedded system
q0458.short: "Undervoltage makes the system misbehave: slower logic, corrupted RAM, half-written flash, weak I/O, so you add brown-out reset and a supervisor. Overvoltage damages it: breakdown above the absolute maximum, and a pin above Vdd forward-biases the ESD diodes and can trigger latch-up. So I use brown-out detection, series resistors and clamps on exposed inputs, proper power sequencing, and a fuse or OVP on the rail, plu

q0459.title: Limiting the current a load can draw
q0459.short: "Match it to the fault. A fuse is cheap and reliable but one-shot, a PTC polyfuse resets, and a series resistor only suits things like LEDs because of the drop and heat. For real rails I'd use an active limiter: a pass FET with a sense resistor and a transistor that throttles the gate at about 0.6 V across the sense resistor, so the limit is roughly 0.6 over R, or an eFuse that integrates the limit, soft-start, therm

q0460.title: What a PCB is and where it's used
q0460.short: "A PCB is an insulating board, usually fibreglass-epoxy FR-4, with copper traces etched on it that connect components soldered to pads. Vias connect layers, soldermask protects the copper and silkscreen labels the parts. We use them because they're repeatable, compact, machine-assembled and let you control impedance and return paths. They're in everything from remote controls to servers, from a single layer up to twe

q0461.title: PCB vs breadboard vs perfboard vs wiring vs IC
q0461.short: "A breadboard is fastest to change but has flaky contacts and a few picofarads and nanohenries of parasitics, so it's for exploration at low frequency. Perfboard or point-to-point is permanent but slow and not repeatable. A PCB takes days to fab but is repeatable, compact, with controlled impedance and cheap at volume. An IC has the biggest up-front cost but the best size, power and performance at high volume. So you

q0462.title: PCB versus IC
q0462.short: "An IC is a piece of silicon with transistors and nanometre-scale wiring fabricated together, put in a package. A PCB is the board that ICs and other parts are soldered onto, with copper traces connecting them. So ICs are the active devices and a PCB is mostly interconnect and support. IC features are nanometres to microns, PCB traces about a tenth of a millimetre. ICs take months in a cleanroom with huge tooling cos

q0463.title: Parasitic elements on a PCB
q0463.short: "Every feature on a board has parasitics. Traces have resistance, about 0.1 ohm for 50 millimetres in 1 oz copper, and inductance of roughly 0.3 nanohenries per millimetre over a plane, which really depends on the loop area. They have capacitance to planes and neighbours, about 0.1 picofarad per millimetre, which causes crosstalk. Vias add about a nanohenry and half a picofarad, pads and component packages add more,

q0464.title: Types of PCBs, trade-offs and uses
q0464.short: "By layer count: single-sided is cheapest for simple products, double-sided is the default, multilayer adds planes for signal integrity and density. By rigidity: rigid, flex for bending, and rigid-flex combining both. By material: FR-4 for most, PTFE or Rogers-type laminates for RF, ceramic for high temperature, metal-core with an aluminium base for LEDs and power. And HDI with microvias for dense designs like phones

q0465.title: Flex PCBs: construction, trade-offs, uses
q0465.short: "A flex PCB is a circuit on a polyimide film instead of rigid fibreglass, with rolled-annealed copper traces, a coverlay instead of soldermask, and stiffeners where parts go. It's thin, light and bendable, so it fits tight 3D spaces, handles dynamic flexing like hinges, and replaces cables and connectors, which improves reliability under vibration. The trade-offs are higher cost, delicate handling, special design rul

q0466.title: PCB layers and their materials
q0466.short: "A rigid PCB is copper foil layers on FR-4, which is fibreglass cloth in epoxy. Multilayer boards are built from cores, which are cured laminate with copper on both sides, and prepreg, partly cured glass-epoxy that bonds the layers under heat and pressure. Outside, there's soldermask, a green epoxy coating that covers everything but the pads, silkscreen ink for labels, and a surface finish such as ENIG or HASL on the

q0467.title: Best conductor material for PCB layers
q0467.short: "Copper, almost always. It has the second-lowest resistivity of any practical metal, about 1.7 times ten to the minus eight ohm-metres, close to silver but vastly cheaper. It's ductile, easy to etch and to electroplate, solders well and conducts heat. Standard foil is 35 microns, one ounce. Silver is costly and tarnishes, gold is worse and very expensive so it's only a thin finish, and aluminium is hard to solder and

q0468.title: Gold versus copper for PCB conductors
q0468.short: "Copper for the conductors, gold only as a thin finish. Gold is actually a worse conductor, about 45% higher resistivity, and thousands of times more expensive per unit mass, so gold traces make no sense. Its advantage is that it's noble: it doesn't oxidise, so pads stay solderable and contacts stay low resistance. That's why we use ENIG, nickel with about 0.1 micron of gold, and gold-plated edge connectors. Downside

q0469.title: PCB insulation materials and trade-offs
q0469.short: "The default is FR-4, glass-fibre in epoxy: cheap, strong and easy to process, with a dielectric constant around 4.3 and a loss tangent around 0.02, fine up to about a gigahertz. Its limits are high-frequency loss, a permittivity that varies, a modest glass transition and poor heat conduction. Alternatives: high-Tg FR-4 for lead-free assembly, polyimide for flex and heat, PTFE or ceramic-filled laminates with loss of

q0470.title: What "FR4" means
q0470.short: "FR-4 means Flame Retardant grade 4. FR means the laminate is self-extinguishing, tested to UL 94 V-0; the 4 is just a grade number in the NEMA system, not four layers. It's woven fibreglass in epoxy resin, the standard PCB substrate: strong, cheap, easy to process, with a dielectric constant around 4.3, loss tangent around 0.02, and a glass transition around 130 to 180 degrees depending on grade. It's the flame-reta

q0471.title: Why PCBs are green; other colours
q0471.short: "The colour is the soldermask, the polymer coating over the copper, not the fibreglass. Green is the default because it's the most mature and cheapest mask chemistry, it gives good contrast with copper and white silkscreen, it's easy on the eyes, and inspection systems are tuned to it. There's also some military-spec folklore. Other colours, red, blue, black, white, yellow, work electrically the same: black looks pre

q0472.title: The silkscreen (legend) layer
q0472.short: "It's the silkscreen, also called the legend or nomenclature: a layer of ink, usually white epoxy, printed on top of the soldermask. It carries reference designators, component outlines, polarity and pin-1 marks, test points, connector labels, and the board name and revision. Keep it off the pads, because ink on a pad blocks soldering and the fab will clip it, use legible sizes, and choose a colour that contrasts wit

q0473.title: What soldermask is and does
q0473.short: "Soldermask is the thin polymer coating over the copper on a PCB, the green layer, with openings at the pads. It's an LPI epoxy about 20 to 30 microns thick. It stops solder bridging between pads and keeps solder on the pads during assembly, protects the copper from oxidation and moisture, and insulates the traces. In layout you set the opening slightly bigger than each pad, keep a minimum mask dam between fine-pitch

q0474.title: PCB layers in a stackup and their materials
q0474.short: "A PCB is a stack of copper layers separated by FR-4 glass-epoxy. From the top: silkscreen, solder mask, top copper, a prepreg glue layer, inner copper, a thick cured core, more inner copper, prepreg, bottom copper, mask and silkscreen. Copper carries signals and current, FR-4 insulates and gives stiffness, mask protects against solder bridges, silkscreen is labeling. Plated holes link the layers. The dielectric thic

q0475.title: Choosing the PCB layer count
q0475.short: "I'd choose the fewest layers that satisfy routing, signal integrity and EMI, and I'd name the reason for each layer. Dense BGAs drive signal layers, about two rows of balls per layer. Fast edges or controlled impedance need an adjacent ground plane, so I'd go to four layers: signal, ground, power, signal. Multiple rails, DDR or SerDes push me to six or eight. Cost goes up with each pair, so I only add layers when so

q0476.title: Choosing a board stackup
q0476.short: "I'd start with a few rules: every signal layer next to a solid reference plane, power and ground planes adjacent and tightly coupled, a symmetric stack so the board stays flat, and dielectric thicknesses that give sensible trace widths for 50 ohms. For four layers that's signal, ground, power, signal. For six, signal, ground, signal, power, ground, signal. Then I get the fab's real thicknesses and permittivity and r

q0477.title: What to route on inner vs outer layers
q0477.short: "Outer layers are for component access: fanouts, short links, test points, RF tuning and power pours. Inner signal layers, between planes, are for long runs and fast or noisy signals, because the field stays inside the board, so there's less emission and pickup. I route adjacent signal layers orthogonally to cut crosstalk, keep each bus or differential pair on one layer type to avoid skew from the different propagati

q0478.title: Which layers should be ground
q0478.short: "Ground goes directly next to the signal layers: layer 2 on a four-layer board, layers 2 and 5 on a six-layer. High-frequency return current flows in the plane right under the trace, so a close, solid ground gives a small loop, less radiation and crosstalk, and predictable impedance. A ground plane between two signal layers also shields them. The plane has to be continuous, so I don't cut it with slots or route acros

q0479.title: Layers for high-speed signal routing
q0479.short: "I route fast signals directly next to a solid ground plane, usually as an inner stripline between two grounds for long, noisy runs, or as a short microstrip on the top layer when via stubs would hurt. I keep each interface on one layer pair, with the same via count for every bit in a bus or pair. I avoid plane splits and adjacent signal layers with no plane between them, and at layer changes I put a ground via next

q0480.title: Which layers for power planes
q0480.short: "Power planes go on inner layers, right next to a ground plane with a thin dielectric between them. That pair forms a low-inductance capacitor that helps decoupling at high frequency and keeps current loops small. In four layers that's layer 3 under the layer 2 ground; in six layers, layer 4 next to the layer 5 ground. I keep full planes off the outer layers, use pours there for high-current rails, split inner planes

q0481.title: Components that need more PCB layers
q0481.short: "Dense, fast or power-hungry parts push the layer count up. Fine-pitch BGAs need extra layers to escape their signals, roughly two rows of balls per layer at 0.8 mm pitch. High-speed interfaces like DDR, PCIe and USB 3 need a reference plane next to each routing layer. Processors and FPGAs with many rails need power planes and decoupling space. RF and mixed-signal sections need isolation, and big connectors need laye

q0482.title: General PCB routing rules of thumb
q0482.short: "Place first, then route the critical nets in order: power, clocks and fast signals, sensitive analog, then the rest. Keep traces short, keep a continuous ground plane under every signal so the return is directly beneath it, and keep loop areas small. Put decoupling right at the pins. Size traces for current, space traces to limit crosstalk, avoid stubs and acute angles, keep noisy and quiet circuits apart, and respe

q0483.title: Floorplanning subsystems on a PCB
q0483.short: "I floorplan before routing. I start from the block diagram, mark noisy blocks (switching supplies, clocks, drivers), sensitive ones (ADC, reference, RF receive) and hot ones, and place connectors and mounting holes per the enclosure. Then I let the signal flow run in a line through the board, keep noisy and sensitive blocks apart, put each supply close to its load, decoupling and crystals at their ICs, and keep the

q0484.title: What PCB grounding is and why it matters
q0484.short: "Ground on a PCB is the reference node and the return path for every current. It's real copper with resistance and inductance, so return currents create voltage drops, I·R at low frequency and L·di/dt at high frequency. If circuits share a ground conductor they couple through it, which shows up as noise, offset errors, resets or emissions. A solid ground plane, short low-inductance connections, and keeping large curr

q0485.title: Basic grounding layout techniques
q0485.short: "I give return currents a short, well-defined path. A solid ground plane right next to the signal layers, never cut by slots; a via at every ground pad, placed right at the pad; the shortest possible loop for decoupling capacitors, since each millimetre of trace is about a nanohenry; separate noisy and sensitive returns by placement rather than by cutting the plane; a star point only where I need one; and stitching v

q0486.title: Ground plane pros and cons
q0486.short: "A ground plane is a solid copper layer used as the reference and return path. Pros: very low impedance, tiny return loops so less radiation, pickup and crosstalk, controlled-impedance traces, shielding between layers, heat spreading, and capacitance with a nearby power plane. Cons: extra layers and cost, parasitic capacitance on high-impedance or RF nodes, shared-impedance noise if big currents flow through it, dama

q0487.title: Ground stitching vias
q0487.short: "Ground stitching means connecting ground layers and pours together with vias in a regular pattern. It removes floating islands, gives return currents a short path at layer changes, forms a via fence for shielding RF or sensitive traces and the board edge, and reduces plane resonances. The spacing rule of thumb is about a twentieth of a wavelength in the board at the highest frequency of concern, which is around 8 mm

q0488.title: Ground plane vs ground traces
q0488.short: "A ground plane gives much lower impedance than ground traces: about 0.5 mΩ per square and sub-nanohenry spreading, versus roughly 190 mΩ and 140 nH for a 100 mm thin trace. It also puts the return directly under each signal, so loops are small, and it avoids the common-impedance buildup of a daisy chain. Traces cost less and let you force a deliberate single-point return, so they're right for one- or two-layer board

q0489.title: Other jobs of a ground plane
q0489.short: "Beyond being the reference, a ground plane is the return path that keeps loops small, so it cuts radiation, pickup and crosstalk; it defines trace impedance; it shields between layers; next to a power plane it adds high-frequency decoupling capacitance; it spreads heat; it gives ESD and surge currents a low-inductance path; it balances copper to limit warp; and it's the counterpoise for antennas. Cutting it up gives

q0490.title: Why a ground plane shields signals
q0490.short: "A ground plane is a good conductor, so it shields in three ways. Electric field lines terminate on it instead of passing through, so a plane between two layers kills capacitive coupling. The return current under the trace is equal and opposite to the signal current, so their magnetic fields cancel and the net field falls off fast. And above a few MHz eddy currents absorb the field: about 47 dB for 1 oz copper at 100

q0491.title: Typical ground plane layers and why
q0491.short: "Ground goes on layer 2, directly under the top signals, and on the layer next to the bottom, with more ground planes added so every inner signal layer sits next to one: layers 2 and 5 on six layers, for example. The reason is return current: outer layers have thin prepreg, so a plane there gives tight return loops and narrow 50 ohm traces; ground beside power adds decoupling capacitance; and inner grounds shield sig

q0492.title: Why ground probe points matter
q0492.short: "The probe's ground lead is a real inductor, about 1 nH per millimetre, and with the probe's roughly 10 pF tip capacitance it forms an LC circuit. A 150 mm clip lead resonates near 130 MHz and shows about 50% overshoot on a fast edge that isn't really there; it also picks up magnetic fields through its loop. A ground pad right next to the test point, with a spring ground, brings the resonance up to hundreds of MHz an

q0493.title: When and why to separate grounds
q0493.short: "I separate grounds for specific reasons: safety isolation, breaking ground loops between systems, keeping large or noisy return currents out of a sensitive reference like a shunt or an ADC, different voltage references, and chassis/ESD handling. On one board I usually partition by placement over a single plane and join returns at one deliberate point rather than cutting the plane. Where the separation is real, signa

q0494.title: Ground layout schemes
q0494.short: "The main ground layout schemes are single-point, which can be series daisy-chain or parallel star, multipoint, which is a solid ground plane, and hybrids. Star grounding keeps circuits from sharing return impedance and suits low-frequency analog. A plane gives the lowest inductance and is the right answer for fast digital. In practice I use a solid plane, partition the board so noisy and quiet circuits don't share r

q0495.title: Star grounding
q0495.short: "Star grounding gives every circuit its own return path to one common point, so no two circuits share a return segment. That matters because ground has resistance and inductance, and a shared segment turns one circuit's current into noise on another's reference. It works best at low frequency, where legs are resistive, and for mixing power, digital and analog. The risks are long inductive legs at high frequency and a

q0496.title: Combined vs separate analog, digital, power grounds
q0496.short: "Combining grounds gives every signal a short, low-inductance return right beneath it, which is simple and robust, but noisy return currents can pass through quiet areas if placement is sloppy. Separating them keeps noisy currents out of the analog region, but any signal crossing the split loses its return path, which creates loops, crosstalk and EMI. My default is one solid plane partitioned by placement, with separ

q0497.title: Ground potential differences across a board
q0497.short: "Every voltage on the board is measured against a local ground, so if grounds differ, I get errors everywhere. Logic levels arrive shifted, so noise margin shrinks and I get bit errors or false triggers. Analog measurements shift by the offset, which can be several LSBs. Large or fast offsets can exceed pin ratings, cause latch-up, or drive cables as antennas and fail EMC. It comes from current times ground impedance

q0498.title: Sources of ground potential variation
q0498.short: "I group the sources into resistive, inductive and coupled. Resistive is IR drop through copper, about half a milliohm per square for one-ounce copper, made worse by neck-downs, vias and connectors. Inductive is L di/dt from fast current: simultaneous switching, switching-regulator loops, package pins and connectors, and it's usually larger on fast boards. Coupled covers return paths detoured by slots, shared returns

q0499.title: Keeping ground variation small
q0499.short: "I keep ground variation small by lowering the impedance and shrinking the currents. Impedance: a solid unbroken plane right under the signal layers, no slots or neck-downs, stitching vias at layer changes, and many ground pins on connectors. Currents: tight decoupling at every power pin, compact switching loops, slower edges and fewer simultaneous switches. Then I partition by placement so noisy returns stay away fr

q0500.title: Designing for ground disturbance resilience
q0500.short: "I assume ground will move and design around it. For links, I use differential or isolated signalling so a ground offset is rejected or irrelevant. For measurements, I use differential, Kelvin or ratiometric methods so offsets cancel. I add margin with hysteresis, RC filtering, slower edges and sampling away from switching. Then recovery: CRC and retry, watchdog and brown-out reset. And big events get clamped at the

q0501.title: Decoupling capacitors and when needed
q0501.short: "A decoupling capacitor is a small ceramic, about 100 nF, placed right at a chip's supply pin. Chips draw current in fast bursts, and the regulator is too far away and too slow, with inductance in between, to provide it. The capacitor supplies that burst locally and gives high-frequency noise a short path to ground, so the rail doesn't dip or ring. You need one on essentially every IC power pin, and more as edge spee

q0502.title: Common decoupling capacitor values
