q0502.short: "The standard is 100 nF ceramic, X7R or X5R, at every supply pin, because its self-resonance is around 20 MHz and it covers the first tens of nanoseconds of a burst. Around it, 10 nF or smaller for higher frequency, 1 to 10 µF for the mid range, and 47 to 470 µF bulk near the regulator. You need a range of values because each capacitor's parasitic inductance makes it inductive above its self-resonance. I check the di

q0503.title: Placing and routing decoupling capacitors
q0503.short: "All the rules are about shrinking the loop inductance of capacitor, pin and planes. Put the capacitor as close to the supply pin as possible, same side as the chip, smallest value nearest. Connect with short, wide traces or vias right at the pads, power and ground vias next to each other, one capacitor per pin, no other routing in between. Keep power and ground planes near the surface to shorten the vias. For BGAs,

q0504.title: Why decoupling must sit close to the package
q0504.short: "Because everything between the capacitor and the pin is inductance, about half to one nanohenry per millimetre, and the pin voltage drops by L times di/dt. A chip stepping 50 mA per nanosecond through just 1 nH loses 50 mV, regardless of capacitor size. Farther away also means the loop inductance resonates with the chip's own capacitance at a lower frequency, and the bigger loop radiates. It's inductance, not signal

q0505.title: Which signals to decouple and why
q0505.short: "Supply pins first: every VDD, including separate analog, I/O and PLL supplies, because that's where fast current bursts and noise coupling occur. Then reference and bias pins, since their noise goes straight into accuracy and their buffers often need a specified capacitor. Regulator inputs and outputs for stability and load steps, and LDO noise-reduction pins. I would not decouple arbitrary signal lines, since a cap

q0506.title: Why many decoupling capacitors, not one big one
q0506.short: "Because real capacitors have series inductance, and above their self-resonant frequency they act like inductors. A single big capacitor resonates low and is inductive where fast current lives. N smaller capacitors in parallel divide ESL and mounting inductance by N, and let you place charge near every supply pin. Different values also cover different frequency bands. The catch is anti-resonance peaks between mixed v

q0507.title: Laying out and routing multiple decoupling capacitors
q0507.short: "I arrange them as tiers: the smallest values against the supply pins or under the BGA balls, mid-value a bit further, bulk near the regulator. Each capacitor gets its own power and ground via pair, side by side, to adjacent power and ground planes, with no daisy-chains or shared vias, and with neighbours' polarity alternated so fields cancel. The planes carry current between tiers. Then I check the combined impedanc

q0508.title: Symptoms of decoupling capacitors placed too far
q0508.short: "If the capacitors are too far, the connection inductance limits how fast they can supply current, so the pin sees L di/dt spikes regardless of capacitance: 100 mA in a nanosecond through 10 nH is a volt. You see resets, corrupted data when outputs switch together, ADC and PLL noise, and failures at low-voltage corners. The bigger loop also shifts the PDN anti-resonance lower and radiates more, so EMC suffers. I'd co

q0509.title: Parasitic inductance and decoupling performance
q0509.short: "A real capacitor is a series RLC. Below its self-resonant frequency it's a capacitor; at resonance the impedance dips to the ESR; above it the inductance dominates and the impedance rises as 2 pi f L, so it's effectively an inductor. That sets the useful bandwidth: a 100 nF with 0.5 nH resonates near 22 MHz, but with 3 nH of mounting it drops to 9 MHz and is six times worse at 100 MHz. It also limits di/dt and creat

q0510.title: Sources of parasitic inductance in decoupling
q0510.short: "The inductance comes from every piece of the current loop: the capacitor's own ESL, the pads and fan-out trace, the power and ground vias, current spreading in the planes, and the IC package's bond wires, leads or balls. They add in series, a bit offset by mutual inductance when power and ground run side by side. On a typical board the vias and fan-out often outweigh the capacitor, so I put vias at the pads, keep pl

q0511.title: How packaging affects decoupling effectiveness
q0511.short: "Packaging acts on two levels. The capacitor's case size and construction set its ESL: 0201 and 0402 are around 0.3 to 0.5 nH, 1206 over a nanohenry, with reverse-geometry and array capacitors lower still, and electrolytics far higher. The IC's package sets a floor: a QFP lead and bond wire are several nanohenries, a BGA or flip-chip much less, and big processors put capacitors on the package. I pick small, low-ESL p

q0512.title: Capacitor self-resonant frequency in decoupling
q0512.short: "SRF is where a capacitor's parasitic inductance and capacitance resonate: 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}). Below it the part is capacitive, at it the impedance is just the ESR, and above it the part is an inductor. A 100 nF ceramic with 0.5 nH resonates around 22 MHz. It matters because it marks the useful band, so I choose values whose SRFs cover the range, and remember mounting inductance lowers the SRF on the real board."

q0513.title: When not to use decoupling capacitors
q0513.short: "Decoupling is the default, so the exceptions are specific. Don't add capacitance beyond what the datasheet allows: LDOs with ESR windows, references and op-amp outputs with capacitive-load limits. Be careful where capacitance causes problems: hot-plugged inputs where ceramic plus cable inductance overshoots toward twice the input, large capacitors that cause inrush, and bad value mixes that create anti-resonance. An

q0514.title: Rules of thumb for routing high-speed signals
q0514.short: "High-speed routing is about keeping the trace a uniform transmission line with a clean return path. I route on a solid reference plane without crossing splits, keep one width for controlled impedance, avoid stubs, minimise vias and put a ground via beside each signal via, use 45° bends, keep about three trace widths of spacing, match lengths on buses and pairs, and terminate if the trace is long compared with the ed

q0515.title: Vias in high-speed traces
q0515.short: "I avoid vias on fast signals where I can, because each one adds around 1 nH of series inductance, a few tenths of a picofarad of shunt capacitance and a stub that resonates. A 1 nH via reflects about 1% of a 1 ns edge but about 10% of a 100 ps edge, so it depends on edge rate. When I must use one I keep the count low, put a ground via next to it for the return current, shorten or back-drill the stub, and make the tw

q0516.title: Shape of high-speed traces: bends and widths
q0516.short: "Straight where possible, and 45° mitres or curves when they have to turn, with constant width, no stubs and no acute angles. A 90° corner puts extra copper over the plane, which is a little capacitance and a small impedance dip. For a 50 Ω line that's around ten femtofarads, so well under a percent of reflection for a 100 ps edge, mostly negligible below several GHz. It costs nothing to route it right, though, and i

q0517.title: Serpentining for bus synchronization
q0517.short: "Serpentining means adding zig-zag length to the shorter traces in a group so that all the signals arrive within the timing budget. In a clocked bus the receiver samples data relative to a clock or strobe, so skew eats directly into setup and hold. On FR-4 it's about 6 ps per millimetre, so a few mm of mismatch is tens of ps. I match delay rather than length, keep meander legs at least three or four trace widths apar

q0518.title: Differential pair and its tradeoffs
q0518.short: "A differential pair is two complementary traces where the data is the voltage difference between them. Noise that hits both lines equally is common-mode and gets subtracted out, the opposite currents make the pair radiate less, and you get a bigger signal difference for a given swing. The costs are double the pins and traces, strict length matching and constant spacing, differential termination, and the fact that an

q0519.title: Routing differential pairs: layout guidelines
q0519.short: "I route the two traces as one object: same layer, constant spacing set by the stackup for the target impedance, matched length, identical vias and symmetric bends, over a continuous reference plane. The big differences from single-ended routing are that matching is within the pair and done locally at each bend or via, spacing sets the impedance, and there should be no stubs or one-sided obstacles. Anything asymmetri

q0520.title: Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix
q0520.short: "If the two lines of a pair don't arrive together, part of the differential signal turns into common-mode. That's a voltage the receiver ignores, but it's also current that radiates and a signal-dependent disturbance, so skew costs eye width, adds jitter and creates EMI. The mode conversion, in S-parameter terms, goes as tan of pi times frequency times skew, so 20 ps at 5 GHz is about minus 10 dB. To avoid it I match

q0521.title: Serpentining a differential pair
q0521.short: "Serpentining a pair means adding a small jog or accordion to the shorter trace so both halves have equal delay. It matters because intra-pair skew converts differential signal to common-mode: that closes the eye and causes EMI. A 90 degree bend can leave about 0.7 mm, around 4 ps, of imbalance, so I add compensation right after the bend, with 45 degree corners, legs spaced several trace widths apart, and without pul

q0522.title: Transmission line components on a PCB
q0522.short: "A PCB transmission line is a signal trace over a reference plane with FR-4 dielectric between them. It's microstrip if it's on an outer layer, stripline if buried between two planes. Electrically it's a ladder of series R and L and shunt C and G per unit length; Z0=\sqrt{L'/C'} and delay is \sqrt{L'C'}, about 50 Ω and 6 ps/mm for a typical trace. Along the path you also have lumped pieces, vias, pads, connectors and

q0523.title: Common characteristic impedance values
q0523.short: "50 Ω single-ended is the default for RF and most PCB traces, 75 Ω for video. For differential pairs, 100 Ω is the usual value, covering Ethernet, SATA, HDMI, PCIe and LVDS, with USB at 90 Ω, and 120 Ω for CAN and RS-485. DDR has its own 40-60 Ω single-ended values. 50 Ω comes from the coax compromise between lowest loss near 77 Ω and highest power handling near 30 Ω. In practice the standard sets the target and I se

q0524.title: Changing a trace's characteristic impedance
q0524.short: "Impedance is square root of L over C, so anything that adds capacitance lowers it. Wider trace, thinner dielectric, higher dielectric constant, thicker copper or nearby coplanar ground all lower Z0; narrower, thicker dielectric and lower epsilon raise it. Width is my layout knob, dielectric height is the strongest physical one. On 0.2 mm FR-4, 0.36 mm is 50 Ω, and ±10% width moves it about 2.6 Ω. For pairs, spacing

q0525.title: Trace impedance versus frequency
q0525.short: "The ideal impedance is square root of L over C, independent of frequency. A real line has Z0=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)/(G+j\omega C)}. Below roughly a megahertz, R dominates and the trace looks like an RC line with large impedance falling as 1/\sqrt f and a −45° phase. Above that it flattens to \sqrt{L'/C'}, about 50 Ω, and stays nearly flat through GHz, with small drifts from skin effect, dielectric loss and dielectric d

q0526.title: Sources of reflection on a PCB and fixes
q0526.short: "A reflection occurs wherever the impedance seen by the wave changes: \Gamma=(ZL-Z0)/(ZL+Z0). On a board that means the driver and receiver ends, stubs and T-junctions, vias, pads, connectors, width and layer changes, and gaps in the reference plane. I minimise them by avoiding the discontinuity, making the unavoidable ones small compared with the edge, and terminating the line so any remaining reflection is absorbed

q0527.title: Interfaces in the signal path and distortion
q0527.short: "Every interface in the path (package, ball, via, AC cap, connector, cable) is a small impedance discontinuity. Each reflects part of the edge and also acts as a low-pass filter: 1 nH in a 50 Ω line adds about 22 ps of rise time, 0.5 pF about 27 ps, and they combine in RSS. Spaced discontinuities also resonate, and connectors add crosstalk and mode conversion. I minimise their number and parasitics, match impedance t

q0528.title: Substrate twice as thick: impedance impact and fixes
q0528.short: "Doubling the substrate thickness lowers the trace's capacitance to the plane and raises its loop inductance, so Z0 goes up by about 45%: a 50 Ω trace on a 0.8 mm core becomes about 73 Ω at 1.6 mm. That gives \Gamma\approx0.18 against 50 Ω. If the trace is electrically short for the edge rate I may live with it. Otherwise the best fix is to have the board remade; else I re-terminate for the real impedance, slow the e

q0529.title: Where to place termination components
q0529.short: "Series termination goes at the source, right next to the driver pin, so that driver plus resistor equals Z0 and absorbs the reflection coming back. Parallel termination goes at the far end, at or just past the last receiver, so it absorbs the wave on arrival. In both cases the stub to the resistor must be short compared with the edge. Never in the middle: a mid-line series resistor splits the line into mismatched pi

q0530.title: Routing termination components
q0530.short: "The signal should flow through the termination, not branch off to it. A series resistor sits in-line right at the driver pin; a parallel termination sits at the end of the line, after the receiver pad, with a very short tap. Its return goes to the solid plane (or a decoupled VTT) through a via right next to the pad. I use 0402-or-smaller parts, keep the stub delay under about a tenth of the rise time, and for differ

q0531.title: When external termination is needed
q0531.short: "I terminate when the trace is electrically long, meaning one-way delay above about a sixth of the rise time, and the driver and receiver aren't matched, so reflections would cause overshoot or ringing beyond the receiver's limits and noise margin. That's typical for fast clocks, multi-drop buses, differential and high-speed links, and anything with an EMI problem. I skip it for short, slow nets and for receivers wit

q0532.title: Termination networks
q0532.short: "The common termination networks are: series, a resistor at the source so R{out}+Rs=Z0, no DC power; parallel, Z0 from the end of the line to ground or V{TT}, which costs DC power; Thevenin, two resistors to the rails with parallel value Z0, which also sets a bias; AC, Z0 in series with a capacitor, no DC current; diode clamps for overshoot; and a differential resistor across a pair, often on-die. I pick by topology

q0533.title: Series versus parallel termination
q0533.short: "Series termination puts a resistor at the driver so driver plus resistor equals Z0: the line gets a half-amplitude step, it doubles at the far end, and the reflection is absorbed at the source. It costs no DC power, but only the end receiver sees a clean edge. Parallel termination puts Z0 at the end of the line: the full step arrives and is absorbed, so any receiver along the line sees it cleanly, but the driver fee

q0534.title: High-current layout rules of thumb
q0534.short: "I treat copper as a resistor: about 0.5 mΩ per square for 1 oz. So I keep high-current paths short and wide, use pours or planes, size the width from an IPC temperature-rise chart and then check the voltage drop separately. I use several vias in parallel, avoid necking down at pads, and route the return path as carefully as the supply. Then I verify with a thermal camera on the first board."

q0535.title: Power planes and shapes vs traces
q0535.short: "A power plane is a full layer of copper on one net; a shape or pour is a copper area on a layer shared with routing. They beat traces because current spreads in two dimensions, so resistance only grows with the log of distance instead of linearly, giving much less drop and heating. A plane close to its return also has very low inductance and some built-in capacitance, and it spreads heat. The catches are splits that

q0536.title: Long vs short power traces and shapes
q0536.short: "Shorter is better for power and ground. Resistance scales with length, so the drop and the heating do too: 50 mm of 1 mm trace at 5 A is 120 mV and 0.6 W. Inductance grows with length as well, about a nanohenry per millimetre, so a fast load step makes volts across it. Long traces are also better antennas and resonators. The exceptions are deliberate ones like length matching, fuses and sense elements."

q0537.title: Skinny vs thick traces and shapes
q0537.short: "For current, thicker is better: resistance and heating fall as one over the width. But not everywhere. Sense and feedback lines want to be skinny to cut coupling and antenna area, the switching node should be only as big as its current needs because it's a high dV/dt node, controlled-impedance lines are sized for impedance, and a thin neck into a small pad prevents tombstoning. So wide for current, narrow where area

q0538.title: What a thermal relief pad is
q0538.short: "A thermal relief connects a pad to a plane or pour through a few narrow spokes with a gap around the rest of the pad. It limits how fast heat leaves the pad during soldering so the joint reaches temperature and doesn't cold-solder or tombstone, and rework is easier. The cost is higher electrical and thermal resistance and less current, so I use it on ordinary pins and turn it off on high-current or thermal pads."

q0539.title: Via stitching and when to use it
q0539.short: "Via stitching is placing many vias that tie same-net copper on different layers together, usually ground. I use it to keep return paths short when a signal changes layers, to build a via fence around an RF trace or the board edge for shielding, with spacing under a twentieth of a wavelength, to share current or heat between layers, and to damp plane resonances. I avoid over-stitching, since a tight row can slot the

q0540.title: Reducing component heating on the board
q0540.short: "First dissipate less, for example a buck instead of an LDO. Then give heat a path: solder the exposed pad to a big top-layer copper area with a solid connection and an array of thermal vias into inner planes and the bottom side, use as much copper as possible, and heavier copper if needed. Spread hot parts apart, keep them near airflow and away from sensitive parts, and finally check with a thermal camera. If the bo

q0541.title: When to use a heat sink
q0541.short: "I use a heat sink when the board alone can't keep the junction under its derated limit at worst-case power and ambient. I check with Tj = Ta + P(\theta{JC}+\theta{CS}+\theta{SA}) and solve for the required sink resistance. For 3 W at 50 °C ambient and 110 °C junction I need 20 K/W total, so about 18 K/W for the sink. Before that I try dissipating less, adding copper and vias, or airflow, and I handle paste, insulati

q0542.title: Where to place the power supply
q0542.short: "Place the supply close to its load, because distance costs IR drop, loop inductance, slower transient response and noise pickup. Keep the input loop tiny and near where power enters. Account for heat, since a regulator dissipates real watts, and keep switchers away from sensitive analog, RF and crystals, because magnetic coupling falls fast with distance. Allow room for tall parts, give it a solid ground plane and t

q0543.title: Why the supply goes close to the load
q0543.short: "Distance adds resistance and inductance to the supply path. At 1 V and 10 A, 20 mm of 1 mm trace each way drops about 190 mV, and 10 nH with a 5 A step in 100 ns droops half a volt. The regulator can't compensate, because its feedback senses its own output, not the load, and the extra inductance hurts the loop. Long traces also radiate and pick up noise. So I place the regulator and output capacitors next to the loa

q0544.title: Overcurrent load on a long supply trace
q0544.short: "The voltage at the load sags by current times trace resistance, because the regulator senses locally and can't compensate, so the load may brown out. The trace dissipates I^2R and can overheat, damage the board or fuse: 1 mm of 1 oz copper fuses around 10 A in a second. The supply may hit current limit, fold back or hiccup, and a constant-power load can collapse. The fix is copper sized for fault current, a fuse or

q0545.title: Laying out power supply components
q0545.short: "I lay it out in priority order. The hot loop first: input capacitor right at VIN and ground pins, with both switches, so the loop is tiny. Then the switch node, short and compact with no vias or sensitive routing near it, then the inductor and output capacitors. The feedback divider and compensation go close to their pins on the quiet side, away from the switch node. A solid ground plane sits underneath, and the exp

q0546.title: Critical nodes of a switch-mode supply
q0546.short: "I sort nodes by mechanism. The input hot loop (input cap and both switches) carries nanosecond pulses of the full load current, so its inductance causes overshoot and EMI. The switch node swings the full input voltage, so it couples through capacitance and radiates; keep it short and small. The feedback and compensation nodes are high impedance and pick up noise, so they stay short and away from the inductor. Ground

q0547.title: Noisy nodes of a supply and how to route them
q0547.short: "The noisy nodes are the switch node, which swings the input voltage in nanoseconds, the hot loop of input capacitor and switches, which has fast pulsed current, the inductor's stray field, and the gate-drive and bootstrap loops. I keep them short, small and on one layer with no vias, over a solid ground plane, with nothing sensitive nearby or underneath. I partition the converter away from analog and RF, use a shiel

q0548.title: Routing the buck input capacitor
q0548.short: "The input capacitor closes the hot loop with the two switches, so I put a small ceramic, 0.1 to 1 µF in 0402 or 0603, right against the VIN and power-ground pins on the same layer, with short wide copper, no vias in between, and the ground via at the capacitor pad over a solid plane. A larger ceramic goes next to it and a bulk capacitor farther away. The reason is inductance: 3 nH with 5 A in 3 ns is 5 V of overshoo

q0549.title: Input capacitor placed too far away
q0549.short: "A far input capacitor puts extra inductance in the hot loop, so the switch node sees L\,di/dt overshoot and rings with the FET's output capacitance, at roughly 100 MHz. At 5 A in 3 ns, 10 nH is about 17 V of potential overshoot, which can exceed the FET rating, fail EMI, and disturb the controller. The fix is a small ceramic right at the VIN and ground pins, then shortening the loop, slowing the edge and adding a sn

q0550.title: Routing the buck switch node
q0550.short: "Short and just wide enough. The switch node carries the inductor current, so I size the width from the IPC chart, about 2 mm for 5 A, but it swings the input voltage in nanoseconds, so any extra area couples noise, since i = C\,dv/dt. So: direct from the SW pins to the inductor pad, one layer, no vias, no pour, a solid ground plane beneath, nothing sensitive nearby, bootstrap capacitor tight, and a small test pad."

q0551.title: Routing the buck inductor
q0551.short: "The inductor goes right next to the SW pins, with the switch-node copper short and small, because that end swings the input voltage in nanoseconds. The other end carries smooth ripple current, so it goes to the output capacitors with wide, short copper. The body is a magnetic field source, so I keep feedback and sensitive traces away, rotate neighbouring inductors, and prefer a shielded part. I check the vendor's gu

q0552.title: Routing the buck feedback network
q0552.short: "The feedback divider is the most sensitive node, so I put it right at the FB pin with the high-impedance tap only a few millimetres long, its bottom resistor on the quiet analog ground, and the whole thing on the far side of the IC from the switch node and inductor. Any long run goes on the low-impedance sense line from the output, taken after the output capacitors at the load. I never route it under or beside the i

q0553.title: Routing decoupling and bulk capacitors
q0553.short: "I route decoupling as small loops: the smallest low-ESL ceramic, say 0.1 µF in 0402, goes right at the power pin on the same side, a short wide connection to the pin, and a via beside the ground pad straight to the plane. Mounting inductance is what limits it: 1.5 nH gives a 13 MHz resonance, 6 nH only 6.5 MHz. Bulk capacitors go near the regulator and power entry, on wide copper with several vias, and their ESR dam

q0554.title: Routing a current sense resistor
q0554.short: "I route it as a four-wire measurement. The load current runs through wide copper into the resistor pads, and two thin sense traces tap the inside edge of each pad, so the measurement only sees the drop across the resistor. Those two traces go to the amplifier as a short, tight differential pair over a ground plane, away from the switch node and inductor, with the small input filter right at the amplifier pins. Skip

q0555.title: Why sense traces should be short
q0555.short: "For the power copper between the resistor and the tap point, short matters because copper resistance adds to the measurement, about half a milliohm per millimetre at 1 mm wide, and it drifts with temperature. For the sense pair, resistance doesn't matter but noise does: pickup is loop area times dB/dt, and loop area is length times gap. A 50 mm pair with a 0.2 mm gap near a 5 amp, 20 ns edge can pick up tens of mill

q0556.title: Sense resistor far from the amplifier
q0556.short: "The long run is the weak point, because a millivolt-level signal picks up noise in proportion to length and the noise doesn't care how big the signal is. So I'd move the amplifier to the resistor: a gain of 50 improves signal-to-noise on the long run by 34 dB, and I send a volt-level, low-impedance signal, or digital data from a power monitor. If I can't, I'd route the raw pair tight, matched and over a plane, filte

q0557.title: Kelvin connection for a sense resistor
q0557.short: "A Kelvin connection uses four terminals: two to force the current and two to sense the voltage right at the resistive element. The sense wires carry almost no current, so the IR drop in the solder joints, pads and copper is outside the measurement. It's most useful below about 10 milliohms, where those parasitic resistances are a real fraction of the resistor. The costs are a more expensive or larger four-terminal p

q0558.title: Why board-level noise matters
q0558.short: "Noise at board level is mostly interference: switching regulators, fast edges and radios coupling into sensitive nodes through shared impedance, capacitance, inductance and radiation. The PCB layout sets all of those paths. The consequences are real: a millivolt of noise costs a 12-bit ADC bits, ground bounce can false trigger a digital input, in-band noise cuts radio sensitivity, and an EMC failure means a respin.

q0559.title: What is EMI?
q0559.short: "EMI is unwanted electromagnetic energy that disturbs a circuit. It has a source, a coupling path and a victim, it can be conducted along wires and grounds or radiated through the air, and it's made of differential-mode and common-mode currents. On a PCB, radiation mostly comes from current loops and from common-mode current on cables, driven by fast edges: the harmonics extend to about 1 over pi times the rise time,

q0560.title: Sources of EMI on a PCB
q0560.short: "I group sources by mechanism. Fast di/dt in loops: a buck converter's hot loop or a chip's supply loop. Fast dv/dt on conductors: the switch node and clock traces. Common-mode current on cables, which act as antennas. And transients like ESD or relay kick. Underneath many of them is a broken return path, such as a signal crossing a plane split, and parasitic ringing that moves energy up to 100 MHz or more. The usual

q0561.title: Why avoid radiated EMI
q0561.short: "Mainly four reasons. It's regulated: you can't sell a product that fails FCC or CISPR limits. It interferes with other radios, including your own, because noise in the Wi-Fi or GPS band desensitises your receiver. By reciprocity, anything that radiates well also picks up interference well. And it's a symptom of bad layout: big loops and cable common-mode current also cause ringing and crosstalk. It's very sensitive

q0562.title: Board techniques to minimize radiated EMI
q0562.short: "I attack it by mechanism. Make loops small: solid ground plane under every fast signal, no splits, ground vias at layer changes, tight decoupling and a compact switcher hot loop. Reduce the source: slow edges with series resistors or slew control, damp ringing with snubbers or gate resistors. Deal with cables: common-mode chokes or ferrites and a proper chassis bond at the connector, and keep fast traces off the edg

q0563.title: External EMI and its impact on circuits
q0563.short: "External EMI is energy from phones, radios, motors, mains transients and ESD that couples in through loops, traces and cables. A 10 V/m field at 100 MHz induces about 20 millivolts in a 10 square centimetre loop, as big as a sensor signal. Semiconductor junctions also rectify RF, so a sensor's DC reading can shift when a phone is nearby. Digital lines can glitch, and ESD or surge can reset or damage the board. So th

q0564.title: Board techniques to protect against EMI
q0564.short: "I defend in layers. At every connector: a TVS for transients with a short, wide return to chassis, a ferrite bead or common-mode choke for RF, and a small capacitor, all placed right at the connector. At the victim: an RC filter at sensitive inputs, low and balanced source impedance, short high-impedance traces. In the layout: solid planes for small loops, differential signalling, partitioning away from connectors,

q0565.title: How signals couple and how to prevent it
q0565.short: "There are four mechanisms. Conductive coupling through a shared impedance, like a common ground trace, where V = IZ or L\,di/dt. Capacitive coupling between conductors, i = Cm\,dv/dt, worst for high-impedance victims. Inductive coupling between loops, v = M\,di/dt, worst for large loops and long parallel runs. And radiation. To prevent it: separate returns and planes for common impedance, spacing and shielding for c

q0566.title: Board techniques to minimize coupling
q0566.short: "Geometry first: keep traces close to their reference plane and separate aggressor and victim by several times that height, with the 3W rule as a check; avoid long parallel runs and cross at 90 degrees. Then return paths: solid planes, separate returns for noisy and quiet circuits. For sensitive nets, a grounded, via-stitched guard. Then slow aggressor edges, lower the victim's impedance, use differential pairs, and

q0567.title: Clock and analog on adjacent layers
q0567.short: "Directly overlapping traces on adjacent layers form a parallel-plate capacitor, so the clock injects C dv/dt into the analog node: roughly 1.9 pF over 50 mm, which can put half a volt on a 10 pF node. Best fix is a ground plane between the layers. If that's not possible, cross them at 90 degrees so the overlap is a tiny square, about 250 times less capacitance, and keep them laterally separated. Then slow the clock

q0568.title: Desense: what, why, and how to avoid
q0568.short: "Desense is loss of receiver sensitivity caused by noise from elsewhere, usually the same product. In-band interference adds to the thermal noise floor, and the sensitivity loss is 10 log of one plus I over N: 3 dB when interference equals noise, 0.4 dB at 10 dB below. It costs range and throughput and can pass regulatory tests because the receiver floor is tens of dB below the limits. To avoid it: separate and shiel

q0569.title: What EMI shields are and when to use them
q0569.short: "An EMI shield is a conductive barrier, usually a soldered metal can on the PCB or a conductive enclosure, that keeps electromagnetic energy from leaving a noisy circuit or entering a sensitive one. I'd use it for RF sections, noisy sources I can't fix at the source, very sensitive analog, or to fix a compliance or desense problem. But it adds cost, height, heat and rework difficulty and leaks at seams, so I treat it

q0570.title: How EMI shields work
q0570.short: "A shield works by reflection and absorption. The metal's surface impedance is milliohms against 377 ohms for a far-field wave, so most of it reflects; what gets in is absorbed because eddy currents oppose it, decaying over a skin depth, 6.6 microns for copper at 100 MHz. Electric fields are easy to shield with any grounded conductor. Low-frequency magnetic fields are hard, because reflection is weak and thin copper

q0571.title: What EMI shields connect to, and why
q0571.short: "Board-level cans are connected to the PCB ground plane at many points around the perimeter; cable shields and enclosures are bonded to chassis with a 360 degree low-inductance connection at the connector. Shielding an electric field means giving the displacement current a path to return, so the shield has to be grounded, and at RF the connection impedance matters: 10 nanohenries is 6 ohms at 100 MHz. A floating shie

q0572.title: Where to place EMI shields
q0572.short: "I put the shield over the block that's most localised and matters most: the RF section, or a noisy source like a switching regulator or processor and memory, and sometimes sensitive analog. It sits on a closed ground ring, stitched to the plane with a via fence so the planes form the floor and walls of a cage. Anything crossing the wall gets filtered or goes through an inner layer. I keep the antenna outside, watch

q0573.title: What is a Faraday cage?
q0573.short: "A Faraday cage is a closed conductive enclosure, solid or fine mesh, that keeps external electric fields and EM waves out of its interior, and internal ones in. Free charges rearrange on the surface until the field inside the metal is zero, and for a charge-free cavity the interior field is zero too. For waves, surface and eddy currents reflect and absorb them. Holes leak in proportion to size versus wavelength, so

q0574.title: What a via is and why
q0574.short: "A via is a plated hole that electrically connects copper on different layers of a PCB. We need them because traces only run in 2-D on each layer, so signals have to drop through the stack to cross each other, reach power and ground planes, escape from BGAs, and move heat. A via isn't ideal: a typical one is about a milliohm, around 1 nH and a few tenths of a picofarad, so at high frequency I treat it as a small indu
terms: Drill size vs finished hole size

q0575.title: Connecting one signal across two layers
q0575.short: "I connect them with a via: a plated hole with pads on both layers, and I'd use the router's layer-change command to drop it. For a slow signal one through via is fine, for power I use several in parallel, and for a fast signal I add a ground via right next to the signal via so the return current can change layers too. If the stack-up allows, I'd use blind or microvias where space is tight."

q0576.title: Via types and their tradeoffs
q0576.short: "The main types are through vias, which go top to bottom and are cheapest; blind vias, which go from an outer layer to an inner one; buried vias, which connect inner layers only; and microvias, which are tiny laser-drilled vias spanning one layer, sometimes stacked. The tradeoff is cost and complexity against density and signal integrity: blind, buried and micro need extra lamination or laser steps, so I default to t

q0577.title: Vias between inner layers
q0577.short: "I'd use a buried via. It connects two inner layers, never reaches the surface, and is drilled and plated in a core before the final lamination. That saves outer-layer space and avoids a stub, but it needs sequential lamination, so it costs more and can't be inspected or reworked. If density or signal integrity doesn't justify it, a through via, possibly back-drilled, is the cheaper alternative."

q0578.title: When to use filled vias
q0578.short: "I use filled vias when a via has to sit in a solder pad, like under a BGA or QFN, because an open barrel wicks solder away and starves the joint. The fab fills the barrel with epoxy and plates copper over it so the pad is flat. I also use copper-filled vias for stacked microvias in HDI and for better thermal conduction. The cost is extra process steps, so I specify it only where it solves a problem."

q0579.title: When to use plugged vias
q0579.short: "A plugged via has its barrel blocked with soldermask or epoxy, but it isn't ground flat or plated over like a filled via. I use plugging to stop solder wicking and shorts near pads or on wave-soldered sides, to make the board airtight for vacuum test fixtures, and to avoid trapped chemicals or ingress. It's not enough for via-in-pad, which needs filled and capped, and it costs more than tenting, so I use it only whe

q0580.title: Common via failure modes
q0580.short: "The main via failures are barrel and corner cracks from Z-axis thermal expansion mismatch between FR-4 and copper, which show up as intermittent opens after thermal cycling or lead-free reflow. Next are plating voids and thin plating in high-aspect-ratio holes, interconnect separation between barrel and inner pad, annular-ring breakout, and CAF, copper migration along glass fibres between close vias in humidity. At

q0581.title: When to avoid using vias
q0581.short: "I avoid vias where their cost outweighs their convenience. On fast edges, a 1.3 nH via on a 50 ohm line can reflect up to roughly 13 percent of a 100 picosecond edge, so for multi-gigabit lanes, clocks and RF I stay on one layer or minimise layer changes, add ground vias, and remove stubs. I also avoid open vias in solder pads, vias near board edges, single vias for power, and via fields that perforate planes."

q0582.title: Vias on surface-mount pads
q0582.short: "Yes, but not open. An open via in a pad wicks solder away and gives starved joints and voids. So I either fill and cap it, use laser microvias, or move it off the pad with a short dogbone and tent it. The normal exception is the thermal pad of a QFN or power part, where I use an array of small vias, tented on the back, with a windowed paste pattern."

q0583.title: Problems from too many vias
q0583.short: "Too many vias eat routing space because each has a pad on every layer, perforate the planes so antipads merge and break return paths, add inductive bumps on signals, raise drill cost and yield loss, and add more barrels that can fail. I keep counts down, stagger vias so antipads don't line up, and use blind or microvias when density demands it."

q0584.title: Too many vias in a power plane
q0584.short: "Each via that doesn't connect to a power plane still cuts an antipad hole. Too many and the copper between holes becomes narrow necks, so resistance, IR drop and current density rise, causing hot spots; the plane inductance rises and signals referencing it lose their return path. I stagger vias, shrink antipads, keep wide copper bridges, and use heavier copper or more planes."

q0585.title: Swiss cheesing a plane
q0585.short: "Swiss cheesing is a plane so perforated by via antipads that it looks like Swiss cheese, typically under BGAs when via rows align. The copper between holes becomes narrow necks, raising resistance and inductance and creating slots that break return paths, so crosstalk and EMI worsen. I stagger vias, shrink antipads, leave copper bridges, and use fewer or blind vias."

q0586.title: Tests you can run on a PCB
q0586.short: "I test in stages: bare-board continuity and isolation, visual/AOI/X-ray after assembly, resistance of each rail to ground before power, a current-limited first power-up, then rail, sequencing and clock checks with a scope, board-level IC checks like JTAG or ID reads, functional tests, and finally validation of thermal and margin conditions. In production this becomes ICT, flying probe and functional test."

q0587.title: What you look for when testing
q0587.short: "I compare measurements to expected values and sort the findings into manufacturing defects like shorts, opens and wrong parts; design errors like wrong dividers, footprints or sequencing; and marginal behaviour like ripple, timing, ringing and heat. I check rail voltage and ripple, current, power sequencing and reset, clocks, communication, signal levels and temperature, including at voltage and temperature corners.

q0588.title: Challenges when testing PCBs
q0588.short: "The main challenges are access, since BGAs, inner layers and tiny pads hide nodes; measurement effects, because probes load the circuit and long ground leads ring; localising shorts and intermittent faults; telling hardware, assembly, firmware and setup problems apart; and doing all this at scale with fixtures and coverage. I plan test points, use proper probing, and isolate variables one at a time."

q0589.title: Common PCB failure modes
q0589.short: "I group PCB failures by origin: fabrication defects like etch shorts, plating voids and delamination; assembly defects like solder bridges, cold joints, tombstones and wrong parts; design faults like wrong footprints, undersized copper and thermal hot spots; and field wear-out like solder-joint and via fatigue from CTE mismatch, contamination and CAF, corrosion and ESD. Symptoms such as rail shorts, intermittent ope

q0590.title: Testing ICs at board level
q0590.short: "I use a ladder: confirm supply, ground, reset, clock and strap pins at the IC; check supply current and temperature; use diode-mode checks on pins for a damage signature; read the ID register over I2C or SPI; use JTAG boundary scan where available; program and read back or run self-tests; and compare with a known-good board. A successful ID read proves the part and its solder joints work in the circuit."

q0591.title: Testing components on a board
q0591.short: "On a board a meter measures everything across the part, so a 10 k resistor with a 10 k path reads 5 k. I lift a leg or infer from powered voltages and currents; ICT uses guarding. Capacitors get shorts and LCR/ESR checks; diodes and LEDs diode-mode; transistors junction and bias checks; crystals via a low-capacitance probe or buffered output; regulators under load; and low-value shunts with 4-wire measurement."

q0592.title: Test plan for a board with x
q0592.short: "I'd first ask what x is, its specs and hazards, and whether it's a prototype or production. Then I'd decompose the block diagram and test in layers: unpowered checks, current-limited power-up with rail, ripple and sequencing checks, each block with known stimuli, the full system against numeric specs, then corners and fault injection. For production I'd add test points and a fixture. I'd adapt the instruments to x:

q0593.title: PCB fabrication process steps
q0593.short: "A PCB starts as copper-clad fiberglass. Inner layers are patterned with photoresist and etched, then stacked with prepreg and laminated under heat and pressure. Holes are drilled and plated to connect the layers, the outer layers are patterned and etched, solder mask and silkscreen go on, a surface finish like ENIG or HASL protects the pads, and the boards are routed out of the panel and electrically tested for open

q0594.title: What is panelization
q0594.short: "Panelization is arranging several boards in one panel so they're fabricated and assembled together. Rails add conveyor grip, tooling holes and fiducials, which makes small or odd-shaped boards easy to run through paste print, pick-and-place and reflow, and it cuts cost per board. The boards are held with V-scores or with tabs and mousebites, and then broken apart at the end. I keep sensitive parts like ceramic caps

q0595.title: Mousebites on PCB panels
q0595.short: "Mousebites are rows of small, non-plated drilled holes through the narrow tabs that hold a routed board in a panel. They perforate the tab so it snaps cleanly where I want it when I break the board out. They're used for odd shapes where V-score can't work. The trade-off is a small stub on the edge, so I keep parts and copper clear of the tabs and make sure the stub doesn't interfere with the enclosure."

q0596.title: Fiducials on a PCB
q0596.short: "Fiducials are alignment marks on a board, typically a 1 mm bare-copper dot with a clear mask opening around it, that a camera uses to find the real position of the board. The paste printer, pick-and-place and AOI use them to correct for offset, rotation and scale. Global fiducials on the panel or board corners fix the whole board, and local ones near fine-pitch parts refine placement of that part. They need clean co

q0597.title: PCB manufacturing and assembly flow
q0597.short: "A typical SMT line prints solder paste through a stencil, inspects the paste, places components with a pick-and-place machine, then sends the board through a reflow oven that melts the paste into joints, followed by AOI. Double-sided boards are flipped and repeated, through-hole parts are soldered by wave, selective or hand soldering, and then the board goes through in-circuit or flying-probe test and a functional t

q0598.title: Surface-mount vs through-hole
q0598.short: "Through-hole parts have leads that go through the board and are soldered on the back; surface-mount parts sit on pads on the surface and are reflow soldered. SMT is smaller, denser, cheaper at volume because it's fully automated, and better at high frequency because it has almost no lead inductance. Through-hole is mechanically stronger and easier to prototype and rework, so I'd still use it for connectors, large po

q0599.title: How components are soldered on PCBs
q0599.short: "SMT parts are soldered by reflow: paste is printed, parts are placed, and an oven melts it. Through-hole parts are soldered by wave, selective or hand soldering. On a double-sided board you reflow one side, flip, and reflow the other, putting heavy parts on the last side or gluing them, because surface tension only holds light parts upside down. On mixed boards I'd reflow the SMT first and then do selective solderin

q0600.title: What is pick-and-place
q0600.short: "Pick-and-place is the machine that puts surface-mount components on a board. A vacuum nozzle picks a part from a feeder, usually a tape reel, a camera checks its position, and the head places it on the paste-printed pads at the programmed X, Y and rotation, using fiducials to align to the board. A centroid file from CAD tells it where each part goes. Chip shooters place passives at tens of thousands per hour; flexib

q0601.title: Optimizing pick-and-place paths
q0601.short: "It's a routing and resource-assignment problem. I'd optimise the placement order, which is like a travelling-salesman problem, using heuristics like nearest-neighbour plus 2-opt; assign feeders so frequently used and co-placed parts are close to the board and to each other; use multi-nozzle collect-and-place to cut trips; group parts by nozzle to avoid changes; and balance parts across machines so no one is the bott

q0602.title: What is reflow soldering
q0602.short: "Reflow is the oven step that solders surface-mount parts. Paste is printed on the pads, parts are placed on it, and the board travels through a multi-zone oven that follows a profile: gentle preheat, a soak to even out temperature and activate the flux, a peak around 240 to 250 °C above the solder's roughly 217 °C melting point so it wets, then controlled cooling. The profile has to fit between the solder's melting

q0603.title: What is wave soldering
q0603.short: "Wave soldering solders through-hole boards in bulk. The board's underside is fluxed, preheated, and then passes over a standing wave of molten solder, around 250 °C for lead-free, for a few seconds. Capillary action fills the holes and forms the joints. Bottom-side SMT parts have to be glued and wave-compatible, and designs need spacing, orientation and thermal reliefs to avoid bridging and poor hole fill. Few throu

q0604.title: How and when PCBs are tested
q0604.short: "Boards are tested in layers. The fab tests bare boards for opens and shorts. In assembly, SPI and AOI check paste and placement and X-ray checks hidden joints. After assembly, in-circuit or flying probe test finds opens, shorts and wrong or missing components, and functional test powers the board and checks it works. Some products get burn-in or thermal cycling too. The idea is to catch defects as early as possible

q0605.title: Testing PCBs at large scale
q0605.short: "At scale, test is a throughput and cost problem. I'd use fixtured in-circuit and fast functional test with automatic handling, test several boards or a panel in parallel, and size the number of stations from test time versus line takt. Fixtures cost thousands but run in seconds, so above some volume, around a couple of thousand boards in a typical example, they beat flying probe. Every board is serialised and logged

q0606.title: Assembly-line tests and their steps
q0606.short: "After reflow I'd expect AOI, and X-ray for BGAs, then an unpowered electrical test, in-circuit or flying probe, for shorts, opens and component values. Then a current-limited first power-up, programming the firmware and calibration, and a functional test of rails, clocks, interfaces, sensors and outputs. Mains products get a safety test like hipot, some get burn-in, and then final inspection and packing. The order i

q0607.title: Test stations on an assembly line
q0607.short: "After reflow I'd expect AOI with cameras checking part presence and solder, X-ray for BGAs, then an electrical test station: in-circuit test with a bed-of-nails fixture, or a flying probe machine. Then a programming station for firmware and serial numbers and a functional test station that powers and exercises the board. Depending on the product there's also RF calibration, hipot, and a burn-in chamber, with final i

q0608.title: Automated optical inspection (AOI)
q0608.short: "AOI is camera-based inspection of an assembled board, usually after reflow. Multi-angle lighting and cameras image each component and joint, and software compares them to a golden board or CAD rules to flag missing, shifted, rotated or tombstoned parts, bridges and bad fillets. It's fast and needs no fixture, but it only sees the surface: no hidden BGA joints, no component values, no function, so it's combined with

q0609.title: In-circuit testing (ICT)
q0609.short: "In-circuit test checks a populated board by contacting test points with a bed-of-nails fixture and measuring each component in place, using guarding so parallel paths don't corrupt the reading. It finds shorts, opens, missing or wrong parts, wrong values and reversed polarity, and it points to the exact component. It's very fast, seconds per board, but needs test points on the nets and a fixture that costs thousands

q0610.title: Functional testing (FCT) of PCBs
q0610.short: "Functional test powers up an assembled board in a fixture and exercises it like the real product: rails and sequencing, clocks, boot, communication buses, sensors with known inputs, outputs into loads and current in each mode, all compared against limits. It captures system-level faults, analog accuracy errors and firmware-hardware problems that structural tests can't see, and it's often where calibration happens. I

q0611.title: Flying probe testing
q0611.short: "Flying probe test checks a board without a custom fixture: a few motorised probes touch down on pads, vias and leads one after another and measure opens, shorts and component values, programmed straight from CAD. It's flexible, so great for prototypes, low volume and changing designs, and can reach fine features on both sides. But it takes minutes per board and can't test at speed or check real function, so above so

q0612.title: Bed-of-nails test fixtures
q0612.short: "A bed-of-nails fixture is a custom plate of spring-loaded pogo pins positioned to match the test pads on one board. A vacuum or clamshell presses the board onto all the probes at once, and the tester measures through them. It captures shorts, opens, component values and polarity for ICT, and powered and functional behaviour for FCT, in seconds. The costs are the fixture, test pads and layout constraints, mechanical

q0613.title: Designing a PCB for manufacturing
q0613.short: "I design to the factory's real capability with margin. For the fab: comfortable trace/space, annular ring and drill aspect ratio, copper pulled back from the edge, and mask dams between fine-pitch pads. For assembly: proper land patterns, courtyards, fiducials, consistent orientation, thermally balanced small passives, and filled via-in-pad only. I think about the panel and test access up front, then run DRC with th

q0614.title: Testability at high volume
q0614.short: "I'd design test access at layout time: one-sided test pads on the nets that matter, at fixture-friendly size and pitch, with boundary scan for nets I can't reach. For functional test I'd add a test mode and a simple port so the station can command, read results and program the board. Then I'd do the math, test seconds times volume gives stations, fixture cost divided by volume gives cost per board, and I'd log every

q0615.title: Component tombstoning causes and fixes
q0615.short: "Tombstoning is when a small chip component stands on one end during reflow, leaving an open. It happens when one pad's solder melts before the other, so surface tension pulls that end down and lifts the far end. Causes are unequal heating, like one pad on a plane, unequal pads or paste, misplacement and a fast profile. I'd prevent it with symmetric pads and thermal reliefs, balanced stencil apertures, accurate place

q0616.title: Designing a PCB for testing
q0616.short: "Design for test means building in controllability and observability. I give each rail, clock, reset and key signal a test pad with a nearby ground, add programming and debug connectors, series jumpers so I can power and measure blocks separately, and test modes, loopbacks or boundary scan in firmware and silicon. For the factory I put pads on one side at fixture-friendly size and pitch. I prioritise by risk and keep

q0617.title: PCB design choices for prototyping
q0617.short: "For prototypes I optimise for debuggability and changeability, not size or cost. I add test points with nearby grounds, a debug header, LEDs and spare-pin breakouts. Where I'm unsure, I add alternate footprints, trimmers and 0 Ω links so I can change values or isolate blocks without cutting traces. I use bigger, hand-solderable parts with rework room, keep rules conservative for a cheap fab, put margin on power, and

q0618.title: Ground probes and ground test points
q0618.short: "A ground probe point is a pad tied to the ground plane through vias, placed right beside a signal test point so a scope's ground can attach with a very short loop. It's needed because a probe measures tip minus ground, and a long ground lead adds inductance that rings with the probe capacitance and picks up noise. I use them next to any fast or sensitive test point and power rail. In fixtures, ground probes serve th
terms: Ground probe point / ground test point

q0619.title: What test points are and what they do
q0619.short: "A test point is a deliberate, labelled pad, loop or via on a net so something can measure or drive it. Engineers use them during bring-up and debug to probe rails and signals, factories use them for in-circuit and functional test, programming and calibration, and technicians use them for diagnosis in the field. They cost a little area and, on fast nets, some capacitance, so I place them on the nets where observabili

q0620.title: Types of PCB test points
q0620.short: "The main styles are SMD pads, which are small and fixture-friendly; through-hole loops or posts, which are easy to clip a scope onto; exposed vias for tight boards; headers and connectors for programming and debug; and RF connectors like SMA or U.FL for high-speed signals. I pick by who measures it, a fixture, an engineer or a technician, and by how fast and sensitive the net is."

q0621.title: Layout guidelines for test points
q0621.short: "Make each test point a bare, flat pad of about a millimetre or more, on one side of the board, on a grid with at least about 1.27 mm spacing, clear of tall parts and the edge, with tooling holes for alignment. Connect it in-line to the net with minimal stub, put ground pads nearby, label it on the silkscreen, and check against the factory's DFT rules. On fast nets, I keep the stub tiny or skip the pad."

q0622.title: When to use and skip test points
q0622.short: "I add test points where the information is worth the cost: rails, ground, resets, power-good, programming lines, slow buses and key analog nodes. I skip or modify them on high-speed, RF, high-impedance and oscillator nets, where the pad adds capacitance and a stub, and on nets I can already see through a connector, boundary scan or self-test. High-voltage nets need guarded points. I decide per net by value, user, al

q0623.title: Test points on high-speed or sensitive signals
q0623.short: "I avoid or special-case them on fast and sensitive nets. A pad plus stub adds roughly half a picofarad that reflects about 12% on a 50 ohm line at 100 ps edges, and the stub can resonate and close an eye. On sensitive analog nodes, pads and probes add loading, leakage and pickup. So I use in-line pads, tiny stubs with an isolation resistor, coax footprints, buffered monitors or built-in eye scan and measure at the r

q0624.title: Who and what uses test points
q0624.short: "Engineers during bring-up and validation use them with scopes and meters. In production, in-circuit and flying-probe testers, functional test stations, programmers and calibration stations contact them, driven by test software that logs by serial number. Boundary-scan controllers use the JTAG port. Afterwards, field technicians and failure-analysis engineers use them. Each user needs something different, like fixtur

q0625.title: Prioritizing test points when space is short
q0625.short: "I'd rank nets by value over cost. Value is fault likelihood times severity times how much information the pad gives that nothing else does. Cost is area, signal-integrity impact and a fixture pin. That puts ground, main rails, reset, power-good and programming at the top, then clocks, console and key analog nodes. I'd make space by sharing connector pins, using boundary scan or firmware readback, and bottom-side pad

q0626.title: Detecting, finding and root-causing a PCB short
q0626.short: "I power from a current-limited supply or check resistance to ground to detect it. To find it, inspect under magnification, then use physics: thermal camera or freeze spray for the hot spot, or force a known current and map the voltage drop along the copper, since copper is about half a milliohm per square. I bisect the net by lifting links or removing parts. For root cause I use microscope, X-ray or cross-section, a

q0627.title: Measuring signals on a PCB
q0627.short: "I pick the instrument by the quantity, DMM for DC, scope for dynamic signals, logic analyser for buses, then make sure the measurement doesn't lie. That means scope bandwidth well above the signal's knee frequency (0.35 over rise time), a probe whose resistance and capacitance don't load the node, and a short ground connection, because a long ground lead rings and picks up noise. I measure at the receiver, using tes

q0628.title: Measuring signals through test points
q0628.short: "I connect the instrument's return to the ground pad next to the test point and measure with the right tool: a DMM for DC rails, a scope with tip-and-barrel and a bandwidth limit for ripple, several scope channels for sequencing, a logic analyser for buses, and a millivolt reading across a shunt's pads for current. I can also use test points to force or inject signals. I watch for probe loading and slips, and sanity-

q0629.title: The ground loop in a measurement
q0629.short: "The ground loop is the closed loop made by the probe tip, the signal path, the ground lead and the board's return path. It has inductance, about 1 nH per mm, which rings with the probe's capacitance, and it has area, which picks up magnetic fields. It's part of the measurement, not just the board. Separately, 'ground loop' can mean multiple earth connections that carry current and inject mains hum."

q0630.title: Why the ground loop should be small
q0630.short: "Because the loop is part of the measurement. Its inductance, about 1 nH per mm, rings with the probe's capacitance (130 MHz for a 150 nH clip lead) and distorts fast edges. Its area picks up magnetic fields in proportion to area, so a loop 80 times bigger sees 80 times more noise from a nearby switch node. A longer return also shares copper with other currents and radiates and receives more. Small loop, accurate wav

q0631.title: Reducing the measurement ground loop
q0631.short: "I'd shrink the loop in order of effectiveness: remove the long clip and use a spring ground tip or tip-and-barrel; ground at the nearest quiet ground pad, which I design in next to test points with vias to the plane; use soldered leads, SMA connectors or low-capacitance active probes for fast signals; and use differential or isolated probes for floating nodes. For mains loops, one earth point or isolation, never lif

q0632.title: What PCB rework is
q0632.short: "Rework is removing, replacing or modifying parts or connections on a board that's already been assembled. Usually that's desoldering a bad component and soldering in a new one, or adding jumper wires for a design change. It needs a controlled thermal profile, flux, preheat and ESD care, because every rework cycle stresses the pads and laminate. It's a last resort that gets weighed against scrapping the board, and go

q0633.title: Describing your rework experience
q0633.short: "On my [project] board, a [part] failed, so I diagnosed it with a multimeter and thermal camera, then replaced it with a hot-air station: flux, preheat, low airflow, Kapton on the neighbours. I lifted a pad on the first attempt, patched it with a wire, and learned to wait until every joint is liquid. Afterwards I checked under the microscope, re-measured the rail, and fixed the footprint error that caused the failure

q0634.title: Types of rework on a PCB
q0634.short: "I split rework into component replacement (through-hole, SMD, or BGA/QFN with a rework station), connection changes like cut-and-jump bodge wires, population changes like swapping values or fitting DNP parts, repairs of lifted pads or traces, and cleanup of bridges or coating. Each has risks: wires add about a nanohenry per millimetre, so fine for slow signals and bad for fast ones, and every thermal cycle stresses

q0635.title: Why PCB rework is needed
q0635.short: "Rework is needed for four reasons: manufacturing defects like bridges, opens or tombstones, design errors like a wrong footprint or missing pull-up, component failures from ESD or bad lots, and changes like ECOs or obsolescence. Even a tiny per-joint defect rate adds up: 1000 joints at 50 ppm gives about 5% of boards needing rework. I try to find the root cause so we fix the process or the design, not just the board

q0636.title: Designing a board for reworkability
q0636.short: "I'd leave keepouts around BGAs and big parts so a nozzle can sit there, keep tall parts away, add thermal reliefs on plane-connected signal pins, and put alternate footprints and zero-ohm links where I expect changes. I'd keep heavy parts off the bottom under rework areas because they can fall during reheat, avoid hiding parts under BGAs, add test points to diagnose faults, and mark pin 1 and polarity clearly."

q0637.title: Thermal relief pads and rework difficulty
q0637.short: "Thermal reliefs make rework easier because a pad tied solidly to a plane sits on a heat sink; the plane carries away the heat from the iron or nozzle, so the joint struggles to reach solder liquidus. Spokes limit that heat flow. But power and ground pads often need the low-resistance connection, so reliefs get omitted there and those joints become the hardest to rework. I'd compensate with bottom preheat, a bigger t

q0638.title: Eagle, Altium, KiCad, Allegro experience
q0638.short: "I've used [tool] for [board]: library parts from datasheets, schematic with ERC, layout with design rules set to the fab's limits, DRC, then Gerbers, drill, BOM and pick-and-place. I know the others conceptually: Eagle is simple and library-centric, Altium is integrated with strong rules and collaboration, KiCad is open source with Python scripting, and Allegro is the high-end constraint-driven tool. The workflow is

q0639.title: Describing your ECAD experience
q0639.short: "I've done [N] boards in [tool], including [project], end to end: libraries from datasheets, schematic with ERC, a four-layer stackup, net classes with trace widths sized from current, USB as a 90-ohm differential pair, DRC with the fab's rules, and Gerber, drill, BOM and pick-and-place. At bring-up I found a footprint error, fixed the board with a bodge, and then fixed the library. I'm weaker on DDR and RF and want

q0640.title: Scripting and automation in ECAD
q0640.short: "My scripting is [level]. I've done [e.g. a KiCad Python script that places LEDs on a circle using x = cx + r cos θ, y = cy + r sin θ, and a BOM checker in Python that groups lines and flags missing part numbers]. The other tools have hooks too: Altium scripting and API, Eagle ULPs, Allegro SKILL. I'd run any editing script on a copy, check with DRC, and keep it in version control so releases are repeatable."

q0641.title: Design rule checks (DRC)
q0641.short: "DRC is an automated check of the PCB layout against rules: clearance between nets, minimum trace width, drill and annular ring, solder mask and silkscreen rules, board-edge distance and connectivity. I set the rules from the fab's capability sheet plus my electrical needs, and run it after every routing session. A clean DRC means it's manufacturable by those rules, not that it's correct, so I still need ERC, review

q0642.title: Common IC packages and trade-offs
q0642.short: "Packages fall into families: through-hole like DIP and TO-220, leaded SMD like SOIC and QFP, leadless like QFN with an exposed pad, area-array BGAs with balls under the package, and wafer-level or stacked packages for phones. Moving along that list gives more pins per area, lower inductance and better thermals, but harder inspection, rework and PCB routing. I choose by pin count, heat, speed and what my assembly pro

q0643.title: Surface-mount vs through-hole
q0643.short: "Surface-mount parts sit on pads and are placed by machine and reflowed, so they're small, cheap to assemble in volume, usable on both sides and have short leads and low inductance. Through-hole parts go through plated holes and are wave or selectively soldered; they're bigger and costlier to assemble but mechanically strong and good for power, so connectors and heavy parts often stay through-hole. Most boards are mi

q0644.title: Ball grid array packages and trade-offs
q0644.short: "A BGA has solder balls in a grid under the package instead of leads at the edge. It packs a lot of pins into a small area, has short, low-inductance connections, good heat flow into the board and self-aligns during reflow. The costs are hidden joints that need X-ray, rework stations and reballing, tough escape routing that can force via-in-pad and more layers at fine pitch, and thermal-cycling fatigue, worst at the

q0645.title: Die vs wafer vs package
q0645.short: "A wafer is a thin disc of silicon, usually 300 millimetres, on which hundreds of identical circuits are fabricated at once. Each rectangular copy is a die. The wafer is tested, cut into dies, and the good dies are mounted in packages, which connect the tiny die pads to board-scale balls or leads, protect the silicon, remove heat and make it solderable. Dies per wafer is roughly wafer area over die area minus edge lo

q0646.title: Process node sizes and what 3nm means
q0646.short: "A node name like 3 nm used to mean a real feature size, such as gate length or half-pitch, but since roughly the 2000s it's a marketing label for a generation. Real dimensions on a '3 nm' process are tens of nanometres, a contacted gate pitch around 45 to 50 nm and metal pitch about 20 to 30 nm, though a few features like fin or sheet thickness are a few nanometres. Density gains per node are about 1.6 to 1.8×, not

q0647.title: Package-on-package chips and trade-offs
q0647.short: "Package-on-package stacks a memory package, usually LPDDR, on top of a processor package, joined by solder balls. It saves board area and gives a very short, low-capacitance memory interface, so less delay and I/O power: 3 mm of stack versus about 25 mm of PCB trace is roughly 19 versus 156 ps. The downsides are thermal coupling since the DRAM sits on the hottest die, extra height, warpage at reflow, yield compoundi

q0648.title: PoP thermal behavior
q0648.short: "With PoP, the memory sits right on top of the SoC, so heat can't easily go up through the package top; most flows down through the balls into the board, and the DRAM gets heated from below. As a thermal circuit, an extra 15 K/W in the top path takes the SoC's junction-to-ambient from about 12.3 to 16.7 K/W, so at 3 W the SoC runs about 13 K hotter. DRAM needs faster refresh above about 85 degrees, so thermals limit

q0649.title: Which chips are PoP and why
q0649.short: "PoP is mostly for mobile application processors, the SoCs in phones and tablets, with LPDDR stacked on top, and similar compact embedded SoCs. They fit because they're area- and height-constrained, use LPDDR where a very short link saves power and timing, run at a few watts so the thermal penalty is manageable, and ship in huge volumes. Servers, desktop CPUs, GPUs and FPGAs don't use it: too much power and heat, and

q0650.title: Chip fabrication yield considerations
q0650.short: "Yield is the fraction of good units, and it multiplies across stages: line, die, assembly and test. For die yield the basic model is Poisson, Y = e^{-AD0}: with 0.1 defects per cm², a 1 cm² die is about 90% and a 6 cm² die about 55%, so area hurts exponentially. That plus fewer dies per wafer makes big dies much more expensive per good die. Designers respond with smaller dies or chiplets, redundancy, binning, design

q0651.title: Why chips can't be arbitrarily large
q0651.short: "The hard limit is the reticle: the scanner exposes about 26 by 33 millimetres, around 858 square millimetres, in one shot. The softer, economic limit is yield: it falls exponentially with area, so an 858 square millimetre die yields about 42% at 0.1 defects per cm² versus 90% at 100 square millimetres, and fewer dies fit on a wafer, so cost per good die is about 20 times higher. Workarounds: chiplets in one package

q0652.title: What are chiplets?
q0652.short: "A chiplet is a small die that is one building block of a bigger chip. You make several small dies, test them, and combine the good ones in one package so it acts like a single processor. It wins on yield, because small dies catch fewer defects, it breaks past the reticle size limit, and it lets you mix process nodes. The cost is slower, more power-hungry links between dies and harder packaging, test and cooling."

q0653.title: What are 3D chips?
q0653.short: "A 3D chip stacks active dies vertically and connects them with through-silicon vias or hybrid bonds, so signals travel tens of microns instead of centimetres. That gives much higher bandwidth and lower energy per bit, which is how HBM and stacked cache work. The trade-offs are heat, since lower dies must push heat through the others, plus harder power delivery, test and yield. 3D NAND is a related but different idea

q0654.title: What are bond wires?
q0654.short: "Bond wires are the very thin gold, copper or aluminum wires, typically 15 to 50 microns, that connect pads on the die to the package leads. A machine welds them with ball and wedge bonds. They're cheap and flexible, but a few millimetres of wire has roughly a nanohenry per millimetre of inductance and a few tenths of an ohm, so they cause ground bounce and limit high-speed and RF performance. Power pins use several

q0655.title: Thin bond wires carrying high current
q0655.short: "A single 25 micron bond wire only handles roughly an amp or so, so for high current you reconcile it by using many wires in parallel, because resistance drops as 1/n and heating per wire as 1/n squared. You also make them short, use fatter copper or aluminum wire or ribbon, or replace them with copper clips or flip-chip bumps. For vertical power MOSFETs the drain current uses the backside. The caveat is that paralle

q0656.title: What are flip chips?
q0656.short: "A flip chip is a die mounted face-down, connected to the package or board through solder bumps or copper pillars across its whole surface instead of wires from its edge. Connections are tens of microns long, so inductance and resistance are far lower, you can have thousands of I/Os, and the back of the die is free for cooling. Underfill is needed because silicon and the substrate expand differently. The cost is a fa

q0657.title: Why chip ground potential varies
q0657.short: "Ground isn't ideal. It has resistance and inductance, so current through it makes voltage. The big one is ground bounce: when many outputs switch, their current changes fast through bond wire and pin inductance, and L\,di/dt lifts the die's ground above board ground. Add IR drop in the grid and planes, shared return paths, substrate coupling and ground loops. Fix with more ground pins, decoupling at the die, slower

q0658.title: How are ICs made?
q0658.short: "ICs are built on a pure single-crystal silicon wafer by repeating a loop: deposit a film, pattern it with photolithography, etch or implant, and clean and polish. The front end builds transistors, and the back end adds copper wiring layers. Then you probe-test each die, dice the wafer, package the good dies and test again. It's done in a cleanroom because one particle can kill a die."

q0659.title: What is a wafer?
q0659.short: "A wafer is a thin, polished disc of ultra-pure single-crystal silicon, usually 300 mm across and about 0.775 mm thick, on which hundreds or thousands of identical chips are built at the same time. It's grown as a crystal ingot by the Czochralski method, sliced and polished. Dies are cut from it later. Bigger wafers mean more dies per processing step, which lowers cost per chip."

q0660.title: From wafer to packaged chip
q0660.short: "After processing, you probe-test every die on the wafer and map the good ones. Then the wafer is thinned by back-grinding, mounted on tape and diced into individual dies with a saw or laser. Good dies are attached to a lead frame or substrate, connected by wire bonds or flip-chip bumps, encapsulated in mould compound, and finished with leads or solder balls. Final test and binning sort the parts by performance befor

q0661.title: What is photolithography?
q0661.short: "Photolithography transfers a pattern to the wafer with light. You coat the wafer with photoresist, shine light through a mask or reticle, and project a reduced image onto the resist with a lens. After a bake and develop, the resist forms a stencil that you then etch through or implant through. The minimum feature is about k1\lambda/NA, so the industry uses shorter wavelengths, immersion and higher NA, going from 248

q0662.title: What is etching?
q0662.short: "Etching selectively removes material to transfer the resist pattern into the actual film. Wet etching uses liquid chemicals: cheap and selective but mostly isotropic, so it undercuts. Dry or plasma etching, reactive-ion etching, uses reactive gas plus ion bombardment to cut vertical sidewalls, which is what fine features need. The key specs are etch rate, anisotropy and selectivity to the mask and underlying layer."

q0663.title: What is atomic layer deposition?
q0663.short: "ALD builds a film one atomic layer at a time by alternating two self-limiting surface reactions with purges in between. For example, TMA reacts with surface hydroxyls until they're used up, then water restores the hydroxyls, adding about an angstrom per cycle. That gives atomic-level thickness control and perfect conformality on tall 3D structures, so it's used for high-k gate dielectrics, spacers and barriers. The

q0664.title: Printing features smaller than the wavelength
q0664.short: "Resolution isn't set by wavelength alone: it's k1\lambda/NA. With 193 nm light you push NA above 1 using water immersion, lower k1 with OPC, phase-shift masks and off-axis illumination, and then go beyond the single-exposure limit with multiple patterning, where spacers deposited by ALD and etched back divide the pitch by two or four. EUV at 13.5 nm does it in one shot for the finest layers. And node names aren't re

q0665.title: Analog versus digital signals
q0665.short: "Analog signals are continuous in time and amplitude, like a microphone voltage. Digital signals are discrete in both: sampled at intervals and quantized to a finite number of levels, usually represented as bits. An ADC converts analog to digital, adding quantization error of about LSB over root 12. Digital wins on noise immunity, because gates regenerate clean levels, and on storage and processing. Analog is still n

q0666.title: What is the Fourier Transform?
q0666.short: "The Fourier Transform rewrites a signal as a sum of sinusoids: X(f)=\int x(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}dt gives the amplitude and phase at each frequency, and the inverse transform rebuilds the signal. It matters because linear circuits act on each frequency independently, so a circuit's output spectrum is the input spectrum times its frequency response, convolution becomes multiplication, and rise time maps to bandwidth. In pra

q0667.title: Fourier Transform vs Fourier Series
q0667.short: "Fourier series is for periodic signals: a sum of sinusoids at the fundamental and its harmonics, so the spectrum is discrete lines. The Fourier transform is for aperiodic signals and gives a continuous spectrum. They're connected: a periodic signal's series coefficients are samples of one period's transform, spaced 1/T apart, and as the period goes to infinity the lines merge into the continuous transform. The FFT t

q0668.title: Sample rate needed to measure a sine wave
q0668.short: "The Nyquist criterion says more than twice the signal frequency, so for a 1 kHz sine, over 2 kS/s. That's the theoretical minimum, though: exactly 2× can sample zero crossings, and real systems need an anti-alias filter, so I'd use about 2.5 to 4×. For viewing a waveform on a scope I'd use 5 to 10× with interpolation, and for peak amplitude from raw samples the worst-case error is 1 minus cosine of pi over N, so abo

q0669.title: Nyquist rate and why it matters
