q0669.short: "The Nyquist rate is twice the signal's highest frequency, the minimum sample rate that preserves it: 40 kS/s for 20 kHz audio. The Nyquist frequency is half your actual sample rate. It matters because sampling replicates the spectrum around multiples of fs; above 2B the copies don't overlap and you can reconstruct perfectly, below it high frequencies fold down as aliasing and can't be recovered. That's why you need

q0670.title: What is aliasing?
q0670.short: "Aliasing is when a signal above half the sample rate folds back and appears as a lower frequency in the sampled data. The apparent frequency is the distance to the nearest multiple of fs: a 900 Hz tone sampled at 1 kHz looks like 100 Hz. It's irreversible, so you prevent it with an analog anti-alias low-pass before the ADC, often with oversampling. It also folds noise in, and a quick test is to change fs: aliases mo

q0671.title: What a square wave is and its properties
q0671.short: "A square wave is a periodic two-level signal that spends half of each period high and half low, so it's a 50% duty rectangular wave. For 0 to V the average is V over two and the RMS is about 0.71 V. In the frequency domain it has only odd harmonics, falling as one over n, with a fundamental of 4A over pi for a plus-minus A wave. The ideal one has infinite bandwidth because the edges are instant. Real ones have a fin

q0672.title: PWM and its characteristics
q0672.short: "PWM is a fixed-frequency rectangular wave where the duty cycle, the fraction of time it's high, carries the information. The average is duty times amplitude, so 30% of 3.3 V is about 1 V. A load or a low-pass filter does the averaging. It's efficient because the switch is either fully on or off. The key characteristics are frequency, duty cycle and resolution, average and RMS value, and the harmonics at multiples of

q0673.title: Spectrum of a square wave and pulse train
q0673.short: "A periodic pulse train has a line spectrum: a DC line equal to the average, then lines at multiples of the repetition frequency. The line heights follow a sinc envelope set by the pulse width, with the nth harmonic equal to 2V times sine of n pi D over n pi. Nulls fall at multiples of f0 over D, so a 50% square wave has only odd harmonics falling as 1 over n, and 25% duty loses every fourth. Finite rise time adds a

q0674.title: Why square waves are noisy and how to cut noise
q0674.short: "Square waves are noisy because sharp edges contain a very wide band of harmonics. On a real board those edges charge capacitance and force current spikes through inductance, which disturbs supplies and grounds, couples into neighbouring traces, and radiates from current loops. To reduce it, I'd slow the edges, since high harmonics scale as one over rise time, keep loops small over a solid return plane, decouple, fil

q0675.title: Highest frequency in real vs ideal square wave
q0675.short: "An ideal square wave has instant edges, so it contains harmonics out to infinity, falling only as one over n. A real one has a finite rise time. It still has infinitely many harmonics mathematically, but above a knee of about one over pi times the rise time they fall off at 40 dB per decade, and real drivers and traces low-pass it further. So the highest significant frequency is set by the edge, roughly 0.35 to 0.5

q0676.title: Rule of thumb for real square wave bandwidth
q0676.short: "The rule is bandwidth equals 0.35 over the 10 to 90 percent rise time. It comes from a single-pole RC: rise time is 2.2 RC, and the 3 dB bandwidth is one over 2 pi RC, so the product is 0.35. A 1 ns edge needs about 350 MHz. For spectral content the knee is often taken as 0.5 over the rise time. I use it to size scopes, probes and filters, and to see that the edge, not the clock rate, sets the bandwidth."

q0677.title: Trade-offs of sharper square-wave edges
q0677.short: "Sharper edges buy timing margin, less jitter from noise because jitter is noise over slew rate, and lower switching loss in power stages. The price is more high-frequency content: more EMI, more crosstalk, more ground bounce and supply droop, and reflections and ringing from every discontinuity, so you need controlled impedance, termination and a tighter layout. I try to use the slowest edge that still meets timing,

q0678.title: Spectrum of sharp vs slow-edged square waves
q0678.short: "Sharp and slow-edged square waves share the same fundamental and low harmonics. The sharp one falls at 20 dB per decade, one over n, all the way up. The slow-edged one follows that until a knee near one over pi times the rise time, then falls at 40 dB per decade because of the extra sinc factor, and it has nulls at multiples of one over the rise time. So high-frequency energy scales inversely with rise time: a 10 ti

q0679.title: What a differential pair is and how it works
q0679.short: "A differential pair is two wires carrying the same signal with opposite polarity, and the receiver responds to the difference between them. Noise that couples equally onto both wires is common-mode and cancels in the subtraction, while the signal, being opposite on each wire, doubles. The equal and opposite currents also keep the loop small, which lowers EMI. It's terminated across the pair, typically 100 ohms, and

q0680.title: Single-ended vs differential signals
q0680.short: "Single-ended means one wire measured against a shared ground; differential means two complementary wires and the signal is the voltage between them. Single-ended depends on the ground reference, so ground offset and noise on the wire go straight into the signal. Differential cancels anything common to both wires, tolerates ground shifts, has lower EMI because the currents cancel, and can use smaller, faster swings.

q0681.title: When differential signaling is used
q0681.short: "Differential signalling is used wherever noise, ground offset, speed or EMI matter. Long cables and different grounds: RS-485, CAN, Ethernet. High-speed links: USB, PCIe, SATA, HDMI, LVDS, where small differential swings give low EMI. Low-level analog: balanced microphone lines and sensor bridges, where the signal is tiny and noise is common-mode. And precision ADC inputs and clocks. I would not bother for short, sl

q0682.title: How differential signals improve noise immunity
q0682.short: "Noise couples about equally onto both wires of a closely routed pair, so it's common-mode, and the differential receiver subtracts it away. The receiver's common-mode rejection ratio sets how well: 60 dB turns half a volt of common-mode noise into half a millivolt. Beyond that, the signal is twice as large, the threshold is the crossing of the two wires so it doesn't depend on ground or supply, and the equal and opp

q0683.title: Common-mode voltage of a differential pair
q0683.short: "Common-mode voltage is the average of the two wires, V-plus plus V-minus over two: the part that's the same on both. The signal is the difference. In a clean link it's a DC offset the driver sets, like 1.2 volts for LVDS, and in a real system it also carries noise and ground offset. It matters because the receiver only works within a common-mode input range, its CMRR sets how much leaks through, and common-mode curr

q0684.title: Differential voltage of a pair
q0684.short: "The differential voltage is the voltage between the two wires, V-plus minus V-minus. It's the signal: positive reads as one, negative as zero, and the zero crossing is the threshold. Watch the factor of two: for LVDS the differential voltage is plus or minus 350 millivolts, 700 peak to peak, while each wire swings 350 peak to peak around a 1.2 volt common-mode. The receiver needs about 100 millivolts differential to

q0685.title: What SI/PI are and why they matter
q0685.short: "Signal integrity is whether a signal arrives intact: reflections, ringing, crosstalk, loss, jitter and ground bounce. Power integrity is whether the chips get a clean, stable supply: IR drop, ripple, and transient droop, handled by designing the power delivery network impedance below a target of allowed ripple over transient current. They are linked, because supply noise becomes jitter and shared return paths couple

q0686.title: SI/PI simulation experience
q0686.short: "[Honest version of your experience.] For example, I simulated a driver, 50 ohm transmission line and capacitive load in LTspice and checked it against the bounce diagram: with a 20 ohm source into an open line the load overshoots to 4.7 V from a 3.3 V step and rings, and adding a 30 ohm series resistor matches the source to the line and removes it. I know the limits: ideal models, no package parasitics. In a real de

q0687.title: Characterizing signal quality
q0687.short: "I check the signal at the receiver against what the receiver needs. Amplitude: levels clear the thresholds with noise margin, with limited overshoot and undershoot. Timing: rise time, skew and jitter that leave enough setup and hold margin. Shape: monotonic edges with little ringing or reflections. For serial links I use an eye diagram, eye height and width, jitter and BER. And I make sure my scope bandwidth and pro

q0688.title: Ground bounce
q0688.short: "Ground bounce is the voltage that appears on a chip's local ground when many outputs switch at once. The return current flows through package and bond-wire inductance, so V = N\,L\,di/dt lifts the die ground relative to the board. Quiet outputs glitch and input thresholds shift, causing false triggers. I reduce it by lowering the inductance, with more ground pins and a better package, or by lowering di/dt with slowe

q0689.title: Edge rate too slow vs too fast
q0689.short: "Too slow, and the edge sits near the threshold: noise turns into timing jitter or even multiple crossings, setup margin shrinks, and CMOS inputs draw shoot-through current. Too fast, and the line behaves like a transmission line so you get reflections and ringing, more crosstalk, ground bounce from the current spikes, and more EMI. So I pick the slowest edge that still meets timing, using drive strength, a series re

q0690.title: Signal monotonicity
q0690.short: "Monotonic means the edge goes one way only through the receiver's threshold region, with no reversal. A rising edge shouldn't dip back toward V{IL} after it passes V{IH}. Overshoot is fine if it stays high, but ringback into the threshold window means the receiver can see multiple edges. It comes from impedance mismatches, stubs, or noise like crosstalk, and I check it at the receiver pin and fix it with termination

q0691.title: Why monotonic edges matter
q0691.short: "Receivers react to every threshold crossing, so a non-monotonic edge shows up as extra edges. On a clock or counter input that means double-clocking; on reset or interrupt lines, spurious events. It also moves the crossing time and eats setup and hold margin, and in the threshold window different parts may disagree. Data that's sampled after it settles can tolerate it, but clocks and control lines can't. I fix it wi

q0692.title: Hysteresis and Schmitt triggers
q0692.short: "Hysteresis gives a circuit two thresholds: it switches high at an upper threshold when the input rises and low at a lower threshold when the input falls. You build it with positive feedback, like feeding some of the comparator output back to the non-inverting input. It's used so a slow or noisy input switches the output once instead of chattering around a single threshold. The window must be bigger than the noise, a

q0693.title: Setup and hold times (SI view)
q0693.short: "Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge, and hold time is how long it must stay stable after it. Together they form a window around the edge. If data changes inside it, the flop may capture the wrong value or go metastable, with an output that hangs between levels before randomly settling. Setup is a period constraint, so a slower clock fixes it; hold depends only on the fastest path, so I f

q0694.title: Crosstalk
q0694.short: "Crosstalk is coupling from an aggressor trace onto a nearby victim trace through mutual capacitance, which injects Cm\,dV/dt, and mutual inductance, which induces Lm\,dI/dt. On a line it appears as near-end and far-end pulses, both growing with edge rate and coupled length, and with closeness to the neighbour relative to the ground plane. I'd reduce it with more spacing, a closer ground plane, shorter parallel runs,

q0695.title: Jitter
q0695.short: "Jitter is the deviation of edges from their ideal time positions. It's measured as period jitter, cycle-to-cycle jitter, or TIE against an ideal clock, and split into random jitter, which is Gaussian, and deterministic jitter, which is bounded. It comes from noise converted at the threshold, supply and ground noise, crosstalk, ISI, and oscillator phase noise. It matters because it eats setup and hold margin, limits

q0696.title: Ringing
q0696.short: "Ringing is oscillation after a fast edge, caused by an underdamped resonance: inductance and capacitance in the path with too little resistance. The ring frequency is 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) and the damping ratio is \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{C/L}. It comes from lumped parasitics like stubs, probe grounds and gate loops, or from reflections on an unterminated transmission line. It causes overshoot, false triggering and EMI, and I'd

q0697.title: Characterizing a differential pair's SI
q0697.short: "I'd look at three levels. The structure: differential impedance on a TDR, typically 100 ohms, and the skew within the pair. The channel: mixed-mode S-parameters on a VNA, so SDD21 for insertion loss, SDD11 for return loss, SCD21 for mode conversion, and crosstalk to neighbours. And the link: an eye diagram with eye height, width, jitter and mask margin, or a BER. The eye is the result; the others tell me why."

q0698.title: What an eye diagram shows
q0698.short: "An eye diagram overlays all the bits of a serial data stream onto one unit interval, usually by triggering a scope from the clock with persistence. The open area in the middle is where the receiver can sample safely. Eye height shows voltage margin after ISI and noise, eye width shows timing margin, UI minus jitter, and the crossings and trace thickness show duty cycle, jitter and noise. A big clean opening means a

q0699.title: Small eye: consequences and Q/BER
q0699.short: "A small eye means little margin, so noise and jitter push samples across the threshold and you get bit errors. Because noise is Gaussian, BER rises exponentially as the eye closes. It's represented by eye height and width in mV and ps or UI, by the Q factor, which is level separation over the sum of noise sigmas, and by BER, related by BER = \frac12\mathrm{erfc}(Q/\sqrt2). Q of 7 is about 10^{-12}. Bathtub curves an

q0700.title: Eye mask and mask violations
q0700.short: "An eye mask is a pass/fail template overlaid on the eye: a hexagon or rectangle in the middle plus limits above and below, defined by the standard in normalised time and voltage. A compliant signal keeps out of it. If some of the signal enters the mask, that's a violation, a hit: the signal doesn't give enough margin in voltage or timing, so it fails compliance. Where the hits are tells you whether it's jitter, nois

q0701.title: Expanding the eye
q0701.short: "First I'd see which direction the eye is closed. For vertical closure from loss and ISI, I'd add equalization: transmitter de-emphasis, a CTLE and DFE at the receiver, tuned together because over-equalizing closes the eye too. And I'd fix the channel: shorter or wider traces, lower-loss material, back-drilled vias and controlled impedance for reflections, spacing for crosstalk. For horizontal closure I'd reduce jitt

q0702.title: Keeping the eye out of the mask
q0702.short: "I'd work from the spec to a budget, simulate the channel before layout, protect the budget with controlled impedance, matched lengths, back-drilled vias, spacing and clean supplies, then measure mask margin on real hardware across corners with aggressors running. I'd aim for comfortable margin, not just a pass, and tune equalization or fix the biggest budget item if margin is thin."

q0703.title: Jitter and noise on an eye diagram
q0703.short: "Timing jitter is the horizontal spread of the eye: the crossing points blur sideways and the eye width shrinks. Amplitude noise is the vertical spread: the rails get thick and the eye height shrinks. You quantify them with histograms, a horizontal one at the crossing for jitter and a vertical one at the sampling point for noise. Gaussian fuzz is random, distinct bands are deterministic like ISI, and noise on a slope

q0704.title: Characterizing power supply quality
q0704.short: "I'd characterise a supply against the load's tolerance budget. DC: set-point accuracy, line and load regulation, temperature drift. AC: ripple at the switching frequency, broadband noise and spikes, quoted with the measurement bandwidth. Dynamic: droop and overshoot on a load step, output impedance and PSRR. Start-up: monotonic, controlled inrush, sequencing. Plus efficiency, thermal and protection. I'd measure with

q0705.title: What power supply ripple is and where it comes from
q0705.short: "Ripple is the periodic AC component on a DC rail at the switching frequency, or twice the line frequency for a rectified supply. It arises because the supply delivers energy in pulses and the output capacitor smooths them. In a buck, the capacitor absorbs the inductor's current ripple, giving \Delta IL/(8f{sw}C) plus \Delta IL\times ESR. In a rectifier the capacitor discharges between charging pulses, giving I/(2fC)

q0706.title: Power sequencing and why it matters
q0706.short: "Power sequencing is controlling the order, timing and ramp of the rails on a multi-rail board, up and down. It matters because chips have rules between their rails: ESD diodes back-power an unpowered rail, I/O above core can cause latch-up or contention, resets must release only when everything is stable, and analog and memory rails have ordering. It also matters for power integrity: starting every regulator at once

q0707.title: Supply spikes: causes and capture
q0707.short: "Spikes are brief, fast excursions on a rail caused by fast current changes through small inductances, V=L\,di/dt: converter hot loops and switch-node edges, diode recovery, capacitor ESL, simultaneous switching outputs, inductive loads, hot-plug and ESD. To capture them I use a scope with enough bandwidth and sample rate for the edge (hundreds of MHz), no 20 MHz limit, a very short ground connection or coax with a D

q0708.title: What transmission line theory is
q0708.short: "Transmission line theory models a wire as distributed series inductance and shunt capacitance, because signals take real time to travel along it. That gives a characteristic impedance Z0=\sqrt{L'/C'}, a propagation delay, and reflections wherever impedance changes, with \Gamma=(ZL-Z0)/(ZL+Z0). We need it when the trace delay is a meaningful fraction of the signal's rise time, because then ordinary node-voltage analy

q0709.title: When transmission line analysis applies
q0709.short: "I'd say transmission line analysis is needed when the line is electrically long compared with the edge: the one-way delay is more than roughly a sixth of the rise time, or the length is beyond about a tenth of a wavelength at 0.35/tr. For a 1 ns edge on FR-4 that's about 3 cm. It's edge rate, not clock rate. And the model itself is only valid for a uniform two-conductor line with a good return path and TEM-like prop

q0710.title: Characteristic impedance explained
q0710.short: "Characteristic impedance is the ratio of voltage to current in a single wave travelling down the line. It comes from the charge and magnetic field the wave front has to build per unit length, so Z0=\sqrt{L'/C'}. It depends only on geometry and dielectric, not length, and it isn't a loss: a lossless line has a real Z0. Until the first reflection comes back, the source sees the line as a resistor of value Z0, and a lo

q0711.title: Reflections and why they matter
q0711.short: "A reflection is the part of a wave that bounces back at an impedance change. The reflected fraction is \Gamma=(ZL-Z0)/(ZL+Z0): +1 for an open, −1 for a short, zero when the load equals Z0. If the source isn't matched either, the wave bounces back and forth and you see ringing and overshoot. I care because it can push a 3.3 V line to 5.5 V, cause false clock edges, close the eye and radiate EMI. You fix it by matchin

q0712.title: Sketching signals with and without reflections
q0712.short: "I'd draw voltage versus time at both ends of a 50 ohm line with 1 ns delay. Matched: the source steps to 2.75 V and the load sees the same step 1 ns later, flat. Unterminated with a 10 ohm driver: the open end doubles the wave to 5.5 V, the driver reflects it back inverted so the load drops to 1.8 V, then 4.3 V, and so on, ringing around 3.3 V with a 4 ns period, while the source end shows a staircase. Series termin
terms: Source end / load end (near end / far end)

q0713.title: What causes reflections
q0713.short: "Reflections happen wherever the impedance the wave sees changes. That's first the source and load terminations, since a CMOS input is nearly open and a driver is rarely 50 ohms. Then discontinuities along the path that change the local inductance or capacitance: vias, stubs and T-junctions, connectors and packages, width or layer changes, gaps in the reference plane, and component pads and ESD capacitance. Their siz

q0714.title: Impedance matching: what, why, when
q0714.short: "Impedance matching means making source, line and load impedances equal so there's no reflection: \Gamma=(ZL-Z0)/(ZL+Z0)=0. In RF it's also the condition for maximum power transfer. I match when the line is electrically long compared with the edge, roughly delay over a sixth of the rise time, or any time it's RF; I don't match short or slow nets, or power rails, where I want a low source impedance and a high load imp

q0715.title: How R, L and C set Z0: microstrip vs coax
q0715.short: "Per unit length, Z0=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)/(G+j\omega C)}, which at high frequency is \sqrt{L/C}: more L raises it, more C lowers it, and R and G just add loss and matter for Z0 only at low frequency. Geometry sets L and C: wider or closer to the plane means more C and less L, so lower Z0. Coax has all its field in one dielectric, so Z0=(60/\sqrt{\varepsilonr})\ln(D/d) exactly and it's shielded. Microstrip's field is p

q0716.title: Series vs parallel termination tradeoffs
q0716.short: "Series termination puts a resistor at the driver so driver plus resistor equals Z0: the line launches half the swing, the open end doubles it, and the reflection is absorbed at the source. It's cheap, uses no DC power, but only works with receivers at the end, and the full level arrives after a round trip. Parallel termination puts Z0 at the receiver and absorbs the wave on arrival, so it suits multi-drop and fast l

q0717.title: Source vs sink termination and matching
q0717.short: "Source termination matches the driver so reflections coming back are absorbed at the near end: cheap, no DC power, but the full level only appears after a round trip, so it suits one receiver at the end. Sink termination matches the receiver so the wave is absorbed on arrival: clean edges for every receiver, tolerant of driver impedance, but costs DC power and swing. Doing both is double termination, standard in RF

q0718.title: Real TL distributed RLGC model
q0718.short: "A real transmission line is a ladder of small sections, each with a series R' and L' and a shunt G' and C' per unit length. L' and C' are the stored magnetic and electric energy and set Z0=\sqrt{L'/C'} and the speed. R' is copper loss, G' is dielectric loss. The ideal line sets R' and G' to zero, so no loss, no dispersion, and a constant real Z0. A real one attenuates high frequencies more, from skin effect and diel

q0719.title: Controlling characteristic impedance
q0719.short: "Z0 is \sqrt{L'/C'}, so I steer it with geometry and material. For a PCB trace over a plane: wider trace or thinner dielectric means more capacitance and less loop inductance, so lower Z0. Higher \varepsilonr also lowers it. Thicker copper acts like a wider trace. About 0.39 mm over 0.2 mm FR-4 is roughly 50 Ω on microstrip. I'd confirm in a field solver and ask the fab for controlled impedance at ±10%. For coax it's

q0720.title: Standard termination and Z0 values
q0720.short: "50 Ω is the default for RF, test gear and single-ended PCB traces, picked as a compromise between lowest loss near 77 Ω and highest power handling near 30 Ω in coax. 75 Ω is video, close to lowest loss. Differentials are mostly 100 Ω (Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS), 90 Ω for USB, about 85 Ω for PCIe, and 120 Ω for CAN and RS-485. Terminations equal those values, so a 50 Ω line gets a 50 Ω load, and everything in the path has

q0721.title: Parasitic R, L, C and Z0
q0721.short: "Per unit length, L' is the magnetic energy of the trace-plus-return loop, C' is the electric energy between trace and plane, and together they set Z0=\sqrt{L'/C'}. R' and G' add loss and only matter for Z0 at low frequency. On a real board the bigger problem is lumped parasitics from vias, pads and connectors: a shunt capacitance dips the impedance, a series inductance bumps it, and the size of the reflection depend

q0722.title: TL loss and distortion sources
q0722.short: "Loss comes from conductor resistance (skin effect, roughness, rises as \sqrt f), dielectric loss (rises roughly with f), radiation, and energy lost to reflections at discontinuities. Because the loss grows with frequency, the line is a low-pass filter, so edges smear and ISI closes the eye. I minimize it with short, clean, impedance-controlled routing, smooth copper and low-loss laminate. Then I compensate actively:

q0723.title: Dielectric loss and frequency
q0723.short: "Dielectric loss is heat generated in the insulator because the polarization of its molecules lags the alternating field. It's captured by the imaginary part of the permittivity, and the ratio to the real part is the loss tangent, \tan\delta. On a transmission line it acts as a shunt conductance G'=\omega C'\tan\delta, so the attenuation rises about linearly with frequency: roughly \pi f\sqrt{\varepsilonr}\tan\delta/

q0724.title: TL impedance vs frequency
q0724.short: "I'd separate three things. The characteristic impedance is essentially constant with frequency above a few MHz, \sqrt{L'/C'}, with a small drift from loss. The input impedance of a finite line depends on frequency through its electrical length: matched, it's Z0 at all frequencies; unmatched, it oscillates, like an open line looking capacitive, then a short at the quarter-wave frequency, then open at the half-wave. A

q0725.title: Skin effect and where it matters
q0725.short: "The skin effect is high-frequency current crowding into a thin layer at the surface of a conductor. Induced eddy currents oppose current in the middle and reinforce it at the edges. The skin depth is \delta=\sqrt{\rho/\pi f\mu}: 66 µm at 1 MHz for copper, 2.1 µm at 1 GHz. Since the effective area shrinks, resistance rises as \sqrt f. In transmission lines it's the dominant conductor loss: R' and attenuation grow as

q0726.title: Preemphasis: why and how
q0726.short: "Preemphasis boosts the high-frequency part of the transmitted signal to cancel the low-pass response of a lossy channel, so the received signal is flat and ISI is small. In the time domain it overshoots the first bit after a transition, or equivalently de-emphasizes repeated bits. It's usually a short FIR filter in the driver, like y[n]=(1-a)x[n]-a\,x[n-1], which boosts Nyquist by 1/(1-2a). It can also be a passive

q0727.title: Signal with and without preemphasis
q0727.short: "Time domain: preemphasis keeps full swing on the first bit after a transition and lowers the following repeated bits, a shoulder after each edge. Frequency domain: the NRZ sinc-squared spectrum is multiplied by a high-pass shape, so DC drops by 6 dB while the Nyquist region stays put. Since the channel is a low-pass, the two combine to a flatter overall response, and at the receiver the isolated bits and long runs r

q0728.title: Components of an embedded system
q0728.short: "An embedded system is a processor, usually an MCU, with its memory, plus the supporting blocks that make it run: power and decoupling, a clock, reset, and a debug port. Around that are inputs, like sensors and buttons, and outputs like LEDs, motors and displays, plus communication buses such as I2C, SPI, UART, CAN and USB. Protection like ESD, a watchdog and brown-out detection makes it robust, and the firmware, inc

q0729.title: Examples of embedded systems
q0729.short: "An embedded system is a computer dedicated to one job inside a product: a microwave, a thermostat, a TV remote, a car's engine and ABS controllers, a pacemaker, a drone's flight controller, a router, a 3D printer. They differ by what constrains them: pacemakers are ultra-low power and safety-critical, ABS and engine control are hard real-time, remotes are cost-driven, routers are throughput-driven. For example, an e

q0730.title: Common microcontrollers and microprocessors
q0730.short: "Microcontrollers integrate CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals: AVR like the ATmega328P in Arduino, PIC, the low-power TI MSP430, and above all 32-bit ARM Cortex-M parts like STMicro's STM32, Nordic's nRF52, the RP2040, plus the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth ESP32. Microprocessors are CPUs needing external DRAM and an OS: Cortex-A chips such as the Raspberry Pi's Broadcom SoC, NXP i.MX, TI Sitara, and x86. The boundary is blurry, sin

q0731.title: Microcontroller vs microprocessor
q0731.short: "A microcontroller integrates the CPU, flash, SRAM and peripherals on one chip, so it runs on its own: low cost, microamp sleep, millisecond boot, deterministic timing, bare-metal or an RTOS. A microprocessor is mainly the CPU and relies on external DRAM, storage and a PMIC; it's faster and runs Linux with an MMU, but costs more, draws watts, needs a complex board, and has non-deterministic timing. Use an MCU for con

q0732.title: Blocks of an MCU and an MPU
q0732.short: "An MCU is a CPU core connected through a bus matrix to on-chip flash and SRAM, plus clock and reset logic, an interrupt controller, DMA, and peripherals: GPIO, timers, serial ports, ADC/DAC, a watchdog and a debug port, all memory-mapped. A microprocessor has the CPU cores with caches and an MMU, a DRAM controller, an interrupt controller and I/O blocks, but the DRAM, boot storage and power management are separate c

q0733.title: How an MCU talks to peripherals
q0733.short: "The firmware talks to hardware through memory-mapped registers: configure a peripheral, then read and write its data and status registers. Depending on the device, the pins are GPIO for on/off signals, ADC for analog in, timers and PWM for waveforms, or a serial bus like I2C, SPI, UART or CAN for smart peripherals. Data moves by polling, interrupts or DMA, depending on rate and latency. And electrically I make sure

q0734.title: MCU vs ASIC vs FPGA
q0734.short: "Default to an MCU: it's cheapest, quickest to develop and the most flexible, but it executes sequentially. Use an FPGA when you need massive parallelism, nanosecond deterministic latency or custom interfaces, with low NRE and reprogrammability but higher unit cost and power. Use an ASIC only at very high volume with a stable design, since NRE is in the millions and a bug means a respin. The break-even is NRE plus un

q0735.title: How to spec an MCU
q0735.short: "I derive the spec from the requirements. CPU: cycles per loop, such as 3,600 cycles per 20 kHz iteration at 72 MHz, with at most about half used. Memory: flash for code, bootloader and update image, RAM for buffers, plus 30–50% margin. Peripherals: enough timers, ADC channels and rate, buses and DMA, checked against pin muxing. Power: supply range, µA/MHz and sleep current. Then temperature grade, package, ecosystem

q0736.title: Reset signal: what and why
q0736.short: "A reset signal forces the chip into a known state: registers go to defaults, peripherals are disabled, and the CPU restarts from the reset vector. It comes from power-on reset, brown-out detection, an external active-low pin, the watchdog, or software. It matters because flip-flops power up randomly, supplies ramp slowly, and firmware can hang: reset gives a deterministic start and a way to recover, and keeps the ch

q0737.title: I2C, SPI and UART: how each works
q0737.short: "UART is two wires and no clock: start bit, data LSB first, stop bit, and both sides just agree on a baud rate. SPI is synchronous: the controller drives a clock, data goes out on MOSI and comes back on MISO at the same time, and each device gets its own chip-select, so it's fast but uses more pins. I2C is two shared open-drain wires, SCL and SDA, where each device has a 7-bit address and acknowledges every byte, so

q0738.title: I2C versus SPI differences
q0738.short: "SPI is four-plus wires, push-pull, full duplex and fast, but every extra device costs a chip-select pin. I2C is two shared open-drain wires with pull-ups, devices selected by address, half duplex and slower, but it adds ACK, multi-master and clock stretching. So I2C scales better in pins, SPI scales better in speed. I'd use I2C for many slow sensors and SPI for flash, displays, or high-rate ADCs."

q0739.title: Why SPI is faster than I2C
q0739.short: "SPI is faster for two reasons. First, its push-pull outputs drive both edges hard, so you can clock at tens of MHz. I2C's rising edge is an RC charge through a pull-up, about 0.85\,RpCb, which caps it around 100 kHz to 1 MHz. Second, I2C has more overhead: 9 clocks per byte plus an address and often a register byte. So a 14-byte read is roughly 380 µs on 400 kHz I2C versus 12 µs on 10 MHz SPI."

q0740.title: How chips talk to each other
q0740.short: "Chips talk by agreeing on four layers. Electrical: compatible logic levels and a shared ground. Timing: either a shared clock like SPI and I2C, or an agreed baud rate with start bits like UART. Framing: a chip-select or an address to say who a message is for. And meaning: usually a register map, so reading a sensor means writing a register address then reading bytes back. I pick the bus by data rate, pin count, devi

q0741.title: Asynchronous versus synchronous communication
q0741.short: "Synchronous means the sender and receiver share a clock, so the receiver samples on that clock's edge. SPI and I2C work this way. It's fast and low overhead but costs a clock wire and has setup and hold timing to meet. Asynchronous, like UART, has no clock wire: both sides agree on a baud rate, a start bit resynchronizes the receiver, and it samples each bit with its own clock. That saves a wire but adds about 20% o

q0742.title: What logic levels are
q0742.short: "Logic levels are the voltage ranges treated as 0 and 1. A driver guarantees V{OL} at most and V{OH} at least; a receiver requires V{IL} at most for a 0 and V{IH} at least for a 1, with an undefined gap in between. The link works if V{OH} is above V{IH} and V{OL} is below V{IL}; the leftover is noise margin. CMOS thresholds scale with the supply, roughly 30% and 70% of V{DD}, so mixed-voltage systems need level check

q0743.title: Common logic levels and standards
q0743.short: "The main single-ended ones are 5 V TTL and CMOS, 3.3 V LVTTL/LVCMOS, 2.5 V, 1.8 V and 1.2 V. TTL thresholds are fixed, 0.8 V and 2.0 V; CMOS thresholds are roughly 30% and 70% of the supply. So 3.3 V can drive 5 V TTL-compatible inputs but not 5 V CMOS inputs, and anything lower than the receiver's supply needs a translator. Then there are non-logic-supply standards: RS-232 at plus and minus several volts, and diffe

q0744.title: What I2C is and what it stands for
q0744.short: "I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit. It's a two-wire serial bus, SCL for the clock and SDA for data, both open-drain with pull-up resistors, invented by Philips for connecting chips on one board. Each device has an address, the controller sends START, address and read/write bit, the target ACKs, then bytes follow, each ACKed, until STOP. It's slow, 100 to 400 kHz typically, but lets many devices share two pins."

q0745.title: How I2C transactions work step by step
q0745.short: "Both lines idle high. The controller pulls SDA low while SCL is high, that's START, then clocks out a 7-bit address and a read/write bit, MSB first, changing SDA only while SCL is low. On the ninth clock the addressed device pulls SDA low to ACK. Data bytes follow, each with its own ACK; on a read the controller NACKs the last byte. A STOP, SDA rising while SCL is high, ends it. Register reads use a repeated START b

q0746.title: Interfacing an MCU with I2C targets
q0746.short: "All targets share SDA and SCL with one pull-up per line, and each is addressed by its 7-bit address. In firmware I configure the MCU's I2C peripheral for 100 or 400 kHz, then for a sensor I write the register pointer, do a repeated START with the read bit, and read the data bytes. I read an ID register first to prove the wiring and address, check for NACKs and timeouts, and use burst reads for efficiency."

q0747.title: How many targets fit on an I2C bus
q0747.short: "Addressing-wise, 7 bits give 128 codes, 16 reserved, so 112 targets; 10-bit addressing gives about a thousand. But the real limit is electrical: total bus capacitance is capped at 400 pF, and each device and each centimetre of trace adds capacitance, which slows the rise time. In practice that's around 20 to 40 devices. Beyond that, or when addresses collide, you use address pins, an I2C multiplexer or a bus buffer.

q0748.title: When an I2C bus needs multiple controllers
q0748.short: "You need multiple controllers when two devices both need to start transactions on the same bus: a main processor plus a sensor hub, a host and a charger sharing a fuel gauge, redundant controllers. I2C handles it with arbitration: both drive open-drain lines; whoever releases a 1 but reads back a 0 has lost, stops, and waits for a STOP, while the winner continues uncorrupted. SCL is wired-AND too, so clocks synchron

q0749.title: I2C address and data frames
q0749.short: "Each frame is nine clocks. The address frame is 7 address bits MSB first plus a read/write bit, with the target pulling SDA low on the ninth clock to ACK; address 0x48 becomes 0x90 for a write and 0x91 for a read. Data frames are 8 bits MSB first plus an ACK, driven by the controller on a write and by the target on a read. There's no length field: bytes continue until STOP. What the bytes mean, such as a register po

q0750.title: Changing or resolving an I2C target address
q0750.short: "Usually you don't change it in firmware; you set it in hardware. Many parts have address pins strapped to ground, supply, SDA or SCL to pick among two to eight addresses. Some parts have a programmable address register, so with identical parts you use their enable pins to bring them up one at a time and give each a new address. If neither is possible, isolate them with an I2C multiplexer or a second bus. SMBus ARP a

q0751.title: I2C ACK and NACK
q0751.short: "The ninth clock after every byte is the acknowledge. The receiver of the byte pulls SDA low for an ACK; if nobody pulls it, the pull-up leaves it high, which is a NACK. A NACK after the address means no device answered; after a written data byte it means the target rejected it; and on a read the controller deliberately NACKs the last byte so the target lets go of SDA for the STOP. EEPROMs use NACK on their address w

q0752.title: I2C clock stretching
q0752.short: "Clock stretching is a target holding SCL low to make the controller wait. Because SCL is open-drain, the bus only goes high when both release it. After releasing SCL, the controller must read it back and wait for it to actually go high before continuing. It's used by slow targets like MCUs running an ISR or sensors mid-conversion. The downside is lower throughput and, if a target never lets go, a hung bus, which is

q0753.title: I2C wire count and adding slaves
q0753.short: "I2C takes two wires, SDA and SCL, plus a shared ground, and one pull-up on each line for the whole bus. More slaves go on the same two wires and are picked by their 7-bit address, so there are no extra pins. The limits are address collisions, which you fix with address straps or an I2C mux, and the 400 pF bus capacitance limit, which you fix with smaller pull-ups, a slower clock, or a buffer."

q0754.title: Drawing an I2C bus connection
q0754.short: "I draw the master, then two shared lines, SCL and SDA, running to every slave, straight through with no crossover. At one point on the bus I add one pull-up resistor from each line to the supply, around 2.2 to 4.7 kΩ at 3.3 V. Grounds are tied together, every chip gets a decoupling cap, and address pins are strapped so no two slaves collide. The pull-ups matter because every driver is open-drain, so it can only pull

q0755.title: I2C pull-ups: why and how to size
q0755.short: "I2C drivers are open-drain, so they can only pull low; the pull-up resistor makes the high level. To size it I use a window. The minimum is (V{DD}-V{OL})/I{OL}, about 970 Ω at 3.3 V and 3 mA, so the weakest device can still pull the line low. The maximum is rise time over 0.85 times bus capacitance, about 3.5 kΩ for 300 ns and 100 pF. I pick a value inside, then check power and parallel pull-ups."

q0756.title: What is I2C bus capacitance
q0756.short: "Bus capacitance is the total capacitance from an I2C line to ground: device pins and ESD structures, PCB trace, connectors and cable. The pull-up has to charge it, so rise time is about 0.85 times Rp times Cb. The spec caps it at 400 pF for Standard and Fast mode. As a rule of thumb I use 5 to 10 pF per device and about 1 pF per centimetre of trace, and I measure the real rise time to confirm."

q0757.title: What changes I2C bus capacitance
q0757.short: "Bus capacitance goes up with everything you hang on the line. Each device pin is a few pF, the trace adds about 1 pF per centimetre and grows with width and shrinks with dielectric thickness, and connectors and cables add tens of pF. It also changes at run time: hot-plugging a module or selecting a mux channel adds or removes branches, and junction capacitance depends on voltage. I'd control it by keeping traces sho

q0758.title: Changing I2C rise time
q0758.short: "I'd clarify the direction, but assuming I want it faster: rise time is about 0.85 times Rp times Cb, so I lower Rp, down to the sink-current limit of about 970 Ω at 3.3 V, or I reduce capacitance with shorter traces, fewer devices, or a mux. If the window is closed I use a rise-time accelerator or current-source pull-up, or slow down. To make it slower on purpose I'd do the opposite, a bigger resistor or a small ser

q0759.title: Why I2C rise time is too slow
q0759.short: "Rise time is about 0.85 times Rp times Cb, so slow means too much R, too much C, or something extra in the path. On the R side: pull-up too big, only internal pull-ups, pull-up on the wrong rail, or a series resistor. On the C side: too many devices, a cable or connector, big ESD parts, or the scope probe. I measure the 30-to-70% rise, back out the capacitance from the known pull-up, and compare it with my budget."

q0760.title: I2C logic low not low enough
q0760.short: "The low level is a divider between the pull-up and the pulling-down device's on-resistance plus anything in series, so I look for what raises it: pull-ups too strong or stacked in parallel so the device sinks more than its rating, a weak driver, series resistance in the path, a ground offset between boards, contention from a push-pull pin, or a receiver on a lower supply with a lower V{IL}. I measure the low level a

q0761.title: Advantages of open-drain outputs
q0761.short: "Open-drain outputs can only pull low; a pull-up makes the high. That gives a wired-AND, so devices can share a wire without contention: if two disagree, low simply wins, instead of a shoot-through current between a PMOS and an NMOS. It's what enables I2C's arbitration, clock stretching and ACK. It also makes level mixing easy and tolerates hot-plug. The cost is a slow rising edge set by RpCb and static current when

q0762.title: Typical I2C logic levels
q0762.short: "I2C levels are ratiometric: a low is below 0.3 times the device's supply, a high is above 0.7 times, and outputs pull low to at most 0.4 V at 3 mA. The high level is just the pull-up rail. Common bus voltages are 3.3 V, 1.8 V and 5 V, so at 3.3 V the thresholds are about 1 V and 2.3 V. The gotcha is mixing supplies, such as a 5 V device needing 3.5 V to see a high, which is where level translators come in."

q0763.title: Typical I2C clock speeds
q0763.short: "The standard speeds are 100 kHz Standard, 400 kHz Fast, 1 MHz Fast-mode Plus, and 3.4 MHz High-speed, plus a 5 MHz write-only Ultra-fast mode. Most sensors run at 100 or 400 kHz. Those are ceilings set by rise time, since the pull-up has to charge the bus capacitance within 1 µs, 300 ns or 120 ns, and by the slowest device. Each byte costs nine clocks, so 400 kHz is at most about 44 kilobytes per second."

q0764.title: What SPI is and stands for
q0764.short: "SPI is Serial Peripheral Interface: a synchronous, full-duplex bus with one master and one or more slaves, using SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a chip select. It works as two shift registers in a ring: on each clock the master and slave swap one bit, so after eight clocks they've exchanged a byte. Push-pull drivers make it fast, but there's no addressing, ACK or formal standard. The master picks the slave with CS and sets the

q0765.title: How many SPI slaves
q0765.short: "SPI has no addresses, so the slave count is limited by how many chip-selects I can make and how loaded the bus gets. The simple scheme is one CS per slave, costing 3 plus N pins. If I'm short on pins I can use a decoder on the CS lines, three GPIOs for eight slaves, or daisy-chain slaves that support it so they share one CS. The electrical limits are bus loading and making sure unselected slaves tri-state MISO."

q0766.title: Interfacing with SPI slaves
q0766.short: "I read the datasheet for mode, max clock, bit order and word size, and configure the master. A transaction is: pull CS low, clock out a command, then for a write clock out data, and for a read clock out dummy bytes while capturing the reply on MISO, then raise CS. I watch the mode matching, that the reply usually arrives a byte after the command, and that CS stays low for the whole transaction with proper timing. Wi

q0767.title: Wiring an SPI bus
q0767.short: "Four wires, function to function: SCLK to SCLK, MOSI from the master's output to the slave's data input, MISO from the slave's data output to the master's input, and CS from a master GPIO to the slave's active-low select. Common ground and a decoupling cap on each chip. No pull-ups on the data lines since the drivers are push-pull, but a pull-up on CS keeps the slave deselected at boot, and series resistors help at

q0768.title: SPI daisy-chaining explained
q0768.short: "Daisy-chaining connects SPI slaves in series: MOSI goes into the first device, each device's output feeds the next input, and the last output returns on MISO, with SCLK and CS shared. The chain behaves as one long shift register, so a frame is N words of clocks with CS low, the first word ends up in the last device, and the CS rising edge latches everything at once. It saves pins and updates simultaneously, but ever

q0769.title: Typical SPI logic levels
q0769.short: "SPI defines no logic levels. It's push-pull CMOS at whatever the devices' I/O rails are, commonly 3.3 V, 1.8 V or 5 V, with thresholds around 30% and 70% of the supply from each datasheet. Each output drives its own rail, unlike I2C where the pull-up sets the high. If the two sides differ, check both directions against V{IH} and absolute maximum, and use a push-pull level translator fast enough for the clock, with M

q0770.title: Typical SPI clock speeds
q0770.short: "SPI has no standard speed grades. Sensors and ADCs typically run 1 to 10 MHz, SD cards, displays and flash 10 to 50 MHz, and fast flash 100+ MHz, with dual and quad modes multiplying throughput. The limits are the slave's datasheet max, the MCU's clock divider, signal integrity, and the MISO timing: the slave's clock-to-output delay plus round-trip propagation plus setup has to fit in half a period. At 10 MHz you ge

q0771.title: What UART is and stands for
q0771.short: "UART is Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter. It's a peripheral that serialises a byte onto a TX pin and rebuilds bytes from an RX pin. Asynchronous means there's no shared clock wire. Both ends just agree on a baud rate, like 115200, and each byte is framed with a start bit, the data bits LSB first, and a stop bit so the receiver can lock on. You wire it TX to RX, RX to TX, plus ground. It's slow but simple,

q0772.title: How UART transmits and receives
q0772.short: "Transmit: the UART loads a byte into a shift register and sends a frame, a low start bit, the data bits LSB first, optional parity, then a high stop bit, each lasting one baud period. Receive: it watches for the falling start edge, waits half a bit to confirm it and to centre itself, then samples every bit time in the middle of each bit and shifts the bits into a register. It checks parity and that the stop bit is h

q0773.title: How many wires UART needs
q0773.short: "The minimum for full duplex is three wires: TX, RX and a common ground. TX and RX are separate so each direction has its own wire. Ground is the reference for the logic levels, so I always count it. If you only need data one way you can use two. Add RTS and CTS for hardware flow control and you're at five. RS-485 variants use differential pairs instead, but it's the same framing. Compared with SPI, which needs four

q0774.title: Wiring a UART connection
q0774.short: "Cross the data lines, so each TX goes to the other device's RX, and tie the grounds. Before powering up I check logic levels match: 3.3 V to 3.3 V is direct; a 5 V TX into a 3.3 V MCU needs a level shifter or at least a divider like 1 k and 2 k. To a PC I use a USB-UART bridge at the right voltage. To a real RS-232 port I'd use a MAX3232-type transceiver, and for long noisy runs RS-485. And I double-check baud and f

q0775.title: Standard UART baud rates
q0775.short: "The classic ones are 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200, then 230400, 460800, 921600 and a megabaud or more on modern parts. 9600 is the old default for GPS and sensors, 115200 for debug consoles. Baud is bits per second, and at 8N1 each byte takes ten bits, so 115200 gives about 11.5 kilobytes per second. The numbers come from dividing a 1.8432 MHz clock, which gives exact rates; with other clocks you get a divid

q0776.title: UART device count and direction
q0776.short: "Basic UART is point to point: two devices, each wire with one driver. TX of one goes to RX of the other, and vice versa, so both directions work at once, which is full duplex. You can't just wire more TX pins together because push-pull drivers would fight. To reach more devices, use one UART each, or RS-485 with tri-state drivers and an addressing protocol like Modbus, which is half duplex, or the 9-bit address mode

q0777.title: UART: synchronous or asynchronous
q0777.short: "Asynchronous. There's no clock wire. Both sides pick the same baud rate and each uses its own oscillator. To make that work, each byte is framed by a start bit and a stop bit, so the receiver can lock onto the falling start edge and then sample each bit in the middle using its own clock. Compare that with SPI or I2C, where the clock is on a wire and the receiver samples on its edges. Async saves a wire and tolerates

q0778.title: Reading UART data without a clock
q0778.short: "The line idles high, so the receiver waits for the falling start edge. From that edge it counts its own bit times using the agreed baud rate. It waits half a bit to land in the middle of the start bit and confirms it's still low, then samples once per bit time, so every sample lands in the middle of a bit, where the signal is steadiest. After the data it checks the stop bit is high. Because it re-syncs on every star

q0779.title: UART oversampling and common rates
q0779.short: "Oversampling means the receiver samples the line at a multiple of the baud rate, typically 16x. A counter runs at 16 times the baud. When it sees the falling start edge it counts 8 ticks to reach the middle of the start bit, confirms it's low, then samples every 16 ticks, so each sample lands mid-bit. It often takes three samples around the centre and majority-votes. It's needed because there's no clock: finding the

q0780.title: What a GPIO is and does
q0780.short: "GPIO is General-Purpose Input/Output: a microcontroller pin whose direction and function you choose in software. As an output it drives high or low; as an input it reads the level, optionally with a pull-up or pull-down and edge interrupts. Typical uses: LEDs, buttons, chip selects, enables and resets, interrupt lines, driving transistors for bigger loads, and bit-banging simple protocols. The thing to remember is t

q0781.title: Meaning of "general purpose" in GPIO
q0781.short: "GP means general-purpose: the pin has no fixed job, so software decides whether it's an input or an output and what level it drives. That contrasts with dedicated pins like power, ground, reset or the crystal, which always do one thing. In practice GPIO pins are multiplexed with peripherals, so the same pad can be a GPIO, a UART TX, a PWM output or an ADC input depending on configuration. And general doesn't mean id

q0782.title: When you run out of GPIOs
q0782.short: "First I'd see if I can free pins or step up to a bigger package. Otherwise: for outputs a 74HC595 shift register turns three pins into eight outputs and chains for more; for inputs a 74HC165; for both, an I2C or SPI I/O expander like the MCP23017 gives 16 pins on two wires. For buttons and LEDs I'd use a matrix, so 8 pins read 16 keys, Charlieplexing for LEDs, or a resistor ladder on one ADC pin. A decoder gives chi

q0783.title: GPIO pin circuit and operation
q0783.short: "The pad connects to a CMOS pair: a PMOS to VDD and an NMOS to ground, driven by the output data and an enable. Data 1 turns on the PMOS and pulls high, data 0 turns on the NMOS and pulls low, and with the enable off both are off, so the pin is high impedance, which is input mode. The input goes through a Schmitt-trigger buffer into the input register. There are optional pull-up and pull-down resistors with switches,

q0784.title: Push-pull vs open-drain trade-offs
q0784.short: "The two types are push-pull and open-drain. Push-pull has a PMOS and NMOS and drives both high and low: fast edges, no static current, but two drivers on one line fight. Open-drain only pulls low and needs an external pull-up for high: the rise is an RC curve, about 400 ns for 4.7 kΩ and 100 pF, and it burns current when low. But devices can share the line safely as a wired-AND, and the pull-up can be at a different

q0785.title: Open-drain and push-pull meaning
q0785.short: "Push-pull means the output has two transistors: a PMOS that pushes the pin up to VDD and an NMOS that pulls it to ground, so it actively drives both high and low. Open-drain means there's only the NMOS, and its drain is left open: it can pull the pin low, or release it. To get a high you need an external pull-up resistor. So push-pull is fast and needs nothing else, while open-drain needs a resistor but lets several

q0786.title: When and how to size pull-ups
q0786.short: "They're needed wherever a node could be undriven: buttons and switches, tri-stated or unused inputs, open-drain lines like I2C and interrupts, and safe defaults like a MOSFET gate pull-down or an active-low enable pull-up. Sizing is two-sided. Too large and leakage, RC rise time and noise hurt, so for I2C at 400 kHz and 100 pF the pull-up is under about 3.5 kΩ. Too small and you burn V over R whenever it's pulled th

q0787.title: Typical configurable GPIO settings
q0787.short: "I think of three groups. What the pin is: mode (input, output, alternate function, analog) and which alternate function. How it drives: output type, push-pull or open-drain, initial value, drive strength and slew rate, which trade edge speed against EMI and ground bounce. How it senses: pull-up, pull-down or none, Schmitt trigger or filter, and interrupt edge, enable and wake-up. Plus housekeeping: atomic set/reset

q0788.title: Bus contention causes and cures
q0788.short: "Bus contention is two drivers actively driving the same wire to opposite levels. With push-pull outputs that's a path from supply to ground through two on-resistances: with 25 Ω each at 3.3 V, about 66 mA, and the wire sits near 1.65 V, an invalid logic level, while the output stages get hot. It happens with two masters, software bugs, a device that won't release the bus, or overlapping enables on a bidirectional bu

q0789.title: What a microcontroller timer is
q0789.short: "A timer is a hardware counter that counts clock ticks independently of the CPU. A prescaler slows the clock, and a compare or reload register tells it when to raise a flag, fire an interrupt, or toggle a pin. So with 16 MHz and a prescaler of 16 I get a 1 MHz tick, and counting to 1000 gives me an exact 1 ms event regardless of what the code is doing. The same hardware is used for PWM, measuring pulse widths with in

q0790.title: What you can do with timers
q0790.short: "Timers let you generate, measure and count in hardware. Generate: periodic interrupts for a system tick or ADC sampling, and output compare for PWM, servo pulses or one-shot strobes. Measure: input capture timestamps an edge with one-tick resolution, so I can time an echo or tach pulse. Count: clock the timer from a pin to count pulses or run a quadrature encoder. Plus watchdog and RTC variants. It's all determinist

q0791.title: Keeping accurate time in a microcontroller
q0791.short: "The counter is exact; the clock isn't. So I pick the clock for the accuracy I need: the internal RC is about 1% (14 minutes a day), a crystal is around 20 ppm (1.7 seconds a day), and a 32 kHz watch crystal into the RTC gives low-power timekeeping. In software I let the timer free-run, use auto-reload so no error accumulates, and use unsigned subtraction for elapsed times so counter wrap doesn't matter. For better t

q0792.title: How timers work and are implemented
q0792.short: "A timer is a synchronous binary counter made of flip-flops with an incrementer, a prescaler that is itself a small counter giving an enable pulse every N clocks, and comparators that check the count against a value in a register. A match sets a flag that can interrupt, toggle a pin, or reload the counter. For input capture, an external edge goes through a synchroniser and loads the count into a capture register. The

q0793.title: Timer applications in embedded systems
q0793.short: "The big ones are the system tick, which drives scheduling, debounce and timeouts; PWM for LEDs, motors, servos and converters; and input capture for measuring things like an ultrasonic echo or a tachometer to a microsecond. Timers can also trigger the ADC at an exact rate so sampling has no software jitter. And the special timers, the watchdog for fault recovery and the RTC for low-power wake-ups. In every case I ch

q0794.title: Reacting right when an external event occurs
q0794.short: "It depends on how fast 'right when' has to be. Polling the pin in the main loop is simplest but the latency is a full loop time and the CPU stays busy. The standard answer is an interrupt on the pin: the hardware jumps to an ISR in about a dozen cycles, around 170 ns on a 72 MHz Cortex-M, and the CPU can sleep in between. For hard deadlines I'd skip the CPU entirely: use timer input capture, a comparator tied to a P

q0795.title: What interrupts are
q0795.short: "An interrupt is a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause what it's doing, save its state, run a short handler called an ISR for the event, and then resume exactly where it left off. It exists so the processor doesn't have to poll for things like a button, a UART byte or a timer tick, and it can even sleep until something happens. A controller handles enables and priorities, and the main rule is to keep ISRs short.

q0796.title: How interrupts work and are implemented
q0796.short: "The peripheral sets a flag, and if its enable bit is on, signals the interrupt controller, which tracks enable, pending and priority per line and picks the winner. At the next instruction boundary the core pushes its state onto the stack, reads the handler address from the vector table, and jumps to my ISR. When it returns, hardware pops the state and resumes. In firmware I enable the peripheral interrupt, the contr

q0797.title: ISRs at the hardware and software level
q0797.short: "In hardware, the NVIC picks the interrupt, the core finishes its instruction, pushes eight registers onto the stack, reads the handler address from the vector table and switches to handler mode, about 12 cycles on a Cortex-M. Because the caller-saved registers are already saved, the ISR is a plain C function: it reads the data, clears the flag and touches volatile shared variables. Returning with the special EXCRETU

q0798.title: Interrupt applications in embedded systems
q0798.short: "Interrupts handle communication (UART/SPI/I2C bytes into ring buffers), timing (periodic ticks and fixed-rate control or ADC sampling), inputs (button or sensor data-ready pins, and waking from sleep), and faults (overcurrent, brown-out, watchdog warnings). They keep the CPU free or asleep until something happens. The limit is event rate: very fast streams or encoders go to DMA or timer hardware, and interrupts are

q0799.title: What can trigger an ISR
q0799.short: "Almost any event: an external pin edge or level, timer overflow, compare or input capture, UART or SPI or I2C events like byte received and transfer complete, ADC conversion complete or out-of-range, comparator output, DMA complete, RTC alarm, watchdog early warning, brown-out, plus software-triggered interrupts like PendSV and CPU faults. Sources can be edge or level triggered, and many flags share one vector, so t

q0800.title: Limitations of interrupts
q0800.short: "The main limits are latency and jitter, since masked sections and higher-priority ISRs delay response, so worst case matters. Events can be lost because there's only one pending bit and a long ISR misses the next event. Entry and exit overhead makes very high rates infeasible, so those need DMA or timer hardware. Shared data between ISR and main creates race conditions, nesting uses stack, and ISRs can't block or do

q0801.title: What an ISR is
q0801.short: "An ISR is the function that the hardware calls when an interrupt happens: its address is in the vector table, it takes no arguments and returns nothing, and it interrupts the main code asynchronously. A good one identifies the source, clears the flag, does the minimum work, like storing a received byte, and signals the main code through a volatile flag or buffer. It must be short, can't block, and any data it shares

q0802.title: Rules of thumb for writing ISRs
q0802.short: "Keep ISRs short, a few microseconds, since they delay everything else. Clear the flag correctly and only what you handled. Never block or call printf, malloc or anything slow or non-reentrant. Make shared variables volatile and update them atomically, ideally one writer per variable or a ring buffer. Defer the real work to main or a task by setting a flag or posting to a queue. Assign priorities by deadline, budget

q0803.title: Interrupt inside an ISR: nesting
q0803.short: "On a Cortex-M it depends on priority. A higher-priority interrupt preempts: the hardware stacks another frame, runs it, and returns into the first ISR, which is nesting. Equal or lower priority waits as pending and runs after, and the same interrupt can't preempt itself, so a repeat just pends. On AVR the global interrupt flag is cleared on entry, so no nesting unless you re-enable. To avoid problems, set priorities

q0804.title: Connecting a sensor to a microcontroller
q0804.short: "It depends on the sensor type, so I'd ask. For an analog sensor like an NTC thermistor, a divider from 3.3 V with the midpoint into an ADC pin through a small RC filter, ratiometric so supply error cancels. For an I2C sensor, SDA and SCL with 4.7 kΩ pull-ups to 3.3 V, a 100 nF decoupling cap at the sensor's VDD, and a common ground. If the sensor is 5 V, I'd divide or level-shift so I don't exceed the MCU's 3.3 V in

q0805.title: Connecting a button to a microcontroller
q0805.short: "The standard way is a pushbutton from the GPIO pin to ground with a pull-up resistor, 10 kΩ, to 3.3 V, or the MCU's internal pull-up. Open, the pull-up holds the pin high; pressed, it reads low, so it's active-low. The pull-up is needed so the pin doesn't float. Because contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, I debounce either with an RC and a Schmitt trigger input, or in software by requiring about 20 ms of stable

q0806.title: Driving LEDs, high-power and dimming
q0806.short: "For a small LED I'd use a series resistor from a GPIO: R=(V{DD}-Vf)/I, so for a 2 V red LED at 5 mA on 3.3 V that's 260 Ω, so a 270 Ω resistor. For a high-power LED the pin can't supply the current, so I'd drive a logic-level N-MOSFET low-side switch from the pin, and regulate current with a constant-current driver rather than a lossy resistor. To change brightness I'd use PWM from a timer at around 1 kHz with a gam

q0807.title: Driving a motor, isolation and speed control
q0807.short: "For one direction I'd use a logic-level N-MOSFET as a low-side switch, gate through about 100 Ω with a pull-down, and a flyback diode across the motor to catch the inductive kick, plus a bulk capacitor. For direction, an H-bridge with dead time to avoid shoot-through. For speed, PWM at around 20 kHz so the average voltage is duty times supply, ideally with encoder feedback. If isolation is needed, optocouplers or di

q0808.title: How an ADC works
q0808.short: "An ADC samples the input, holds it steady, then compares it to a reference to pick one of 2^N levels and outputs that level as a binary code. Resolution is the reference divided by 2^N, so a 12-bit ADC on 3.3 V has about 0.8 mV per step. How it finds the level depends on architecture: flash uses one comparator per level for speed, SAR does a binary search in N steps and is what most microcontrollers use, and delta-s

q0809.title: How a flash ADC works
q0809.short: "A flash ADC compares the input against every possible threshold at once. A resistor ladder makes 2^N-1 evenly spaced reference voltages, one comparator per threshold. The comparators output a thermometer code, ones up to the input level, and an encoder turns that into binary. It's the fastest ADC architecture, one comparator delay, but the comparator count, area and power double with each bit and offsets must be bel

q0810.title: How a SAR ADC works
q0810.short: "A SAR ADC is a binary search. After sampling and holding the input, it tests the MSB by setting the internal DAC to half of full scale and asking a comparator whether the input is above that. Yes means keep the bit, no means clear it. Then it tests the next bit at the new midpoint, and so on. N bits means N comparisons, using one comparator and a capacitor-array DAC, which is why it's small, low power, and the stand

q0811.title: Design an ADC
q0811.short: "I'd start with requirements: range, bandwidth, resolution, supply and power. For a 0 to 3.3 V, 10 kHz sensor with 1 mV resolution, that's 12 bits at 100 kS/s, so a SAR ADC. The sampling capacitor is sized for kT/C noise and settling, a few picofarads. The clock is about 15 cycles per conversion. I'd add a clean reference, an RC anti-alias filter, and verify it with a ramp for linearity and a sine for ENOB. If I had

q0812.title: Converting an ADC reading to volts
q0812.short: "Voltage equals the low reference plus code times the reference span divided by 2 to the N. For a 12-bit ADC on 3.3 V with ground as the low end, each code is 0.806 mV, so a reading of 3000 is 2.417 V. Some people divide by 2 to the N minus 1 instead, a 0.02% difference. Then undo any divider in front of the pin, and remember the reading is only as good as the reference."

q0813.title: What is sampling?
q0813.short: "Sampling is measuring a continuous signal at regular time intervals, giving a sequence of numbers. If the signal's highest frequency is below half the sample rate, which is Nyquist, the samples contain all the information. If not, higher frequencies fold back as aliases: a 900 Hz tone sampled at 1 kHz looks like 100 Hz. So you put an anti-alias low-pass filter ahead of the ADC and sample comfortably faster than twic

q0814.title: What is sample and hold?
q0814.short: "A sample and hold captures the input voltage at one instant and holds it constant while the ADC converts. It's a switch plus a capacitor, usually followed by a buffer. Close the switch and the capacitor tracks the input. Open it and the capacitor holds the value. It's needed because a conversion takes time, and if the input moves during it, different bits would be decided at different voltages. Real ones have droop,

q0815.title: How a sample is held steady
q0815.short: "The sample is stored as charge on a capacitor. When the switch opens, the capacitor has nowhere to dump that charge, as long as the switch is highly off and the next stage is a high-impedance buffer like a MOSFET input. What remains is leakage, which gives droop dV/dt=I{leak}/C: 1 nA on 10 pF is 0.1 mV per microsecond. To keep it steady I use a bigger capacitor, low-leakage switches and buffers, a short hold time, a

q0816.title: Design a sample and hold circuit
q0816.short: "I'd start from the spec: 12 bits, 3.3 V, 100 kHz, 1 MS/s. The circuit is an input buffer, an NMOS or transmission-gate switch, a hold capacitor and an output buffer. I'd pick 10 pF so kT/C noise is about 20 µV and droop is tiny, then size the switch so settling to half an LSB, nine time constants, fits in the track window: under 4 kΩ at 0.4 µs. I'd use a dummy switch to cancel charge injection and a bootstrapped gat

q0817.title: Fast versus slow sample-and-hold durations
q0817.short: "The sampling window must be long enough for the sampling capacitor to charge through source plus switch resistance, about nine time constants for 12 bits, or the reading is wrong, with gain error and memory of the previous channel. Too long and you waste throughput: on a 14 MHz ADC, 1.5 cycles gives 1 MS/s but 240 cycles gives 55 kS/s. On the hold side, too short means the conversion can't finish and too long means

q0818.title: Common ADC front ends
q0818.short: "The ADC front end is everything between sensor and pin. It protects the input with a series resistor and clamps, scales the signal into 0 to V{ref} with a divider or amplifier (plus a level shift if it's bipolar), and drives the pin with a low impedance or a charge-reservoir capacitor so the sampling cap can settle. It adds an RC anti-alias filter, and for particular sensors uses an instrumentation amp, a current-se

q0819.title: ADC precision and effective resolution
q0819.short: "Resolution is one LSB, full scale over 2^N: 0.806 mV for a 12-bit, 3.3 V ADC, which is 0.024% of range, with ±½ LSB quantization error. Accuracy is worse: add offset, gain error including the reference, INL and noise. In my example that's about 11 LSB worst case or 5.7 LSB RSS, so roughly 9.5 real bits. For dynamic performance, ENOB is SINAD minus 1.76, over 6.02. Calibration removes offset and gain; noise needs ave

q0820.title: How a DAC works
q0820.short: "A DAC turns an N-bit code into a voltage, V{ref}\cdot\text{code}/2^N, by summing binary-weighted contributions: the MSB is half the reference, the next a quarter, and so on. The classic circuit is an R-2R ladder: two resistor values, and the ladder to the right of every node looks like 2R, so each bit's contribution halves per stage. The output resistance is R, so you buffer it with an op-amp, and the staircase outp

q0821.title: Design a DAC
q0821.short: "I'd start from requirements: bits, range, update rate, accuracy, load. For 8 bits at 100 kS/s on 3.3 V, I'd use an R-2R ladder on eight GPIOs with an op-amp buffer. Resistor tolerance sets linearity: 1% gives up to 2 LSB of DNL and possible non-monotonicity, 0.1% keeps it near 0.2 LSB, so I'd use 0.1% resistors. The ladder settles in well under a microsecond. For slow signals, PWM plus a two-stage RC works with a ri

q0822.title: DAC precision and error budget
q0822.short: "A DAC's resolution is one LSB, the reference over 2^N: 0.806 mV for 12 bits at 3.3 V, with a maximum output one LSB below the reference. Accuracy is different: add offset, gain error, reference error and INL. With 3 mV offset, 0.2% gain, 0.1% reference and 2 LSB INL, that's about 18 LSB worst case, 10 LSB RSS, so about 8 to 9 real bits. Calibrating offset and gain leaves INL, about 11 bits. DNL above −1 LSB guarante

q0823.title: How a microcontroller stores data
q0823.short: "A microcontroller keeps program code and constants in non-volatile flash, working variables and the stack in fast volatile SRAM, and uses registers both inside the CPU and as memory-mapped peripheral controls. They all share one address space, so the CPU uses ordinary loads and stores for everything. The linker decides placement: code in flash, initialised globals copied from flash to RAM at startup, locals on the s

q0824.title: Needing more memory than the MCU has
q0824.short: "First I'd identify whether I'm short of code space, working RAM or persistent storage. Then I'd shrink what I can, and if that isn't enough, add external memory: QSPI flash for code or assets, PSRAM or external SRAM for working data, EEPROM or SD for logs, picking by capacity, bandwidth, pin count and wear. Or I'd move to a bigger part in the same family. The trade-off is always cost, board pins and speed against ef

q0825.title: Making data persist after power-off
q0825.short: "I'd store it in non-volatile memory: on-chip flash or EEPROM for settings, FRAM for data that changes constantly, and external flash or SD for large data. A coin-cell backup domain can keep a clock and a few bytes alive too. The important part is robustness: respect the endurance limit with wear levelling, and protect against power loss mid-write using CRCs, sequence numbers and alternating slots."

q0826.title: What non-volatile memory means
q0826.short: "Non-volatile memory retains its data without power, unlike SRAM or DRAM. Flash and EEPROM do it by trapping charge on an insulated floating gate, which shifts the transistor's threshold voltage; FRAM and MRAM use ferroelectric or magnetic states. The trade-off is slower, more power-hungry writes and limited endurance, so firmware lives in flash while running variables live in SRAM."

q0827.title: What ROM is
q0827.short: "ROM is read-only memory: non-volatile storage whose contents are set at manufacturing, or programmed once, and only read during operation. Physically it's a decoder plus an array of connections, essentially a hard-wired lookup table. Variants like PROM, EPROM, EEPROM and flash allow progressively easier rewriting. In an MCU, ROM typically holds the boot code that runs first after reset."

q0828.title: What an EEPROM is
q0828.short: "An EEPROM is non-volatile memory you can erase and rewrite electrically, one byte or small page at a time. Cells are floating-gate transistors written by tunnelling, so data lasts decades without power but wears out after roughly 10^5 to 10^6 writes. Typically it's a small I2C or SPI chip for calibration or settings. Writes take a few milliseconds, and you poll for completion. For big or frequently changing data, us

q0829.title: What registers are
q0829.short: "A register is a small group of flip-flops holding a few bits. There are CPU registers, which hold operands and the program counter, and peripheral registers, which are memory-mapped control, status and data locations that firmware reads and writes to control hardware, like setting a GPIO pin or starting a timer. They're split into bit fields, changed with mask-and-shift read-modify-write, and declared volatile in C.

q0830.title: Decoding register fields from hex
q0830.short: "I convert the hex to binary four bits per digit, number the bits from zero at the right, then read each field [msb:lsb] as a binary number, using shift and mask in code. For 0xB5A3 that's 1011 0101 1010 0011, so a 16-bit map with EN at bit 15, MODE at 14:12 and so on gives EN 1, MODE 3, GAIN 5, RATE 10. Then I check reserved bits, signed fields and byte order, and translate the codes into real meaning."

q0831.title: Debugging a microcontroller: hardware vs software
q0831.short: "I partition the problem. First check hardware basics with a multimeter and scope: power rails, clock, reset and boot pins. Then connect a debugger over SWD or JTAG to halt, step, and inspect registers and memory. For timing-sensitive bugs I use non-intrusive tools: GPIO toggles on a scope, a logic analyzer on buses, or trace. Challenges are intermittent hardware faults, probes disturbing circuits, and real-time soft

q0832.title: What a debugger is
q0832.short: "A debugger lets me control and inspect a program running on the microcontroller: halt it, step through code, set breakpoints, and read or modify variables, registers and memory. It's a chain of host software, a USB debug probe, a two-wire SWD or four-wire JTAG link, and dedicated debug hardware inside the chip with a few breakpoint comparators. The same link programs flash. Its limit is that halting is intrusive for

q0833.title: Debugging without a hardware debugger
q0833.short: "Without a hardware debugger I rely on observability from the outside: UART or buffered printf logging, GPIO toggles measured on a scope or logic analyzer for timing, LEDs for state, and a logic analyzer for buses. I also log events to a RAM ring buffer, save registers in a fault handler, and test algorithms on the PC. I'd pick the least intrusive method, and consider a cheap probe, since SWD adapters are inexpensive

q0834.title: Microcontroller not booting: what to check
q0834.short: "I check in dependency order. Power at the MCU pins with a scope, including every VDD and the regulator-capacitor pin. Then reset: is NRST released high? Then the clock: is the crystal oscillating, or is it falling back to the internal oscillator? Then boot pins and option bytes. Then I attach a debugger, possibly under reset, to see where the program counter is. If it connects and runs, it's firmware: vector table,

q0835.title: What an operating system is
q0835.short: "An operating system is the software layer that manages hardware resources and gives applications a clean interface to them. It handles scheduling of tasks, memory management, device drivers and I/O, and synchronisation between tasks. On a PC that's Windows or Linux; on a microcontroller it's typically a small RTOS like FreeRTOS with a scheduler and queues. It costs memory and CPU overhead, but makes concurrent, modu

q0836.title: Examples of operating systems
q0836.short: "Three families. General-purpose: Windows, macOS, Linux; mobile: Android and iOS. Embedded Linux, built with Yocto or Buildroot, for application-class processors with an MMU.
