And RTOSes for microcontrollers: FreeRTOS, Zephyr, ThreadX, VxWorks, QNX, µC/OS, RTEMS. I'd pick by hardware and requirements: FreeRTOS or Zephyr on small Cortex-M parts, Linux on Cortex-A devices, a certified commercial RTOS where safety standa

q0837.title: When an operating system is needed
q0837.short: "You need an OS when you have several concurrent activities with different timing, when a long task mustn't delay a short deadline, or when you use middleware like TCP/IP, USB or a file system that expects threads. You need Linux-class OS for memory protection and big ecosystems. Don't use one on tiny, ultra-low-power or very simple devices, where a super-loop plus interrupts is cheaper and simpler. I'd decide with R

q0838.title: What bare-metal programming is
q0838.short: "Bare-metal means firmware running directly on the hardware with no operating system. After reset, startup code initialises memory and calls main, which configures clocks and peripherals via registers and then runs a super-loop, with interrupts handling urgent events. It gives minimal overhead, full control and low power, but I must handle scheduling, drivers and concurrency myself, which gets harder as the system gr

q0839.title: Advantages of an OS over bare-metal
q0839.short: "The advantages are structure and predictable timing. Each activity becomes a task that can block on events, and priority preemption bounds the latency of urgent work regardless of how much other work exists, while a super-loop's latency grows with every feature. You also get tested mutexes, queues and timers, reusable middleware like TCP/IP and USB, portability and cleaner team boundaries. The costs are RAM for stac

q0840.title: What a real-time operating system is
q0840.short: "A real-time OS is one whose timing is predictable: real-time means meeting deadlines reliably, not being fast. It uses a priority-based preemptive scheduler, so the highest-priority ready task runs within a bounded, small latency, with short, bounded interrupt-disabled sections and deterministic primitives. Hard real-time means a miss is a failure; soft means degraded. FreeRTOS, Zephyr, VxWorks and QNX are examples.

q0841.title: What is a sensor?
q0841.short: "A sensor converts a physical quantity, like temperature, light, motion or pressure, into an electrical signal a circuit can use. The sensing element does the physics, then signal conditioning, an ADC and firmware turn that into a calibrated number. I judge a sensor by range, sensitivity, resolution, accuracy, noise, bandwidth and drift. For example, an NTC thermistor is very sensitive but nonlinear, while a thermoco

q0842.title: Applications of sensors
q0842.short: "Sensors close control loops, protect systems and improve user experience. Motor drives measure current and position, battery packs measure cell temperature and current for safety, phones use light, proximity and motion sensors for brightness, screen-off and rotation, cars use accelerometers for airbags, and factories use vibration sensors for predictive maintenance. For each one the requirement differs: bandwidth fo

q0843.title: Types of sensors and uses
q0843.short: "I group sensors by measurand. Temperature: NTC thermistors, RTDs and thermocouples. Motion: accelerometers, gyros, encoders and Hall sensors. Light: photodiodes and image sensors. Force and pressure: strain gauges in bridges and piezoresistive diaphragms. Electrical: shunts and Hall sensors for current. Each has a principle, a typical readout and a typical weakness: thermistors are nonlinear and self-heat, thermocou

q0844.title: What is a transducer?
q0844.short: "A transducer converts energy from one form to another, for example sound to voltage in a microphone or voltage to motion in a motor. A sensor is a transducer used to measure something, so it outputs an electrical signal carrying information. An actuator is a transducer in the other direction, electrical energy to physical action. So microphone and thermocouple are sensors, speaker and heater are actuators, and some

q0845.title: What is sensor fusion?
q0845.short: "Sensor fusion combines several sensors to get an estimate better than any one alone. They have complementary weaknesses: a gyro is smooth but drifts, an accelerometer is absolute for tilt but noisy. A complementary filter trusts the gyro in the short term and the accelerometer in the long term, and a Kalman filter does the same optimally by weighting each sensor by its noise variance. Other examples are GPS plus IMU

q0846.title: What is a gyroscope / accelerometer?
q0846.short: "An accelerometer measures specific force: a tiny MEMS proof mass on springs shifts when the case accelerates and the capacitance change is read out. At rest it reads 1 g up and in free fall zero, which lets it find the gravity direction. A gyroscope measures angular rate: a vibrating mass feels a Coriolis force when the chip rotates, and the sideways motion is proportional to the rate. To get an angle from a gyro yo

q0847.title: Gyro/accelerometer applications
q0847.short: "Accelerometers and gyros give a system its sense of motion and orientation. Phones use them for screen rotation, step counting and image stabilisation, drones for attitude control at kilohertz rates, cars for airbag deployment and stability control, laptops and drives for free-fall protection, and factories for vibration-based predictive maintenance. The applications differ in range, bandwidth and power: an airbag n

q0848.title: Gyroscope vs accelerometer, why pair them
q0848.short: "An accelerometer measures specific force, so at rest it gives an absolute gravity reference for tilt with no drift, but it is noisy and corrupted by real acceleration. A gyroscope measures rotation rate, so integrating it gives a smooth, responsive angle, but bias integrates into unbounded drift. Their errors are complementary, so a complementary or Kalman filter trusts the gyro at high frequency and the acceleromet

q0849.title: Position and velocity from accelerometer
q0849.short: "You integrate acceleration once for velocity and again for position, after removing gravity using the orientation. But bias integrates twice: a bias b gives position error b t squared over two, so 1 milli-g is about 18 metres after a minute. Tilt error leaks gravity into the horizontal axes, and 0.1 degrees is about 31 metres per minute. So with a consumer IMU it only works for seconds, unless you reset velocity wit

q0850.title: IMU definition and tradeoffs
q0850.short: "An IMU packages a three-axis accelerometer and gyroscope, often plus a magnetometer and barometer, to measure motion and orientation. The trade-offs: noise versus bandwidth versus power, bias stability which sets how long you can free-run, range versus resolution, bus bandwidth for the output rate, and the vibration, temperature and magnetic environment. Consumer MEMS gyros drift tens of degrees per hour or more, na

q0851.title: Measuring light: what it means
q0851.short: "Measuring light means measuring optical power on a surface, radiometrically in watts per square metre or photometrically in lux, which weights the power by the eye's response with 683 lumens per watt at 555 nm. The common sensor is a photodiode: photons create carriers and the photocurrent is proportional to power, about 0.5 A/W for silicon in the near infrared. A transimpedance amplifier converts the nanoamps to a

q0852.title: Properties of light and detection
q0852.short: "Light has several measurable properties and each has its own detector. Intensity uses a photodiode and transimpedance amplifier. Wavelength uses filters, as in colour sensors, or a grating and detector array in a spectrometer. Position uses a quadrant photodiode with difference over sum. Timing and distance use fast detectors and time of flight. Polarisation uses a rotating polariser and Malus's law. To reject ambie

q0853.title: Photoresistor vs photodiode tradeoffs
q0853.short: "A photoresistor is a light-dependent resistor, usually CdS: cheap, passive, big signal and a roughly logarithmic response that covers a wide range with a divider and an ADC, but slow, nonlinear, temperature dependent, part-to-part variable and cadmium-based. A photodiode gives current linear in light, nanosecond to microsecond speed and repeatability, but needs a transimpedance amplifier. I use LDRs for slow, rough

q0854.title: Applications of light measurement
q0854.short: "Light measurement is used passively and actively. Passive: ambient light sensors for screen brightness, camera exposure meters and colour sensors. Active: a proximity sensor pulses an IR LED and measures reflection, a smoke detector measures scattered light, and a pulse oximeter uses red and IR LEDs through the skin and the ratio of the pulsatile components to get oxygen saturation. Transmissive: encoders and light

q0855.title: Light sensing combined with other sensors
q0855.short: "I pick the quantity I want and let each sensor cover the others' blind spots. A wrist PPG uses an accelerometer as a noise reference to remove motion artefacts. A phone combines ambient light, proximity and motion to know it is in a pocket. A drone gets velocity from optical flow plus a rangefinder for height plus a gyro to subtract rotation: v equals height times flow minus gyro rate. LiDAR and cameras use an IMU t

q0856.title: How a camera works
q0856.short: "A camera focuses the scene with a lens onto a sensor made of millions of photodiodes. Each pixel converts photons to electrons during the exposure, under a Bayer color filter. The charge is converted to a voltage, amplified, which is the ISO gain, and digitized by an ADC into a raw mosaic. An image signal processor then demosaics, white-balances, denoises, tone-maps and compresses it, while an autofocus, auto-exposu

q0857.title: OIS vs EIS image stabilization
q0857.short: "OIS physically moves the lens or sensor, driven by a gyro in a closed loop with position feedback, so the image stays still on the sensor during the exposure. That removes blur in each frame, which helps photos and low light. EIS is software: it uses gyro and image data to shift and crop frames after capture, so it has no moving parts, but it can't fix blur within an exposure and it costs field of view. OIS is mostl

q0858.title: How smartphone night mode works
q0858.short: "Night mode fights photon shot noise by collecting more light than one handheld exposure could. The phone takes a burst of short frames, picks the exposure length from the gyro so it stays sharp, aligns the frames, and merges them while rejecting moving regions. Averaging N frames improves SNR by the square root of N. Then it tone-maps to brighten, denoises, and fixes white balance. OIS and fast compute make it pract

q0859.title: Techniques to reduce image noise
q0859.short: "I group it into three: more signal, quieter electronics, and cleanup. For signal, shot noise dominates so use more photons: wider aperture, longer exposure, bigger pixels or binning, and frame stacking, which gives root N. For electronics: low-read-noise sensor with correlated double sampling, clean analog supply, low gain, cooling. For fixed patterns, calibrate with dark frames, flat fields and a defect map. Then d

q0860.title: Ambient light effects on cameras
q0860.short: "Light affects a camera three ways. Level: signal scales with lux, shot noise means SNR goes as root signal, so dim scenes need longer exposures or more gain and get noisy or blurry, and autofocus struggles. Spectrum: different lights shift raw color, so white balance has to estimate the illuminant, and LED spectra can cause color errors. And time structure: mains and PWM lights flicker, which causes banding unless e

q0861.title: Characterizing camera quality
q0861.short: "I'd measure it category by category with calibrated charts and lighting: sharpness via slanted-edge MTF50, noise via SNR on flat patches at several lux, dynamic range with a step chart and a stated SNR threshold, color via ColorChecker delta E under standard illuminants, tone via OECF, and geometry for distortion, vignetting and flare. Plus speed: autofocus, shutter lag and rolling shutter. I'd test raw to isolate s

q0862.title: The camera image processing pipeline
q0862.short: "The ISP takes linear raw Bayer data through, in order: black level, defective pixel and lens shading correction, optional raw denoise, demosaic, white balance, a 3 by 3 color matrix, then non-linear gamma and tone mapping, followed by chroma denoise, luma sharpening, conversion to YCbCr and JPEG compression. The order follows the math: linear operations first, non-linear after. Statistics from the pipeline drive aut

q0863.title: What happens when you press the shutter
q0863.short: "Before the press, the sensor streams continuously over MIPI, the ISP makes the preview and statistics, and firmware closes three loops: auto exposure, autofocus and white balance, while face detection runs and a ring buffer holds recent full-resolution frames for zero shutter lag. On the press, the phone locks focus and exposure, chooses or captures frames, merges them in raw if it's HDR or night, runs the full ISP,

q0864.title: What is LiDAR
q0864.short: "LiDAR is Light Detection And Ranging: an active sensor that fires laser pulses and times how long they take to come back. Distance is c times the round-trip time over two, so 200 nanoseconds is 30 meters. By steering the beam, with a spinning head, MEMS mirror or flash illumination, it builds a 3D point cloud of the scene. It gives accurate geometry in any lighting, but has lower resolution than a camera and no colo

q0865.title: How a LiDAR measures range
q0865.short: "A controller fires a few-nanosecond laser pulse and starts a timer. The light scatters off the target and a faint return hits an avalanche photodiode. A transimpedance amplifier boosts it, a comparator or ADC detects the pulse, and a time-to-digital converter stops the timer. Range is c times the time over two: 15 centimeters per nanosecond. Pair that with the scanner's angle and you get an x, y, z point. Precision

q0866.title: Applications of LiDAR
q0866.short: "LiDAR gives direct 3D geometry in any lighting, so it's used wherever machines need to know the shape of the world: autonomous driving and driver assistance, mobile robots and safety scanners, airborne and terrestrial surveying and forestry, drones, and small depth sensors in phones for autofocus and AR. The use sets the specs: a highway car needs 150 to 250 meters of range, a vacuum robot needs cheap short range 36

q0867.title: LiDAR versus a camera
q0867.short: "A camera is passive and gives a dense 2D image with color and texture but no direct depth; LiDAR is active and gives direct, accurate 3D range, day or night. Stereo camera depth error grows as range squared, so it's meters at 100 meters, while LiDAR stays at centimeters. But cameras have far higher resolution and read signs and colors, are cheaper, and LiDAR struggles in fog and has no color. So real systems fuse th

q0868.title: Mapping 360 degrees with LiDAR
q0868.short: "For 360°, a spinning head carries a vertical stack of lasers around an axis at 10 to 20 revolutions per second, and an encoder gives each return its azimuth; range, azimuth and the channel's elevation convert to x, y, z. Alternatives are mirrors or several solid-state units stitched together. To make a map, I timestamp every point, use the IMU to deskew the motion during a scan, register consecutive scans with ICP o

q0869.title: What a LiDAR outputs: the point cloud
q0869.short: "The product is a point cloud: a time-stamped set of 3D points on the visible surfaces, produced 10 to 20 times a second, each with x, y, z, an intensity from the return strength, and usually the laser channel and return number. It's sparse and irregular, density falls with the square of range, there's no color, and it carries noise like edge artifacts and ghost points. A 64-channel unit gives around a million points

q0870.title: What limits LiDAR accuracy
q0870.short: "I'd split it into five buckets: timing electronics (jitter is rise time over SNR, plus walk, quantization, clock and temperature drift, where 100 ps is 1.5 cm); signal level set by target reflectivity, incidence angle and range; geometry like beam footprint, mixed pixels and angular encoder error; the environment: sun, fog, rain and other LiDARs; and platform effects like motion distortion and calibration. Mitigate

q0871.title: Calibrate, validate and test a sensor
q0871.short: "Calibration fixes the systematic error against a reference that's at least four times better than the sensor: offset and gain at minimum, more points if it's nonlinear. Validation checks that correction on points I did not fit, across range and temperature, against the spec. Testing stresses it with supply changes, warm-up, vibration and noise. My experiment is a sweep up and down over the full range with many sampl

q0872.title: What to validate in a sensor
q0872.short: "I group it: static accuracy (offset, gain, nonlinearity, hysteresis), noise and repeatability, dynamics (bandwidth, response time, latency), environment (temperature, supply, vibration, EMI), long-term drift, and fault behavior like saturation, startup and open-circuit. For each one I'd define a method, a reference and a pass limit. Which ones get priority depends on the application, a gyro cares about bias stabilit

q0873.title: Characterizing measurement error
q0873.short: "I take many readings against a reference and compute error as reading minus truth. The mean is the bias, which I can calibrate out. The standard deviation is the random error, which averaging reduces as one over root N until drift sets a floor. I check the histogram for Gaussian shape and outliers and plot error against time and temperature. Independent sources combine in quadrature into a total uncertainty. I then

q0874.title: Analog versus digital signals
q0874.short: "Analog signals are continuous in value and time, so the exact voltage carries the information. Digital signals are limited to a few levels, usually two, so the information is just which side of a threshold you're on. That gives you noise immunity, exact copying and easy processing, at the cost of needing ADCs and DACs and some bandwidth. And remember a digital wire is still an analog waveform: edges, ringing and noi

q0875.title: Big versus little endian
q0875.short: "Endianness is the order a multi-byte value's bytes are stored at increasing addresses. Big-endian puts the most significant byte first, so 0x12345678 is 12 34 56 78. Little-endian puts the least significant byte first: 78 56 34 12. Same number, different layout. x86, ARM-in-practice and RISC-V are little-endian, network order is big-endian. It matters whenever bytes cross a boundary, like sensor registers, packets o

q0876.title: MSB and LSB meaning
q0876.short: "The MSB is the most significant bit, the one with the largest weight, 2^{N-1} in an N-bit number, and the LSB is the least significant, weight one. Flipping the MSB changes the value by half the range, flipping the LSB by one count. The MSB is the sign bit in two's complement, an ADC's LSB is its smallest voltage step, and serial links differ in whether they send LSB or MSB first, UART LSB first and SPI usually MSB

q0877.title: Interfacing different logic levels
q0877.short: "I check each direction: the driver's guaranteed high must exceed the receiver's input-high threshold, the low must be under the input-low threshold, and nothing may exceed the receiver's absolute maximum. If that works, connect directly. If not, step down with a 5 V-tolerant input, a divider for slow signals or a translator; step up with a translator or transistor stage. Open-drain buses like I²C get a single-FET sh

q0878.title: Design a level shifter
q0878.short: "I'd ask for rails, direction, push-pull versus open-drain and speed first. For a fast or multi-bit push-pull bus I'd use a dual-supply translator IC. For a slow single signal I'd use an NMOS with the gate on the low rail and a pull-up to the high rail on the drain, inverting, with the pull-up sized from 2.2RC and the quiescent current. For open-drain buses like I²C I'd use the single-FET bidirectional shifter. On ch

q0879.title: Single-FET bidirectional level shifter
q0879.short: "One N-channel FET, gate to the low rail, source on the low-voltage side, drain on the high-voltage side, and a pull-up on each side to its own rail. Idle, Vgs is zero so it's off. If the low side pulls down, Vgs becomes the low rail and the FET pulls the high side down. If the high side pulls down, the body diode drags the source down to 0.6 V, Vgs rises above threshold, and the FET finishes the job. It's bidirectio

q0880.title: Setup and hold times
q0880.short: "Setup time is how long data must be stable before the active clock edge, and hold time is how long it must stay stable after it. They exist because the flip-flop's internal latches need time to capture the data. Violating either can capture the wrong value or put the flip-flop into metastability. Setup limits clock frequency, since the period must cover clock-to-Q plus logic plus setup, so you fix it by slowing the

q0881.title: Flip-flop versus latch
q0881.short: "A latch is level-sensitive: it's transparent while its enable is active and holds when it isn't. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples D at one clock edge and ignores the input otherwise. A flip-flop is two latches in series, master and slave, with opposite clock phases, so there's never a transparent path from D to Q. Flip-flops give simple, predictable timing; latches are smaller and allow time borrowing but p

q0882.title: How a flip-flop or latch works
q0882.short: "Feedback is the key. Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch with two stable states, so it stores a bit: set, reset, or hold, with both inputs high forbidden. Gate the inputs with an enable and tie them to D and its complement and you get a D latch, which is transparent while enabled. Put two D latches in series with opposite enables and you get a flip-flop: the master captures D while the clock is low, and at

q0883.title: Design a memory cell
q0883.short: "I'd first ask volatile or not, and speed versus density. For fast on-chip storage I'd use a 6T SRAM cell: two cross-coupled CMOS inverters hold the bit, and two NMOS access transistors on a word line connect the storage nodes to the bit lines. Write by driving the bit lines and overpowering the cell; read by precharging and sensing which line droops. Sizing is the trade-off: the pull-downs must beat the access devic

q0884.title: Why digital systems need clocks
q0884.short: "Logic takes time to settle and glitches on the way, so we need a point at which values are guaranteed valid. The clock provides it: flip-flops capture on the edge, and between edges the logic can glitch freely. That makes the design a simple state-to-next-state machine, lets us pipeline for speed, orders operations, and gives timers and protocols a time base. The costs are clock power, skew and jitter, and EMI; the

q0885.title: What happens when a clock is too fast
q0885.short: "If the clock period is shorter than clock-to-Q plus the longest logic delay plus setup, flip-flops sample before data has settled: setup violations. The longest paths fail first, so you get pattern-dependent wrong results, worse when hot or at low voltage, and possibly metastability. Power and heat rise with frequency too, and interfaces like memory or SPI slaves have their own limits. Hold violations aren't affecte

q0886.title: What is a register
q0886.short: "A register is a group of flip-flops sharing a clock that stores a multi-bit value: on the active edge, when enabled, all bits load together, and in between it holds. An 8-bit register is eight D flip-flops. In logic design it's the state between combinational stages; in a CPU it's the fast register file; a shift register moves bits along each clock; and in firmware, peripheral registers are memory-mapped addresses y

q0887.title: What is metastability
q0887.short: "Metastability is when a flip-flop samples a data change inside its setup/hold window and its internal bistable loop is left near the unstable midpoint. Positive feedback then amplifies the tiny difference exponentially, so the output eventually settles to 0 or 1, but after a random and unbounded time, during which it may sit at an in-between level. You can't prevent it for asynchronous inputs, so you use synchronize

q0888.title: What is a mux
q0888.short: "A mux is a digitally controlled switch: N data inputs, log-two-of-N select lines, one output that follows whichever input the select picks. A 2-to-1 is Y equals not-S times A plus S times B, so an inverter, two ANDs and an OR, or just two transmission gates in CMOS. You can tree them to make bigger ones. They're used for register source selection, ALU result select, and every if-else in RTL. They're also universal:

q0889.title: Draw logic gate symbols
q0889.short: "I draw inputs on the left, output on the right. A triangle is a buffer, and a triangle with a bubble is NOT. AND is a D shape, OR is the curved-back shield shape. Add a bubble on the output of those and you get NAND and NOR. XOR is OR with an extra curved line at the back, XNOR adds a bubble. The bubble always means inversion. I'd write the expression next to each one: A·B, A+B, A⊕B. And the symbol only tells you th

q0890.title: Logic gates from CMOS transistors
q0890.short: "The base cell is the CMOS inverter: a PMOS from VDD to the output, an NMOS from the output to ground, gates tied together. Input low pulls the output up, input high pulls it down, and one is always off so there's no static current. A NAND has two NMOS in series on the bottom and two PMOS in parallel on top; a NOR is the dual. The rule is: pull-down implements the complement of the function, AND as series, OR as para

q0891.title: Truth tables for logic gates
q0891.short: "With two inputs there are four rows: 00, 01, 10, 11. AND is 0, 0, 0, 1. OR is 0, 1, 1, 1. NAND and NOR are those inverted: 1, 1, 1, 0 and 1, 0, 0, 0. XOR is 0, 1, 1, 0, high when the inputs differ, and XNOR is 1, 0, 0, 1. NOT just flips its one input. I remember the rule rather than the columns: AND needs all ones, OR needs any one, XOR needs an odd number of ones. For n inputs the table has 2 to the n rows."

q0892.title: The universal logic gate
q0892.short: "NAND, and also NOR, is universal: any logic function can be built from that single gate. For NAND: tie both inputs together for a NOT, add a NOT after a NAND for AND, and NAND the two inverted inputs for OR by De Morgan. Since AND, OR and NOT can build anything, NAND can. NOR is the dual. AND and OR alone aren't universal because they can't invert. NAND is preferred in CMOS because its series stack is NMOS, so it's

q0893.title: Converting between number bases
q0893.short: "Every base is positional, so to get to decimal I add digit times power of the base: 0xAF is 10 times 16 plus 15, which is 175. Going from decimal, I divide repeatedly by the target base and read the remainders bottom to top. For binary to hex or octal I just group the bits, 4 per hex digit and 3 per octal digit, starting from the right: 1010 1111 is AF, and 10 101 111 is 257 in octal. Then I check by converting back

q0894.title: What is a truth table?
q0894.short: "A truth table lists every possible combination of a circuit's inputs and the output for each one. With n inputs there are 2^n rows. It fully specifies a combinational function, and I can get the Boolean expression straight from it by ORing the minterms of the rows where the output is 1. Then I'd simplify with a K-map. It doesn't work for circuits with memory, because there the output also depends on state, so you'd

q0895.title: Do the K-map for a truth table
q0895.short: "I lay out the K-map with the variables in Gray code so neighbouring cells differ in one bit, fill in the 1s from the truth table, and circle the biggest rectangles of 1s in powers of two, wrapping around the edges. Each group becomes one product term containing just the variables that don't change within it. OR the terms together and I have a minimal sum of products. Don't-cares can be used to enlarge groups, and I

q0896.title: What is an FSM?
q0896.short: "An FSM is a clocked circuit that is in one of a finite number of states and moves between them based on its inputs. Hardware-wise it's a state register of flip-flops, next-state logic that depends on state and inputs, and output logic. If outputs depend only on state it's Moore; if they also depend on inputs it's Mealy. I'd use one for anything with history: protocol handlers, sequence detectors, arbiters, controlle

q0897.title: Mealy vs Moore FSM
q0897.short: "In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the current state; in a Mealy machine they depend on the current state and the current inputs. So a Moore output changes only on clock edges and is clean, while a Mealy output can respond within the same cycle, which is one cycle faster and usually needs fewer states, but it can glitch if the inputs do. For an overlapping 101 detector, Moore needs four states and Mealy t

q0898.title: Name some computer architectures
q0898.short: "I'd split them up. By memory: von Neumann, with one shared memory for code and data, and Harvard, with separate ones; real CPUs are modified Harvard with split L1 caches. By instruction set: CISC like x86 and RISC like ARM, RISC-V and MIPS. By execution style: in-order pipelined, superscalar out-of-order, VLIW, SIMD/vector, GPU-style SIMT, and multicore. Then special-purpose ones like DSPs and neural accelerators. E

q0899.title: Architectures in phones and consumer electronics
q0899.short: "Phones and most consumer electronics use Arm-based RISC cores, because they're very efficient per watt and the licensing model lets each vendor build its own SoC. A phone chip is heterogeneous: big out-of-order cores for bursts, small efficient cores for background work, plus a GPU, image processor, DSP, neural engine and modem on the same die. Small devices like earbuds use Cortex-M style microcontrollers, and RISC

q0900.title: What is a CPU?
q0900.short: "A CPU is the circuit that executes a program. It repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory using the program counter, decodes it, and executes it using an ALU and a register file. Internally it's a datapath controlled by a finite state machine, all synchronized by a clock. Its speed is instruction count times CPI times clock period, and modern ones use pipelining, caches and branch prediction to execute many ins

q0901.title: Blocks inside a CPU
q0901.short: "Following an instruction: the program counter addresses the instruction cache, the decoder and control unit turn the opcode into control signals, the register file supplies operands, the ALU computes, the load/store unit talks to the data cache and memory, and the result is written back to the register file. Real CPUs add a branch predictor, MMU and TLB, a floating-point unit, an interrupt controller, and in high-en

q0902.title: What is an ALU?
q0902.short: "The ALU is the combinational block in a CPU that does arithmetic and logic. It takes two operands and control bits selecting the operation, like add, subtract, AND, OR, shift or compare, and outputs a result plus flags like zero, negative, carry and overflow. It's built from a full-adder chain, with subtraction done by inverting the second operand and adding one, plus logic gates and a mux. Carry propagation is the

q0903.title: What is the program counter?
q0903.short: "The program counter is a register that holds the address of the next instruction to fetch. Normally it increments by the instruction size each cycle; branches, jumps, calls, returns, interrupts and exceptions load a new value into it instead. In hardware it's a clocked register, an incrementer and a mux selecting between PC+4, a branch target, a register jump target and an exception vector. On reset it's loaded with

q0904.title: How the PC changes over time
q0904.short: "The PC normally steps forward by the instruction size, so by 4 for 32-bit instructions. A taken branch or jump loads a new address, so loops jump backward and repeat; a call loads the function's address and saves the return address, and the return restores it; an interrupt saves the PC and loads a handler address, then returns; and reset loads the reset vector. Plotted over time it's a staircase with occasional jump

q0905.title: Fetch/execute cycle
q0905.short: "It's the loop every CPU runs. Fetch: read the instruction at the address in the PC into the instruction register and increment the PC. Decode: work out what the instruction is and read its source registers. Execute: the ALU computes the result, a memory address, or a branch condition. Memory: loads and stores access memory. Writeback: write the result to a register. Then repeat. A simple CPU does this in 3 to 5 cycl

q0906.title: The five-stage pipeline
q0906.short: "Five stages: instruction fetch, decode and register read, execute in the ALU, memory access, and writeback. Pipeline registers between them let five instructions be in flight, so once it's full one instruction completes per cycle, a throughput of up to five times, though latency per instruction stays five cycles. Hazards break the ideal: data hazards are fixed with forwarding plus a one-cycle stall for load-use, and

q0907.title: Offloading work from the CPU
q0907.short: "I'd push repetitive or time-critical work to hardware: peripherals like timers, PWM and serial FIFOs, interrupts rather than polling, DMA to move blocks without the CPU, and accelerators or extra cores for heavy compute. In parallel you can run DMA and peripherals while the CPU computes, using double buffering. The trade-offs are area and power for the hardware, less flexibility, shared-bus contention, setup and syn

q0908.title: Increasing CPU throughput
q0908.short: "I'd use the iron law: time is instruction count times CPI times clock period. To cut the clock period, make stages shorter, with a power cost. To cut CPI, use pipelining, superscalar and out-of-order execution, branch prediction and caches so the CPU is never waiting. To cut instruction count, use better compilers and SIMD. Beyond that, add parallelism with multithreading, multiple cores and accelerators. The limits

q0909.title: What is pipelining?
q0909.short: "Pipelining splits an instruction's work into stages separated by registers so several instructions are in flight at once, each in a different stage. The clock only has to cover the slowest stage instead of the whole path, so you get a much higher clock and, once full, roughly one instruction per cycle. Latency for a single instruction doesn't improve, it gets slightly worse, so it's a throughput win. The speedup is

q0910.title: Branch prediction and its algorithms
q0910.short: "Branch prediction is the CPU guessing a branch's direction and target before it resolves, so a pipeline can keep fetching instead of stalling. A wrong guess flushes the speculative instructions and costs the pipeline depth in cycles. Static schemes are always-not-taken or backward-taken. The standard dynamic one is a table of 2-bit saturating counters indexed by the PC, which mispredicts a loop only once at the exit
terms: Branch History Table (BHT) / pattern history table

q0911.title: Interrupts in computers vs embedded systems
q0911.short: "An interrupt is a signal that makes the CPU pause its current program, jump through a vector table to a handler, and then resume where it left off. It lets hardware events like timers, incoming data or faults get attention without the CPU polling, which saves cycles and gives fast response. They're also how an OS regains control for multitasking. On a PC the OS kernel owns the interrupts and defers heavy work to thr

q0912.title: What is microarchitecture?
q0912.short: "Microarchitecture is how a specific processor implements its ISA: the pipeline, issue width, in-order or out-of-order execution, execution units, caches, branch predictors and buses. The ISA is the contract software sees; the microarchitecture is the implementation and it can differ wildly while running identical programs, like an Arm Cortex-A53 versus an A76. It's what determines CPI and clock speed, so performance

q0913.title: What is an ISA?
q0913.short: "An ISA, or instruction set architecture, is the contract between software and a processor: the instructions and their encodings, the registers, data types, addressing modes, memory model and exception behaviour. Software only depends on the ISA, so different microarchitectures can implement the same ISA and run the same binaries. RISC ISAs like Arm and RISC-V use simple fixed-length load/store instructions, while CI

q0914.title: Microarchitecture vs ISA
q0914.short: "The ISA is the contract software sees: instructions, registers, memory model, exceptions. The microarchitecture is how one chip implements that contract: pipeline, issue width, caches, branch predictor. One ISA, like x86 or Arm, has many microarchitectures, from tiny in-order cores to wide out-of-order ones, and they all run the same binaries. That split lets hardware improve every generation without breaking softwa

q0915.title: What is RISC-V
q0915.short: "RISC-V is an open, royalty-free instruction set architecture, started at Berkeley and now run by RISC-V International. It's a clean load/store RISC with fixed 32-bit instructions and 32 registers, built modularly: a small base like RV32I plus optional extensions such as M, F, C and V. It's only the spec, not a chip, so anyone can build their own core."

q0916.title: RISC-V: ISA or microarchitecture
q0916.short: "It specifies the ISA. RISC-V defines the instructions, registers, privilege modes, traps, virtual memory and memory model, but not the pipeline, caches or branch predictor. Those are microarchitecture, chosen by whoever builds the core. That's why in-order cores like Rocket and out-of-order cores like BOOM can both be RISC-V and run the same software at very different speeds and power."

q0917.title: RISC vs CISC advantages
q0917.short: "RISC uses simple, fixed-length, load/store instructions with lots of registers. That makes decode cheap and pipelining clean, so you get low CPI, a fast clock and less area and power. CISC packs more work into each instruction and has better code density, which lowers instruction count. By the Iron Law it's a trade between IC and CPI. Today x86 translates to micro-ops internally, so the difference is mostly the cost

q0918.title: Characterizing CPU performance
q0918.short: "Performance is execution time. The Iron Law says time is instruction count times CPI times clock period, so clock speed alone is meaningless. I'd measure with representative benchmarks like SPEC, summarize with a geometric mean, and separate latency from throughput. Then look at what limits it: memory stalls, branch mispredicts, Amdahl's law, and finally performance per watt and thermal throttling."

q0919.title: What is a GPU
q0919.short: "A GPU is a throughput-oriented parallel processor with thousands of small lanes that run the same program on many threads at once, backed by very high memory bandwidth and fixed-function graphics units. Graphics is perfect for it because millions of pixels are independent. It hides memory latency with massive multithreading instead of big caches. Today the same hardware also runs compute and machine learning."

q0920.title: How a GPU works
q0920.short: "You write a kernel for one thread and launch it over a huge grid. The hardware groups threads into warps of 32 that run the same instruction in lockstep on an SM. Each SM holds many warps, and when one stalls on memory the scheduler instantly issues another, so latency is hidden by parallelism. Divergent branches and uncoalesced memory accesses are what cost performance."

q0921.title: The GPU graphics pipeline
q0921.short: "Vertices go through a vertex shader that transforms them to screen space, then primitive assembly builds and clips triangles. The fixed-function rasterizer finds the pixels each triangle covers, the fragment shader colors them using textures and lighting, and the ROP stage does depth test and blending and writes the framebuffer. The shaders are programmable and share the same cores, while raster, texture and ROP har

q0922.title: GPU vs CPU
q0922.short: "A CPU is latency-optimized: a few big out-of-order cores with big caches and branch prediction to run one thread fast. A GPU is throughput-optimized: thousands of simple lanes running in lockstep, hiding memory latency by switching among tens of thousands of threads, with very high memory bandwidth. CPUs win on branchy serial code, and GPUs win on regular data-parallel work like graphics and matrix math. In practice

q0923.title: GPU optimizations and trade-offs
q0923.short: "GPUs exploit massive independent parallelism: SIMT amortizes fetch and decode over 32 lanes, thousands of threads hide latency instead of caches, very wide memory like GDDR or HBM feeds them, and fixed-function raster, texture and blend units do common work very efficiently. Compression and on-chip tiles cut bandwidth. The costs are weak single-thread speed, divergence and memory-pattern sensitivity, huge register f

q0924.title: Characterizing GPU performance
q0924.short: "I'd look at compute, memory and efficiency. Peak FLOPS is SMs times lanes times two times clock, about 35 TFLOPS for a typical card. Memory bandwidth is bus width times data rate over eight, say 512 GB/s. The ratio, the ridge point of the roofline, tells me whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound. For graphics I add fill rate and frame-time percentiles. Then performance per watt and achieved versus peak, measur

q0925.title: GPU compute beyond graphics
q0925.short: "GPUs excel at anything that's the same operation over lots of independent data: machine learning, which is mostly matrix multiplies, scientific simulation, image and video processing, FFTs, Monte Carlo and hashing. The reasons are thousands of parallel threads, regular memory access that uses the wide high-bandwidth memory, and high arithmetic intensity. They struggle with branchy, serial or pointer-chasing code, sm

q0926.title: What is a system on chip
q0926.short: "A SoC integrates a whole system, CPU cores, memory controllers, often a GPU and accelerators, peripherals like UART, SPI, USB and PCIe, plus clocks, power management and security, onto a single die, tied together by an on-chip interconnect and a shared address map. It cuts size, power and board cost at volume, though you still need DRAM, regulators and a crystal outside, and the design effort is large. A microcontro

q0927.title: SoC applications
q0927.short: "SoCs power phones and tablets, wearables, IoT sensor nodes, laptops and consoles, cars, networking gear, smart TVs, cameras, drones and industrial controllers. The architecture is the same, but the mix of blocks and the constraint differ: phones are limited by battery and heat, sensor nodes by microamps of sleep current, cars by safety and temperature range, routers by throughput. Integration is what makes the small

q0928.title: Components on a SoC
q0928.short: "I group them by function. Compute: CPU cores with caches, a GPU, and accelerators like NPU, DSP, ISP and video codec. Memory: on-chip SRAM, boot ROM, a DRAM controller and PHY, flash in MCUs. A bus matrix or network-on-chip with DMA and an interrupt controller ties them together. Peripherals: GPIO, UART, SPI, I2C, ADC, USB, PCIe, Ethernet, camera and display. Infrastructure: PLLs, resets, power management, security

q0929.title: SoC versus separate components
q0929.short: "Integration wins on size, power, speed and unit cost at volume: on-die wires are shorter and cheaper to drive than package pins and traces, and you cut packages, passives and board area. It loses on upfront NRE, schedule, flexibility and process compromises, and heat is concentrated. So integrate when volume and size or power limits justify the NRE, and use discrete parts or a module for low volume or uncertain requ

q0930.title: Components needed around a SoC
q0930.short: "Beyond the SoC you need power: a PMIC or regulators with the right rails, sequencing and decoupling, plus a charger if it's a battery product. Clocks and reset: a crystal or oscillator, a 32 kHz RTC crystal and a reset supervisor. Memory: DRAM and boot flash or eMMC unless they're on-chip. I/O parts: PHYs, connectors, ESD protection, level shifters and radios. Then sensors, display and user I/O, plus debug access, b

q0931.title: System on module versus SoC
q0931.short: "A SoM is a small board containing a SoC plus DRAM, flash and power management, plugged into your carrier board. The SoC is the silicon; the SoM is a ready-made mini-system around it. A SoM cuts time to market and layout risk, since DDR routing, sequencing and the software support are done, but costs more per unit and locks you into its form factor. Chip-down with the bare SoC wins at high volume."

q0932.title: Trade-offs of integration
q0932.short: "Integration gives lower energy, higher bandwidth, lower latency and smaller, cheaper systems. The costs: yield drops with die area so cost per good die rises faster than linearly; one process can't suit logic, analog, RF and memory; digital noise couples into sensitive blocks; heat concentrates; and verification, NRE and respin risk grow. Chiplets are the modern compromise: smaller dies in the best process, joined b

q0933.title: Which SoC blocks use the most power
q0933.short: "Under load it's the compute blocks, the CPU cluster and GPU, and NPU if it's running, followed closely by the memory subsystem, because moving data from DRAM costs far more than computing on it. Dynamic power goes as alpha C V squared f, so high-voltage, high-frequency blocks dominate; at idle, leakage in SRAM and powered domains does. Designers manage it with clock and power gating, DVFS, heterogeneous cores and fi

q0934.title: Where data and program live
q0934.short: "Program and data are both just bits, so they can live in registers, caches, SRAM, DRAM, flash and disk. At rest the program sits in non-volatile memory like flash or an SSD. When it runs, instructions and data are brought into RAM and then into caches and registers. On a microcontroller, code and constants stay in flash, variables and the stack live in SRAM, and the startup code copies initialized globals from flash

q0935.title: Data memory vs program memory
q0935.short: "Program memory holds the instructions the CPU fetches with the program counter; data memory holds the variables and buffers the instructions load and store. Program memory is mostly read-only at run time and often non-volatile flash, while data memory is read/write, usually SRAM. In a Harvard architecture they're physically separate so you can fetch and access data in the same cycle; in von Neumann they share one me

q0936.title: The memory hierarchy and its trade-offs
q0936.short: "The memory hierarchy stacks storage levels, each bigger, slower and cheaper than the last: registers, L1/L2/L3 SRAM caches, DRAM main memory, then SSD or disk. No one technology is fast, large and cheap, so we exploit locality: keep the working set in small fast levels and most accesses never reach the slow ones. Registers hold live operands, caches hold copies of hot code and data, DRAM holds running programs, stor

q0937.title: What a cache is and how it works
q0937.short: "A cache is a small, fast SRAM between the CPU and main memory that holds copies of recently used data and instructions. It works because of locality: programs reuse data and use neighbouring data. The address is split into tag, index and offset; the index selects a set, tags are compared, and a match is a hit in a cycle or few; otherwise it's a miss and a 64-byte line is fetched from the next level. With a 95 percen

q0938.title: What registers are
q0938.short: "A register is a small, very fast storage element inside the CPU made of flip-flops: an n-bit register is n D flip-flops sharing a clock and write enable. Registers are the top of the memory hierarchy: the ALU reads operands from them and writes results back in about a cycle. There are general-purpose registers, plus special ones like the program counter, stack pointer and status flags, and pipeline registers between

q0939.title: What RAM is (SRAM vs DRAM)
q0939.short: "RAM is random-access, read/write, normally volatile working memory. There are two main types. SRAM stores a bit in a six-transistor latch, so it's fast and needs no refresh but takes a lot of area; it's used for caches and on-chip RAM. DRAM stores a bit as charge on a capacitor with one access transistor, so it's dense and cheap but slower, reads are destructive, and the charge leaks, so rows must be refreshed every

q0940.title: What "random access" means
q0940.short: "Random access means any address can be read or written in about the same time, independent of where you accessed last, because an address decoder selects the cell directly. It doesn't mean the data is random. It's contrasted with sequential access like tape, where reaching a location means winding past everything before it, and semi-random media like hard disks, where seek and rotation depend on position. Real DRAM

q0941.title: What is stack overflow?
q0941.short: "A stack overflow is when the call stack outgrows the region of memory reserved for it. Each function call pushes a frame with the return address and locals, so very deep or infinite recursion, or big local arrays, can push the stack pointer past the limit. On a PC the OS has a guard page, so you get a segfault. On a microcontroller with no MMU it silently overwrites globals or the heap. You prevent it by avoiding un

q0942.title: Stack versus heap
q0942.short: "The stack holds function-call frames: locals and return addresses. It's allocated by moving the stack pointer, freed automatically on return, fast and cache friendly, but small and strictly LIFO. The heap holds data that has to outlive a call or has a runtime-determined size. It's allocated with malloc and freed explicitly, so it's flexible but slower and can leak or fragment. In embedded I prefer stack and static a

q0943.title: Memory management unit (MMU)
q0943.short: "The MMU sits between the CPU and memory and translates the virtual addresses programs use into physical addresses, using page tables, with a TLB caching recent translations. It also checks read, write and execute permissions on every access. We need it for isolation between processes and the kernel, for giving every program a clean contiguous address space on top of fragmented RAM, and for features like demand pagin

q0944.title: Radiation-induced memory errors in space
q0944.short: "Radiation particles can deposit charge in silicon and flip a stored bit, a single-event upset, which silently corrupts data or instructions. Worse events include latch-up, which can burn the chip, and accumulated dose that degrades transistors. To be resilient I'd use ECC on all memories with scrubbing so errors don't accumulate, triple modular redundancy or lockstep for critical logic, radiation-tolerant parts with

q0945.title: Clock frequency, power and thermals
q0945.short: "Dynamic power is \alpha C V^2 f, so at fixed voltage it's linear in frequency. Performance also rises with frequency, but only for the part of the workload not waiting on memory. The catch is that higher frequency needs higher voltage to meet timing, so along a DVFS curve power grows much faster than linearly, about 3x for 2x frequency in a typical example. All that power becomes heat, Tj = Ta + P\theta, and leakage

q0946.title: Why multiple clock domains
q0946.short: "Different blocks need different clock rates: CPUs run at GHz, peripherals at a few MHz, an always-on timer at 32 kHz, and interfaces like USB or DDR have clocks set by their standards. Separate domains let me save dynamic power, apply DVFS and clock gating per block, and keep clock trees manageable. The price is clock domain crossing: signals between unrelated clocks can go metastable, so I use synchronizers for sin

q0947.title: Supply voltage, power and thermals
q0947.short: "Dynamic power goes as V squared, so a 20% voltage cut saves 36% of dynamic power, and leakage falls even faster. Performance also depends on voltage: drive current scales with V minus Vt, so delay shrinks and maximum frequency rises with voltage, with diminishing returns at high V and a steep slowdown near threshold. Less power means less heat. So voltage is the most effective power knob, limited below by SRAM and t

q0948.title: Why multiple supply voltages
q0948.short: "Because different blocks want different voltages. Dynamic power scales with V squared, so non-critical logic runs at lower voltage and each domain, like big cores, little cores and GPU, gets its own DVFS. Also SRAM needs a higher minimum voltage than logic, I/O must match external standards like 1.8 or 3.3 V, analog wants a clean rail, and an always-on domain lets the rest power off. The cost is more regulators, lev

q0949.title: PVT impact on power and performance
q0949.short: "PVT is process, voltage and temperature, the three sources of variation. Process: die-to-die and within-die differences, where fast silicon has lower thresholds, more drive current and much more leakage. Voltage: supply tolerance, IR drop and droop; higher voltage is faster but burns V squared dynamic power and more leakage. Temperature: hot means lower mobility, so usually slower, and exponentially more leakage, wi

q0950.title: Process corners explained
q0950.short: "Process corners bound global manufacturing variation, usually at about three sigma. They're named NMOS then PMOS: SS slow-slow, TT typical, FF fast-fast, plus the skewed FS and SF where one device type is fast and the other slow. Fast means lower threshold and more current, but more leakage. Slow corners are used for setup timing, fast for hold and for leakage and power, and the skewed ones for SRAM, ratioed logic a

q0951.title: Typical validation temperature ranges
q0951.short: "Typical grades: commercial 0 to 70 °C, industrial -40 to 85 °C, automotive AEC-Q100 from -40 to 85 (Grade 3) up through 105, 125 and 150 °C (Grades 2, 1, 0), and military or space about -55 to 125 °C. Validation is really at junction temperature, ambient plus power times thermal resistance. We test cold, room and hot across voltage and process corners, plus temperature cycling and high-temperature life for reliabili

q0952.title: Techniques to reduce power consumption
q0952.short: "I'd go through the power equation. Dynamic power is activity times capacitance times V squared times frequency, so: lower voltage and frequency with DVFS and multiple voltage domains; cut activity with clock gating, operand isolation and architectural choices that avoid work; reduce capacitance with smaller devices and shorter wires. For leakage use high-Vt cells, and power gating with retention for idle blocks. The

q0953.title: Ways to throttle performance
q0953.short: "The main throttle is DVFS: lower voltage and frequency together, which cuts power by roughly V squared times f. Faster, cruder options are clock modulation, which gates the clock for some fraction of cycles, and microarchitectural throttling of fetch and issue width; coarser ones park cores or cap memory and accelerator bandwidth. Triggers are temperature, power or current limits, with hysteresis. DVFS is the most e

q0954.title: Temperature control loops in chips and systems
q0954.short: "Thermal control is a stack of feedback loops. On-chip sensors drive fast throttling, via DVFS, clock reduction or power caps, often with hysteresis or a stepped governor. At the system level, a fan controller runs a PWM curve or a PID loop on temperature. Underneath all that is a hardware thermal trip as the last resort. Because the thermal plant is slow and lagged, the loops have to be tuned so they don't oscillate

q0955.title: PPA: power, performance, area trade-offs
q0955.short: "PPA is power, performance and area, the three axes you trade in chip design. Power is switching, alpha C V squared f, plus leakage. Performance is speed, frequency times work per cycle. Area is silicon cost. Raising voltage or deepening the pipeline buys speed but costs power or area. Relaxing timing saves power and area. Which trade you make depends on the product: a phone wants low power, a server wants performanc

q0956.title: Describing your RTL experience
q0956.short: "My RTL experience is [your project, for example a UART or a small processor] in [language] on [FPGA or ASIC flow]. I wrote the FSM and datapath with clocked registers and combinational logic, verified it with a self-checking testbench, then ran synthesis and looked at timing and utilization. The biggest lesson was [a real bug you hit]. I'm comfortable going into any part of it."

q0957.title: Design a clock divider
q0957.short: "I'd clarify the ratio, duty cycle and whether it's a true clock or a tick. For an even N I count N/2 input cycles and toggle an output flip-flop, giving 50% duty at f over N. Odd N needs a rising-edge and a falling-edge counter whose pulses are ORed to fix the duty cycle. For internal logic I'd rather generate a one-cycle clock-enable, which keeps a single clock domain and avoids generated-clock and glitch problems.

q0958.title: Design an arbiter and compare types
q0958.short: "An arbiter picks one winner among simultaneous requests. Fixed priority is a priority encoder, req & -req, tiny and fast but it can starve low-priority requesters. Round-robin keeps a mask or pointer so every requester gets a turn, with a worst-case wait of N minus 1 grants. Other schemes are weighted round-robin, matrix or LRU, age-based and time-division, each trading fairness and latency guarantees against area a

q0959.title: Design a multiplexer (mux)
q0959.short: "A mux picks one of several inputs based on a select. For a 2:1 it's Y equals not-S times A plus S times B, one inverter, two ANDs, an OR. In RTL I'd write a parameterized assign y = sel ? b : a, or an indexed array for N inputs with no latch. Scaling to N inputs gives a tree of N minus one 2:1 muxes, log2 N deep, or a flat AND-OR if the select is one-hot. I'd also mention that an AND-OR mux can glitch when both inpu

q0960.title: What a module is in RTL
q0960.short: "A module is the basic design unit in Verilog or SystemVerilog: a named block with ports for its inputs and outputs, and a body containing logic or instances of other modules. You write it once as a template and instantiate it as many times as you like, and each instance is separate hardware running in parallel, unlike a software function call. Modules give you hierarchy, so teams can split a chip into blocks, test e

q0961.title: RTL reuse and why it matters
q0961.short: "RTL reuse is writing a block once, with parameters and clean interfaces, so it can drop into many designs. Tools are parameters, generate statements, packages, interfaces, and standard bus protocols. It matters because it saves schedule and, more importantly, verification effort, and a block already proven in silicon is lower risk. The cost is that a reusable block needs documentation, a limited and well-tested conf

q0962.title: What assembly is, versus C and Python
q0962.short: "Assembly is the human-readable form of a processor's machine instructions, roughly one line per instruction, so it's specific to one instruction set like RISC-V, ARM or x86. C is compiled down to it: one C statement becomes several assembly instructions, and the same C can target many processors. Python is interpreted, so it's another layer further from the hardware. I'd use assembly for boot code, interrupt entry,

q0963.title: Read a program, time it, count calls
q0963.short: "I'd do three passes. First read it: find the loops and calls, identify inputs and outputs, trace two iterations, and summarize it in a sentence. Second, count instructions: setup plus iterations times loop-body instructions plus exit, remembering to include instructions inside called subroutines, then time equals instructions times CPI over clock frequency, stating my pipeline assumption. Third, the subroutine count

q0964.title: Describing your coding experience
q0964.short: "My coding is mostly applied to hardware work. The biggest example is [project], where I wrote [language] to [goal]. The interesting technical part was [one specific mechanism], and I debugged it by [method]. It ended up [measured result]. Beyond that I've used C for embedded work, Python for scripting and plotting, and Git for version control. I'm strongest in [language] and actively building depth in [other]."

q0965.title: Experience in C, C++ and Python
q0965.short: "Yes, at different levels. C I've used on [microcontrollers or coursework]: pointers, structs, bit manipulation for registers, and volatile for ISR flags. C++ I've used for [project], so classes, references, RAII and the STL containers, intermediate level. Python is what I use most, for scripting, data analysis and instrument automation. I'd pick C for hardware-level control, Python for fast scripting and analysis, a

q0966.title: Strongest languages and honest self-rating
q0966.short: "My strongest is [language], roughly [3.5 out of 5]: I can build a working project and debug it on my own, and I can explain the details like [pointers / dictionaries]. I haven't done large-scale design or deep optimization yet. My second is [language] at about [2.5]: fine for basics, but I'd look up the details. I'd pick [language] for any coding exercise because it's where I'm most accurate, and I'm happy to be tes

q0967.title: What a regular expression is
q0967.short: "A regex is a compact pattern language for describing sets of strings so you can search, extract or replace text. Building blocks are literals, character classes, quantifiers like and +, anchors, groups and alternation. I use them to parse logs and reports, like pulling VDD=3.29V out of a test log with VDD=(\d+\.\d+)V. Watch out for greedy versus lazy matching and catastrophic backtracking. Theoretically they corresp

q0968.title: Basic variable types and their limits
q0968.short: "The basic types are integers, characters, floating-point numbers, booleans and pointers. Sizes are platform dependent, so in firmware I use fixed-width types like uint8t and int32t. An unsigned 8-bit holds 0 to 255, a signed one minus 128 to 127 in two's complement, and unsigned arithmetic wraps on overflow. Floats are 32-bit IEEE 754 with about seven decimal digits, so they can't represent 0.1 exactly. Python is dy

q0969.title: Strings versus chars and string implementation
q0969.short: "A char is a single character, in C a one-byte integer, so 'A' is 65. A string is a sequence of chars. In C it's usually a null-terminated array, so "Hi!" is four bytes: 48 69 21 00. That makes length an O(n) walk and requires one extra byte, and it's why overruns are a classic bug. Other designs store the length, like Pascal strings or C++'s std::string with small-string optimization, and Python uses immutable Unico

q0970.title: The volatile keyword and when to use it
q0970.short: "volatile tells the compiler a variable can change outside the program's flow, or that accesses have side effects, so every read and write in the source must actually happen, in order. Without it the optimizer can cache a flag in a register and loop forever. I use it for memory-mapped hardware registers, variables shared between an ISR and main code, and polling loops. But it isn't atomic, isn't a lock and isn't a me

q0971.title: Writing pseudocode from a spec
q0971.short: "I'd restate the spec, ask about inputs, units, rates and error cases, and name the state the code has to remember. Then I write a short, language-neutral procedure with a clear loop and conditions, trace a normal case and an edge case through it by hand, and say the cost, like 'one pass, constant memory'. For firmware I'd also say whether it blocks and how long the worst case takes. A debounce routine is a good exam

q0972.title: Walking through a given program
q0972.short: "I'd first summarise what it does in a sentence, then go top-down: entry point, state, anything asynchronous like an ISR. I'd walk a concrete input through any loop with a trace table, check bit tricks by plugging in a real number, and look for hardware hazards like a missing volatile, overflow or a race between the ISR and main. Last I'd estimate runtime as iterations times cost per iteration at the clock rate."

q0973.title: String, file and API coding tasks
q0973.short: "Reverse and palindrome are two-pointer loops: indices at both ends moving inward, swapping or comparing, O(n) time and O(1) space, with care for empty strings and, for palindromes, case and punctuation. Substring search checks the needle at every offset, O(nm) worst case, and KMP makes it linear, though in real code I'd use the library. File tasks stream line by line with a regex and write to a new file. For an API

q0974.title: Smartphone and laptop components
q0974.short: "A phone or laptop is a processor SoC, DRAM and flash, a power subsystem (battery, charger, PMIC with many rails), radios (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GNSS), display and touch, audio, cameras and sensors, all connected by high-speed buses like DDR, MIPI and PCIe and low-speed ones like I2C and SPI. The design is dominated by battery life, heat, size and cost, and by keeping radios and fast digital from interfering."

q0975.title: Design six small systems end to end
q0975.short: "I'd run the same method on each: clarify requirements, draw sense-decide-act with power and comms, then size the critical numbers. Variable LED is a PWM-driven MOSFET with gamma correction. Ambient-compensated adds a photodiode and a slow feedback loop. Security is low-power sensing with false-alarm rejection and backup power. A camera is a bandwidth and memory problem, a tracker is a battery problem, and eye tracki

q0976.title: Redundancy in system design
q0976.short: "Redundancy means having more than one way to do a critical function so a single failure doesn't stop the system. I'd use it when failure is dangerous, expensive or can't be repaired, like aircraft, cars, medical devices and satellites. You can run parallel units, keep a standby, or use three-way voting. The catches are that you must detect failures, the switch can itself fail, and common-cause faults like a shared s

q0977.title: Design constraints across industries
q0977.short: "The same circuit is designed differently because failure costs differ. Consumer is driven by cost, size and battery life with commercial parts and EMC marks. Automotive adds minus 40 to 125 degrees, 10 to 15 year life, a rough 12 volt supply with load dump, AEC-Q parts and ISO 26262. Aerospace, space and defense add radiation, vacuum, shock, no repair and heavy screening and documentation. Medical is dominated by pa

q0978.title: Measurement tools and when to use each
q0978.short: "I choose by quantity. A multimeter for accurate DC voltage, current and resistance. An oscilloscope for waveforms, edges and ripple. A spectrum analyzer or scope FFT for frequency content. An LCR meter or VNA for impedance and RF behaviour. A logic analyzer for digital buses, an SMU or power supply with readback for source-and-measure, a power analyzer and electronic load for power electronics, and thermocouples or

q0979.title: Familiarity with DMMs, scopes, VNAs, SMUs
q0979.short: "DMMs and scopes I use routinely: DMM for accurate DC, resistance and current, aware of averaging, burden voltage and true-RMS; scope for waveforms, choosing bandwidth for the edge rate and using a proper probe and trigger. A VNA sources a swept sine and measures S-parameters like return loss and gain after a calibration; I understand it well conceptually [and have used it for ]. For supplies I know constant-voltage

q0980.title: Choosing scope bandwidth and sample rate
q0980.short: "I size bandwidth from the fastest feature and sample rate from the bandwidth. For a sine I want bandwidth 3 to 5 times the frequency. For an edge, content extends to about 0.5 over the rise time, and a scope's own rise time is 0.35 over its bandwidth, so to keep rise-time error near 2 percent I need roughly 1.75 over the rise time: about 900 MHz for a 2 ns edge. Sample rate is then at least 2.5 to 5 times that, givi

q0981.title: How to measure a given signal
q0981.short: "I'd first ask what the signal is: DC or AC, amplitude, speed, source impedance, grounded or floating, and required accuracy. Then I pick the tool: DMM for steady DC, scope for waveforms with bandwidth from the rise time and a 10x probe with a short ground, active probe for high-impedance nodes, differential or isolated probe for floating or high voltage, spectrum analyzer for frequency content. Then I sanity-check t

q0982.title: Ways to measure current
q0982.short: "Current is measured indirectly. The simple ways are a multimeter in series, which is accurate for DC but adds burden voltage and breaks the circuit, or a small sense resistor with the voltage across it read by a DMM, scope or current-sense amplifier. That trades signal against loss: 10 milliohms gives 10 millivolts and 10 milliwatts at 1 amp, but amplifier offset limits small currents. Without breaking the circuit,

q0983.title: Bandwidth versus sampling rate
q0983.short: "Bandwidth is the analog front end's limit: the frequency where amplitude has dropped 3 dB. Sample rate is how often the ADC samples, and Nyquist says you can only represent frequencies below half of it. They're separate but linked: anything above half the sample rate that gets through the front end aliases down to a false lower frequency, so the bandwidth or anti-alias filter must cut it first.
