q0984.title: What a vector network analyzer is
q0984.short: "A VNA is a swept RF instrument that measures how a network reflects and transmits signals, with magnitude and phase, which are the S-parameters. It sources a sine, uses couplers and coherent receivers to measure incident, reflected and transmitted waves. S11 gives input match: return loss, VSWR and impedance. S21 gives gain or insertion loss. You calibrate with short, open, load and through standards so you're measu

q0985.title: Measuring R, C, L and impedance
q0985.short: "Resistance with a DMM, using four-wire mode for small values and measuring out of circuit. Capacitance and inductance with an LCR meter at a test frequency near use, which reports the value plus D, Q or ESR. Without one, a capacitor in an RC with a known R gives C from the time constant on a scope, and an inductor with a known C gives L from the resonant frequency. For impedance across frequency, including self-reso

q0986.title: What a digital multimeter is
q0986.short: "A DMM measures voltage, current and resistance and displays a number. Internally it's an ADC with conditioning: attenuators for volts, a shunt for current, a current source for resistance, an RMS converter for AC. Key specs are digits or counts for resolution, accuracy as percent of reading plus counts, input impedance around 10 megohms, and burden voltage in current mode. It's great for accurate, slow measurements

q0987.title: What a DMM can measure
q0987.short: "A DMM measures DC and AC voltage, DC and AC current and resistance, plus continuity, diode test, usually capacitance, frequency and duty cycle, and temperature with a thermocouple. For AC I want true-RMS, because an average-responding meter is only right for sine waves. Limits to remember: 10 megohm input loads high-impedance nodes, current ranges add burden voltage and need the right jack and fuse, resistance shoul

q0988.title: DMM sample rate and whether it matters
q0988.short: "A DMM's sample rate is really readings per second, set by how long it integrates, usually a number of power-line cycles. At 1 NPLC on 60 Hz that's about 16.7 ms, so up to ~60 readings a second; handhelds give a few per second. Longer integration gives lower noise, roughly one over root-time, and better 50/60 Hz rejection. It matters for anything that changes within a reading: glitches, ripple, transients get average

q0989.title: Choosing a DMM or a scope
q0989.short: "The DMM is for a number, the scope is for a picture. A DMM gives accurate, quiet, high-resolution DC, resistance and current, and it's isolated, but it averages over tens of milliseconds so it can't show ripple, glitches or timing. A scope shows voltage over time with high bandwidth and triggering, but has only about 8 bits and a percent or two of DC accuracy, and its ground is tied to earth. So I use the DMM to che

q0990.title: What is an oscilloscope?
q0990.short: "An oscilloscope plots voltage versus time, so instead of one number like a multimeter I see the actual waveform: edges, ripple, ringing, glitches, timing between signals. The specs that matter are bandwidth, sample rate, memory depth, vertical resolution and channel count. Modern ones sample the input with an ADC and store it. I always remember that the probe loads the circuit and the scope's bandwidth limits what I

q0991.title: How a digital oscilloscope works
q0991.short: "A digital scope conditions the input with coupling, an attenuator and an amplifier, then a fast ADC samples it into a circular memory. A separate trigger comparator decides which moment is time zero, so the scope can stop after enough post-trigger samples and show the history before it too. The processor interpolates, decimates and draws the waveform. So bandwidth, sample rate, ADC bits and memory depth each limit t

q0992.title: Scope triggers and how to use them
q0992.short: "A trigger tells the scope when to start each sweep, so repeating signals line up and sit still. For an edge trigger I pick the source, a level on the clean part of the edge, and a slope. Auto mode always shows something, normal waits for the condition, single captures one event. Holdoff handles bursts. For hard problems I use pulse-width, runt, timeout or serial triggers, and the pre-trigger history shows what led t

q0993.title: Current from a sense-resistor voltage
q0993.short: "I divide the voltage by the resistor value: 20 mV across 10 milliohms is 2 amps. I'd have the scope do it with a scale setting or a math channel. I check where the resistor sits, because on the high side I need a differential probe, and I probe right at its pads with bandwidth limit on because the signal is tiny. For very fast edges I remember the resistor's inductance can add a fake spike, so I'd cross-check with a

q0994.title: When you need multiple scope channels
q0994.short: "I use multiple channels whenever the debug question is about how signals relate in time. For example trigger on a reset on one channel and watch the supply on another to see if it drooped first. They're also used for sequencing several rails, delay between clock and data, multi-wire buses like SPI, and math like volts times amps for power. I watch for shared grounds, probe skew, and that some scopes drop sample rate

q0995.title: Differential probe and when to use it
q0995.short: "A differential probe measures the difference between two points and ignores the voltage they share, so neither point has to be at ground. I need it for floating signals: a high-side gate drive on a half-bridge, a shunt on a high-side rail, or a differential pair. Its limits are CMRR, which falls with frequency, plus input range, noise and cost. For huge common-mode swings and fast edges I'd use an isolated probe."

q0996.title: Active probe and when to use one
q0996.short: "An active probe has a small buffer amplifier at the tip, so it has high resistance and very low input capacitance, around a picofarad, versus 10 to 15 pF for a passive 10x. That means much less loading at high frequency, so I use it for fast edges, clocks, high-speed buses and sensitive high-impedance nodes. The costs are price, limited voltage range, noise, fragility and needing power from the scope."

q0997.title: What a 10x probe attenuator does
q0997.short: "The 10x probe is a built-in voltage divider: 9 megaohms in the tip and the scope's 1 megaohm give a 10:1 reduction, so the circuit sees about 10 megaohms and roughly 10 picofarads instead of 1 megaohm and about 100 pF. A trimmer capacitor across the 9 megaohm resistor equalizes the time constants, R1C1=R2C2, so the ratio stays 10:1 at all frequencies. I adjust it with the square-wave output. The cost is ten times le

q0998.title: What is a current probe
q0998.short: "A current probe senses the magnetic field around a wire so I can see current without breaking the circuit or adding a series resistor. An AC probe is a clamp-on transformer, a Hall-effect probe adds DC capability, and a Rogowski coil is an air-cored coil giving di/dt that is integrated. I zero or degauss it, clamp one conductor with the arrow along the current, and watch bandwidth, saturation and noise floor. For ti

q0999.title: Probe input impedance: what and why
q0999.short: "The probe impedance should be much higher than the source impedance at every frequency of interest, at least 10 times, so it doesn't load the node. A 10x passive probe is about 10 megaohms with 10 to 15 picofarads, but at high frequency the capacitance dominates: 12 pF is only about 130 ohms at 100 MHz. For high-speed or high-impedance nodes I use an active probe with about a picofarad. For 50 ohm transmission lines

q1000.title: When to use a different probe impedance
q1000.short: "I choose probe impedance by what I'm measuring. For normal nodes, 10x or 1 MΩ high impedance. For 50 ohm lines and RF, the scope's 50 ohm input so the line is terminated without reflections. For very fast signals on low-impedance nodes, a low-Z resistive divider probe like 500 ohms for 10 to 1, which has tiny capacitance. For sensitive high-impedance nodes, an active probe with about 1 pF. And 1x for tiny slow signa

q1001.title: Tools for debug, test and validation
q1001.short: "I choose the tool by the question. A DMM and a current-limited supply for power, a scope with a proper probe for signals in time, a logic or protocol analyzer for buses, a spectrum analyzer or VNA for frequency-domain and impedance, a thermal camera for hot spots, a microscope or X-ray for physical issues, and a debugger plus UART logs and GPIO toggles for firmware. I also use simulation, version control and automat

q1002.title: Your approach to debug, test, validate
q1002.short: "My approach is a loop: define what correct looks like, reproduce the failure, gather evidence without changing things, then split the system in half to isolate it. I rank hypotheses by likelihood and cost, test one variable at a time, and once something fixes it I verify I understand why and check for side effects. I document the root cause. For validation I start from requirements, test corners and margin, automate

q1003.title: Design a system to test X
q1003.short: "I'd start by asking what X is and what the test must prove, volume, cycle time and accuracy. Then I'd define the tests and limits from the spec, and build a fixture with Kelvin contacts, programmable supply and load, a DMM and scope controlled by a script that sequences the tests, applies limits and logs results by serial number. I'd choose instruments about four times more accurate than the limits, set guard bands,

q1004.title: How you debug software
q1004.short: "I use the same loop as hardware: reproduce the bug, read the evidence like logs and fault registers, then localize with a debugger, watchpoints, assertions and git bisect. On an embedded target I toggle a GPIO and watch it on a scope for timing, decode hard faults from the stacked PC, and check stack overflow, ISR races and volatile. I watch for observer effects like printf changing the timing, and I add a regressio

q1005.title: Running tests 24/7 through outages
q1005.short: "I'd layer it. A UPS, ideally online, on the PC and instruments sized by load: about 29 minutes for 300 watts from a small battery, which covers short outages and a graceful shutdown. A generator with an automatic transfer switch for long ones. Then make it self-recovering: power-on-after-AC-loss, a test script that checkpoints its state and logs atomically, and a watchdog.
